Second, comparing nodes: use `node is target` (identity) when the problem hands you node OBJECTS, and `node.val == target` when it hands you values — duplicated values make `==` on values ambiguous. Third, default mutable arguments: `def dfs(node, path=[])` shares ONE list across all top-level calls; pass the accumulator explicitly or create it inside a wrapper.
sections.code:
import sys
from collections import deque

sys.setrecursionlimit(200_000)   # default ~1000 frames dies on skewed trees

class TreeNode:                  # the entire "data structure" is this class
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left         # reference to another TreeNode, or None
        self.right = right       # same for the right child

def build(values):
    # Build from a LeetCode-style level-order list; None marks a hole.
    # Example: [1, 2, 3, None, 5] -> 1 has children 2,3; 2 has right child 5.
    if not values or values[0] is None:
        return None
    root = TreeNode(values[0])
    q = deque([root])            # parents still waiting for their children
    i = 1
    while q and i < len(values):
        parent = q.popleft()
        if values[i] is not None:              # left slot of this parent
            parent.left = TreeNode(values[i])
            q.append(parent.left)
        i += 1                                 # consume the slot even if None
        if i < len(values) and values[i] is not None:   # right slot
            parent.right = TreeNode(values[i])
            q.append(parent.right)
        i += 1
    return root

sections.title: Pattern: The Three DFS Traversals (Recursion and an Explicit Stack)
sections.content:
Depth-first traversal walks as deep as possible before backtracking. There are exactly three orders, and they differ only in WHEN the root is processed relative to its subtrees: preorder (Root, Left, Right), inorder (Left, Root, Right), postorder (Left, Right, Root). Recognize the pattern instantly: the sheet questions Preorder Traversal, Inorder Traversal and Postorder Traversal ask for these directly, but the deeper point is that almost every other tree problem is one of these orders in disguise — 'process node before children' is preorder, 'process node after children' is postorder.

The invariant of the recursive form: when the function returns for a node, that node's entire subtree has been emitted in the correct order. The base case `if node is None: return` handles every edge (empty tree, missing child) in one line.

Interviewers routinely follow up with 'now do it without recursion'. The iterative versions replace the call stack with your own list-as-stack. Iterative inorder is the one to drill: keep sliding left while pushing nodes, then pop (that pop is the leftmost unvisited node), visit it, and switch to its right subtree. Iterative preorder pushes right child before left so left pops first. Iterative postorder has a beautiful shortcut: run a Root-Right-Left preorder and reverse the output. All six variants are O(N) time and O(H) auxiliary space.
sections.code:
# The three DFS orders differ ONLY in where the "visit" line sits.
def preorder(node, out):
    if node is None:                # base case covers every missing child
        return
    out.append(node.val)            # visit root FIRST  (Root, L, R)
    preorder(node.left, out)        # then the entire left subtree
    preorder(node.right, out)       # then the entire right subtree

def inorder(node, out):
    if node is None:
        return
    inorder(node.left, out)         # finish the left subtree first
    out.append(node.val)            # visit root BETWEEN subtrees (L, Root, R)
    inorder(node.right, out)

def postorder(node, out):
    if node is None:
        return
    postorder(node.left, out)
    postorder(node.right, out)
    out.append(node.val)            # visit root LAST — children already done

# Iterative inorder: an explicit stack simulates the recursion frames.
def inorder_iter(root):
    out, stack, cur = [], [], root
    while cur or stack:
        while cur:                  # dive as far left as possible,
            stack.append(cur)       # remembering every node on the way down
            cur = cur.left
        cur = stack.pop()           # leftmost not-yet-visited node
        out.append(cur.val)         # its left side is complete: visit it
        cur = cur.right             # then explore its right subtree
    return out

sections.title: Pattern: BFS Level Order and Its Variants
sections.content:
Breadth-first search processes the tree one horizontal slice at a time using a queue. The invariant that makes every variant easy: at the top of the outer loop, the queue contains EXACTLY one complete level. Snapshot `len(q)` before the inner loop, pop exactly that many nodes, and push their children — the children form the next level, cleanly separated from the current one.

Recognize this pattern whenever the problem says 'level by level', 'per row', 'nearest to the root', or asks about widths. On this sheet: Level Order Traversal is the base template; Zig Zag Traversal is the same loop plus `level.reverse()` on odd depths (or an appendleft deque); Left View and Right View can be read straight off the levels as the first and last element of each; Maximum Width of Binary Tree is BFS where each node carries a virtual heap index (children of i are 2i+1 and 2i+2) and a level's width is last index minus first index plus one, counting the internal gaps of missing nodes.

Two implementation notes. Use `collections.deque`, never `list.pop(0)`. And in the width problem, subtract the level's first index from every index in that level — otherwise indices double each level and, in languages with fixed-size integers, overflow (Python survives, but the interviewer wants to hear you say it). Complexities: O(N) time; queue holds at most one level, so O(W) space, up to N/2 for the bottom of a full tree.
sections.code:
from collections import deque

def level_order(root):
    if root is None:
        return []
    ans, q = [], deque([root])          # the queue holds the CURRENT level
    depth = 0
    while q:
        level = []
        for _ in range(len(q)):         # snapshot: pop one level exactly
            node = q.popleft()          # O(1) — this is why we use deque
            level.append(node.val)
            if node.left:               # children belong to the NEXT level
                q.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                q.append(node.right)
        if depth % 2 == 1:              # Zig Zag = same code + this reverse
            level.reverse()
        ans.append(level)
        depth += 1
    return ans

def max_width(root):
    # Pair each node with a virtual heap index: children of i -> 2i+1, 2i+2.
    if root is None:
        return 0
    best, q = 1, deque([(root, 0)])
    while q:
        base = q[0][1]                  # renormalize so indices stay small
        last = 0
        for _ in range(len(q)):
            node, i = q.popleft()
            i -= base                   # index relative to the level's start
            last = i                    # remember the level's last index
            if node.left:
                q.append((node.left, 2 * i + 1))
            if node.right:
                q.append((node.right, 2 * i + 2))
        best = max(best, last + 1)      # first index is 0 after renormalizing
    return best

sections.title: Pattern: Post-Order Aggregation (the Answer Bubbles Up)
sections.content:
This is the most important pattern in all of tree interviews. The shape: a helper function returns a small summary of its subtree (usually its height or best downward sum), and while those summaries flow upward, a `nonlocal best` variable captures the real answer as a side effect at whichever node it happens to peak. It is postorder because a node can only compute its summary AFTER both children have reported theirs.

Recognize it whenever the answer involves 'longest/largest ... anywhere in the tree' but the natural recursive return value is something smaller and local. Sheet questions: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree is the pure form (return 1 + max of child heights, no side variable needed). Check if Binary Tree is Balanced adds the sentinel trick — return -1 upward the instant any subtree is unbalanced, keeping one O(N) pass instead of the naive O(N^2) height-per-node version. Diameter of Binary Tree returns height but records leftHeight + rightHeight at every node, because the longest path bends at some node. Maximum Path Sum in Binary Tree returns the best DOWNWARD gain (clamping negative branches to 0) while recording val + leftGain + rightGain. Children Sum Property is the same traversal checking node.val against the sum of its children's values.

The invariant to state in an interview: 'my helper returns X for the subtree; the global answer is updated at the bend node; the parent only ever needs X, not the full answer.' Getting this separation wrong — returning the bent path upward — is the classic diameter/path-sum bug, because a parent cannot extend a path that already bends.
sections.code:
def diameter(root):
    # Diameter = number of EDGES on the longest node-to-node path.
    best = 0                            # global answer, updated as a side effect
    def height(node):
        nonlocal best
        if node is None:
            return 0                    # empty subtree has height 0
        lh = height(node.left)          # postorder: children report first
        rh = height(node.right)
        best = max(best, lh + rh)       # path BENDING at this node
        return 1 + max(lh, rh)          # parent only needs the taller arm
    height(root)
    return best

def max_path_sum(root):
    best = float('-inf')                # values can be negative: not 0!
    def gain(node):
        # Best sum of a downward path STARTING at node.
        nonlocal best
        if node is None:
            return 0
        lg = max(gain(node.left), 0)    # negative branch? skip it (take 0)
        rg = max(gain(node.right), 0)
        best = max(best, node.val + lg + rg)   # bend the path here
        return node.val + max(lg, rg)   # parent may extend ONE arm only
    gain(root)
    return best

sections.title: Pattern: Coordinates on a Tree — Views, Vertical Order, Boundary
sections.content:
Give every node a pair of coordinates as you traverse: column `hd` (horizontal distance: root is 0, left child hd-1, right child hd+1) and row `depth`. Suddenly a family of 'draw the tree as seen from somewhere' problems becomes bookkeeping over a dictionary keyed by coordinate. Recognize the pattern from words like view, vertical, column, top, bottom.

Sheet mapping. Top View of Binary Tree: BFS, keep the FIRST value seen for each hd — BFS order guarantees that first means topmost. Bottom View of Binary Tree: identical loop, but keep overwriting, so the LAST value per hd survives. Vertical Order Traversal: collect every (row, val) per hd, then sort columns by hd and entries by row (with value as tie-break if the problem demands it, as LeetCode 987 does). Left View and Right View use only the row coordinate: track the first node reached at each new depth using a DFS that visits the favored side first — when `depth == len(ans)`, you are the first visitor at this depth and therefore visible. Boundary Traversal is a composite: root, then the left edge walking down (skipping leaves), then every leaf left to right via DFS, then the right edge collected downward and appended in reverse — with leaf-vs-edge checks to avoid printing corner nodes twice.

Why BFS for top/bottom but DFS for left/right? Top/bottom need 'topmost wins' across DIFFERENT columns, which BFS's row-by-row order gives for free; a DFS version must also compare rows explicitly. Left/right views only need per-level firsts, which a side-biased DFS delivers in five lines. All of these run in O(N) time; vertical order pays an extra O(C log C) to sort C columns.
sections.code:
from collections import deque

def top_and_bottom_view(root):
    # Coordinates: root hd=0, left child hd-1, right child hd+1.
    if root is None:
        return [], []
    first, last = {}, {}                 # hd -> value
    q = deque([(root, 0)])
    while q:
        node, hd = q.popleft()
        if hd not in first:              # never overwrite -> TOP view
            first[hd] = node.val
        last[hd] = node.val              # always overwrite -> BOTTOM view
        if node.left:
            q.append((node.left, hd - 1))
        if node.right:
            q.append((node.right, hd + 1))
    hds = sorted(first)                  # emit columns left to right
    return [first[h] for h in hds], [last[h] for h in hds]

def right_view(root):
    # First node reached at each depth, visiting the RIGHT side first.
    ans = []
    def dfs(node, depth):
        if node is None:
            return
        if depth == len(ans):            # first visitor at this depth wins
            ans.append(node.val)
        dfs(node.right, depth + 1)       # right first -> rightmost node wins
        dfs(node.left, depth + 1)        # (swap these two for the LEFT view)
    dfs(root, 0)
    return ans

sections.title: Pattern: Two-Tree Recursion (Compare in Lockstep)
sections.content:
Some problems hand you TWO trees (or two halves of one tree) and ask whether they relate in some structural way. The pattern: recurse on a PAIR of nodes simultaneously, and write the base cases as a truth table over which of the two is None. Both None: the empty trees match, return True. Exactly one None: shapes differ, return False. Both present: compare values, then recurse on the child pairs.

The entire art is choosing WHICH children get paired. Check Identical Trees pairs the same sides: (p.left with q.left) and (p.right with q.right). Symmetric Binary Tree is the same skeleton with the pairing crossed: a tree is symmetric if its left subtree is the MIRROR of its right subtree, so you compare (a.left with b.right) — the outer pair — and (a.right with b.left) — the inner pair. Say that insight out loud in an interview; it is the whole problem. The same lockstep skeleton solves 'is T2 a subtree of T1' (run identical-check at every node of T1) and 'merge two trees'.

Invariant: a call `same(a, b)` returns True exactly when the subtree rooted at a is structurally identical (or mirror-identical, for symmetry) to the subtree at b, values included. Complexity: O(min(N1, N2)) time because you stop at the first mismatch, O(H) stack. A common slip is writing `if p is None or q is None: return False` BEFORE the both-None case — order the truth table so both-None is checked first, or combine: both None is True, then any single None is False.

sections.title: Pattern: Root-to-Node Paths and Lowest Common Ancestor
sections.content:
Two closely related tools for questions about WHERE nodes sit relative to each other. The first is path building by backtracking: walk down with DFS, append each node to a shared path list on the way in, and — the crucial move — pop it back off when the subtree fails to contain the target. The invariant: at any moment, `path` holds exactly the chain from the root to the current node. When the target is found, return True all the way up without popping, freezing the path. That is the sheet question Root to Node Path, and the identical skeleton solves root-to-leaf path sums and 'print all ancestors'.

The second tool is the one-pass Lowest Common Ancestor, for the sheet question Lowest Common Ancestor in Binary Tree. The recursion returns a node meaning 'in my subtree I found this much': None (neither target here), p or q (found one), or the LCA itself. The rules: if root is None, p, or q, return root immediately — note this is correct even when one target is an ancestor of the other, because the search never needs to look below the first target found. Then recurse both sides. If BOTH sides return non-None, p and q are split across this node, so this node is the LCA — return it. Otherwise forward whichever side is non-None.

Complexity: both are O(N) time, O(H) space. The two-pass alternative — build both root-to-node paths, then walk them together until they diverge — is also O(N) and easier to reason about, but uses O(H) extra lists; know both and offer the one-pass version as the refinement. Careful: the elegant one-pass LCA assumes both targets EXIST in the tree; if existence is not guaranteed, verify at the end or count matches during the recursion.

sections.title: Pitfalls & Common Mistakes
sections.content:
1) Calling height() inside a recursion over every node — the balanced-tree and diameter problems become O(N^2) on skewed trees. Fix: one postorder pass that returns height while updating the answer (sentinel -1 for imbalance).

2) Returning the bent path upward in diameter/max-path-sum. A parent can extend only ONE arm of a child's path; return `val + max(leftGain, rightGain)`, never `val + leftGain + rightGain`. The bent value goes only into the global best.

3) Forgetting negatives in Maximum Path Sum: initialize best to -infinity (not 0) because the answer may be a single negative node, and clamp child gains with max(gain, 0) so a harmful branch is dropped.

4) `list.pop(0)` as a queue — silently O(N^2). Always `collections.deque.popleft()`.

5) Recursion depth: 10^5-node skewed tree = 10^5 frames; CPython's default limit is about 1000. Fix: `sys.setrecursionlimit(200_000)` or rewrite with an explicit stack.

6) None-order bugs in two-tree recursion: testing `p is None or q is None` before `p is None and q is None` returns False for two empty trees. Order the truth table both-None first.

7) Mixing up depth conventions: height in nodes (leaf = 1) versus edges (leaf = 0) changes diameter by exactly the fencepost you will get wrong under pressure. Pick nodes-convention, say it, and note diameter-in-edges = lh + rh with node-heights.

8) Width problem without renormalizing indices: indices double per level and reach 2^depth; subtract each level's first index. 9) Mutable default `path=[]` accumulating across calls — build the list inside the function. 10) Using `==` on node values when the problem gives node objects and values repeat — compare with `is` on the objects.

sections.title: Interview Recognition Checklist
sections.content:
Cues that a problem is this topic: the input is a TreeNode/root; words like subtree, leaf, depth, level, ancestor, view, path; a diagram with branching; 'level by level' or 'zigzag' (BFS); 'as seen from the top/side' (coordinates); 'longest/largest anywhere in the tree' (postorder aggregation with a global best); two roots given (lockstep recursion).

Thirty-second checklist before coding: (1) DFS or BFS? Per-level wording means BFS; everything else defaults to DFS. (2) Which DFS order? Need children's answers first: postorder. Need to process/record before descending: preorder. (3) What does my helper RETURN, and is the true answer a side effect (nonlocal best) rather than the return value? (4) Base case: what is the answer for None — 0, True, -infinity, empty list? Get this one line right and half the bugs vanish. (5) Values or node objects — compare with == or is? Are duplicates possible? (6) Can the tree be skewed — do I need to raise the recursion limit or go iterative? (7) State the complexity before coding: almost always O(N) time and O(H) or O(W) space.

Then dry-run on three tiny inputs: the empty tree, a single node, and a two-node chain. Those three catch most base-case and None-handling errors before the interviewer does. If the problem smells like search-by-value in O(log N), pause — that is a BST assumption; confirm whether the ordering property actually holds before using it.

implementations.title: TreeNode, level-order builder, and all six traversals (recursive + iterative + BFS)
implementations.code:
# =====================================================================
# TreeNode, a level-order builder, and ALL core traversals from scratch:
# three recursive DFS, three iterative DFS, and BFS level order.
# =====================================================================
from collections import deque

class TreeNode:
    # A binary-tree node is just a value plus two child references.
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left        # None means "no left child"
        self.right = right

def build(values):
    # Build a tree from a level-order list where None marks a hole.
    # Example: [1, 2, 3, None, 5] gives 1 -> (2 -> (None, 5), 3).
    if not values or values[0] is None:
        return None
    root = TreeNode(values[0])
    q = deque([root])                     # parents still owed children
    i = 1
    while q and i < len(values):
        parent = q.popleft()
        if values[i] is not None:         # this parent's left slot
            parent.left = TreeNode(values[i])
            q.append(parent.left)
        i += 1
        if i < len(values) and values[i] is not None:   # right slot
            parent.right = TreeNode(values[i])
            q.append(parent.right)
        i += 1
    return root

# ---------- recursive DFS: moving ONE line changes the order ----------
def preorder(node, out=None):
    if out is None:
        out = []                          # fresh list per top-level call
    if node:
        out.append(node.val)              # Root first
        preorder(node.left, out)          # then Left subtree
        preorder(node.right, out)         # then Right subtree
    return out

def inorder(node, out=None):
    if out is None:
        out = []
    if node:
        inorder(node.left, out)           # Left first
        out.append(node.val)              # Root in the middle
        inorder(node.right, out)          # Right last
    return out

def postorder(node, out=None):
    if out is None:
        out = []
    if node:
        postorder(node.left, out)         # Left
        postorder(node.right, out)        # Right
        out.append(node.val)              # Root LAST (children finished)
    return out

# ---------- iterative DFS: an explicit stack replaces the call stack ----
def preorder_iter(root):
    out, stack = [], ([root] if root else [])
    while stack:
        node = stack.pop()                # LIFO: last pushed pops first
        out.append(node.val)              # visit on pop
        if node.right:                    # push right FIRST so that the
            stack.append(node.right)      # left child is popped first
        if node.left:
            stack.append(node.left)
    return out

def inorder_iter(root):
    out, stack, cur = [], [], root
    while cur or stack:
        while cur:                        # slide to the leftmost node,
            stack.append(cur)             # remembering the path down
            cur = cur.left
        cur = stack.pop()                 # left subtree exhausted here
        out.append(cur.val)               # so visit this node now
        cur = cur.right                   # then switch to its right side
    return out

def postorder_iter(root):
    # Trick: produce Root, Right, Left with a stack, then reverse it.
    out, stack = [], ([root] if root else [])
    while stack:
        node = stack.pop()
        out.append(node.val)              # building Root, Right, Left ...
        if node.left:
            stack.append(node.left)
        if node.right:
            stack.append(node.right)
    return out[::-1]                      # reversed -> Left, Right, Root

# ---------- BFS ----------
def level_order(root):
    ans = []
    q = deque([root]) if root else deque()
    while q:
        level = []
        for _ in range(len(q)):           # exactly one level per pass
            node = q.popleft()
            level.append(node.val)
            if node.left:
                q.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                q.append(node.right)
        ans.append(level)
    return ans

if __name__ == "__main__":
    t = build([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, None, 6])
    print(preorder(t))                    # [1, 2, 4, 5, 3, 6]
    print(inorder(t))                     # [4, 2, 5, 1, 3, 6]
    print(postorder(t))                   # [4, 5, 2, 6, 3, 1]
    assert preorder(t) == preorder_iter(t)     # iterative matches recursive
    assert inorder(t) == inorder_iter(t)
    assert postorder(t) == postorder_iter(t)
    print(level_order(t))                 # [[1], [2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]

implementations.title: One-pass tree metrics: depth, balance, diameter, max path sum, children-sum
implementations.code:
# =====================================================================
# One postorder recursion, five classic answers: max depth, balanced
# check, diameter, maximum path sum, children-sum property.
# All O(N) time and O(H) call-stack space.
# =====================================================================
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def max_depth(root):
    # Height counted in NODES: empty tree = 0, single leaf = 1.
    if root is None:
        return 0
    return 1 + max(max_depth(root.left), max_depth(root.right))

def is_balanced(root):
    # Balanced = at EVERY node |height(L) - height(R)| <= 1.
    # Sentinel trick: return -1 upward the moment imbalance appears,
    # keeping ONE O(N) pass (no repeated height() calls -> not O(N^2)).
    def check(node):
        if node is None:
            return 0
        lh = check(node.left)
        if lh == -1:                    # left side already failed
            return -1
        rh = check(node.right)
        if rh == -1:                    # right side already failed
            return -1
        if abs(lh - rh) > 1:            # imbalance found right here
            return -1
        return 1 + max(lh, rh)          # otherwise report normal height
    return check(root) != -1

def diameter(root):
    # Diameter = number of EDGES on the longest node-to-node path.
    best = 0
    def height(node):
        nonlocal best
        if node is None:
            return 0
        lh = height(node.left)          # postorder: children answer first
        rh = height(node.right)
        best = max(best, lh + rh)       # longest path BENDING at node
        return 1 + max(lh, rh)          # only the taller arm goes upward
    height(root)
    return best

def max_path_sum(root):
    # A path may start and end anywhere; it bends at exactly one node.
    best = float("-inf")                # answer can be negative: not 0
    def gain(node):
        # Best sum of a DOWNWARD path starting at this node.
        nonlocal best
        if node is None:
            return 0
        lg = max(gain(node.left), 0)    # drop harmful negative branches
        rg = max(gain(node.right), 0)
        best = max(best, node.val + lg + rg)   # bend the path here
        return node.val + max(lg, rg)   # a parent extends ONE arm only
    gain(root)
    return best

def children_sum_ok(root):
    # Children Sum Property: every non-leaf equals the sum of its
    # children's values (a missing child counts as 0; leaves pass).
    if root is None or (root.left is None and root.right is None):
        return True
    left_val = root.left.val if root.left else 0
    right_val = root.right.val if root.right else 0
    if root.val != left_val + right_val:
        return False                    # property broken at this node
    return children_sum_ok(root.left) and children_sum_ok(root.right)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Tree:      -10
    #            /  \
    #           9   20
    #               / \
    #             15   7
    r = TreeNode(-10, TreeNode(9), TreeNode(20, TreeNode(15), TreeNode(7)))
    print(max_depth(r))                 # 3
    print(is_balanced(r))               # True
    print(diameter(r))                  # 3   (9 -> -10 -> 20 -> 15, in edges)
    print(max_path_sum(r))              # 42  (15 + 20 + 7)
    ok = TreeNode(5, TreeNode(2), TreeNode(3))
    print(children_sum_ok(ok))          # True: 5 == 2 + 3

implementations.title: Views toolkit: left/right/top/bottom views, vertical order, boundary traversal
implementations.code:
# =====================================================================
# The "views" toolkit — every answer is bookkeeping over coordinates:
# hd (column: left = -1, right = +1) and depth (row).
# =====================================================================
from collections import deque, defaultdict

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def left_view(root):
    # First node of every level: DFS visiting the LEFT child first;
    # the first arrival at each new depth is the visible node.
    ans = []
    def dfs(node, depth):
        if node is None:
            return
        if depth == len(ans):            # first visitor at this depth
            ans.append(node.val)
        dfs(node.left, depth + 1)        # left first -> leftmost wins
        dfs(node.right, depth + 1)
    dfs(root, 0)
    return ans

def right_view(root):
    ans = []
    def dfs(node, depth):
        if node is None:
            return
        if depth == len(ans):
            ans.append(node.val)
        dfs(node.right, depth + 1)       # right first -> rightmost wins
        dfs(node.left, depth + 1)
    dfs(root, 0)
    return ans

def top_bottom_view(root):
    # BFS with horizontal distance: BFS order = top-to-bottom order,
    # so FIRST value per hd is the top view, LAST is the bottom view.
    if root is None:
        return [], []
    first, last = {}, {}
    q = deque([(root, 0)])
    while q:
        node, hd = q.popleft()
        if hd not in first:              # never overwrite: top view
            first[hd] = node.val
        last[hd] = node.val              # always overwrite: bottom view
        if node.left:
            q.append((node.left, hd - 1))
        if node.right:
            q.append((node.right, hd + 1))
    hds = sorted(first)                  # columns from left to right
    return [first[h] for h in hds], [last[h] for h in hds]

def vertical_order(root):
    # Group (row, val) by column; sort columns by hd, entries by row
    # (value breaks ties in the same cell — LeetCode 987 convention).
    cols = defaultdict(list)             # hd -> list of (row, val)
    q = deque([(root, 0, 0)]) if root else deque()
    while q:
        node, hd, row = q.popleft()
        cols[hd].append((row, node.val))
        if node.left:
            q.append((node.left, hd - 1, row + 1))
        if node.right:
            q.append((node.right, hd + 1, row + 1))
    return [[v for _, v in sorted(cols[h])] for h in sorted(cols)]

def boundary(root):
    # Anticlockwise boundary = root + left edge (no leaves) + all
    # leaves left-to-right + right edge (no leaves) reversed.
    def is_leaf(n):
        return n.left is None and n.right is None
    if root is None:
        return []
    ans = [] if is_leaf(root) else [root.val]   # avoid double counting
    cur = root.left                      # 1) walk the left edge down
    while cur:
        if not is_leaf(cur):             # leaves are added in step 2
            ans.append(cur.val)
        cur = cur.left if cur.left else cur.right
    def leaves(n):                       # 2) plain DFS emits leaves in order
        if n is None:
            return
        if is_leaf(n):
            ans.append(n.val)
        leaves(n.left)
        leaves(n.right)
    leaves(root)
    tmp, cur = [], root.right            # 3) right edge, collected downward
    while cur:
        if not is_leaf(cur):
            tmp.append(cur.val)
        cur = cur.right if cur.right else cur.left
    ans.extend(reversed(tmp))            # appended bottom-up
    return ans

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Tree:        1
    #            /   \
    #           2     3
    #          / \     \
    #         4   5     6
    r = TreeNode(1, TreeNode(2, TreeNode(4), TreeNode(5)),
                 TreeNode(3, None, TreeNode(6)))
    print(left_view(r))                  # [1, 2, 4]
    print(right_view(r))                 # [1, 3, 6]
    print(top_bottom_view(r))            # ([4, 2, 1, 3, 6], [4, 2, 5, 3, 6])
    print(vertical_order(r))             # [[4], [2], [1, 5], [3], [6]]
    print(boundary(r))                   # [1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 3]

implementations.title: Paths and ancestors: root-to-node path, LCA, and maximum width
implementations.code:
# =====================================================================
# Root-to-node path via backtracking, single-pass lowest common
# ancestor, and maximum width via virtual heap indices.
# =====================================================================
from collections import deque

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def root_to_node_path(root, target):
    # Backtracking: extend the path going down; if a subtree cannot
    # reach the target, POP the node before returning False.
    path = []
    def dfs(node):
        if node is None:
            return False
        path.append(node.val)            # tentatively on the path
        if node.val == target:
            return True                  # found: keep the frozen path
        if dfs(node.left) or dfs(node.right):
            return True                  # found deeper: keep this node
        path.pop()                       # dead end: undo, then report up
        return False
    dfs(root)
    return path                          # [] means target is absent

def lca(root, p, q):
    # Single pass; p and q are NODES guaranteed to be in the tree.
    if root is None or root is p or root is q:
        return root                      # hit bottom, or found a target
    left = lca(root.left, p, q)          # what the left subtree found
    right = lca(root.right, p, q)        # what the right subtree found
    if left and right:                   # one target on each side:
        return root                      # this node is the split point
    return left if left else right       # both on one side (or none)

def max_width(root):
    # Virtual heap indices: children of index i are 2i+1 and 2i+2.
    # Width of a level = last - first + 1, counting internal holes.
    if root is None:
        return 0
    best = 0
    q = deque([(root, 0)])
    while q:
        base = q[0][1]                   # renormalize each level so the
        last = 0                         # indices never grow unbounded
        for _ in range(len(q)):
            node, i = q.popleft()
            i -= base                    # index relative to level start
            last = i
            if node.left:
                q.append((node.left, 2 * i + 1))
            if node.right:
                q.append((node.right, 2 * i + 2))
        best = max(best, last + 1)       # first index is 0 after shift
    return best

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Tree:      3
    #           / \
    #          5   1
    #         / \ / \
    #        6  2 0  8
    n6, n2, n0, n8 = TreeNode(6), TreeNode(2), TreeNode(0), TreeNode(8)
    n5, n1 = TreeNode(5, n6, n2), TreeNode(1, n0, n8)
    r = TreeNode(3, n5, n1)
    print(root_to_node_path(r, 2))       # [3, 5, 2]
    print(lca(r, n5, n1).val)            # 3 (targets split at the root)
    print(lca(r, n6, n2).val)            # 5 (both under node 5)
    print(max_width(r))                  # 4 (bottom level is full)

Binary Tree Part-II.summary:
Part-I gave you the traversal machinery: DFS in three orders, BFS by levels, postorder aggregation with a global best, coordinates for views, and path/LCA recursions. This tab assumes all of that is muscle memory and goes after the questions interviewers use to separate strong candidates: moving UPWARD through a tree, rebuilding trees from traversal arrays, turning trees into strings and back, restructuring trees in place, and traversing in O(1) extra space.

The unifying theme of Part-II is that the tree stops being a read-only structure you walk down. Nodes at Distance K and Burn a Binary Tree need edges pointing toward the root, so you manufacture them with a child-to-parent hash map and then run plain graph BFS. Construct-from-traversals and Serialize/Deserialize treat the tree as data to be encoded and decoded, teaching you which traversal combinations carry enough information to pin down a unique shape (preorder+inorder does; preorder alone does not, unless you also record the None holes). Morris traversal mutates the tree itself — temporarily threading right pointers through it — to walk it with no stack and no recursion, then heals every change. Flatten reuses that exact splice to rewire a tree into a linked list in place. Count Nodes in a Complete Tree shows how a structural guarantee (completeness) buys you O(log^2 N) where a generic tree forces O(N).

These nine problems share remarkably little boilerplate but a lot of ideas: hash maps as auxiliary indexes over trees, index arithmetic on traversal arrays, and the discipline of mutating pointers without losing the rest of the tree. Master them and the hard end of tree interviews becomes routine.
preRequisites: Total fluency with Part-I traversals: you can write recursive and iterative preorder/inorder and BFS level order without pausing to think — Part-II composes them.
Hash maps (`dict`) as auxiliary indexes: value-to-position maps for O(1) lookups during tree construction, and node-to-parent maps for walking upward.
Graph-style BFS with a visited set on `collections.deque` — once parents are recorded, a tree is an undirected graph where every node has at most 3 neighbors.
Index arithmetic over subarrays: passing (lo, hi) bounds instead of slicing, because `arr[a:b]` copies and turns an O(N) build into O(N^2).
String building with `','.join(parts)` and `str.split(',')` — repeated `s += piece` is O(N^2); serialization must collect parts in a list and join once.
Bit shifts and powers of two: a perfect tree of height h has 2^h - 1 nodes, computed as `(1 << h) - 1`.
The inorder predecessor concept: the rightmost node of a node's left subtree — Morris traversal is built entirely on finding and re-finding it.
cheatSheet: Parent map in one BFS: parent[child] = node for each real child; afterwards every node has neighbors {left, right, parent[node]} — a graph of degree <= 3.

Distance K / Burn: BFS from the target over those 3 neighbors with a visited set; distance-K answer = the frontier after exactly K expansions; burn time = number of expansions until the queue empties.

Complete-tree count: if leftmost-spine height == rightmost-spine height, the subtree is perfect with 2^h - 1 nodes; else 1 + count(left) + count(right). O(log N) levels x O(log N) spine walks = O(log^2 N).
Build pre+in: next preorder element is the root; its inorder index m splits inorder into left [lo, m-1] and right [m+1, hi]; a val-to-index dict makes each split O(1), total O(N).
Build post+in: identical split but consume postorder from the END and build the RIGHT subtree before the left (postorder reversed = Root, R, L).
Uniqueness: preorder+inorder or postorder+inorder determine a unique tree (distinct values assumed); preorder+postorder alone is ambiguous unless every node has 0 or 2 children.
Serialize with null markers: preorder DFS emitting '#' for None (or BFS emitting '#per missing child') makes ONE traversal sufficient to rebuild the exact shape.

Morris inorder: pred = rightmost node of cur.left; if pred.right is None, thread pred.right = cur and go left; if pred.right is cur, unthread, visit cur, go right. O(N) time, O(1) space — each edge is traversed at most 3 times.
Morris preorder = same threading, but visit cur when the thread is CREATED (first touch) instead of when it is removed.

Flatten to linked list: either reverse-preorder recursion (visit Right, Left, Root; set node.right = prev, node.left = None), or the Morris-style loop: splice the left subtree between cur and cur.right, repeat down the right spine.

sections.title: Recap & What Part-II Adds
sections.content:
Quick recap of Part-I: a binary tree is nodes with `val`, `left`, `right`; DFS gives preorder/inorder/postorder in O(N) time and O(H) stack; BFS processes levels with a deque; hard problems decompose as 'helper returns a subtree summary, nonlocal best captures the answer'. If any of that feels shaky, reread the Binary Tree tab first — nothing there is repeated here.

Part-II adds five genuinely new capabilities. (1) Walking UP: child links only point down, so problems like Nodes at Distance K and Burn a Binary Tree require you to build a child-to-parent map, converting the tree into an undirected graph you can BFS in any direction. (2) Reconstruction: given traversal arrays (preorder+inorder, postorder+inorder), rebuild the unique tree they describe using index arithmetic and a value-to-index hash map. (3) Serialization: encode a tree into a single string with explicit null markers and decode it back — the round-trip discipline behind Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree and, conceptually, behind every system that ships trees over a network. (4) O(1)-space traversal: Morris inorder and preorder thread temporary right-pointers through the tree so you can traverse with no stack and no recursion, then repair every mutation. (5) In-place restructuring: Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List rewires the same nodes into a right-spine list, and Count Total Nodes in a Complete Binary Tree exploits structural guarantees to beat O(N). Different problems, one attitude shift: the tree is now something you index, encode, and rewire — not just walk.

sections.title: Pattern: Parent Map — Walking Up the Tree
sections.content:
Recognize this pattern whenever distance or spreading is measured in ALL directions from some starting node: 'all nodes at distance K from a target' (Nodes at Distance K) or 'fire starts at a node and spreads one edge per minute' (Burn a Binary Tree). Child pointers only let you go down, but distance-K neighbors and fire spread also go UP through the parent. The fix is two clean steps that you should narrate in the interview.

Step 1: one BFS (or DFS) pass building `parent[child] = node` for every node. Now every node has at most three neighbors: left child, right child, parent. The tree has become an undirected graph — and a tree-shaped graph has no cycles, so a plain visited set is all the protection you need against walking back and forth between child and parent forever.

Step 2: standard ring-by-ring BFS from the target. For Nodes at Distance K, expand exactly K rings; whatever sits in the queue after the K-th expansion IS the answer. For Burn a Binary Tree, keep expanding until the queue empties and count the expansions — each ring is one minute of fire spread, so the number of non-trivial expansions is the total burn time. Both run in O(N) time and O(N) space (the parent map dominates).

The pattern generalizes: any 'distance between two nodes', 'closest leaf', or 'spread/infection' phrasing on a tree is this same parent-map + BFS combination. A popular alternative for distance-K uses a recursive function returning the distance from each ancestor to the target and scanning the other side — it works, but the parent-map version is shorter, harder to get wrong, and the interviewer sees a reusable idea rather than a one-off trick.
sections.code:
from collections import deque

def parent_map(root):
    # Step 1 of every walk-upward problem: child -> parent in one pass.
    parent = {root: None}                # root has no parent
    q = deque([root])
    while q:
        node = q.popleft()
        for child in (node.left, node.right):
            if child:
                parent[child] = node     # record the upward edge
                q.append(child)
    return parent

def nodes_at_distance_k(root, target, k):
    # Step 2: ordinary graph BFS; each node has <= 3 neighbors.
    if root is None:
        return []
    par = parent_map(root)
    seen, q, d = {target}, deque([target]), 0
    while q and d < k:                   # expand exactly k rings
        for _ in range(len(q)):
            node = q.popleft()
            for nb in (node.left, node.right, par[node]):
                if nb and nb not in seen:    # visited set stops us from
                    seen.add(nb)             # bouncing child <-> parent
                    q.append(nb)
        d += 1
    return [n.val for n in q]            # the frontier IS the answer

sections.title: Pattern: Exploiting Completeness — Counting Nodes in O(log^2 N)
sections.content:
Count Total Nodes in Complete Binary Tree looks like a trick question — `count = 1 + count(left) + count(right)` finishes it in O(N). The real question is hidden in the word COMPLETE: every level is full except possibly the last, which fills left to right. The interviewer wants you to beat O(N) using that guarantee.

The key observation: in a complete tree, walk down the leftmost spine and count its length, then the rightmost spine. If the two heights are EQUAL, the last level under this root is completely full, so the subtree is perfect and has exactly 2^h - 1 nodes — no traversal needed, one bit-shift. If they differ (by exactly 1 — completeness allows no more), you cannot shortcut this root, so recurse: 1 + count(left) + count(right). Here is why that recursion stays cheap: in a complete tree, at every node AT LEAST ONE of the two children is the root of a perfect subtree. That child's count returns immediately from the height check, so only ONE side ever recurses deeper. The recursion therefore descends a single path of O(log N) nodes, and each visit pays O(log N) for the two spine walks: O(log^2 N) total. For a million-node tree that is roughly 400 operations instead of a million.

State the invariant explicitly: 'left spine height equals right spine height implies perfect implies 2^h - 1'. And know the follow-up: the same completeness guarantee powers binary-searching the last level for a specific node (used in some variants), because positions on the last level map to left/right turn sequences — the same 2i+1 / 2i+2 index arithmetic from Part-I's width problem.
sections.code:
def count_complete(root):
    # Works on any tree, but achieves O(log^2 N) when it is complete.
    def left_h(n):
        h = 0
        while n:                       # hug the left edge downward
            h += 1
            n = n.left
        return h
    def right_h(n):
        h = 0
        while n:                       # hug the right edge downward
            h += 1
            n = n.right
        return h
    if root is None:
        return 0
    lh, rh = left_h(root), right_h(root)
    if lh == rh:                       # spines match -> PERFECT subtree
        return (1 << lh) - 1           # 2^lh - 1 nodes, via bit shift
    # Otherwise recurse; completeness guarantees one child is perfect,
    # so only one side keeps recursing -> O(log N) levels of work.
    return 1 + count_complete(root.left) + count_complete(root.right)

sections.title: Pattern: Rebuilding a Tree from Traversals
sections.content:
Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder, and its sibling Construct Binary Tree from Postorder and Inorder, invert what Part-I taught: instead of tree-to-array, you go array-to-tree. The engine is one fact: the FIRST element of preorder is the root of the whole tree. Find that value in the inorder array at index m; everything left of m is the left subtree's inorder, everything right is the right subtree's — and their sizes tell you how the remaining preorder splits too. Recurse on both halves and the tree assembles itself.

Two optimizations turn a correct O(N^2) sketch into the expected O(N). First, precompute `idx = {value: inorder_position}` so each root lookup is O(1) instead of a linear scan (this assumes distinct values — say so). Second, never slice the arrays: `preorder[1:m+1]` copies memory at every level. Instead keep a single climbing pointer `pre_i` into preorder and pass (lo, hi) bounds over inorder. The invariant: when `rec(lo, hi)` is called, `preorder[pre_i]` is exactly the root of the subtree spanning `inorder[lo..hi]` — this is why you MUST build the left subtree before the right (preorder lists left before right).

For postorder+inorder, mirror everything: consume postorder from the END (its last element is the root), and because postorder read backwards is Root, Right, Left, build the RIGHT subtree first. Finally, know the uniqueness theory cold, because it is a favorite follow-up: inorder + (either preorder or postorder) determines a unique tree; preorder + postorder alone does NOT — a single-child node's side is ambiguous — unless the tree is full (every node has 0 or 2 children). And preorder ALONE suffices only when None holes are recorded, which is exactly the serialization pattern in the next section.
sections.code:
def build_pre_in(preorder, inorder):
    # Next preorder element = root; its inorder index splits Left | Right.
    idx = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(inorder)}   # val -> position, O(1) lookups
    pre_i = 0                                     # climbing pointer into preorder
    def rec(lo, hi):                              # build tree of inorder[lo..hi]
        nonlocal pre_i
        if lo > hi:
            return None                           # empty range -> no node
        root_val = preorder[pre_i]
        pre_i += 1                                # consume this root
        node = TreeNode(root_val)
        m = idx[root_val]                         # root's slot in inorder
        node.left = rec(lo, m - 1)                # LEFT first: preorder order
        node.right = rec(m + 1, hi)
        return node
    return rec(0, len(inorder) - 1)

def build_post_in(postorder, inorder):
    # Same split; consume postorder from the END, build RIGHT first
    # (postorder read backwards is Root, Right, Left).
    idx = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(inorder)}
    post_i = len(postorder) - 1                   # pointer walks backwards
    def rec(lo, hi):
        nonlocal post_i
        if lo > hi:
            return None
        root_val = postorder[post_i]
        post_i -= 1                               # consume from the back
        node = TreeNode(root_val)
        m = idx[root_val]
        node.right = rec(m + 1, hi)               # RIGHT before left here
        node.left = rec(lo, m - 1)
        return node
    return rec(0, len(inorder) - 1)

sections.title: Pattern: Serialization — a Tree as a String and Back
sections.content:
Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree asks for a lossless round trip: `deserialize(serialize(root))` must reproduce the exact structure. The previous section showed why one plain traversal cannot do it — preorder [1,2] could be a left chain or a right chain. The fix is to record ABSENCE explicitly: emit a marker like '#' every time you meet None. With null markers, a single preorder captures the complete shape, because at decode time every token answers the question 'is there a node here?' before you ever have to guess.

The DFS codec is beautifully symmetric. Serialize: preorder DFS appending `str(val)` or '#', then one `','.join` (never `s += piece` in a loop — that is O(N^2) string copying). Deserialize: wrap the tokens in an iterator and recurse: take the next token; '#' means return None; otherwise make the node, then rebuild left, then right. The invariant: the token stream is consumed left to right in EXACTLY the order serialize produced it, so recursion depth and token position stay perfectly synchronized with no index bookkeeping at all.

The BFS codec (used in the implementation below, and the format LeetCode itself prints) emits level order, writing '#' for each missing child of each real node; decoding pairs a queue of waiting parents with the token stream, two tokens per parent. Both are O(N) time and space. Interview notes: delimiters are mandatory (values can be multi-digit or negative — '12' must not read as '1','2'); mention that BFS output matches the platform's format while DFS code is shorter; and connect it back: serialization is 'construct from traversal' made unambiguous, which is a sentence interviewers love to hear.

sections.title: Pattern: Morris Threading — Traversal in O(1) Extra Space
sections.content:
Every traversal so far spends O(H) memory — recursion frames or an explicit stack — to remember how to climb back up. Morris traversal (the sheet questions Morris Inorder Traversal and Morris Preorder Traversal) removes even that, achieving O(N) time with O(1) extra space by storing the return path INSIDE the tree: it temporarily points some right-child pointers back up, then removes every thread it created, leaving the tree exactly as found.

The mechanism, for the current node `cur` with a left child: find `cur`'s inorder predecessor — the RIGHTMOST node of its left subtree. That node's right pointer is None (it is a subtree's last node), so it is free real estate. First visit: set `pred.right = cur` (the thread) and move into the left subtree; the thread guarantees that finishing the left subtree walks you straight back to `cur` with no stack. Second arrival: the predecessor scan now finds `pred.right is cur`, which tells you the left subtree is complete — remove the thread, visit `cur`, and move right. Nodes with no left child are just visited and passed through. Preorder is the same machine with the visit moved: emit `cur` when the thread is CREATED (before descending left) instead of when it is removed.

Why is this O(N) and not O(N x H)? The predecessor scan walks only edges of `cur`'s left subtree's right spine, and each tree edge is traversed at most three times overall (down the spine while threading, again while unthreading, once by `cur` itself). Amortized, the scans cost O(N) total. Caveats to state: the tree is temporarily modified — unacceptable for concurrent readers; and any early exit (searching, k-th element) must first restore outstanding threads or the tree stays corrupted. Morris is THE standard answer to the follow-up 'now do inorder in O(1) space', and it also powers the O(1)-space flatten in the next section.

sections.title: Pattern: In-Place Restructuring — Flatten to a Linked List
sections.content:
Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List asks you to rewire the tree so that all nodes hang off `right` pointers in PREORDER order, with every `left` set to None — using the same node objects, no new allocations. It is the cleanest test of whether you can mutate pointers without losing subtrees, and it has three standard solutions worth knowing in ascending order of elegance.

Solution 1 — reverse preorder with a trailing pointer: visit nodes in the order Right, Left, Root (exactly reversed preorder). Keep `prev`, the head of the already-built list. At each node set `node.right = prev`, `node.left = None`, `prev = node`. The invariant: `prev` always points to the node that comes immediately AFTER the current node in preorder, and everything from `prev` onward is already correctly linked. The subtle safety property: by the time a node's pointers are overwritten, both its subtrees have been fully processed, so nothing is lost. O(N) time, O(H) stack.

Solution 2 — Morris-style splice, the O(1)-space answer: walk down the right spine. Whenever `cur` has a left subtree, find that subtree's rightmost node (the same predecessor from Morris), attach `cur`'s old right subtree to it, move the whole left subtree into `cur.right`, null out `cur.left`, and step right. Each splice is exactly 'insert the left subtree between cur and its right subtree', which preserves preorder by construction.

Recognize the wider pattern: 'convert tree to (doubly) linked list', 'increasing order search tree', and 'populate next-right pointers' are all the same discipline — decide the target order, then rewire while holding a reference to everything not yet linked. The number-one bug is overwriting `node.right` while the old right subtree is only reachable through it; the reverse-order visit (solution 1) or the explicit save (solution 2) is precisely what prevents that.
sections.code:
def flatten_reverse_preorder(root):
    # Visit in REVERSE preorder (Right, Left, Root); prev is the head
    # of the already-flattened tail of the list.
    prev = None
    def dfs(node):
        nonlocal prev
        if node is None:
            return
        dfs(node.right)              # rightmost part of the list first
        dfs(node.left)
        node.right = prev            # everything after node: already linked
        node.left = None             # the list uses right pointers only
        prev = node                  # node becomes the new list head
    dfs(root)

def flatten_morris(root):
    # O(1) space: splice the left subtree between cur and cur.right.
    cur = root
    while cur:
        if cur.left:
            pred = cur.left          # rightmost node of the left subtree
            while pred.right:
                pred = pred.right
            pred.right = cur.right   # old right subtree hangs off its tail
            cur.right = cur.left     # left subtree moves to the right
            cur.left = None          # left pointer must end up None
        cur = cur.right              # walk down the growing list

sections.title: Pitfalls & Common Mistakes
sections.content:
1) Distance-K / Burn without a visited set: BFS bounces forever between child and parent (each is the other's neighbor). Always add every enqueued node to `seen` — including the starting target.

2) Burn-time off-by-one: counting rings from 0 versus 1. Define it precisely: the target burns at minute 0; each BFS expansion that discovers at least one new node adds one minute. Dry-run a 3-node tree to check your counter.

3) Construct-from-traversal with slicing: `rec(preorder[1:m+1], inorder[:m])` copies subarrays at every level — O(N^2) time and memory churn. Pass (lo, hi) bounds and one climbing pointer instead.

4) Forgetting that val-to-index maps assume DISTINCT values; with duplicates, pre+in reconstruction is genuinely ambiguous — say so rather than silently assuming.

5) Building left before right in build_post_in (or right before left in build_pre_in): the shared consumption pointer makes subtree order mandatory, and swapping it scrambles the tree without crashing — the worst kind of bug. Test with an asymmetric 5-node tree.

6) Serializing without delimiters or null markers: '1,12' vs '11,2' ambiguity, and shape ambiguity for single-child nodes. Join with commas; write '#' for every None.

7) Morris with an early return: breaking out mid-traversal leaves threads in the tree — a corrupted structure for any later code. Finish the loop or explicitly unthread before returning.

8) Morris predecessor scan missing the `pred.right is not cur` guard: the scan follows your own thread back to `cur` and loops forever.

9) Flatten losing the right subtree: `cur.right = cur.left` before saving the old right — always attach the old right subtree to the left subtree's tail FIRST.

10) Count-complete recomputing spine heights from scratch at every level is fine (that is the O(log^2 N)), but calling full `count` on BOTH children after the equal-height check never triggers means you wrote plain O(N) — verify the shortcut actually fires by tracing a 6-node complete tree.

sections.title: Interview Recognition Checklist
sections.content:
Cues that you are in Part-II territory: 'distance K from a node', 'burn/infect/spread from a node' (parent map + BFS); 'complete binary tree' plus any request to beat O(N) (spine-height shortcut); arrays named preorder/inorder/postorder as INPUT (reconstruction with a val-to-index map); 'serialize', 'encode', 'save and load', 'convert to string' (null-marker traversal codec); 'O(1) space' or 'no recursion, no stack' attached to any traversal (Morris threading); 'in place', 'rewire', 'flatten', 'convert to linked list' (pointer restructuring with a saved tail).

Thirty-second checklist before coding: (1) Do I need to move upward or measure in all directions? Build the parent map first — it is 8 lines and unlocks everything. (2) Am I consuming a traversal array? Fix which END is the root (front for preorder, back for postorder), which subtree gets built FIRST, and whether values are distinct. (3) Am I encoding? Choose delimiter and null marker before writing a line; confirm the round trip on a single node and on a right-only chain. (4) Am I mutating pointers? For every assignment `x.right = y`, ask what the old `x.right` was and who still references it — if the answer is 'nobody', you just leaked a subtree. (5) Morris specifically: can I articulate the two-visit protocol (thread on first touch, unthread and advance on second) before coding it? (6) Complexity story ready: parent-map BFS O(N)/O(N); reconstruction O(N)/O(N); serialization O(N)/O(N); Morris O(N) time O(1) space; count-complete O(log^2 N). Close by testing the empty tree, a single node, and a skewed chain — Part-II problems break on skew more often than anywhere else.

implementations.title: Nodes at Distance K and Burn a Binary Tree — parent map + graph BFS
implementations.code:
# =====================================================================
# Nodes at Distance K and Burn a Binary Tree, both from the same idea:
# record parents, then BFS the tree as an undirected graph.
# =====================================================================
from collections import deque

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def build_parent_map(root):
    # One BFS pass: parent[child] = its parent node; root maps to None.
    parent = {root: None}
    q = deque([root])
    while q:
        node = q.popleft()
        for child in (node.left, node.right):
            if child:
                parent[child] = node     # remember the upward edge
                q.append(child)
    return parent

def nodes_at_distance_k(root, target, k):
    # Ring-by-ring BFS from target; neighbors = left, right, parent.
    if root is None:
        return []
    parent = build_parent_map(root)
    seen = {target}                      # never revisit (stops bouncing)
    q = deque([target])
    dist = 0
    while q and dist < k:                # expand exactly k rings
        for _ in range(len(q)):
            node = q.popleft()
            for nb in (node.left, node.right, parent[node]):
                if nb and nb not in seen:
                    seen.add(nb)
                    q.append(nb)
        dist += 1
    return [n.val for n in q]            # the frontier after k rings

def time_to_burn(root, target):
    # Fire starts at target and crosses one edge per minute in all
    # three directions; answer = number of BFS expansions performed.
    parent = build_parent_map(root)
    seen = {target}
    q = deque([target])
    minutes = -1                         # the target itself is minute 0
    while q:
        for _ in range(len(q)):
            node = q.popleft()
            for nb in (node.left, node.right, parent[node]):
                if nb and nb not in seen:
                    seen.add(nb)
                    q.append(nb)
        minutes += 1                     # one ring processed = one minute
    return minutes

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Tree:      3
    #           / \
    #          5   1
    #         / \ / \
    #        6  2 0  8
    #          / \
    #         7   4
    n7, n4 = TreeNode(7), TreeNode(4)
    n2 = TreeNode(2, n7, n4)
    n5 = TreeNode(5, TreeNode(6), n2)
    n1 = TreeNode(1, TreeNode(0), TreeNode(8))
    r = TreeNode(3, n5, n1)
    print(sorted(nodes_at_distance_k(r, n5, 2)))   # [1, 4, 7]
    print(time_to_burn(r, n5))                     # 3 (0 and 8 burn last)

implementations.title: Tree codec: BFS serialize/deserialize + construct from pre+in and post+in
implementations.code:
# =====================================================================
# A complete tree codec: BFS serialization with '#' null markers, and
# reconstruction from preorder+inorder / postorder+inorder.
# =====================================================================
from collections import deque

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def serialize(root):
    # Level-order dump; '#' marks each missing child of a real node.
    if root is None:
        return ""
    parts, q = [], deque([root])
    while q:
        node = q.popleft()
        if node is None:
            parts.append("#")            # a hole: nothing to enqueue
        else:
            parts.append(str(node.val))
            q.append(node.left)          # enqueue even if None so the
            q.append(node.right)         # decoder sees the exact shape
    return ",".join(parts)               # single join keeps it O(N)

def deserialize(data):
    # Mirror image: a queue of parents consumes two tokens each.
    if not data:
        return None
    tokens = data.split(",")
    root = TreeNode(int(tokens[0]))
    q = deque([root])                    # parents awaiting children
    i = 1
    while q:
        parent = q.popleft()
        if tokens[i] != "#":             # left-child token
            parent.left = TreeNode(int(tokens[i]))
            q.append(parent.left)
        i += 1
        if tokens[i] != "#":             # right-child token
            parent.right = TreeNode(int(tokens[i]))
            q.append(parent.right)
        i += 1
    return root

def build_pre_in(preorder, inorder):
    # Next preorder element is the root; inorder index splits L | R.
    idx = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(inorder)}   # O(1) root lookups
    pre_i = 0                                     # pointer into preorder
    def rec(lo, hi):                              # subtree = inorder[lo..hi]
        nonlocal pre_i
        if lo > hi:
            return None                           # empty range: no node
        root_val = preorder[pre_i]
        pre_i += 1                                # consume the root
        node = TreeNode(root_val)
        m = idx[root_val]                         # split point in inorder
        node.left = rec(lo, m - 1)                # LEFT first (preorder!)
        node.right = rec(m + 1, hi)
        return node
    return rec(0, len(inorder) - 1)

def build_post_in(postorder, inorder):
    # Consume postorder from the END; build the RIGHT subtree first.
    idx = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(inorder)}
    post_i = len(postorder) - 1
    def rec(lo, hi):
        nonlocal post_i
        if lo > hi:
            return None
        root_val = postorder[post_i]
        post_i -= 1                               # consume from the back
        node = TreeNode(root_val)
        m = idx[root_val]
        node.right = rec(m + 1, hi)               # RIGHT before left here
        node.left = rec(lo, m - 1)
        return node
    return rec(0, len(inorder) - 1)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    t = build_pre_in([3, 9, 20, 15, 7], [9, 3, 15, 20, 7])
    s = serialize(t)
    print(s)                              # 3,9,20,#,#,15,7,#,#,#,#
    print(serialize(deserialize(s)) == s) # True: lossless round trip
    t2 = build_post_in([9, 15, 7, 20, 3], [9, 3, 15, 20, 7])
    print(serialize(t2) == s)             # True: same tree from post+in

implementations.title: Morris machines: O(1)-space inorder/preorder, in-place flatten, O(log^2 N) complete-tree count
implementations.code:
# =====================================================================
# Morris inorder and preorder (O(1) extra space), the Morris-style
# in-place flatten, and the O(log^2 N) complete-tree node count.
# =====================================================================
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def morris_inorder(root):
    out, cur = [], root
    while cur:
        if cur.left is None:
            out.append(cur.val)          # no left side: visit, go right
            cur = cur.right
        else:
            pred = cur.left              # inorder predecessor lives at the
            while pred.right and pred.right is not cur:
                pred = pred.right        # rightmost node of the left subtree
            if pred.right is None:
                pred.right = cur         # FIRST touch: lay the thread
                cur = cur.left           # then dive into the left subtree
            else:
                pred.right = None        # SECOND touch: heal the tree
                out.append(cur.val)      # left subtree done: visit cur
                cur = cur.right
    return out

def morris_preorder(root):
    out, cur = [], root
    while cur:
        if cur.left is None:
            out.append(cur.val)
            cur = cur.right
        else:
            pred = cur.left
            while pred.right and pred.right is not cur:
                pred = pred.right
            if pred.right is None:
                out.append(cur.val)      # preorder: visit BEFORE going left
                pred.right = cur
                cur = cur.left
            else:
                pred.right = None        # thread used up: clean and move on
                cur = cur.right
    return out

def flatten(root):
    # Rewire into a right-spine linked list in preorder, O(1) space:
    # splice the left subtree between cur and its old right subtree.
    cur = root
    while cur:
        if cur.left:
            pred = cur.left              # tail of the left subtree
            while pred.right:
                pred = pred.right
            pred.right = cur.right       # old right hangs off that tail
            cur.right = cur.left         # left subtree slides right
            cur.left = None              # left pointers must be cleared
        cur = cur.right                  # walk down the growing list
    return root

def count_complete(root):
    # If the left spine and right spine have equal height, the subtree
    # is PERFECT: 2^h - 1 nodes with zero traversal.
    def left_h(n):
        h = 0
        while n:                         # walk the left edge only
            h += 1
            n = n.left
        return h
    def right_h(n):
        h = 0
        while n:                         # walk the right edge only
            h += 1
            n = n.right
        return h
    if root is None:
        return 0
    lh, rh = left_h(root), right_h(root)
    if lh == rh:
        return (1 << lh) - 1             # perfect: 2^lh - 1, one shift
    # Completeness => one child is perfect, so only one branch recurses
    # deeper: O(log N) levels x O(log N) spine walks = O(log^2 N).
    return 1 + count_complete(root.left) + count_complete(root.right)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Tree:      1
    #           / \
    #          2   3
    #         / \
    #        4   5
    r = TreeNode(1, TreeNode(2, TreeNode(4), TreeNode(5)), TreeNode(3))
    print(morris_inorder(r))     # [4, 2, 5, 1, 3]
    print(morris_preorder(r))    # [1, 2, 4, 5, 3]
    print(count_complete(r))     # 5 (this tree is complete)
    flatten(r)
    out = []
    while r:                     # walk the flattened right-spine list
        out.append(r.val)
        r = r.right
    print(out)                   # [1, 2, 4, 5, 3] — preorder order

Binary Search Tree.summary:
A Binary Search Tree (BST) is a binary tree with one extra promise: at every node, every key in the left subtree is strictly smaller than the node's key, and every key in the right subtree is strictly larger. The promise is recursive — it holds at the root, at each child, at every grandchild, everywhere. That single rule turns a loose tree into a sorted, searchable structure. Standing at any node, one comparison ("is my target smaller or larger?") tells you which child to visit, and the entire other subtree can be thrown away. It is binary search on an array, rebuilt on linked nodes — but unlike a sorted array, a BST also supports insert and delete without shifting anything.

Interviews love BSTs because that one invariant spawns a dozen distinct problem families: guided descent (Search in BST, Ceil in BST, Lowest Common Ancestor in BST), sorted-order exploitation via inorder traversal (Kth Smallest, Two Sum in BST, Recover BST), constraint propagation with min/max windows (Validate BST, Construct BST from Preorder, Largest BST in Binary Tree), structural editing (Insert, Delete Node in BST), and space-controlled iteration (BST Iterator). They also test whether you give the honest complexity: every descent is O(H) where H is the height — O(log N) only when the tree is balanced, degrading to O(N) when keys arrive in sorted order and the tree collapses into a chain. Saying "O(H), and here is why H may be N" is exactly the nuance interviewers listen for.

The mental model: a stack of sorted decisions. Inorder traversal (left, node, right) of any BST prints the keys in ascending order — that fact alone solves a third of the sheet.

```
        8                inorder walk:
      /   \              1 3 4 6 7 8 10 13 14
     3     10            (always sorted!)
    / \      \
   1   6     14          search(7): 8 -> 3 -> 6 -> 7
      / \    /           three comparisons, each one
     4   7  13           discards half the remaining tree
```
preRequisites: Binary tree fundamentals: a TreeNode class with val/left/right, what a leaf and a subtree are, and the three DFS traversals — inorder especially, since inorder of a BST is sorted.
Recursion with return values: functions that return a computed value (or a rebuilt subtree root) up the call chain, not just print things.
Height vs node count: H = O(log2 N) for a balanced tree of N nodes, but H = N - 1 for a skewed chain — all BST costs are quoted in H.
The binary-search halving mindset from sorted arrays: one comparison eliminates half of the candidates.
Python None handling: `if node is None` guards, and using `float('-inf')` / `float('inf')` as open-interval sentinels.
Using a Python list as an explicit stack (`append` / `pop`) for iterative traversal, since recursion hits Python's ~1000-frame default limit on deep trees (`sys.setrecursionlimit`).
Tuple returns like `return (lo, hi, size)` for recursion that must report several facts at once (used by Largest BST in Binary Tree).
cheatSheet: BST invariant (strict): for every node, ALL left-subtree keys < node.val < ALL right-subtree keys — recursively, not just the two children.
search / insert / delete / floor / ceil / LCA / successor: O(H) time — H = O(log N) balanced, O(N) skewed; iterative versions use O(1) extra space.
Inorder traversal of a BST is strictly increasing — powers Kth Smallest, Validate (prev trick), Two Sum in BST, Recover BST.
Validate: pass an open window (low, high) down; require low < node.val < high; recurse left with (low, node.val), right with (node.val, high).
Delete: 0 children -> return None; 1 child -> return that child; 2 children -> copy inorder successor (min of right subtree), then delete it from the right.
Ceil: when node.val >= target, record candidate and go left; Floor: when node.val <= target, record candidate and go right.
LCA in BST: descend from root; the first node with min(p,q) <= node.val <= max(p,q) is the answer — no parent pointers, no paths.
BST Iterator: stack the left spine; next() pops and pushes pop.right's left spine — amortized O(1) per call, O(H) space.
Build BST from preorder in O(N): consume values with a shared index while they fit the inherited (low, high) window.
Largest BST in Binary Tree: postorder, each subtree reports (min, max, size); node is a BST root iff left.max < node.val < right.min.

sections.title: What & Why
sections.content:
A Binary Search Tree is a binary tree that keeps its keys ordered. The rule: at every node, all keys stored in its left subtree are strictly smaller than the node's key, and all keys in its right subtree are strictly larger. The rule applies recursively at every single node — that word "all" is what beginners miss, and it is the difference between a correct Validate BST and a wrong one.

Real-world analogy: the guessing game "think of a number between 1 and 100". Every question ("is it bigger than 50?") removes half of the possibilities. A BST bakes that game into a data structure: each node is a stored question, and the comparison result tells you which child holds the answer.

Where it shows up in real systems: C++ std::map / std::set and Java's TreeMap / TreeSet are self-balancing BSTs (red-black trees); the Linux kernel schedules processes and tracks virtual-memory regions with red-black trees; database indexes use B-trees and B+ trees, which are wide, disk-friendly generalizations of the same idea; interval trees and order-statistic trees are BSTs with extra bookkeeping.

Why interviews love it: one invariant produces many families — guided descent (Search in BST, Ceil in BST), sorted-order tricks (Kth Smallest Element in BST), constraint propagation (Validate BST), structural surgery (Delete Node in BST), and iterator design (BST Iterator). And it constantly checks whether you say O(H) instead of blindly claiming O(log N).

sections.title: Memory Model & Representation
sections.content:
A BST lives on the heap as scattered node objects connected by references — there is no contiguous block like a Python list. Each node is a tiny object with three fields: the key, a reference to the left child, and a reference to the right child. Leaves hold None in both child slots. The whole tree is reachable from a single `root` reference.

```
  root --> [ 8 ]
           /    \
     [ 3 ]        [ 10 ]
     /   \             \
 [ 1 ]  [ 6 ]         [ 14 ]
        /   \          /
    [ 4 ]  [ 7 ]   [ 13 ]

  One node object in memory:
  +------------------------+
  | val   : 8              |
  | left  : ref to node 3  |
  | right : ref to node 10 |
  +------------------------+
```

Because nodes are linked, every operation is a pointer walk from the root, so cost is measured in height H, not in N. The SHAPE of the tree — which depends entirely on insertion order — decides H:

```
Insert 8,3,10,1,6,14 (mixed)      Insert 1,3,6,8 (sorted!)
        8                             1
      /   \                            \
     3     10                           3
    / \      \                           \
   1   6     14                            6
                                            \
  N=6, H=3: O(log N) walks                   8
                                  N=4, H=4: a linked list
                                  in disguise -- O(N) walks
```

This is why interviewers ask "what if the input is sorted?" — a plain BST degenerates, and the fix in real libraries is self-balancing (AVL, red-black), which you should name-drop but are almost never asked to implement.

sections.title: Core Operations & Complexity
sections.content:
Every "descend from the root" operation costs one node visit per level, so its time is O(H). On a balanced tree H is about log2(N) (a million keys is only ~20 levels); on a skewed tree H = N. Traversals that must touch every node are O(N) no matter the shape.

```
Operation         | Balanced  | Skewed | Why (one clause)
------------------+-----------+--------+--------------------------------
search(x)         | O(log N)  | O(N)   | each compare discards a subtree
insert(x)         | O(log N)  | O(N)   | descend to the first empty slot
```
