```
delete(x)         | O(log N)  | O(N)   | descend + successor splice
min / max         | O(log N)  | O(N)   | walk leftmost / rightmost
floor / ceil      | O(log N)  | O(N)   | descend, remember best candidate
successor(x)      | O(log N)  | O(N)   | min(right) or last left-turn
LCA(p, q)         | O(log N)  | O(N)   | descend to the split point
inorder traversal | O(N)      | O(N)   | must visit every node
kth smallest      | O(H + k)  | O(N)   | inorder, stopped after k pops
validate          | O(N)      | O(N)   | every node must be checked
```

Space: iterative descent uses O(1) extra space; anything recursive (or using an explicit stack, like the BST Iterator) holds one path of the tree, which is O(H). A full inorder that materializes all values into a list costs O(N) — the BST Iterator question exists precisely to make you avoid that.

sections.title: How Python Does It
sections.content:
Python's standard library has no BST. This surprises people coming from C++ (std::map) or Java (TreeMap). What Python offers instead, and why each falls short of a real BST:

`dict` and `set` are hash tables — O(1) average lookup but zero ordering, so no floor/ceil/kth/range queries. `bisect` gives O(log N) binary search over a sorted list, but keeping the list sorted costs O(N) per insert because every later element must shift. `heapq` only ever exposes the minimum — you cannot search it. The third-party `sortedcontainers.SortedList` genuinely provides fast ordered operations, but it is a pip install, not stdlib — in an interview you name-drop it, then build the tree by hand.

So for every sheet question here (Search in BST, Insert Node in BST, Delete Node in BST, BST Iterator...) you write your own TreeNode class. Two Python-specific facts matter: (1) Python has no pointers, only references — rebinding `node = node.left` moves YOUR variable, it never modifies the tree; to change the tree you must assign into an attribute, e.g. `parent.left = new_child`. (2) CPython's default recursion limit is about 1000 frames, and a skewed BST of 100k nodes will blow through it — either write iterative loops or raise the limit.
sections.code:
# Python has NO built-in BST. You always build the node class yourself.
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val):
        self.val = val      # the key stored at this node
        self.left = None    # reference to left child (smaller keys)
        self.right = None   # reference to right child (larger keys)

# What Python DOES give you, and why none of it is a BST:
import bisect                      # binary search over a SORTED LIST
a = [1, 3, 6, 8, 10]
i = bisect.bisect_left(a, 6)       # O(log N) search -- that part is fine
a.insert(i, 5)                     # O(N)! every later element shifts
# dict / set : O(1) average lookup but NO order -> no floor/ceil/kth
# heapq      : only exposes the MIN; cannot search arbitrary keys
# sortedcontainers.SortedList : real ordered ops, but third-party pip
#              package -- name-drop it, then code the BST by hand.

# References, not pointers: rebinding a local moves only YOUR variable.
root = TreeNode(8)
node = root
node = node.left                   # tree untouched -- only `node` moved
root.left = TreeNode(3)            # THIS mutates the tree

import sys
sys.setrecursionlimit(200_000)     # skewed BSTs can be 1e5 levels deep

sections.title: Pattern: Guided Descent (Prune Half Each Step)
sections.content:
Recognize it when: the problem asks about ONE key or one best-candidate key — find it, insert it, find the smallest value >= x, find where two values' paths split. You never need to look at both children; the invariant does the navigation.

Invariant: at every step, "if the answer exists, it is inside the subtree I am standing in." Comparing the target with node.val proves which child can contain the answer, so the other child (and its entire subtree) is discarded. For best-candidate questions (Ceil in BST, floor, Inorder Successor in BST) there is one extra trick: the current node might itself be the answer, so RECORD it as a candidate before moving toward a potentially better one.

Sheet questions using this pattern: Search in BST (pure descent), Ceil in BST (descent + candidate), Insert Node in BST (descend to the first None slot and attach), Lowest Common Ancestor in BST (descend until node.val sits between p and q — the first such node is the split point and therefore the LCA), and Inorder Successor in BST (candidate descent: go left when node.val > target, right otherwise).

Complexity: O(H) time, O(1) space when written iteratively — always say both, and note H can be N. The LCA version is a favorite because the general binary-tree LCA needs O(N); the BST invariant collapses it to a single walk.

sections.title: Pattern: Inorder Is Sorted
sections.content:
Recognize it when: the problem mentions rank or order — "kth smallest", "pairs summing to a target", "two nodes were swapped", "is this a valid BST" — anything that would be trivial on a sorted array. The BST's inorder traversal (left, node, right) IS that sorted array; you just refuse to materialize it.

Invariant: inorder visits values in strictly increasing order. So keep a `prev` reference while traversing: comparing prev.val with the current value is comparing adjacent elements of the sorted sequence, with zero extra memory beyond the traversal itself.

Sheet questions using this pattern: Kth Smallest Element in BST (count pops during an iterative inorder, stop at k — O(H + k), no full list), Validate BST (the prev variant: valid iff every inorder step strictly increases), Recover BST (exactly two nodes were swapped, so the inorder sequence shows one or two positions where prev.val > curr.val — remember the first offender's prev and the last offender's curr, then swap their values), Two Sum in BST (naive version: dump inorder into a sorted list, then two-pointer — the O(H)-space upgrade lives in the iterator pattern), and Inorder Successor in BST (naive version: the node visited right after the target).

Complexity: full inorder is O(N) time; the early-stop kth version is O(H + k). A follow-up interviewers ask after Kth Smallest: "what if the BST is modified often?" — answer: augment each node with a subtree-size counter, making kth a pure O(H) descent.
sections.code:
def kth_smallest(root, k):
    # Inorder = ascending, so the k-th node popped is the answer.
    stack, node = [], root
    while stack or node:
        while node:                  # dive down the left spine
            stack.append(node)
            node = node.left
        node = stack.pop()           # next-smallest value in the BST
        k -= 1                       # consumed one value of the order
        if k == 0:
            return node.val          # early stop: O(H + k) total
        node = node.right            # then its right subtree


def recover_bst(root):
    # Exactly two nodes got swapped -> the inorder sequence has one or
    # two "dips" where prev.val > curr.val.
    #   adjacent swap : ONE dip  -> offenders are prev and curr of it
    #   distant swap  : TWO dips -> first dip's prev, second dip's curr
    first = second = prev = None

    def inorder(node):
        nonlocal first, second, prev
        if not node:
            return
        inorder(node.left)                 # smaller values first
        if prev and prev.val > node.val:   # sorted order violated here
            if first is None:
                first = prev               # first offender (the big one)
            second = node                  # keep updating: last offender
        prev = node                        # slide the adjacency window
        inorder(node.right)                # then larger values

    inorder(root)
    first.val, second.val = second.val, first.val   # O(1) repair

sections.title: Pattern: Bounds Propagation (Min-Max Windows)
sections.content:
Recognize it when: a node's legality depends on ANCESTORS, not just its children — "is this whole tree a valid BST", "rebuild a BST from its preorder", "find the largest BST hiding inside a plain binary tree". The classic beginner failure is checking only node vs its two children; the tree `[10, 5, 15]` with 15's left child 6 passes that local check but is invalid, because 6 sits in 10's right subtree while being smaller than 10.

Invariant: every node must lie inside an open interval (low, high) inherited from its ancestors. The root gets (-inf, +inf). Descending left shrinks the upper bound to node.val; descending right raises the lower bound to node.val. A node is legal iff low < node.val < high. This encodes "ALL left-subtree keys are smaller" exactly.

Sheet questions using this pattern: Validate BST (the canonical form — recurse with the window, O(N)), Construct BST from Preorder Traversal (the O(N) trick: preorder order is root-first, so keep one shared index and let each recursive call consume the next value only if it fits its inherited window; values that do not fit belong to some ancestor's other side), and Largest BST in Binary Tree (the bottom-up mirror: instead of pushing bounds down, each subtree reports (min, max, size) up, and a node roots a BST iff left's max < node.val < right's min — track the best size seen, O(N) one pass).

Complexity: all three are O(N) time, O(H) recursion space. The preorder build without this trick — inserting each value one by one — is O(N*H), which the interviewer will ask you to beat.

sections.title: Pattern: Stack-Based Controlled Iteration
sections.content:
Recognize it when: the problem says "design an iterator", demands O(H) memory instead of O(N), or needs a pause-and-resume walk — including running TWO walks at once, like a two-pointer scan over the tree's sorted order.

Invariant: keep a stack holding the current LEFT SPINE of the not-yet-consumed part of the tree. The top of the stack is always the next-smallest unvisited node. To consume it: pop it, then push the left spine of its right child. Every node is pushed exactly once and popped exactly once across the whole iteration, so next() is amortized O(1), and the stack never holds more than one root-to-node path: O(H) space.

Sheet questions using this pattern: BST Iterator (this pattern verbatim), Kth Smallest Element in BST (an iterator you stop after k calls), and Two Sum in BST done properly — one ascending iterator (left spines) plus one descending iterator (right spines, the mirror image) act as the two ends of the classic sorted-array two-pointer scan: sum too small, advance the ascending side; too big, advance the descending side. That achieves O(N) time with O(H) space, beating the O(N)-space "dump inorder to a list" approach.

This pattern is also the honest answer to "iterate a tree without recursion": the explicit stack replaces the call stack you no longer have, which matters in Python where deep recursion raises RecursionError.
sections.code:
class BSTIterator:
    # Stack = the CURRENT LEFT SPINE: top of stack is the next smallest.
    # next()/has_next(): amortized O(1) -- each node pushed & popped once.
    # Space: O(H), never the whole tree.
    def __init__(self, root):
        self.stack = []
        self._push_left(root)          # prime with the root's spine

    def _push_left(self, node):
        while node:
            self.stack.append(node)    # remember everything passed
            node = node.left           # keep sliding down-left

    def has_next(self):
        return len(self.stack) > 0     # empty spine = walk finished

    def next(self):
        node = self.stack.pop()        # next smallest, by construction
        self._push_left(node.right)    # its successors live down-right
        return node.val


def two_sum_bst(root, k):
    # Ascending iterator (left spines) + descending mirror (right
    # spines) = sorted-array two-pointer in O(H) space, O(N) time.
    fwd, bwd = [], []                  # the two spine stacks

    def push_left(n):                  # feed the ascending side
        while n:
            fwd.append(n)
            n = n.left

    def push_right(n):                 # feed the descending side
        while n:
            bwd.append(n)
            n = n.right

    push_left(root)
    push_right(root)
    while fwd and bwd and fwd[-1] is not bwd[-1]:   # not crossed yet
        s = fwd[-1].val + bwd[-1].val
        if s == k:
            return True                # found a valid pair
        if s < k:                      # sum too small: advance ascending
            push_left(fwd.pop().right)
        else:                          # sum too big: advance descending
            push_right(bwd.pop().left)
    return False

sections.title: Pattern: Structural Surgery (Delete & Successor)
sections.content:
Recognize it when: the tree's SHAPE must change while the invariant survives — Delete Node in BST is the boss fight of this topic, and Insert Node in BST is its gentle warm-up (descend to the first empty slot, attach, done — insertion never restructures anything).

Deletion has exactly three cases, decided by how many children the doomed node has. Zero children: return None to the parent — the leaf vanishes. One child: return that child — the child is spliced up into the node's place, and the invariant holds because the whole subtree was already on the correct side. Two children: you cannot splice two subtrees into one slot, so instead REPLACE the node's value with its inorder successor — the minimum of the right subtree (leftmost node there). That value is larger than everything in the left subtree and smaller than everything else in the right subtree, so the invariant is restored. Then recursively delete that successor from the right subtree — and that second delete is guaranteed to hit case zero-or-one, because a leftmost node has no left child. (Using the inorder predecessor, max of left, is equally valid.)

The Python-critical detail: the recursion must RETURN the new subtree root and the parent must re-link it — `node.left = self._delete(node.left, val)`. Beginners mutate a local variable and wonder why the tree never changed; Python references make the re-link pattern mandatory.

Sheet questions using this pattern: Delete Node in BST, Insert Node in BST, and Inorder Successor in BST (the successor hunt inside delete IS that question: with a right subtree, successor = min of it; without one, it is the last node where you turned left during descent). All O(H) time.

sections.title: Pitfalls & Common Mistakes
sections.content:
1) Validating parent-child only. Checking `node.left.val < node.val < node.right.val` accepts invalid trees like 10 -> right 15 -> left 6 (6 is under 10's right side but smaller than 10). Fix: propagate (low, high) windows, or check strict increase against `prev` during inorder.

2) Forgetting the re-link. Writing `delete(node.left, key)` and dropping the return value leaves the tree untouched — Python rebinding never mutates the parent. Fix: always `node.left = delete(node.left, key)`.

3) Claiming O(log N) unconditionally. Every descent is O(H); a sorted insertion order makes H = N. Fix: say "O(H), log N if balanced", and mention self-balancing trees as the production fix.

4) Duplicates ambiguity. The strict invariant (<, >) has no place for equal keys; "allow duplicates on the left/right" silently breaks Validate BST and Kth Smallest counting. Fix: ask the interviewer, or store a count field per node.

5) RecursionError on deep trees. A skewed BST with 1e5 nodes exceeds CPython's ~1000-frame default. Fix: iterative loops with an explicit stack, or `sys.setrecursionlimit` (and say why).

6) O(N)-space iterator. Dumping the full inorder into a list "implements" BST Iterator but fails the follow-up. Fix: the left-spine stack — O(H) space, amortized O(1) next().

7) Recover BST edge case. When the swapped nodes are ADJACENT in inorder there is only ONE dip, and code that expects two dips crashes with `second = None`. Fix: set `second` at the FIRST dip too, then let a second dip overwrite it.

8) Successor confusion in delete. Taking min of the LEFT subtree (that is the predecessor's side) corrupts the ordering. Fix: successor = leftmost of the RIGHT subtree; predecessor = rightmost of the LEFT — either works, but do not mix them.

sections.title: Interview Recognition Checklist
sections.content:
Cues that scream BST: the phrase "binary search tree" itself; "sorted order" / "kth smallest / largest" on a tree; "closest value" / "floor" / "ceil"; "validate"; "two nodes were swapped"; "iterator with O(h) memory"; "count / report keys in range [L, R]"; a general-tree question (LCA) where the tree is stated to be a BST — the invariant always buys a faster or simpler solution than the generic tree approach.

30-second pre-coding checklist:
- Which pattern? One key -> guided descent. Rank/pairs/sortedness -> inorder. Ancestor-dependent legality -> bounds window. Pause/resume or O(H) memory -> spine stack. Shape change -> delete surgery.
- Duplicates: allowed? Strict < and >, or counts per node? Say your assumption out loud.
- Complexity: quote O(H), then immediately add "log N balanced, N skewed". If the problem promises a balanced tree, use it.
- Recursive or iterative? Iterative for descents (O(1) space) and for anything deep; recursion is fine for O(N) traversals if you mention the depth limit.
- Sentinels: are `float('-inf')` / `float('inf')` safe bounds, or can node values themselves be infinite/None? Prefer None-as-unbounded if values are arbitrary.
- Return contract: does each recursive call return a value, a rebuilt subtree root (delete/build), or a tuple of facts (Largest BST)? Write it as a comment before coding.

implementations.title: Complete BST — insert, search, min/max, floor/ceil, successor, delete, inorder
BSTIterator + Reverse Iterator + O(H)-space Two Sum
Largest BST in Binary Tree — one-pass postorder
implementations.code:
import math


class TreeNode:
    # Plain binary-tree node (the input is NOT necessarily a BST).
    def __init__(self, val, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


def largest_bst_subtree(root):
    # 'Largest BST in Binary Tree' sheet question.
    # POSTORDER: each subtree reports (lo, hi, size) if it is a valid
    # BST; a poison triple otherwise. The parent then checks the
    # bottom-up version of the bounds rule: left.hi < node.val < right.lo.
    # O(N) time (each node visited once), O(H) recursion space.
    best = 0                          # size of the largest BST found

    def solve(node):
        # Returns (lo, hi, size) where lo/hi are the min/max keys of
        # this subtree WHEN it is a BST. Non-BST returns size = -1 with
        # bounds that force every ancestor's check to fail too.
        nonlocal best
        if node is None:
            # Empty subtree: a BST of size 0. lo=+inf / hi=-inf are the
            # identity values -- they can never violate a comparison.
            return (math.inf, -math.inf, 0)
        l_lo, l_hi, l_sz = solve(node.left)     # left child's report
        r_lo, r_hi, r_sz = solve(node.right)    # right child's report
        if l_sz != -1 and r_sz != -1 and l_hi < node.val < r_lo:
            size = l_sz + r_sz + 1              # subtree is a BST here
            best = max(best, size)              # record the champion
            # this subtree's key range: leftmost .. rightmost
            return (min(l_lo, node.val), max(r_hi, node.val), size)
        return (-math.inf, math.inf, -1)        # poison: not a BST

    solve(root)
    return best


if __name__ == "__main__":
    #      10
    #     /  \        the RIGHT subtree rooted at 15 is NOT a BST
    #    5    15       (its left child 6 < 15 is fine, but the whole
    #   / \     \      tree fails because 6 < 10 sits on 10's right)
    #  1   8    7
    tree = TreeNode(10,
                    TreeNode(5, TreeNode(1), TreeNode(8)),
                    TreeNode(15, None, TreeNode(7)))
    # Largest valid BST inside it is {1, 5, 8} -> size 3
    assert largest_bst_subtree(tree) == 3
    # A tree that is entirely a BST reports its full size
    good = TreeNode(2, TreeNode(1), TreeNode(3))
    assert largest_bst_subtree(good) == 3
    print("LargestBST OK")

Tries.summary:
A Trie (from reTRIEval, usually pronounced "try") is a tree that stores strings by their characters: every edge is one character, and every path starting at the root spells a prefix. Words that share a prefix share the beginning of their path — "car", "card" and "cat" all ride the same c-a rails before splitting. A boolean end-of-word flag on a node records "a complete word stops here", which is what separates storing "card" from merely passing through "car". The result: inserting or looking up a word of length L costs O(L) — completely independent of how many words the trie holds, which is exactly what a hash set of strings cannot promise for prefix queries.

Interviews use tries in two costumes. The first is the literal one — Implement Trie asks for insert, search, and startsWith, and is really a test of whether you keep the end-flag and the prefix-path ideas separate. The second is sneakier and more powerful: the binary trie, where the "characters" are the bits of a number from most-significant to least-significant. Storing numbers this way turns "find the pair with maximum XOR" (Maximum XOR of Two Numbers) into a greedy 32-step descent — at each bit you try to walk toward the OPPOSITE bit, because winning bit i is worth more than winning all lower bits combined. Add offline sorting and you solve Maximum XOR Queries, where each query restricts partners to values below a threshold.

```
insert: cat, car, card          (root)
                                 +-- c
  shared prefix "ca"             |    +-- a
  stored ONCE                    |         +-- t*     <- "cat"
                                 |         +-- r*     <- "car"
  * = end-of-word flag           |              +-- d*  <- "card"
                                 +-- d
                                      +-- o
                                           +-- g*     <- "dog"
```
preRequisites: Python dicts as the go-to node map: `d.get(k)`, `k in d`, and `d.setdefault(k, default)` which fetches-or-creates in one call.
Classes and object references: trie nodes are tiny objects linked by references, and `__slots__` keeps millions of them small.
String basics: iterating characters with `for ch in word`, and `ord(ch) - ord('a')` to map lowercase letters to 0..25 array indices.
Bit manipulation: extracting bit i with `(x >> i) & 1`, setting it with `ans |= 1 << i`, and why bit i outweighs all bits below it (2^i > 2^(i-1) + ... + 1).
XOR properties: x ^ x = 0, x ^ 0 = x, and XOR of two numbers has a 1 exactly where their bits DIFFER — maximizing XOR means chasing opposite bits.
Offline query processing: sorting queries, answering them out of order, then writing each answer back to its original index.
cheatSheet: insert(word) / search(word) / startsWith(prefix): all O(L), L = string length — independent of the number N of stored words.
Node = children map (dict, or 26-slot array for lowercase) + end flag; the root represents the empty prefix "".
search = walk the path AND check the end flag; startsWith = walk the path only — forgetting the flag is the classic bug.
Space: O(total stored characters) nodes worst case; each array node burns 26 slots, each dict node stores only the children it has.
Counting trie: keep pass_count (words through this node) and end_count (words ending here) — gives countWordsStartingWith / countWordsEqualTo / erase, all O(L).
Binary trie: insert bits MSB-first (bit 31 down to 0); a number becomes a 32-step path of 0/1 children.
Max XOR with x: at each bit prefer the child (1 - bit); when it exists, ans |= 1 << i — greedy is safe because bit i beats all lower bits combined.
Maximum XOR of a pair over the array: insert each number then query it, keep the best — O(N * 32).
Maximum XOR Queries with threshold m: sort nums and queries by m, insert nums <= m before answering; empty trie -> answer -1. O((N + Q) * 32) after sorting.

sections.title: What & Why
sections.content:
A trie stores a SET of strings as a tree of characters. The root is the empty string. Each child edge appends one character, so the node you reach by walking c-a-r represents the prefix "car". A flag on that node says whether "car" is a complete stored word or just a corridor on the way to "card". Because words that share a prefix share a path, the trie physically deduplicates common beginnings.

Real-world analogy: a contact list on an old T9 phone, or any autocomplete box. As you type "ca", the system is standing on the "ca" node, and everything below that node is exactly the set of completions — no scanning of the full dictionary required.

Where tries run in real systems: search-engine and IDE autocomplete; spell-checkers and word-game solvers; IP routers, whose longest-prefix-match over binary address bits is literally a binary trie walk; compression (the LZ78 family builds a trie of seen phrases); and bioinformatics suffix trees, which are compressed tries over DNA strings.

Why interviews care: the direct question (Implement Trie) checks clean data-structure design — the path/flag separation, O(L) reasoning, dict-vs-array trade-offs. The indirect questions are the interesting ones: Maximum XOR of Two Numbers and Maximum XOR Queries look like math puzzles, but become mechanical once you store numbers as 32-bit paths and walk greedily toward opposite bits. Recognizing "this is secretly a trie problem" is the skill being tested.

sections.title: Memory Model & Representation
sections.content:
A trie is a web of small node objects on the heap. Each node owns (1) a map from character to child node and (2) an end-of-word marker. The words themselves are never stored — a word IS a root-to-flag path, one character per hop.

```
Words stored: cat, car, card, dog

(root)
 +-- c
 |    +-- a
 |         +-- t*            <- "cat" ends here
 |         +-- r*            <- "car" ends here (also a corridor!)
 |              +-- d*       <- "card" ends here
 +-- d
      +-- o
           +-- g*            <- "dog" ends here

 * = end flag True.  8 nodes store 4 words / 13 characters,
 because "ca" and its path are shared.
```

The children map has two standard shapes, and choosing is a real interview talking point:

```
dict flavour                      array flavour (lowercase a-z)
+----------------------+          +---------------------------+
| children: {          |          | children: [None] * 26     |
|   'c': <node>,       |          |   [2] ('c') -> <node>     |
|   'd': <node> }      |          |   [3] ('d') -> <node>     |
| end: False           |          | end: False                |
+----------------------+          +---------------------------+
 stores only real edges            26 slots ALWAYS allocated
 any alphabet (unicode)            fastest constant, fixed a-z
```

Space is the trie's weak spot: worst case (no shared prefixes) it allocates one node per stored character, and every array-flavour node burns 26 pointers regardless of use. A binary trie for 32-bit numbers is the extreme fixed-alphabet case — alphabet {0, 1}, depth exactly 32, so N numbers cost at most 32*N nodes.

sections.title: Core Operations & Complexity
sections.content:
Every trie operation is a walk from the root, one hop per character, doing O(1) work per hop (a dict lookup or an array index). That gives the trie its headline property: cost scales with the LENGTH of the string in hand, never with the NUMBER of stored words. A hash set can check exact membership in O(L) too (hashing reads every character), but it cannot answer prefix questions without scanning every key — the trie answers them by just stopping mid-path.

```
Operation                  | Time        | Why (one clause)
---------------------------+-------------+--------------------------------
insert(word)               | O(L)        | one create-or-walk per char
search(word)               | O(L)        | walk path, then check end flag
startsWith(prefix)         | O(L)        | walk path, flag irrelevant
countWordsEqualTo(w)       | O(L)        | read end_count at final node
countWordsStartingWith(p)  | O(L)        | read pass_count at final node
erase(word)                | O(L)        | decrement counters along path
build from N words         | O(sum L_i)  | each character processed once
list completions of prefix | O(subtree)  | DFS below the prefix node
space                      | O(total chars * alphabet-slot cost)
```

Two footnotes worth saying aloud in an interview: dict-node hops cost an average-O(1) hash lookup with real constant-factor overhead, while 26-array hops are a raw index — faster, but only legal when the alphabet is fixed. And enumeration (autocomplete listing) is the one operation that is NOT O(L): after the O(L) walk you still pay for the size of the answer subtree.

sections.title: How Python Does It
sections.content:
The stdlib has no trie, so you build one — and Python gives you unusually pleasant raw material. The idiomatic lightweight trie is a NESTED DICT: each node is a plain `{}` mapping characters to child dicts, plus a sentinel key (like '$') marking end-of-word. `dict.setdefault(ch, {})` walks to a child, creating it if missing, in one call — that single method is the whole insert loop. This version needs no classes at all and is perfect for quick scripting.

For interview code, an explicit `TrieNode` class reads better and extends naturally to counters (for the counting/erase variant) and to the 26-slot array flavour. Use `__slots__` on node classes: it removes the per-object `__dict__`, cutting memory by roughly half — worth mentioning because tries allocate huge numbers of tiny objects, and memory is the trie's known weakness.

Also know the famous party trick: `Trie = lambda: defaultdict(Trie)` — a defaultdict whose missing-key factory builds another one of itself, giving an infinitely self-nesting trie in one line. It is memorable and worth knowing, but in an interview prefer the explicit class: the one-liner auto-creates paths even on READS, which silently mutates the trie during a lookup — a genuine correctness gotcha.

There is no bit-trie helper in the stdlib either; for the XOR problems you build nodes with a 2-slot child list. Note that Python ints are arbitrary precision, so YOU must fix the bit width (e.g. 32) from the problem's value range — there is no automatic 32-bit ceiling like in C++ or Java.
sections.code:
# Python has no built-in trie -- dicts make a minimal one in ~15 lines.
trie = {}                                # the root: empty prefix
END = '$'                                # sentinel key: "a word ends here"

def insert(word):
    node = trie
    for ch in word:
        node = node.setdefault(ch, {})   # walk to child, creating if absent
    node[END] = True                     # mark the complete word

def search(word):
    node = trie
    for ch in word:
        if ch not in node:
            return False                 # path breaks -> word absent
        node = node[ch]
    return END in node                   # path exists AND is a full word

def starts_with(prefix):
    node = trie
    for ch in prefix:
        if ch not in node:
            return False                 # no stored word has this prefix
        node = node[ch]
    return True                          # reaching the node is enough

insert("car")
insert("card")
assert search("car") and not search("ca")     # "ca" is only a corridor
assert starts_with("ca")                      # ...but a valid prefix

# Party trick: an infinitely self-nesting trie in one line.
from collections import defaultdict
Trie = lambda: defaultdict(Trie)         # missing key -> new sub-trie
root = Trie()
# Caution: root['x'] CREATES 'x' even when you only meant to look --
# reads mutate the structure, so prefer an explicit class in interviews.

sections.title: Pattern: Prefix Trie with End Markers
sections.content:
Recognize it when: the problem manages a DICTIONARY of words and asks prefix-flavoured questions — "does any word start with...", autocomplete, "count words equal to / starting with", spell-check style lookups, or simply "design this data structure". The sheet question Implement Trie is this pattern verbatim, and it is the foundation the two XOR questions build on.

Invariant: the node reached by walking the characters of a string s IS the prefix s; the `end` flag records whether s is additionally a complete stored word. Every operation is the same skeleton — walk the path one character at a time — differing only in what happens at the end: insert creates missing children and sets the flag; search demands the walk succeed AND the flag be set; startsWith only demands the walk succeed. Writing one private `_walk` helper and reusing it for both queries is a clean-code signal interviewers notice.

The standard extension (Striver's "Implement Trie II") replaces the boolean with two counters: `pass_count` (how many stored words pass through this node) incremented on every node of an insert path, and `end_count` (how many words end exactly here). Those turn countWordsStartingWith and countWordsEqualTo into O(L) reads, and make erase a clean O(L) decrement walk — no node restructuring needed, because a node with pass_count 0 is treated as absent.

Complexity: every operation O(L); building from N words totals O(sum of lengths). Space is the trade-off to mention: worst case one node per character stored.

sections.title: Pattern: Binary Trie — Greedy Opposite-Bit Descent
sections.content:
Recognize it when: the problem says "maximum XOR" over pairs or against a query value — Maximum XOR of Two Numbers is the canonical sheet question. Brute force compares all pairs in O(N^2); the binary trie drops it to O(N * 32) by making "find the best partner for x" a 32-step walk.

Setup: treat each number as a 32-character string of bits, MOST significant bit first, and insert it into a trie whose alphabet is {0, 1}. Every number becomes a fixed-depth path; N numbers cost at most 32*N nodes.

Invariant (why greedy is safe): walk the trie level by level from bit 31 down. At bit i, the walk so far has committed to some prefix shared by a set of stored numbers. XOR puts a 1 at position i exactly when the partner's bit DIFFERS from x's bit, and 2^i is strictly greater than the sum of ALL lower powers (2^(i-1) + ... + 1). So if a child with the opposite bit exists, taking it is optimal no matter what happens below — no lower bits can compensate for giving up bit i. If the opposite child does not exist, you are forced to follow the same bit and that XOR bit is 0. This is a rare greedy whose proof is one inequality; say it out loud.

MSB-first order is load-bearing: it makes the greedy decide the most valuable bit first. Inserting LSB-first breaks the argument entirely. For Maximum XOR of Two Numbers, insert each number THEN query it against the trie built so far (insert-before-query also conveniently avoids querying an empty trie), keeping the running best. The same structure with counts also answers "count pairs with XOR less than k"-style variants — same skeleton, different per-level bookkeeping.
sections.code:
class BitNode:
    __slots__ = ("child",)             # child[0] / child[1]
    def __init__(self):
        self.child = [None, None]      # the two bit branches


BITS = 32                              # fixed width: covers 0 <= x < 2^32


def bt_insert(root, num):
    # Store num as a path of bits, MSB first (bit 31 down to bit 0),
    # so the greedy query decides the most valuable bit first.
    node = root
    for i in range(BITS - 1, -1, -1):
        b = (num >> i) & 1             # bit i of num
        if node.child[b] is None:
            node.child[b] = BitNode()  # extend the path
        node = node.child[b]


def bt_max_xor(root, num):
    # Best partner for num: at each level try the OPPOSITE bit.
    # Opposite bit -> XOR bit = 1 -> gain 2^i, which beats ALL lower
    # bits combined (2^i > 2^(i-1) + ... + 1) -> greedy is safe.
    node, ans = root, 0
    for i in range(BITS - 1, -1, -1):
        b = (num >> i) & 1
        if node.child[1 - b] is not None:   # opposite branch exists
            ans |= 1 << i              # scored a 1 at position i
            node = node.child[1 - b]
        else:
            node = node.child[b]       # forced: XOR bit stays 0
    return ans


def find_maximum_xor(nums):
    # Sheet question: 'Maximum XOR of Two Numbers'. O(N * 32).
    root = BitNode()
    best = 0
    for x in nums:
        bt_insert(root, x)             # insert BEFORE query: trie never
        best = max(best, bt_max_xor(root, x))   # empty (x^x=0 harmless)
    return best

sections.title: Pattern: Offline Queries on a Growing Trie
sections.content:
Recognize it when: each query carries a CONSTRAINT limiting which stored values it may use — Maximum XOR Queries is the sheet question: each query (x, m) asks for the maximum of x XOR v over array values v <= m, or -1 if no value qualifies. Answering naively rebuilds a filtered trie per query: O(Q * N). The offline trick shares one growing trie across all queries.

The idea: nothing forces you to answer queries in the order given. Sort the array ascending. Sort the QUERIES by their threshold m (keeping each query's original index — sort indices, or tuples carrying the index). Now sweep: for each query in increasing-m order, first insert every not-yet-inserted array value <= m into the binary trie, then answer with the standard opposite-bit walk. Because thresholds only grow, values inserted for an earlier query remain valid for every later one — the trie only ever gains elements, and a single pointer over the sorted array inserts each value exactly once across ALL queries.

Invariant: when query (x, m) is answered, the trie contains EXACTLY the values <= m — never more, never less. The two sorts make this a two-pointer merge. Guard the edge case: if the pointer is still at 0, no value qualifies and the answer is -1 (query the flag, not the trie).

Complexity: O(N log N + Q log Q) sorting + O((N + Q) * 32) trie work — each value inserted once, each query one walk. Answers are written to ans[original_index], so the output order is untouched. This offline pattern (sort queries by constraint, sweep a growing structure) generalizes far beyond tries — flag it whenever queries have monotone thresholds and the structure only needs insertions.
sections.code:
def maximize_xor(nums, queries):
    # Sheet question: 'Maximum XOR Queries'.
    # query (x, m) -> max(x ^ v) over stored v <= m, else -1.
    # OFFLINE: sort nums; process queries in increasing-m order while
    # a single pointer inserts newly-eligible nums. Each num inserted
    # exactly once across ALL queries.
    nums = sorted(nums)                      # ascending values
    order = sorted(range(len(queries)),      # query ids...
                   key=lambda j: queries[j][1])   # ...sorted by threshold m
    root = BitNode()                         # one shared, growing trie
    ans = [-1] * len(queries)                # default: nothing qualifies
    i = 0                                    # pointer into sorted nums

    for j in order:                          # increasing-m sweep
        x, m = queries[j]
        while i < len(nums) and nums[i] <= m:
            bt_insert(root, nums[i])         # admit newly-eligible value
            i += 1
        if i > 0:                            # trie non-empty for this m
            ans[j] = bt_max_xor(root, x)     # standard greedy walk
        # write-back by ORIGINAL index keeps the output order intact
    return ans

# Reuses BitNode / bt_insert / bt_max_xor from the binary-trie pattern.
# Example: nums = [0,1,2,3,4], queries = [(3,1), (1,3), (5,6)]
#   sorted by m -> (3,1): insert 0,1      -> best 3 ^ 0|1 -> 3
#                  (1,3): insert 2,3      -> best 1 ^ 2   -> 3
#                  (5,6): insert 4        -> best 5 ^ 2   -> 7
#   answers restored to input order: [3, 3, 7]

sections.title: Pitfalls & Common Mistakes
sections.content:
1) search vs startsWith confusion. Returning True just because the path exists makes search("ca") succeed after inserting "car". Fix: search requires the END flag on the final node; startsWith does not. Keep the two ideas physically separate (flag vs path).

2) Shared mutable default. Writing `class TrieNode: children = {}` at CLASS level makes every node share ONE dict — the trie silently collapses into a single node. Fix: create `self.children = {}` inside `__init__`.

3) Reads that mutate. With `defaultdict`-based tries (and careless `setdefault` in lookups), checking a missing path CREATES it. Fix: use `.get(ch)` for reads; reserve creation for insert.

4) Naive deletion breaking shared prefixes. Physically removing the "car" nodes destroys "card". Fix: either counters (decrement pass/end counts; a pass_count of 0 means absent) or bottom-up pruning that only unlinks nodes with no children AND no end flag.

5) LSB-first binary trie. Inserting bits from bit 0 upward makes the greedy walk optimize the LEAST valuable bit first — answers are simply wrong. Fix: always MSB-first, bit 31 (or width-1) down to 0.

6) Wrong bit width. Using 20 bits when values reach 10^9 (needs 30) truncates numbers; Python's arbitrary-precision ints will not stop you. Fix: derive width from the stated max value (or use 32) and use the same width for insert and query.

7) Querying an empty trie. In Maximum XOR Queries, when no value <= m exists the walk crashes (child is None) or fabricates 0. Fix: track insert count and return -1 before walking.

8) Memory blindness. One 26-array node per character can exhaust memory on big dictionaries. Fix: dict children for sparse alphabets, `__slots__` on node classes, and mention compressed tries (radix trees) as the production answer.

sections.title: Interview Recognition Checklist
sections.content:
Cues that scream trie: "prefix" in any form — starts with, longest common prefix across many queries, autocomplete, "count words with prefix"; a dictionary of words hit with MANY lookups (amortize the build); word games / spell-check; "maximum XOR" of pairs or of a query against an array (binary trie); "longest prefix match" (routing); streaming characters where matches must survive across steps.

30-second pre-coding checklist:
- Alphabet: fixed lowercase a-z -> 26-slot array children; anything wider or unknown -> dict children. Say the trade-off (speed vs memory) out loud.
- What lives on a node? Plain membership -> end flag. Counting or erase support -> pass_count + end_count. Autocomplete -> maybe a cached best-suggestion per node.
- Deletions required? Plan counters up front; bolting deletion onto a boolean trie later is painful.
- For XOR problems: bit width from the max value (30 bits for 10^9; default 32); insert MSB-first; insert-then-query to dodge the empty trie; is it pairs within one array, or queries against it?
- Queries with thresholds/constraints? Ask if answering OFFLINE is allowed — sort queries by the constraint and sweep a growing trie.
- Budget check: time O(total characters) or O((N + Q) * bits); space is the same order — confirm it fits before coding, and mention radix/compressed tries if memory is tight.
- State the complexity per operation as O(L) BEFORE coding; interviewers listen for "independent of the number of stored words".

implementations.title: CountingTrie — dict children, word/prefix counts, O(L) erase
ArrayTrie — 26-slot children with true node deletion (pruning)
XorTrie — max XOR pair + offline XOR queries
implementations.code:
class XorTrieNode:
    __slots__ = ("child",)            # tiny node: just two branches
    def __init__(self):
        self.child = [None, None]     # child[0] = bit-0, child[1] = bit-1


class XorTrie:
    # Binary trie over fixed-width non-negative ints, MSB first.
    # insert / max_xor_with are O(B) where B = bit width.

    def __init__(self, bits=32):
        self.root = XorTrieNode()
        self.bits = bits              # width: 32 covers values < 2^32
        self.count = 0                # how many numbers are stored

    def insert(self, num):
        node = self.root
        self.count += 1
        for i in range(self.bits - 1, -1, -1):   # MSB -> LSB
            b = (num >> i) & 1        # bit i of num
            if node.child[b] is None:
                node.child[b] = XorTrieNode()    # extend the path
            node = node.child[b]

    def max_xor_with(self, num):
        # Greedy walk: prefer the OPPOSITE bit at every level. A win at
        # bit i is worth 2^i > sum of all lower bits, so it is safe.
        if self.count == 0:
            return -1                 # empty trie: nothing to pair with
        node, ans = self.root, 0
        for i in range(self.bits - 1, -1, -1):
            b = (num >> i) & 1
            if node.child[1 - b] is not None:    # opposite branch exists
                ans |= 1 << i         # this XOR bit becomes 1
                node = node.child[1 - b]
            else:
                node = node.child[b]  # forced: follow the same bit
        return ans


def find_maximum_xor(nums):
    # 'Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array' -- O(N * 32) total.
    trie = XorTrie(32)
    best = 0
    for x in nums:
        trie.insert(x)                # insert BEFORE query: never empty
        best = max(best, trie.max_xor_with(x))
    return best


def maximize_xor(nums, queries):
    # 'Maximum XOR Queries': for (x, m), max(x ^ v) over v <= m or -1.
    # Offline sweep: sort nums; visit queries by ascending m; a single
    # pointer inserts each eligible num exactly once. O((N + Q) * 32).
    nums = sorted(nums)               # ascending, so one pointer works
    order = sorted(range(len(queries)), key=lambda j: queries[j][1])
    trie = XorTrie(32)
    ans = [-1] * len(queries)         # -1 = no value <= m exists
    i = 0                             # how many nums are in the trie
    for j in order:                   # increasing-threshold order
        x, m = queries[j]
        while i < len(nums) and nums[i] <= m:
            trie.insert(nums[i])      # admit newly-eligible numbers
            i += 1
        ans[j] = trie.max_xor_with(x) # -1 when trie is still empty
    return ans                        # already in ORIGINAL query order


if __name__ == "__main__":
    assert find_maximum_xor([3, 10, 5, 25, 2, 8]) == 28     # 5 ^ 25
    assert maximize_xor([0, 1, 2, 3, 4],
                        [(3, 1), (1, 3), (5, 6)]) == [3, 3, 7]
    assert maximize_xor([5, 2, 4, 6, 6, 3],
                        [(12, 4), (8, 1), (6, 3)]) == [15, -1, 5]
    print("XorTrie OK")

Dynamic Programming.summary:
Dynamic Programming (DP) is recursion that never repeats work. Many problems break into smaller versions of themselves, and the SAME small versions keep reappearing. Naive recursion recomputes them over and over: computing fib(50) by pure recursion makes about 2^50 calls, even though there are only 50 distinct values to know. DP says: solve each distinct subproblem once, write the answer down (in a dict or an array), and after that just look it up. That one idea turns exponential algorithms into polynomial ones — fib(50) drops from centuries to 50 additions.

Interviews love DP because it cannot be faked with a memorized trick. You must design a STATE (the minimal information that identifies a subproblem, like "index i and remaining budget c"), a TRANSITION (how the answer for a state is built from smaller states, usually a max/min/sum over a few choices), and BASE CASES (the states you can answer without any recursion). Those three decisions are the whole game; the code that follows is almost mechanical. The sheet for this topic spans the five families that cover ~90% of interview DP: 1-D position DP (Climbing Stairs, House Robber), knapsack (Coin Change, 0/1 Knapsack), two-string DP (Edit Distance, LCS), the LIS family, and interval DP (Burst Balloons, Matrix Chain Multiplication).

The mental model: a table of already-answered smaller questions. Each cell asks "what is the answer for THIS prefix / THIS budget / THIS segment?", and you fill cells in an order where every cell you need has already been filled.

```
naive fib(5): 15 calls, repeats     DP: 6 cells, each filled once
        f5                          idx:  0   1   2   3   4   5
      f4  f3   <- f3 appears twice  val: [0] [1] [1] [2] [3] [5]
     .. .. ..                             base --> each = sum of prev two
```
preRequisites: Recursion with confidence: you can write a function that calls itself, state its base case precisely, and trace it on paper for a small input like n = 4.
Complexity of recursion trees: why a two-branch recursion without caching costs O(2^n) calls even when there are only n DISTINCT argument values.
Python dicts and functools.lru_cache: how a cache keyed by the argument tuple gives O(1) average lookups, and why cache keys must be hashable (tuples yes, lists no).
Building 2-D lists safely: [[0]*cols for _ in range(rows)] creates independent rows, while [[0]*cols]*rows creates rows that alias the SAME list.
Index conventions for prefixes: s[:i] means 'the first i characters', so DP tables are usually sized len+1, with row/column 0 reserved for the empty prefix.
bisect.bisect_left / bisect_right for binary search over a sorted list — required for the O(n log n) Longest Increasing Subsequence.
Python's recursion limit (~1000 frames by default): why deep top-down DP needs sys.setrecursionlimit or a bottom-up rewrite.
cheatSheet: Total DP cost = (number of distinct states) x (work per transition). Count states FIRST, then multiply.
Fibonacci family: dp[i] = f(dp[i-1], dp[i-2]) — O(n) time, O(1) space with two rolling variables.
0/1 knapsack 1-D: for each item, loop capacity DESCENDING: dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c-wt] + val) — descending keeps each item used at most once.
Unbounded knapsack / Rod Cutting: same recurrence, loop capacity ASCENDING — dp[c-wt] may already contain the same item (unlimited copies).
Coin Change (min): dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a-c] for coin c), dp[0]=0, impossible = inf. Coin Change II (count combinations): coins in the OUTER loop, dp[0]=1.
LCS: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]+1 if s[i-1]==t[j-1] else max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]); O(n*m). Longest Palindromic Subsequence = LCS(s, reversed(s)).
Edit Distance: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] on match, else 1 + min(replace dp[i-1][j-1], delete dp[i-1][j], insert dp[i][j-1]).
LIS in O(n log n): keep tails[]; for each x replace tails[bisect_left(tails, x)] or append; answer = len(tails). tails is NOT the actual LIS.
Interval DP (MCM, Burst Balloons, Cut Stick): dp[i][j] = best over split k of dp-left + dp-right + cost(i,k,j); fill by increasing segment length; O(n^3).
Base cases carry the semantics: minimization -> init inf, counting -> init 0 with dp[empty]=1, maximization -> init 0 or -inf.

sections.title: What & Why: Remembering Instead of Recomputing
sections.content:
Dynamic Programming is a strategy, not a data structure: solve a problem by combining answers to smaller overlapping subproblems, computing each distinct subproblem exactly once. Two properties must hold. First, OPTIMAL SUBSTRUCTURE: the best answer for the whole is built from best answers for parts (the cheapest way to reach stair 10 extends the cheapest way to reach stair 8 or 9). Second, OVERLAPPING SUBPROBLEMS: the same parts are needed many times (reach-stair-8 is needed by stair 9 AND stair 10). If subproblems never repeat (like mergesort's halves), plain divide-and-conquer is enough and caching buys nothing.

A real-world analogy: a cashier counting a drawer writes the running total on paper after every stack of bills. If interrupted, they resume from the last written total instead of recounting from zero. The paper is the DP table; "recounting from zero" is what naive recursion does.

DP is everywhere in real systems: `git diff` and DNA sequence alignment are Edit Distance / LCS; spell-checker suggestions rank candidates by edit distance; TeX's famously good paragraph line-breaking is a 1-D DP; Bellman-Ford routing and currency-arbitrage detection are DP over path lengths; speech recognition (Viterbi) is DP over hidden states; query optimizers pick join orders with interval-DP just like Matrix Chain Multiplication.

Two equivalent implementation styles exist and you should be fluent in both. TOP-DOWN (memoization): write the natural recursion, add a cache; the recursion visits only reachable states. BOTTOM-UP (tabulation): fill an explicit table from base cases upward; no recursion depth limits, easy space optimization. Same states, same transitions, same complexity — the difference is who orders the computation: the call stack or your for-loop.

sections.title: Memory Model: Tables, Memo Dicts, and the Recursion Stack
sections.content:
A DP computation lives in two kinds of memory: the ANSWER STORE (memo dict or table) and, for top-down, the RECURSION STACK.

Top-down: the memo is a dict mapping a state tuple to its answer. `lru_cache` builds exactly this behind the scenes, keyed by the argument tuple. Each in-flight recursive call also occupies a stack frame, so a chain of n un-memoized calls needs n frames — that is why Python's ~1000-frame default limit matters for n = 10^5 inputs.

Bottom-up: the store is a list (1-D) or list-of-lists (2-D). A Python 2-D "grid" is really an outer list of POINTERS to independent row lists — which is why `[[0]*m]*n` (n pointers to ONE row) corrupts DP tables.

```
naive fib(5) call tree (15 calls)      memoized: 6 answers, stored once
          f5                           key   0   1   2   3   4   5
        f4    f3                       val  [0] [1] [1] [2] [3] [5]
      f3  f2  f2 f1                          ^base^   each computed once,
     (f3, f2 recomputed!)                             then O(1) lookups
```

For 2-D DP the table has a DEPENDENCY DIRECTION. Every cell of the LCS grid needs its up, left, and diagonal neighbors, so filling row by row, left to right, guarantees dependencies are ready:

```
     ""   a   c   e         dp[i][j] (LCS of "abcde"[:i], "ace"[:j]) needs:
 "" [ 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 ]          dp[i-1][j-1]   diagonal (match case)
 a  [ 0 | 1 | 1 | 1 ]          dp[i-1][j]     up       (drop char of s)
 b  [ 0 | 1 | 1 | 1 ]          dp[i][j-1]     left     (drop char of t)
 c  [ 0 | 1 | 2 | 2 ]
 d  [ 0 | 1 | 2 | 2 ]       row 0 / col 0 = empty prefix -> base answers 0
 e  [ 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 ]       answer = bottom-right cell dp[5][3] = 3 ("ace")
```

Space optimization falls out of this picture: if transitions only ever read the PREVIOUS row, you never need the whole grid — keep two rows, or one row swept in the right direction (the knapsack trick). That converts O(n*m) space to O(m) while time stays O(n*m).

sections.title: Core Operations & Complexity: States x Transitions
sections.content:
There is no fixed API like a stack's push/pop; the "operations" of DP are design steps. Each has a cost you should be able to state before writing code.

```
Operation                          Time            Why
---------------------------------  --------------  --------------------------------------
memo lookup / insert (dict)        O(1) average    hash of the state tuple
fill 1-D table, lookback k         O(n*k)          n states, up to k candidate transitions
fill knapsack table                O(n*W)          n*W states, O(1) pick/skip transition
fill two-string table              O(n*m)          n*m prefix pairs, O(1) transition
LIS via tails + bisect             O(n log n)      n elements, one binary search each
interval DP (MCM, Burst Balloons)  O(n^3)          O(n^2) segments, O(n) split points each
reconstruct one optimal solution   O(path length)  walk stored parent/choice links backward
```

The golden formula: TOTAL = (#states) x (work per transition). It converts complexity analysis from guesswork into counting. Frog Jump with K Distance: n states, k transitions each -> O(n*k). Burst Balloons: n^2 segments, n choices of last balloon -> O(n^3). If your recursion has no repeated states, memoization changes nothing — the speedup comes purely from collapsing repeats.

Two subtleties. First, knapsack-style DP is PSEUDO-POLYNOMIAL: O(n*W) is polynomial in the VALUE W, but W takes only log W bits of input, so the same algorithm is exponential in input SIZE — this is why Coin Change with amount 10^9 needs a different idea. Second, reconstruction (which items? which subsequence? which bracketing?) is cheap if you stored the table or parent links: one backward walk, no re-solving. Interviewers often ask for it as a follow-up, so build tables you can walk back through.

sections.title: How Python Does It: lru_cache, Dicts, Lists, and Their Traps
sections.content:
Python gives you three memo mechanisms and one big trap.

`functools.lru_cache(maxsize=None)` (alias `functools.cache` in 3.9+) wraps a function with a dict keyed by its argument tuple. It is the fastest DP style to WRITE, with three gotchas: (1) arguments must be hashable — pass indices into a shared list, never the list itself; (2) the cache lives as long as the function does, so call `.cache_clear()` between test cases and avoid decorating methods (the cache would keep `self` alive — define the cached helper INSIDE the method instead); (3) each recursive call still costs a Python stack frame, and the default limit is about 1000 — raise it with `sys.setrecursionlimit` or convert to bottom-up for inputs around 10^5.

An explicit dict memo does the same thing with more control. A bottom-up list table is the most robust: no recursion limit, obvious space optimization, and usually the fastest constant factor because it avoids function-call overhead. `float('inf')` is the standard "impossible" sentinel — it flows through `min()` correctly and survives `+ 1`. `bisect` powers O(n log n) LIS.
sections.code:
from functools import lru_cache
import sys

# --- Style 1: top-down with lru_cache (fastest to WRITE) --------------
@lru_cache(maxsize=None)          # dict cache keyed by the args tuple (n,)
def fib(n):
    if n < 2:                     # base cases stop the recursion
        return n
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)   # each distinct n computed once

# --- Style 2: explicit dict memo (full control, clearable) ------------
def fib_memo(n, memo=None):
    if memo is None:
        memo = {}                 # fresh dict per top-level call
    if n < 2:
        return n
    if n not in memo:             # compute a state only on first request
        memo[n] = fib_memo(n - 1, memo) + fib_memo(n - 2, memo)
    return memo[n]                # afterwards: O(1) dict hit

# --- Style 3: bottom-up rolling variables (no recursion at all) -------
def fib_table(n):
    if n < 2:
        return n
    prev2, prev1 = 0, 1           # answers for i-2 and i-1
    for _ in range(2, n + 1):
        prev2, prev1 = prev1, prev2 + prev1   # slide the window forward
    return prev1                  # O(n) time, O(1) space

# --- THE 2-D grid trap ------------------------------------------------
rows, cols = 3, 4
bad  = [[0] * cols] * rows        # WRONG: 3 pointers to ONE shared row
good = [[0] * cols for _ in range(rows)]   # RIGHT: 3 independent rows
bad[0][0] = 9                     # silently "edits" every row of bad!

# --- Deep top-down DP needs a bigger stack ----------------------------
sys.setrecursionlimit(300000)     # default ~1000 frames dies near n=1000

sections.title: Pattern: 1-D DP on Positions (Fibonacci Family)
sections.content:
RECOGNIZE IT: the input is a line of positions (stairs, stones, houses) and the answer at position i depends only on a few earlier positions. This is the entry-level DP family and the fastest to master.

THE INVARIANT: dp[i] = the answer for the prefix ending at position i, and by the time you compute dp[i], every dp[j] with j < i is final and correct.

Sheet questions in this family: **Climbing Stairs** — dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2], literally Fibonacci, because the last move was a 1-step or a 2-step and the two option sets are disjoint. **Frog Jump** — dp[i] = min(dp[i-1] + |h[i]-h[i-1]|, dp[i-2] + |h[i]-h[i-2]|): a MIN over the same two choices instead of a SUM (counting -> sum over choices, optimizing -> min/max over choices; the skeleton is identical). **Frog Jump with K Distance** — the lookback window widens from 2 to k, so cost becomes O(n*k). **Maximum Sum of Non-Adjacent Elements** and **House Robber** — at each house choose rob (x + dp[i-2]) or skip (dp[i-1]); House Robber's circular street is handled by running the line version twice, once excluding the first house and once excluding the last, because the only new constraint is that those two can't BOTH be robbed.

SPACE: when the lookback is a constant (1 or 2 positions), the whole array collapses to rolling variables — O(1) space. With lookback k, keep the last k entries. Reflex to build: write the recurrence over the full dp array first, get it right, THEN collapse.

sections.title: Pattern: Knapsack — Pick or Skip Under a Budget
sections.content:
RECOGNIZE IT: a set of items, each with a "size" and a "value", a budget (capacity, amount, rod length), and per item the decision is pick or skip. The state is (items considered, budget left).

THE INVARIANT (2-D form): dp[i][c] = best answer using only the first i items with budget c — the choice for item i is resolved by comparing "skip" (dp[i-1][c]) with "take" (val + dp[i-1][c-wt] for 0/1, or val + dp[i][c-wt] for unbounded). That one index difference — previous row vs SAME row — is the entire distinction between the two variants, and in the 1-D compressed form it becomes the LOOP DIRECTION: descending capacity for **0/1 Knapsack** (so dp[c-wt] still holds the previous item's row), ascending for **Unbounded Knapsack** (so an item may feed into itself).

Sheet questions: **0/1 Knapsack** is the canonical form. **Unbounded Knapsack** allows repeats. **Rod Cutting Problem** IS unbounded knapsack in disguise: piece lengths are weights, piece prices are values, the rod length is the capacity. **Coin Change** is min-knapsack: dp[a] = fewest coins for amount a, base dp[0] = 0, unreachable = inf. **Coin Change II** counts COMBINATIONS: put coins in the OUTER loop so coins are considered in a fixed order and {1,2} is never recounted as {2,1}; swapping the loops counts permutations, a different question (that ordered variant is exactly the Climbing-Stairs shape).

Complexity O(n*W) time — pseudo-polynomial, fine for W up to a few million. Reconstruction ("which items?") needs the full 2-D table: walk from dp[n][W] backwards, checking which choice produced each cell.

sections.title: Pattern: Two-String DP (LCS Family and Matching)
sections.content:
RECOGNIZE IT: two strings (or one string compared against a transformed copy of itself), and the question is about aligning, matching, or transforming them. The state is a PAIR of prefix lengths: dp[i][j] = answer for s[:i] vs t[:j]. That is (n+1)*(m+1) states with O(1) transitions -> O(n*m).

THE SKELETON every member shares: look at the LAST characters s[i-1] and t[j-1]. If they match, usually consume both (diagonal move). If not, try the ways to make progress and combine with max/min/sum.

Sheet questions: **Longest Common Subsequence** — match: 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]; mismatch: max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). **Longest Palindromic Subsequence** — one line: LCS(s, reversed(s)), because a subsequence common to s and its reverse reads the same both ways. **Edit Distance** — match is free (dp[i-1][j-1]); mismatch costs 1 + min(replace dp[i-1][j-1], delete dp[i-1][j], insert dp[i][j-1]); base row/column are i deletions / j insertions, not 0. **Distinct Subsequences** — COUNTING: dp[i][j] = ways t[:j] appears in s[:i] as a subsequence = dp[i-1][j] (ignore s's char) + dp[i-1][j-1] if the chars match (use it); base dp[i][0] = 1 (empty t appears once). **Wildcard Matching** — boolean DP: '?' behaves like a match (diagonal); '*' gives dp[i][j] = dp[i][j-1] (star matches empty) OR dp[i-1][j] (star eats one more char of s); the base row needs care because a prefix of '*'s matches the empty string.

Notice how the SAME grid holds lengths (LCS), costs (Edit Distance), counts (Distinct Subsequences), and booleans (Wildcard). Master the skeleton once; each problem only changes the cell type, the two case formulas, and the base row/column.

sections.title: Pattern: Longest Increasing Subsequence Family
sections.content:
RECOGNIZE IT: one sequence, and you must select an ordered subsequence obeying a comparison rule (strictly increasing, chainable, rising-then-falling). Unlike prefix DP, "the best answer for the first i elements" is not enough state — whether a[i] can extend a subsequence depends on which element that subsequence ENDS with. So the invariant is: dp[i] = length of the longest valid subsequence that ends EXACTLY at index i, and the final answer is max over all i.

The O(n^2) recurrence: dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j] for j < i if a[j] < a[i]), else 1. Store parent links if you must print the subsequence.

The O(n log n) upgrade keeps `tails`, where tails[k] is the SMALLEST possible tail value of any increasing subsequence of length k+1. tails stays sorted, so each new x either replaces the first tail >= x (bisect_left, keeping future options maximal) or extends the array. The length of tails is the LIS length — but tails itself is NOT a valid LIS (its entries come from different subsequences); recovering an actual LIS needs parent pointers, shown in the implementations below. Strictness control: bisect_left gives strictly increasing; bisect_right would allow equal neighbors (non-decreasing).

Sheet questions: **Longest Increasing Subsequence** is the base form. **Longest String Chain** is LIS in costume: sort words by length, and word w extends word u if deleting exactly one character of w yields u — the "comparison rule" is predecessor-by-deletion, and a dict from word to best chain length replaces the inner scan. **Bitonic Subsequence** runs the machinery twice: inc[i] = LIS ending at i computed left-to-right, dec[i] = longest DECREASING subsequence starting at i computed right-to-left; the best mountain through i has inc[i] + dec[i] - 1 elements (i is counted in both halves, subtract it once).

sections.title: Pattern: Interval / Partition DP (Think About the LAST Move)
sections.content:
RECOGNIZE IT: the answer for a whole range is assembled by choosing where to split it (or which operation happens LAST inside it), and both sides then become independent subranges. State: a segment. Invariant: dp[i][j] = best answer for the segment (i, j), correct by the time any larger segment asks for it — which is why tabulation fills segments in increasing LENGTH order. Cost is usually O(n^2) segments x O(n) split choices = O(n^3), which fits when n <= ~500.

The key mental trick is thinking about the LAST move, not the first. In **Burst Balloons**, choosing the FIRST balloon to burst entangles the sides (they become adjacent afterwards). Choosing the LAST balloon k to burst in segment (i, j) is clean: when k finally pops, every other balloon inside is already gone, so its neighbors are exactly the fixed borders i and j, and the two sides were solved independently. Pad the array with virtual 1-valued balloons to make borders exist.

**Matrix Chain Multiplication** picks the LAST multiplication: splitting the chain i..j at k costs dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + dims[i]*dims[k+1]*dims[j+1] scalar multiplications. **Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick** sorts the cut positions, adds the stick's two ends as sentinels, and defines dp over pairs of cut positions; making a cut inside a segment costs that segment's LENGTH plus the two halves — same skeleton, cost function = segment length.

**Palindrome Partitioning II** is the front-partition cousin: instead of two-sided segments, dp[i] = minimum cuts needed for the suffix s[i:], and you try every j where s[i:j+1] is a palindrome: dp[i] = min(1 + dp[j+1]). To keep transitions O(1), precompute pal[i][j] with its own DP (pal[i][j] = s[i]==s[j] and pal[i+1][j-1]) — total O(n^2). The shared idea across all four: fix the boundary event, and the rest decomposes.
sections.code:
def max_coins(nums):
    # Burst Balloons. Pad with virtual balloons worth 1 on both ends so
    # every real balloon always has two neighbors when it pops.
    a = [1] + nums + [1]
    n = len(a)
    # dp[i][j] = best coins from bursting everything STRICTLY between i, j
    dp = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    # gap = distance between the two fixed borders; solve small gaps first
    for gap in range(2, n):
        for i in range(0, n - gap):
            j = i + gap
            for k in range(i + 1, j):      # k = LAST balloon to pop in (i,j)
                # when k pops last, everything else inside is gone, so its
                # neighbors are exactly the borders a[i] and a[j]
                gain = a[i] * a[k] * a[j]
                dp[i][j] = max(dp[i][j], dp[i][k] + dp[k][j] + gain)
    return dp[0][n - 1]                    # O(n^3) time, O(n^2) space


def min_cut_stick(n, cuts):
    # Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick: add both ends as sentinels, sort
    pos = sorted([0] + cuts + [n])
    m = len(pos)
    dp = [[0] * m for _ in range(m)]       # dp[i][j]: cut everything
    for gap in range(2, m):                # strictly between pos[i], pos[j]
        for i in range(0, m - gap):
            j = i + gap
            best = float('inf')
            for k in range(i + 1, j):      # k = first cut in this segment
                best = min(best, dp[i][k] + dp[k][j])
            # cutting this segment (any order) pays its full length once
            dp[i][j] = best + pos[j] - pos[i]
    return dp[0][m - 1]

sections.title: Pitfalls & Common Mistakes
sections.content:
Every one of these has cost real interviews. Each comes with its fix.

1. `[[0]*m]*n` for a 2-D table. All n rows alias ONE list, so writing dp[2][5] also "writes" dp[0][5]. Fix: `[[0]*m for _ in range(n)]`.

2. Wrong loop direction in 1-D knapsack. Ascending capacity in 0/1 knapsack silently lets an item be taken twice; descending in unbounded silently forbids repeats. Fix: 0/1 -> descending, unbounded -> ascending; if unsure, write the 2-D version first and compress after it works.

3. Coin Change II with amount in the outer loop. That counts ordered sequences (permutations), inflating the answer. Fix: coins outer, amounts inner, and know WHY (each coin's contribution is committed before the next coin exists).

4. Off-by-one between "index" and "prefix length". In an (n+1)-sized table, dp[i] talks about s[:i], and the character being examined is s[i-1]. Fix: pick the convention out loud, and check dp[0]/row 0 means "empty" before writing transitions.

5. Wrong initialization semantics. Min-problems need inf for "unknown" (0 would claim everything is free); counting needs dp[empty] = 1, not 0 (there IS one way to make amount 0). Fix: derive base cases from the English meaning of the state, never copy them from another problem.

6. RecursionError on big inputs. Top-down on n = 10^5 exceeds Python's ~1000-frame limit. Fix: sys.setrecursionlimit(3*10^5) or, better, rewrite bottom-up.

7. lru_cache traps: list arguments are unhashable (pass indices instead); the cache persists across test cases (call .cache_clear()); decorating a method pins `self` in memory forever (define the cached helper inside the method).

8. Treating the LIS `tails` array as the answer subsequence. Its entries come from different subsequences; only its LENGTH is meaningful. Fix: keep parent pointers if the actual sequence is required.

9. Believing memoization fixes a wrong state. If the state is missing information the transition needs (e.g. LIS without "what the subsequence ends with"), the cached answers are WRONG, not slow. Fix: ask "do two situations with the same state tuple truly have the same future?" — if no, the state is incomplete.

sections.title: Interview Recognition Checklist
sections.content:
CUES that a problem is DP: the ask is "count the number of ways", "minimum cost / maximum value", "longest / shortest subsequence", or "is it possible to reach / partition"; each step offers a small set of choices; a greedy pick is easy to break with a counter-example; and brute force is exponential while the number of DISTINCT (position, budget/segment) situations is polynomial. Constraints are loud hints: n <= 20 whispers bitmask or plain backtracking, n <= 1000 suggests O(n^2) table DP, n <= 500 with segments screams O(n^3) interval DP, amount/W around 10^4-10^6 says knapsack over values.

Map the wording to the family: line of positions with short lookback -> 1-D DP (Climbing Stairs, House Robber); items + budget -> knapsack (Coin Change, Rod Cutting); two strings -> prefix-pair grid (Edit Distance, LCS); one sequence with an ordering rule -> LIS family; ranges where a last operation splits the problem -> interval DP (Burst Balloons, Matrix Chain Multiplication); "partition a string, minimize pieces" -> front-partition DP (Palindrome Partitioning II).

The 30-second pre-coding checklist:
1. STATE — what tuple uniquely determines a subproblem? Say it as a sentence: "dp[i][c] = best value using first i items with capacity c."
2. CHOICES — what are the 2-3 moves available at a state?
3. TRANSITION — combine choices with max, min, or sum? Write the one-line formula.
4. BASE — which states are answerable with no recursion, and what value encodes "empty" or "impossible"?
5. ORDER — top-down with memo, or bottom-up (which loop direction makes dependencies ready)?
6. ANSWER — which cell holds it: dp[n][W], max over all dp[i], or dp[0][n-1]?
7. COST — #states x transition work; does it fit the constraints?
8. FOLLOW-UP — can I reconstruct the actual solution and space-optimize if asked?
If any of the eight has no answer, do not start typing — fix the design first.

implementations.title: 0/1 Knapsack Three Ways (Memo, Table, 1-D) + Item Reconstruction
implementations.code:
# =====================================================================
# 0/1 KNAPSACK — built three ways, plus reconstruction of the items.
# Problem: n items; item i has weights[i], values[i]; capacity W.
# Each item may be used AT MOST ONCE. Maximize total value.
# State: (next item to decide, remaining capacity) -> n*W states.
# =====================================================================
from functools import lru_cache


def knapsack_memo(weights, values, W):
    # ---- Top-down: the literal pick / not-pick recursion + a cache ----
    n = len(weights)

    @lru_cache(maxsize=None)             # cache key = the (i, cap) tuple
    def best(i, cap):
        if i == n:                       # no items left to decide
            return 0                     # value of the empty selection
        ans = best(i + 1, cap)           # choice 1: SKIP item i
        if weights[i] <= cap:            # choice 2: TAKE item i (if it fits)
            ans = max(ans, values[i] + best(i + 1, cap - weights[i]))
        return ans                       # best over both choices

    result = best(0, W)
    best.cache_clear()                   # avoid leaking cache across calls
    return result


def knapsack_table(weights, values, W):
    # ---- Bottom-up 2-D: dp[i][c] = best using first i items, capacity c
    n = len(weights)
    # row 0 = zero items -> value 0 everywhere (the base case row)
    dp = [[0] * (W + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        wt, val = weights[i - 1], values[i - 1]   # item i is index i-1
        for c in range(W + 1):
            dp[i][c] = dp[i - 1][c]      # default: skip item i
            if wt <= c:                  # if it fits, try taking it
                dp[i][c] = max(dp[i][c], dp[i - 1][c - wt] + val)
    return dp, dp[n][W]                  # keep the table for reconstruction


def knapsack_1d(weights, values, W):
    # ---- Space-optimized: ONE row, capacity swept DESCENDING ----
    # Descending is what makes this 0/1: dp[c - wt] on the right side
    # still holds the PREVIOUS item's row, so no item is counted twice.
    dp = [0] * (W + 1)
    for wt, val in zip(weights, values):
        for c in range(W, wt - 1, -1):   # high capacity -> low
            dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c - wt] + val)
    return dp[W]                         # O(n*W) time, O(W) space


def reconstruct_items(dp, weights, W):
    # ---- Walk the 2-D table backwards, replaying each decision ----
    chosen = []
    c = W
    for i in range(len(weights), 0, -1):
        if dp[i][c] != dp[i - 1][c]:     # value changed -> item i was TAKEN
            chosen.append(i - 1)         # record its 0-based index
            c -= weights[i - 1]          # give back its weight
        # equal cells mean item i was skipped: just move up a row
    chosen.reverse()                     # collected back-to-front
    return chosen


if __name__ == "__main__":
    weights = [1, 3, 4, 5]
    values = [15, 50, 60, 90]
    W = 8
    table, best_val = knapsack_table(weights, values, W)
    # all three techniques must agree on the optimum
    assert best_val == knapsack_memo(weights, values, W)
    assert best_val == knapsack_1d(weights, values, W)
    assert best_val == 140               # items 1 and 3: 50 + 90, weight 8
    print("best value:", best_val)
    print("chosen item indices:", reconstruct_items(table, weights, W))

implementations.title: LCS & Edit Distance Engine with Diff-Style Reconstruction
implementations.code:
# =====================================================================
# LCS + EDIT DISTANCE engine with full reconstruction — the machinery
# behind `git diff` and spell-checker suggestions.
# dp[i][j] always talks about the prefixes s[:i] and t[:j].
# =====================================================================


def lcs_table(s, t):
    n, m = len(s), len(t)
    # (n+1) x (m+1) grid; row 0 / col 0 = empty prefix -> LCS length 0
    dp = [[0] * (m + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        for j in range(1, m + 1):
            if s[i - 1] == t[j - 1]:              # last chars match
                dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1   # extend diagonal LCS
            else:                                 # they differ: drop one
                dp[i][j] = max(dp[i - 1][j],      # ignore s's last char
                               dp[i][j - 1])      # ignore t's last char
    return dp


def lcs_string(s, t):
    # Backtrack from the bottom-right corner, replaying the decisions
    # the fill made — this recovers an ACTUAL common subsequence.
    dp = lcs_table(s, t)
    i, j = len(s), len(t)
    out = []
    while i > 0 and j > 0:
        if s[i - 1] == t[j - 1]:         # this char is part of the LCS
            out.append(s[i - 1])
            i -= 1                       # consume from both strings:
            j -= 1                       # move diagonally
        elif dp[i - 1][j] >= dp[i][j - 1]:
            i -= 1                       # the max came from "drop s's char"
        else:
            j -= 1                       # the max came from "drop t's char"
    return "".join(reversed(out))        # built back-to-front, so reverse


def edit_distance(s, t):
    # Levenshtein distance: fewest insert/delete/replace ops, s -> t
    n, m = len(s), len(t)
    dp = [[0] * (m + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for i in range(n + 1):
        dp[i][0] = i                     # erase all i chars of s
    for j in range(m + 1):
        dp[0][j] = j                     # type all j chars of t
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        for j in range(1, m + 1):
            if s[i - 1] == t[j - 1]:
