                dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1]        # chars agree: free move
            else:
                dp[i][j] = 1 + min(dp[i - 1][j - 1],   # replace s's char
                                   dp[i - 1][j],       # delete s's char
                                   dp[i][j - 1])       # insert t's char
    return dp[n][m]                      # O(n*m) time and space


def longest_palindromic_subsequence(s):
    # a common subsequence of s and reversed(s) is a palindrome in s
    dp = lcs_table(s, s[::-1])
    return dp[len(s)][len(s)]            # bottom-right = full-string answer


if __name__ == "__main__":
    assert lcs_string("abcde", "ace") == "ace"       # classic sanity check
    assert edit_distance("horse", "ros") == 3        # r-o-s: replace,del,del
    assert longest_palindromic_subsequence("bbbab") == 4   # "bbbb"
    print("LCS(AGGTAB, GXTXAYB) =", lcs_string("AGGTAB", "GXTXAYB"))  # GTAB

implementations.title: LIS: O(n^2) DP and O(n log n) Patience Method, Both Reconstructing
implementations.code:
# =====================================================================
# LONGEST INCREASING SUBSEQUENCE — two engines with reconstruction.
#  1. O(n^2) DP with parent links (easiest to reason about).
#  2. O(n log n) patience method that ALSO recovers a real LIS —
#     something the bare "tails" trick cannot do on its own.
# =====================================================================
import bisect


def lis_quadratic(a):
    n = len(a)
    if n == 0:
        return []                        # empty input -> empty LIS
    dp = [1] * n                         # dp[i] = LIS length ending AT i
    parent = [-1] * n                    # parent[i] = previous index used
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i):
            # a[j] < a[i]: the subsequence ending at j can grow with a[i]
            if a[j] < a[i] and dp[j] + 1 > dp[i]:
                dp[i] = dp[j] + 1
                parent[i] = j            # remember where the best came from
    end = max(range(n), key=lambda i: dp[i])   # the LIS may end anywhere
    seq = []
    while end != -1:                     # walk the parent chain backwards
        seq.append(a[end])
        end = parent[end]
    return seq[::-1]                     # reverse into forward order


def lis_nlogn(a):
    n = len(a)
    tails_val = []      # tails_val[k] = smallest tail of a length-(k+1) subseq
    tails_idx = []      # index into `a` of that tail element
    parent = [-1] * n   # parent pointers make reconstruction possible
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        # leftmost pile whose tail is >= x  (bisect_left -> STRICT increase)
        k = bisect.bisect_left(tails_val, x)
        if k > 0:
            # x extends the best subsequence of length k
            parent[i] = tails_idx[k - 1]
        if k == len(tails_val):
            tails_val.append(x)          # new record length discovered
            tails_idx.append(i)
        else:
            tails_val[k] = x             # smaller tail = better future options
            tails_idx[k] = i
    if not tails_idx:
        return []
    seq = []
    i = tails_idx[-1]                    # end of one optimal LIS
    while i != -1:                       # follow parents to the front
        seq.append(a[i])
        i = parent[i]
    return seq[::-1]                     # O(n log n) time, O(n) space


if __name__ == "__main__":
    data = [10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18]
    s1 = lis_quadratic(data)
    s2 = lis_nlogn(data)
    assert len(s1) == len(s2) == 4       # e.g. [2, 3, 7, 18]
    # both answers must be genuinely increasing subsequences of data
    for s in (s1, s2):
        assert all(x < y for x, y in zip(s, s[1:]))
    print("one optimal LIS:", s2)

implementations.title: Matrix Chain Multiplication with Optimal Parenthesization
implementations.code:
# =====================================================================
# MATRIX CHAIN MULTIPLICATION — the canonical interval DP, with
# reconstruction of the optimal bracketing.
# dims encodes the chain: matrix i has shape dims[i] x dims[i+1].
# dp[i][j] = fewest scalar multiplications to collapse matrices i..j.
# =====================================================================


def matrix_chain(dims):
    n = len(dims) - 1                    # number of matrices in the chain
    INF = float('inf')
    dp = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]     # single matrix (i == j) costs 0
    cut = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]    # cut[i][j] = winning split point
    # solve short chains first so long chains find their parts ready
    for length in range(2, n + 1):       # length = matrices in the segment
        for i in range(0, n - length + 1):
            j = i + length - 1           # segment covers matrices i..j
            dp[i][j] = INF
            for k in range(i, j):        # LAST multiply: (i..k) x (k+1..j)
                # left block is dims[i] x dims[k+1],
                # right block is dims[k+1] x dims[j+1];
                # multiplying them costs the product of the three dims
                cost = (dp[i][k] + dp[k + 1][j]
                        + dims[i] * dims[k + 1] * dims[j + 1])
                if cost < dp[i][j]:      # strict < keeps the FIRST best k
                    dp[i][j] = cost
                    cut[i][j] = k        # remember the winning split
    return dp, cut                       # O(n^3) time, O(n^2) space


def parenthesize(cut, i, j):
    # Rebuild the optimal bracketing recursively from the cut table.
    if i == j:
        return "M" + str(i)              # single matrix: no brackets needed
    k = cut[i][j]                        # the split the optimum used
    left = parenthesize(cut, i, k)       # bracket the left block
    right = parenthesize(cut, k + 1, j)  # bracket the right block
    return "(" + left + " x " + right + ")"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    dims = [40, 20, 30, 10, 30]          # 4 matrices: 40x20 20x30 30x10 10x30
    dp, cut = matrix_chain(dims)
    assert dp[0][3] == 26000             # the classic CLRS answer
    print("min scalar mults:", dp[0][3])
    print("optimal bracketing:", parenthesize(cut, 0, 3))
    # expected: ((M0 x (M1 x M2)) x M3)

Graphs.summary:
A graph is the most general way to store "things and the connections between them": a set of vertices (nodes) plus a set of edges (links). Every structure you have studied so far is secretly a graph — a linked list is a graph where each node has exactly one outgoing edge, and a tree is a connected graph with no cycles. Interviews love graphs because the graph is usually hidden inside a story: courses with prerequisites, cities with road costs, islands of land in an ocean of water, people who follow each other. The hard part is rarely the algorithm itself — it is recognizing "this is a graph problem" and then choosing the right tool from a small, fixed toolbox.

The mental model: draw circles and arrows. Every graph algorithm is a disciplined way of walking the arrows while writing notes on the circles — visited flags, distances, colors, parent pointers. BFS walks in expanding rings, so it finds shortest paths when every edge costs the same. DFS dives as deep as possible before backing up, so it discovers structure: connected components, cycles, and valid orderings. Weighted problems add exactly one new idea, "relaxation": keep a best-known distance for each node and improve it whenever some edge offers a shortcut. Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, and DAG shortest path are the same relaxation step run on four different schedules.

```
  (0)---(1)      circles = vertices, lines = edges
   |     |       one walk: 0 -> 1 -> 3 -> 2
  (2)---(3)      degree of 0 = 2 (two edges touch it)
```

The sixteen sheet problems for this topic cover the complete interview toolbox: both traversals, grid problems (Number of Islands, Flood Fill), cycle detection in undirected and directed graphs, topological sort done two ways, bipartite checking, three shortest-path algorithms, and two minimum-spanning-tree algorithms. Learn each one as a named template with a one-line invariant, and every new graph problem becomes "which template, with what twist?".
preRequisites: collections.deque and why q.popleft() is O(1) while list.pop(0) is O(N) — every BFS depends on this.
Recursion mechanics and Python's ~1000-frame default recursion limit (sys.setrecursionlimit raises it); how to convert recursion to an explicit stack.
heapq basics: heappush/heappop on a plain list give an O(log N) min-heap, and tuples like (distance, node) compare field by field.
dict and collections.defaultdict(list) for building adjacency lists without KeyError checks.
Big-O with two variables: O(V + E) means 'touch each vertex once and each edge a constant number of times', not O(V*E).
2D list indexing plus the direction-array idiom dirs = [(1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)] for walking grid neighbors.
Tree BFS/DFS from the Binary Tree topic — graph traversal is the same idea plus a visited set (trees never revisit, graphs can).
cheatSheet: BFS with a deque: O(V+E); in an UNWEIGHTED graph the layer number IS the shortest distance.
Mark visited when you ENQUEUE, not when you dequeue — otherwise one node enters the queue many times.
DFS: O(V+E); recursion depth can reach V, so raise sys.setrecursionlimit or use an explicit stack.
Undirected cycle: a visited neighbor that is NOT my parent => cycle.
Directed cycle: an edge into a GRAY node (still on the recursion stack) => cycle; BLACK (finished) is safe.
Kahn's topo sort: repeatedly pop indegree-0 nodes; if processed count < V => the graph has a cycle.
Dijkstra (no negative edges): pop min from heap, skip stale pairs with 'if d > dist[u]: continue'; O(E log V).
Bellman-Ford: V-1 rounds of relaxing all E edges = O(V*E); if a V-th round still relaxes => negative cycle.
Floyd-Warshall: dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]) with k as the OUTERMOST loop; O(V^3).
MST: Prim grows one tree with a heap (O(E log V)); Kruskal sorts edges and skips cycle-closers with DSU (O(E log E)).

sections.title: What & Why
sections.content:
A graph G = (V, E) is a set of V vertices and E edges. Vocabulary you must own before anything else: an edge is **directed** (one-way arrow, u -> v) or **undirected** (two-way, u - v); it may carry a **weight** (a cost); a **path** is a sequence of edges linking two vertices; a **cycle** is a path that returns to its start; a **connected component** is a maximal group of vertices that can all reach each other; a **DAG** is a Directed Acyclic Graph; the **degree** of a vertex is how many edges touch it.

Real-world analogy: a city map. Intersections are vertices, streets are edges, one-way streets are directed edges, street lengths are weights. "Find the fastest route" is shortest path; "can I get there at all" is reachability; "visit every district" is traversal.

Where graphs run in real systems: Google Maps and network routers run Dijkstra-family algorithms; build tools (make, npm, cargo) and university course planners run topological sort on dependency DAGs; operating systems detect deadlock as a cycle in the wait-for graph; social networks compute friend suggestions over follower graphs; web crawlers are BFS over pages and links.

Why interviewers love the topic: sixteen sheet problems collapse into about six reusable templates (BFS, DFS, cycle check, topo sort, relaxation-based shortest paths, MST). The interview tests two skills — spotting the hidden graph in a word problem, and picking the correct template from the problem's constraints (directed? weighted? negative weights? all pairs or one source?).

sections.title: Memory Model & Representation
sections.content:
There are three standard representations. In interviews you will use the **adjacency list** 95% of the time, because real interview graphs are sparse (E is much closer to V than to V^2).

```
Graph:              Adjacency list (dict of lists):
  0 --- 1           { 0: [1, 2],
  |     |             1: [0, 3],
  2     3             2: [0],
                      3: [1] }        space O(V + E)

Adjacency matrix (V x V):            Edge list:
       0  1  2  3                    [(0,1), (0,2), (1,3)]
    0[ 0  1  1  0 ]                  space O(E)
    1[ 1  0  0  1 ]                  (what Kruskal and
    2[ 1  0  0  0 ]                   Bellman-Ford want)
    3[ 0  1  0  0 ]  space O(V^2)
```

In Python memory terms the adjacency list is a dict whose values are list objects, and each list holds references to int objects. An undirected edge is stored TWICE (u in v's list and v in u's list), which is why traversal cost is written O(V + 2E) = O(V + E). For weighted graphs each entry becomes a tuple: `g[u] = [(v, w), ...]`.

The matrix wins only when the graph is dense or when you need O(1) "is there an edge u-v?" checks — Floyd-Warshall is the one sheet algorithm that genuinely wants a matrix. Its O(V^2) memory means V above ~3000 will not fit comfortably.

The fourth, most interview-relevant representation is the **implicit graph**: a grid. In Number of Islands and Flood Fill nobody hands you an adjacency list — cell (r, c) is a vertex and its up/down/left/right neighbors are the edges, computed on the fly with a direction array. Recognizing "this grid IS a graph" is the entire first step of those problems.

sections.title: Core Operations & Complexity
sections.content:
Costs below assume V vertices, E edges, adjacency list stored as dict-of-lists. The single most important row is traversal: BFS and DFS are O(V + E) because every vertex is marked visited exactly once, and every adjacency list is scanned exactly once — summing list lengths over all vertices counts each undirected edge twice, giving V + 2E total work.

```
Operation                        Adj list     Adj matrix   Why (one clause)
-------------------------------  -----------  -----------  --------------------------------
add edge u-v                     O(1)         O(1)         append vs set a cell
check edge u-v exists            O(deg(u))    O(1)         scan u's list vs index a cell
iterate neighbors of u           O(deg(u))    O(V)         list stores only real edges
full BFS / DFS                   O(V + E)     O(V^2)       matrix scans a whole row per node
topological sort (both ways)     O(V + E)     O(V^2)       it is one traversal + O(V) bookkeeping
Dijkstra (binary heap)           O(E log V)   —            each edge may push once: E pushes, log each
Bellman-Ford                     O(V * E)     —            V-1 full passes over the edge list
Floyd-Warshall                   —            O(V^3)       triple loop over (k, i, j)
Prim (heap) / Kruskal            O(E log V)   —            heap ops / sort dominate
space                            O(V + E)     O(V^2)       matrix stores absent edges too
```

Two budgeting rules of thumb for interviews: with V, E up to ~10^5 you may spend O(V + E) or O(E log V) but never O(V^2); Floyd-Warshall's O(V^3) is acceptable only when V <= ~400. State this out loud when choosing an algorithm — it is exactly the justification interviewers want to hear.

sections.title: How Python Does It
sections.content:
Python gives you every graph building block in the stdlib — but each has a sharp edge you must know.

**defaultdict(list)** builds adjacency lists without `if u not in g` boilerplate. Gotcha: reading `g[u]` on a missing key CREATES an empty list, so iterate `range(n)` (or a saved key list), not `g.keys()`, if you must not mutate while looping.

**deque** is the only correct BFS queue: `popleft()` is O(1) because deque is a doubly linked block list. `list.pop(0)` is O(N) — on a 10^5-node BFS that turns O(V+E) into O(V^2) and times out.

**heapq** turns a plain list into a binary min-heap: push/pop are O(log N). Store `(distance, node)` tuples — Python compares tuples element by element, so the smallest distance surfaces first. There is no decrease-key operation; every Dijkstra/Prim template instead pushes duplicates and skips stale ones on pop ("lazy deletion").

**Visited tracking**: for vertices labeled 0..n-1, a `[False] * n` list is faster than a set (direct indexing, no hashing). For grids, either a parallel visited matrix or mutating the grid itself ("sink the island") works.

**Recursion**: CPython's default limit is about 1000 frames. A DFS on a 10^5-node path graph or a 500x500 grid will crash without `sys.setrecursionlimit(...)` — or write the DFS with an explicit stack, which interviewers always accept.
sections.code:
from collections import defaultdict, deque
import heapq
import sys

# ---- Building the graph -------------------------------------------
def build_graph(n, edges, directed=False):
    # defaultdict(list): first access to a missing key creates [].
    g = defaultdict(list)
    for u, v in edges:
        g[u].append(v)                 # store edge u -> v
        if not directed:
            g[v].append(u)             # undirected: store BOTH directions
    return g

# ---- The three workhorse containers and their REAL costs ----------
q = deque([0])                         # BFS frontier
q.append(1)                            # enqueue right: O(1)
front = q.popleft()                    # dequeue left: O(1)
# list.pop(0) also "works" but is O(N): it shifts every element left.

pq = []                                # heapq uses a plain list as a heap
heapq.heappush(pq, (7, 2))             # (distance, node) tuples compare
heapq.heappush(pq, (3, 5))             #   field by field: distance first
d, node = heapq.heappop(pq)            # -> (3, 5), the smallest distance
# heapq is a MIN-heap only; push (-value, node) to simulate a max-heap.

seen = [False] * 10                    # visited for nodes 0..n-1: a bool
seen[3] = True                         #   list beats a set (no hashing)
# For non-integer or sparse node ids, fall back to a set().

# ---- Recursion limit: the classic DFS crash -----------------------
sys.setrecursionlimit(300000)          # default ~1000 dies on deep graphs

INF = float("inf")                     # standard "unreached" distance;
# INF + w stays INF-like and any real distance compares smaller.

sections.title: Pattern: BFS — Layered Exploration & 2-Coloring
sections.content:
**Recognize it when**: the problem says "shortest path" or "minimum number of moves/steps" on an UNWEIGHTED graph, asks for level-by-level processing, models something spreading outward one step at a time, or asks whether nodes can be split into two groups (bipartite).

**The invariant**: the queue always holds vertices from at most two consecutive distance layers, and the moment a vertex is dequeued its distance is final. This holds because you mark a vertex visited (and fix its distance) when you ENQUEUE it — the first time BFS reaches a node is via a shortest route, since all shorter layers were fully processed earlier.

**Sheet questions using this**: *BFS Traversal* is the raw template. *Bipartite Graph Check* is BFS plus a color array — paint the source 0, every neighbor the opposite color, and declare failure if an edge connects two same-colored nodes; that failure is exactly an odd-length cycle. *Detect Cycle in Undirected Graph (BFS)* reuses the traversal with a parent carried in the queue (details in the cycle-detection section). *Topological Sort (BFS/Kahn's Algorithm)* is BFS where "distance" is replaced by "indegree reached zero". The same layered idea powers Rotten Oranges (multi-source BFS) in the Stack & Queue Part-II topic.

**Multi-source variant** worth memorizing: push ALL sources into the queue at distance 0 before the loop; nothing else changes. This answers "nearest X for every cell" questions in one pass.

sections.title: Pattern: DFS — Components, Islands & Flood Fill
sections.content:
**Recognize it when**: the problem asks to count regions/islands/provinces, to paint or erase a connected area, to check reachability, or to exhaustively explore all paths. DFS is also the engine inside cycle detection and topological sort, so this template is the most reused code in the whole topic.

**The invariant**: when a DFS call on vertex u returns, EVERYTHING reachable from u through unvisited vertices has been visited. Two consequences do all the work: (1) the number of times the outer loop launches a fresh DFS equals the number of connected components; (2) marking u visited on entry (before recursing) guarantees each vertex is processed once, giving O(V + E).

**Sheet questions using this**: *DFS Traversal* is the raw template. *Number of Islands* runs DFS over the implicit grid graph and counts launches — each launch sinks one whole island. *Flood Fill Algorithm* is a single DFS launch that repaints instead of counting. The same skeleton with extra state solves *Detect Cycle in Undirected Graph (DFS)*, *Detect Cycle in Directed Graph*, and *Topological Sort (DFS)* in the next two sections.

**Grid mechanics to say out loud**: the grid is an implicit graph — cell (r, c) is a vertex, the 4-direction array generates edges, bounds-checking replaces the adjacency list, and mutating the grid ('1' -> '0', or old color -> new color) replaces the visited set at zero extra memory. On huge grids prefer the iterative-stack DFS (or BFS) to dodge the recursion limit.

sections.title: Pattern: Cycle Detection (Undirected vs Directed)
sections.content:
Cycle detection is two DIFFERENT algorithms depending on edge direction, and interviewers deliberately test whether you know why the undirected trick fails on directed graphs.

**Undirected** (*Detect Cycle in Undirected Graph (BFS)* and *(DFS)*): while traversing, remember which node you came from (the parent). Meeting a visited neighbor that is not your parent means two distinct routes reach that neighbor — a cycle. The invariant: in a cycle-free undirected graph, the ONLY visited neighbor a node can ever see is its own parent. Both BFS (carry parent in the queue) and DFS (pass parent as an argument) implement the same test in O(V + E). Run it per component.

**Directed** (*Detect Cycle in Directed Graph*): the parent trick breaks because a directed edge into an already-FINISHED vertex is harmless. Example: edges 0->1, 0->2, 1->2. DFS from 0 visits 1, then 2; later it sees 0's edge to the visited node 2 — not a cycle, because you cannot travel back out of 2 to 0. What does prove a cycle is an edge into a vertex that is still ON the current recursion stack. Hence three colors: WHITE (untouched), GRAY (entered, not finished — the active path), BLACK (fully explored). Edge into GRAY = cycle; edge into BLACK = safe.

**Alternative for directed graphs**: run *Kahn's algorithm* (next section) and check whether it outputs fewer than V vertices — vertices trapped on a cycle never reach indegree 0. Mentioning both earns points.

sections.title: Pattern: Topological Sort & DAG Shortest Path
sections.content:
**Recognize it when**: the problem mentions prerequisites, dependencies, build/course order, "must happen before", or hands you any DAG. A topological order lists vertices so that every edge u -> v has u appear before v. It exists if and only if the directed graph has no cycle.

**Kahn's algorithm** (*Topological Sort (BFS/Kahn's Algorithm)*): compute every vertex's indegree; enqueue all indegree-0 vertices; repeatedly pop one, append it to the order, and decrement each neighbor's indegree, enqueuing any that hit zero. Invariant: a vertex enters the queue only after ALL of its prerequisites have been output. Bonus: if the final order has fewer than V vertices, the leftovers form/feed a cycle — this doubles as the BFS answer to *Detect Cycle in Directed Graph*.

**DFS version** (*Topological Sort (DFS)*): run a normal DFS and append each vertex to a list when it FINISHES (after all its out-neighbors are fully explored), then reverse the list. Invariant: u finishes only after everything it points to has finished, so reversed finish order puts u before them all.

**Shortest Path in DAG** (*Shortest Path in DAG*): topologically sort, then relax each vertex's outgoing edges in that order. When the scan reaches u, no future vertex can improve dist[u] — every path into u travels through vertices earlier in the order, all already processed. One pass, O(V + E), and negative weights are fine because correctness comes from the ordering, not from greedy choice. On a DAG this beats Dijkstra on both speed and generality — say that comparison out loud in the interview.

sections.title: Pattern: Weighted Shortest Paths — Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall
sections.content:
All three algorithms run the same relaxation step — `if dist[u] + w < dist[v]: dist[v] = dist[u] + w` — on different schedules. Choosing between them IS the interview question, so memorize the decision table:

```
Situation                                Tool               Cost
---------------------------------------  -----------------  ----------
unweighted                               plain BFS          O(V+E)
DAG (any weights, even negative)         topo-order relax   O(V+E)
weights >= 0, one source                 Dijkstra           O(E log V)
negative edges possible, one source      Bellman-Ford       O(V*E)
all pairs, V small (<= ~400)             Floyd-Warshall     O(V^3)
```

***Dijkstra's Algorithm***: greedily pop the unfinalized vertex with the smallest tentative distance. Invariant: a popped-and-fresh vertex's distance is FINAL — any other route to it would pass through a vertex that is at least as far away, and with non-negative weights the detour cannot get shorter. That proof is exactly what negative edges destroy, which is why Dijkstra silently produces wrong answers on them. Python has no decrease-key, so push duplicates and skip stale pairs with `if d > dist[u]: continue`.

***Bellman Ford Algorithm***: relax EVERY edge, V-1 times. Invariant: after round k, all shortest paths that use at most k edges are correct; a shortest simple path has at most V-1 edges, so V-1 rounds suffice. If a V-th round still improves anything, a negative cycle is reachable — report it instead of a distance.

***Floyd Warshall Algorithm***: DP over the set of allowed intermediate vertices. After the k-th outer iteration, dist[i][j] is optimal using intermediates from {0..k} only — which is why k must be the OUTERMOST loop. A negative value appearing on the diagonal (dist[i][i] < 0) exposes a negative cycle through i.
sections.code:
import heapq

def dijkstra(wgraph, n, src):
    # wgraph[u] = [(v, w), ...] with every w >= 0 (REQUIRED).
    INF = float("inf")
    dist = [INF] * n
    dist[src] = 0
    pq = [(0, src)]                    # heap of (tentative dist, node)
    while pq:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(pq)       # closest not-yet-final vertex
        if d > dist[u]:
            continue                   # stale pair: u improved after push
        for v, w in wgraph[u]:
            nd = d + w                 # candidate distance through u
            if nd < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = nd           # relax edge u -> v
                heapq.heappush(pq, (nd, v))    # lazy insert a fresh pair
    return dist                        # O(E log V): <= E pushes, log each

def bellman_ford(n, edges, src):
    # edges = [(u, v, w), ...]; negative w allowed. O(V * E).
    INF = float("inf")
    dist = [INF] * n
    dist[src] = 0
    for _ in range(n - 1):             # round k fixes paths of <= k+1 edges
        changed = False
        for u, v, w in edges:
            if dist[u] != INF and dist[u] + w < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w  # same relaxation, brute schedule
                changed = True
        if not changed:
            break                      # nothing moved: already optimal
    # one EXTRA pass: any improvement now proves a negative cycle
    neg = any(dist[u] != INF and dist[u] + w < dist[v]
              for u, v, w in edges)
    return dist, neg

def floyd_warshall(n, mat):
    # mat[i][j] = edge weight or INF; mat[i][i] = 0. O(V^3), all pairs.
    dist = [row[:] for row in mat]     # copy so the input stays intact
    for k in range(n):                 # k OUTERMOST: after iteration k,
        for i in range(n):             #   dist[i][j] is optimal using only
            for j in range(n):         #   intermediate vertices 0..k
                via = dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]
                if via < dist[i][j]:
                    dist[i][j] = via   # routing through k is shorter
    return dist                        # dist[i][i] < 0 => negative cycle

sections.title: Pattern: Minimum Spanning Tree — Prim & Kruskal
sections.content:
**Recognize it when**: "connect all cities/computers/houses at minimum total cable/road cost". A spanning tree of a connected undirected weighted graph picks exactly V-1 edges that connect every vertex with no cycle; the Minimum Spanning Tree is the cheapest such choice.

**The theory both algorithms lean on — the cut property**: split the vertices into any two non-empty groups; the cheapest edge crossing between the groups is ALWAYS safe to include in some MST. (If an MST avoided it, adding it would create a cycle containing another, more expensive crossing edge — swap them and the tree gets cheaper or stays equal.)

***Minimum Spanning Tree (Prim's Algorithm)***: grow ONE tree from any seed vertex. The cut is "tree vs not-yet-tree"; a min-heap holds candidate crossing edges, and each pop adds the cheapest one plus its new vertex. It is structurally Dijkstra with one change — the heap key is the single edge weight, not the accumulated path distance. O(E log V); prefer it when the graph is dense or already in adjacency-list form.

***Minimum Spanning Tree (Kruskal's Algorithm)***: sort ALL edges ascending and scan; take an edge unless its two endpoints are already connected — a test done in near-O(1) by a Disjoint Set Union. Every accepted edge is the cheapest crossing the cut between its two components, so the cut property applies. O(E log E) from the sort; prefer it when input is an edge list or when you also need "are u, v connected yet?" queries. The full DSU (union by rank + path compression) is in the implementations below — interviewers regularly ask for it from scratch.

sections.title: Pitfalls & Common Mistakes
sections.content:
Every one of these mistakes appears constantly in mock interviews — each comes with its fix.

**Marking visited at dequeue instead of enqueue (BFS)**: a node can be pushed by several neighbors before it is ever popped, ballooning the queue to O(E) duplicates and corrupting distance math. Fix: set `seen[v] = True` in the same breath as `q.append(v)`.

**Forgetting disconnected graphs**: BFS/DFS from vertex 0 only touches one component; cycle checks and component counts silently miss the rest. Fix: wrap every traversal in `for s in range(n): if not seen[s]: ...`.

**list.pop(0) as a queue**: turns O(V+E) BFS into O(V^2). Fix: `collections.deque.popleft()`.

**Recursion limit**: DFS on 10^5 chained nodes or a large grid crashes CPython at ~1000 frames. Fix: `sys.setrecursionlimit(3*10**5)` or convert to an explicit stack.

**Dijkstra with negative edges**: no crash, just wrong answers — the greedy finalization proof needs w >= 0. Fix: Bellman-Ford, or topo-relaxation if the graph is a DAG.

**Missing the stale-pair skip**: without `if d > dist[u]: continue`, each vertex may be reprocessed once per duplicate heap entry, inflating the running time. Fix: keep the two-line guard.

**Undirected edge stored once**: traversal then sees a one-way street and misses paths/cycles. Fix: append to both adjacency lists.

**Kahn's without the count check**: on a cyclic graph the queue drains early and you return a partial "order" as if valid. Fix: `if len(order) < n: report cycle`.

**Directed cycle check with the parent trick**: cross edges to finished vertices get misreported as cycles (or worse, real cycles missed). Fix: WHITE/GRAY/BLACK coloring — only GRAY hits are cycles.

sections.title: Interview Recognition Checklist
sections.content:
**Cues that scream "graph"**: the input is pairs/relations (flights, friendships, prerequisites, wires); the input is a grid where you move between adjacent cells; the ask contains "shortest path", "minimum cost to connect", "order such that", "can all be divided into two groups", "number of regions/islands/provinces", or "is it possible to finish" (cycle check in disguise). Word problems about states and moves (locks, jugs, word ladders) are graphs over states.

**30-second pre-coding checklist** — answer these aloud before typing:

```
1. Vertices = ?   Edges = ?          (write it in one sentence)
2. Directed or undirected?  Weighted or unweighted?  Negative weights?
3. Sizes: V = ?, E = ?  ->  which complexities fit the budget?
4. Template:
     unweighted shortest / layers ......... BFS
     regions / reachability / explore ..... DFS
     ordering / prerequisites ............. topo sort (Kahn or DFS)
     cycle?  undirected -> parent trick;  directed -> GRAY set / Kahn
     two groups ........................... bipartite 2-coloring
     weighted shortest .................... DAG-relax / Dijkstra / Bellman-Ford
     all-pairs, small V ................... Floyd-Warshall
     connect everything cheaply ........... Prim / Kruskal (+DSU)
5. Disconnected input possible?  Self-loops / parallel edges?
6. Visited structure chosen?  Recursion depth safe, or go iterative?
```

If you can fill line 1 crisply, the rest of the problem is one of the templates in this chapter — name the template to the interviewer, state its invariant, then code it.

implementations.title: Adjacency-List Graph: BFS, DFS (recursive + iterative), Topological Sort (Kahn + DFS)
Dijkstra's Algorithm with Path Reconstruction (heapq, lazy deletion)
implementations.code:
import heapq


def dijkstra(n, wadj, src):
    # Single-source shortest paths; every weight must be >= 0.
    # wadj[u] = [(v, w), ...]. Time O((V + E) log V), space O(V + E).
    INF = float("inf")
    dist = [INF] * n                   # best known distance per node
    parent = [-1] * n                  # predecessor on the best path
    dist[src] = 0
    pq = [(0, src)]                    # heap of (tentative dist, node)
    while pq:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(pq)       # u = closest unfinalized node
        if d > dist[u]:
            continue                   # stale pair: skip (lazy deletion)
        for v, w in wadj[u]:
            nd = d + w                 # candidate distance through u
            if nd < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = nd           # relax the edge u -> v
                parent[v] = u          # remember how we got to v
                heapq.heappush(pq, (nd, v))    # fresh pair; old one rots
    return dist, parent


def rebuild_path(parent, target):
    # Walk parent pointers back to the source. O(path length).
    path = []
    while target != -1:                # -1 marks "no parent" (the source)
        path.append(target)
        target = parent[target]
    path.reverse()                     # collected backwards, flip it
    return path


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # 0 --4-- 1 --2-- 2 --2-- 3, plus a direct 0 --9-- 3 shortcut edge.
    wadj = {
        0: [(1, 4), (3, 9)],
        1: [(0, 4), (2, 2)],
        2: [(1, 2), (3, 2)],
        3: [(0, 9), (2, 2)],
    }
    dist, parent = dijkstra(4, wadj, 0)
    print(dist)                        # [0, 4, 6, 8] — 8 beats direct 9
    print(rebuild_path(parent, 3))     # [0, 1, 2, 3]

implementations.title: Disjoint Set Union (rank + path compression) and Kruskal's MST
implementations.code:
class DSU:
    """Disjoint Set Union with union by rank + path compression.

    Together the two optimizations make each op effectively O(1)
    (inverse-Ackermann alpha(n), which is <= 4 for any real input).
    """

    def __init__(self, n):
        self.parent = list(range(n))   # each node starts as its own root
        self.rank = [0] * n            # upper bound on each tree height

    def find(self, x):
        # Locate the root, then point every visited node straight at it.
        root = x
        while self.parent[root] != root:
            root = self.parent[root]   # climb to the representative
        while self.parent[x] != root:  # second pass: path compression
            self.parent[x], x = root, self.parent[x]   # rewire and step
        return root

    def union(self, a, b):
        # Merge the sets holding a and b; False if already together.
        ra, rb = self.find(a), self.find(b)
        if ra == rb:
            return False               # same set: this edge closes a cycle
        if self.rank[ra] < self.rank[rb]:
            ra, rb = rb, ra            # ensure ra is the taller tree
        self.parent[rb] = ra           # hang the shorter under the taller
        if self.rank[ra] == self.rank[rb]:
            self.rank[ra] += 1         # equal heights: root grows by one
        return True


def kruskal_mst(n, edges):
    # edges = [(w, u, v), ...]. Time O(E log E) — the sort dominates.
    dsu = DSU(n)
    total = 0                          # accumulated MST weight
    chosen = []                        # the edges we actually keep
    for w, u, v in sorted(edges):      # cheapest edges first
        if dsu.union(u, v):            # reject edges that close a cycle
            total += w
            chosen.append((u, v, w))
            if len(chosen) == n - 1:
                break                  # spanning tree complete: n-1 edges
    if len(chosen) != n - 1:
        return None, []                # graph was not connected
    return total, chosen


if __name__ == "__main__":
    edges = [(1, 0, 1), (2, 1, 2), (4, 0, 2), (3, 2, 3), (5, 1, 3)]
    print(kruskal_mst(4, edges))       # (6, [(0,1,1), (1,2,2), (2,3,3)])

implementations.title: Bellman-Ford and Floyd-Warshall from Scratch
implementations.code:
def bellman_ford(n, edges, src):
    # edges = [(u, v, w), ...]; negative weights allowed. O(V * E).
    # Key fact: a shortest SIMPLE path uses at most V-1 edges, so
    # V-1 full relaxation rounds suffice when no negative cycle exists.
    INF = float("inf")
    dist = [INF] * n
    dist[src] = 0
    for _round in range(n - 1):        # round k fixes paths of <= k+1 edges
        changed = False
        for u, v, w in edges:
            if dist[u] != INF and dist[u] + w < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w  # relax edge u -> v
                changed = True
        if not changed:
            break                      # early exit: everything optimal
    # One EXTRA pass: any improvement now proves a negative cycle.
    neg_cycle = any(
        dist[u] != INF and dist[u] + w < dist[v]   # still improvable?
        for u, v, w in edges
    )
    return dist, neg_cycle


def floyd_warshall(n, mat):
    # All-pairs shortest paths on a V x V matrix in O(V^3).
    # mat[i][j] = direct edge weight (INF if absent); mat[i][i] = 0.
    INF = float("inf")
    dist = [row[:] for row in mat]     # copy: never mutate the input
    for k in range(n):                 # k MUST be outermost: after step k,
        for i in range(n):             #   dist[i][j] is optimal using only
            for j in range(n):         #   intermediate vertices 0..k
                if dist[i][k] == INF or dist[k][j] == INF:
                    continue           # no route through k at all
                via = dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]
                if via < dist[i][j]:
                    dist[i][j] = via   # routing through k is shorter
    # dist[i][i] dropping below 0 exposes a negative cycle through i.
    has_neg = any(dist[i][i] < 0 for i in range(n))
    return dist, has_neg


if __name__ == "__main__":
    INF = float("inf")
    edges = [(0, 1, 4), (0, 2, 5), (1, 2, -3), (2, 3, 4)]
    print(bellman_ford(4, edges, 0))   # ([0, 4, 1, 5], False)
    mat = [
        [0, 4, 5, INF],                # same graph as a matrix
        [INF, 0, -3, INF],
        [INF, INF, 0, 4],
        [INF, INF, INF, 0],
    ]
    print(floyd_warshall(4, mat)[0][0])    # row 0: [0, 4, 1, 5]

Miscellaneous.summary:
"Miscellaneous" is the sheet's design-and-tricks tab: four problems that do not belong to one data structure, but each teaches a reusable engineering idea. *LFU Cache* teaches composition — welding hash maps and doubly linked lists together so every operation stays O(1) while a non-trivial eviction rule (least frequently used, ties broken by least recently used) is enforced. *Online Stock Span* turns the monotonic-stack idea from Next Greater Element into a streaming API, where prices arrive one at a time and each answer must come back immediately. *Power Set* is the canonical bitmask-enumeration exercise: every subset of n items corresponds to one integer between 0 and 2^n - 1. *Maximum XOR Subarray* combines two tricks — prefix XOR, which turns a range question into a pair question, and a binary trie, which answers "which stored number XORs best with x?" in O(bits) time.

Interviewers use these problems to test whether you can design, not just recall. There is no single named algorithm to reach for; you must choose structures, state invariants out loud ("min_freq always points at a non-empty bucket", "prices on the stack are strictly decreasing"), and defend a per-operation complexity budget. That is precisely the skill of real systems work: Redis ships an LFU eviction policy, streaming analytics pipelines compute span-like statistics over tick data, routers match IP prefixes with bit tries on every packet, and XOR parity powers RAID and checksums.

The mental model that unifies the tab: pick the invariant FIRST, then pick structures that can maintain that invariant in O(1) or O(log) per step. Once the invariant is written down, the code is close to mechanical — and saying the invariant before coding is most of what separates a strong candidate from a memorizer.
preRequisites: dict fundamentals: average O(1) get/put/delete via hashing, and the guarantee (Python 3.7+) that dicts preserve insertion order.
Doubly linked list surgery from the Linked List topic: unlinking a node by rewiring prev/next is O(1) once you hold the node.
The monotonic stack idea from Next Greater Element (Stack & Queue topic) — this tab's stock-span problem is its streaming twin.
Python bit operators: << >> & | ^, the fact that ints are arbitrary precision, and x >> i & 1 to read bit i.
Prefix sums from the Arrays topic — prefix XOR is the identical trick with ^ replacing +, since XOR is its own inverse.
Writing small classes: __init__, instance attributes, and __slots__ for lightweight node objects.
collections.OrderedDict: move_to_end(key) and popitem(last=False) both run in O(1).
cheatSheet: LFU = dict key->node + dict freq->DLL + min_freq pointer => O(1) get and put.
LFU access: move the node from bucket f to bucket f+1; if bucket f emptied and f == min_freq, min_freq += 1.
LFU insert of a NEW key: freq = 1 and min_freq = 1, always.
Stock span: pop while stack-top price <= today, absorbing popped spans; push (price, span); amortized O(1).
Power set: masks 0 .. 2^n - 1; bit i set in mask <=> take nums[i]; exactly 2^n subsets.
Prefix XOR: xor(l..r) = P[r] ^ P[l-1] — subarray questions become pair-of-prefixes questions.
Max-XOR query on a bit trie: walk bits high -> low, greedily branch to the OPPOSITE bit; O(32) per query.
Monotonic stack accounting: each element is pushed once and popped at most once => total O(N) over the stream.

sections.title: What & Why
sections.content:
This tab is four problems, four transferable ideas.

**LFU Cache** — design a fixed-capacity key-value store where get and put are O(1) and eviction removes the LEAST FREQUENTLY used key (ties: least recently used among them). The transferable idea is composition: no single structure does this, but a hash map (find anything instantly) fused with doubly linked lists (reorder anything instantly) does. Real systems: Redis's allkeys-lfu eviction policy, CDN object caches, CPU cache replacement research.

**Online Stock Span** — prices arrive one per call; answer "how many consecutive days ending today had price <= today's?" immediately. The idea is the monotonic stack in streaming form: keep only the information the future can still use, compressed. Real systems: streaming analytics over tick data, "how long has this metric been rising" dashboards.

**Power Set** — list all subsets of a set. The idea is the bijection between subsets and binary numbers: n yes/no choices are one n-bit integer. Real systems: generating test-case combinations, feature-flag matrices, brute-force over small search spaces (n <= 20).

**Maximum XOR Subarray** — find the contiguous subarray whose XOR is maximum. Two ideas stack: prefix XOR reduces "best subarray" to "best pair of prefixes", and a binary trie finds the best partner for a number in O(bits). Real systems: bit tries are how routers do longest-prefix matching; XOR itself underlies RAID parity and checksums.

Interviews love this tab because every problem forces you to justify per-operation complexity and to articulate an invariant — the two habits that transfer to system design rounds.

sections.title: Memory Model & Representation
sections.content:
Three memory pictures cover the whole tab.

**LFU cache** — two dicts and a family of doubly linked lists. One dict maps key -> node (so any key is reachable in O(1)); another maps frequency -> a doubly linked list of the nodes at that frequency, kept in recency order; an integer min_freq names the lowest non-empty bucket, i.e. the eviction bucket.

```
kv:  {1: n1, 2: n2, 3: n3}        min_freq = 1
freq buckets (recency inside each: front = newest):
  1:  head <-> n3 <-> tail             <- evict from TAIL of this list
  2:  head <-> n2 <-> n1 <-> tail
```

**Bitwise trie** — a binary tree of depth B (the bit width). Each number is a root-to-leaf path of its bits, most significant first; each node has at most two children (bit 0 / bit 1). Storing 5 (101) and 2 (010) in 3 bits:

```
        root
       /    \
     [0]    [1]        level = bit 2
       \      \
       [1]    [0]      level = bit 1
       /        \
     [0]        [1]    level = bit 0
      = 010 (2)  = 101 (5)
```

**Monotonic stack of (price, span) pairs** — a plain Python list where prices strictly decrease from bottom to top. Every popped day is "absorbed" into the popper's span, so the stack is a lossless compression of all history the future could still query:

```
prices seen: 100  80  60  70  60  75  85
stack now:   [(100, 1), (85, 6)]      <- 85 absorbed 5 earlier days
```

The power set needs no structure at all: the counter mask = 0 .. 2^n - 1 IS the representation, one subset per integer.

sections.title: Core Operations & Complexity
sections.content:
Every complexity below is the number an interviewer expects you to state unprompted, with its one-clause justification.

```
Structure / operation                Time         Why (one clause)
-----------------------------------  -----------  --------------------------------------
LFU get / put                        O(1)         dict lookup + DLL splice, no scans
LFU eviction                         O(1)         min_freq names the bucket; pop its tail
StockSpanner.next  (amortized)       O(1)         each price pushed once, popped <= once
StockSpanner.next  (worst single)    O(N)         one call may pop the whole stack
Power set, bitmask enumeration       O(n * 2^n)   2^n subsets exist; each costs O(n) to emit
Power set, backtracking              O(n * 2^n)   same output bound; recursion tree = 2^n leaves
XorTrie insert / max-xor query       O(B)         one node per bit, B ~ 32 levels
Maximum XOR Subarray total           O(N * B)     one insert + one query per prefix
```

Two of these lines deserve special care in interviews. First, the stock-span worst case: a single call can pop many entries, but the AMORTIZED cost is O(1) because a popped entry never returns — total pushes = total pops <= N over the whole stream. Say "amortized" explicitly. Second, the power-set bound is output-bound: no algorithm can beat O(2^n) because the answer itself has 2^n entries — which is also why the technique is only legal when n <= ~20 (2^20 is about a million; 2^30 is a billion and out of budget).

sections.title: How Python Does It
sections.content:
The stdlib gives you 90% of this tab; knowing which 10% to hand-roll is the design skill.

**dict** is the backbone: O(1) average get/put/delete, and since Python 3.7 it preserves insertion order. **OrderedDict** adds the two O(1) reordering calls a cache needs: `move_to_end(key)` (mark as most recent) and `popitem(last=False)` (evict the least recent). An LRU cache is nothing but an OrderedDict plus those two calls. For LFU you need one recency list PER frequency — a `defaultdict(OrderedDict)` works and is the fast interview version; the from-scratch doubly-linked-list version (in the implementations below) is what you present when the interviewer says "no OrderedDict".

**Bit operations**: Python ints are arbitrary precision, so `1 << n` never overflows, and `x >> i & 1` reads bit i of any size number. `x.bit_length()` tells you the width you actually need — use it to size a bit trie instead of hard-coding 32. `bin(x)` prints the binary string for debugging.

Gotchas worth stating: `functools.lru_cache` is a memoization decorator, not a cache you can query — do not offer it as an LFU/LRU answer. `2 ** n` and `1 << n` are equal in value, but the shift form signals bit-level thinking. And there is no built-in trie anywhere in the stdlib — when a problem needs per-bit prefix matching, you build the node class yourself.
sections.code:
from collections import OrderedDict

# dict: average O(1) get/put/delete, preserves insertion order (3.7+).
d = {}
d["a"] = 1                             # O(1) insert
d["b"] = 2

# OrderedDict adds O(1) REORDERING — enough to build LRU on its own,
# and to serve as the recency list inside each LFU frequency bucket.
od = OrderedDict()
od["x"] = 1
od["y"] = 2
od.move_to_end("x")                    # "x" becomes most recent, O(1)
oldest = next(iter(od))                # peek least recent, O(1)
od.popitem(last=False)                 # evict least recent, O(1)

# Bit tools — Python ints are arbitrary precision, so no overflow ever.
n = 3
for mask in range(1 << n):             # 1 << n == 2**n; masks 0..7
    picked = [i for i in range(n) if mask >> i & 1]    # read bit i

x = 41
print(x.bit_length())                  # 6: highest set bit of 41 is bit 5
print(bin(x))                          # "0b101001" — handy when debugging
print(x ^ x, x ^ 0)                    # 0 41 — xor is its own inverse
# That self-inverse rule is the whole prefix-XOR trick:
# P[r] ^ P[l-1] cancels the shared prefix, leaving xor of nums[l..r].

sections.title: Pattern: Composed O(1) Cache Design (LFU)
sections.content:
**Recognize it when**: the problem says "design a cache/store with capacity, get and put must be O(1)" and eviction depends on how OFTEN keys are used (least frequently used), not just how recently. The sheet question is *LFU Cache*; it is the natural escalation of *LRU Cache* from the Stack & Queue topic, and interviewers frequently chain them in one session.

**Why one structure is not enough**: a dict finds keys in O(1) but cannot rank them by usage; a list ranks but cannot find in O(1); a heap keyed on frequency gives O(log N) and breaks ties by recency only with painful bookkeeping. The O(1) design needs three coordinated pieces — key -> node dict, frequency -> recency-list dict, and a min_freq integer.

**The invariants** (recite before coding): every key sits in exactly one bucket, the one matching its stored frequency; inside a bucket, order is recency (newest at one end, eviction victim at the other); min_freq always names a non-empty bucket. The subtle step that keeps min_freq honest: after any access bumps a key from f to f+1, min_freq can only need to move UP by one (when bucket f was the floor and just emptied) — and after inserting a brand-new key, min_freq is reset to 1 unconditionally, because a frequency-1 key now exists.

**Complexity**: get and put are a constant number of dict operations plus one list splice — O(1) each, O(capacity) space. The template here uses OrderedDict buckets for interview speed; the implementations section carries the fully hand-rolled doubly-linked-list version for the "build it from scratch" follow-up.
sections.code:
from collections import defaultdict, OrderedDict

class LFUCache:
    # Invariants (say these before coding):
    #   kv[key]      = (value, freq)
    #   buckets[f]   = OrderedDict of keys at frequency f, recency order
    #   min_freq     = smallest f whose bucket is non-empty
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.cap = capacity
        self.kv = {}
        self.buckets = defaultdict(OrderedDict)
        self.min_freq = 0

    def _touch(self, key):
        # Move key from bucket f to bucket f+1. All steps O(1).
        value, f = self.kv[key]
        del self.buckets[f][key]
        if not self.buckets[f] and f == self.min_freq:
            self.min_freq += 1         # bucket f emptied: floor rises
        self.kv[key] = (value, f + 1)
        self.buckets[f + 1][key] = None    # append = newest at freq f+1
        return value

    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.kv:
            return -1
        return self._touch(key)        # every hit bumps the frequency

    def put(self, key, value):
        if self.cap == 0:
            return                     # degenerate cache stores nothing
        if key in self.kv:
            self._touch(key)           # update counts as a use
            _v, f = self.kv[key]
            self.kv[key] = (value, f)  # then overwrite the value
            return
        if len(self.kv) == self.cap:
            # Evict least-frequent; ties -> least recent inside bucket.
            victim, _ = self.buckets[self.min_freq].popitem(last=False)
            del self.kv[victim]
        self.kv[key] = (value, 1)      # new keys always start at freq 1
        self.buckets[1][key] = None
        self.min_freq = 1              # a freq-1 key now surely exists

sections.title: Pattern: Monotonic Stack in a Stream (Stock Span)
sections.content:
**Recognize it when**: a stream asks, per new element, "how far back does a run of smaller/greater elements extend?" — consecutive days with price <= today, previous greater element's distance, streaks. The sheet question is *Online Stock Span*; it is the streaming twin of *Next Greater Element* and *Stock Span Problem* (Stack & Queue topics), and the same reasoning powers *Largest Rectangle in Histogram* and the monotonic deque in *Sliding Window Maximum*.

**The reduction to state**: the span of today equals the distance back to the previous STRICTLY GREATER price. Any day with price <= today can never again be "the previous greater" for any future day — today stands in front of it, taller. So those days can be deleted, as long as their span (how many days they represent) is added to today's. That is the entire algorithm: pop while top <= today, summing spans; push (today, total).

**The invariant**: prices on the stack strictly decrease from bottom to top, and the spans on the stack partition all days seen so far. Because each arriving price is pushed exactly once and popped at most once, N calls do at most 2N stack operations — amortized O(1) per call, worst single call O(N). Always present the amortized argument; it is the point of the problem.

**Storing (price, span) pairs rather than indices** is what makes the streaming version work: you never know the global index of a day, only how many days each stack entry has swallowed. The naive alternative — rescanning backwards per query — is O(N) per call and O(N^2) total, exactly what this pattern exists to beat.
sections.code:
class StockSpanner:
    # Invariant: stack holds (price, span) with prices STRICTLY
    # decreasing bottom -> top. A popped day is absorbed into the
    # popper's span, so no information the future needs is lost.
    def __init__(self):
        self.stack = []                # [(price, span), ...]

    def next(self, price):
        span = 1                       # today always counts itself
        while self.stack and self.stack[-1][0] <= price:
            _, s = self.stack.pop()    # that day can never answer a
            span += s                  #   future query: absorb its span
        self.stack.append((price, span))
        return span                    # amortized O(1): push/pop once each

# Trace:  prices  100  80  60  70  60  75  85
#         spans     1   1   1   2   1   4   6
# After 85 the stack is [(100, 1), (85, 6)] — 85 absorbed five days.

sections.title: Pattern: Bitmask Subset Enumeration (Power Set)
sections.content:
**Recognize it when**: "generate ALL subsets / combinations / selections" and n is small (n <= ~20). The sheet question is *Power Set*; the identical enumeration underlies *Subset Sums* and *Subsets II* in the Recursion topic (there with sorting + skip-duplicates added) and any brute force over "take it or leave it" decisions.

**The bijection that is the whole idea**: a subset of n items is n independent yes/no decisions, and n yes/no decisions are exactly one n-bit integer. So counting mask from 0 to 2^n - 1 and reading its bits enumerates every subset exactly once — no recursion, no bookkeeping, impossible to miss or duplicate a subset. Bit i of the mask answers "is nums[i] included?".

**Choosing between the two templates**: the bitmask loop is shorter, iterative, and the interviewer-preferred first answer for plain enumeration. Backtracking earns its keep the moment constraints appear — pruning branches early (sum too big already), handling duplicates (sort, then skip equal neighbors at the same depth, as *Subsets II* requires), or emitting subsets in lexicographic order. Know both; say when each wins.

**Complexity discipline**: 2^n subsets exist, so O(n * 2^n) is output-bound and optimal. State the practical ceiling out loud: 2^20 ~ 10^6 is fine, 2^25 is straining, 2^30 ~ 10^9 is out of budget. If n is 40+, the problem wants meet-in-the-middle or DP instead of enumeration — recognizing that boundary is part of the pattern.
sections.code:
def power_set(nums):
    # Bijection: subset <-> n-bit mask. O(n * 2^n) time — the output
    # itself has 2^n subsets, so this bound cannot be beaten.
    n = len(nums)
    out = []
    for mask in range(1 << n):         # every mask 0 .. 2^n - 1
        subset = []
        for i in range(n):
            if mask >> i & 1:          # bit i set -> include nums[i]
                subset.append(nums[i])
        out.append(subset)
    return out

def power_set_backtrack(nums):
    # Same output via a recursive include/exclude choice per index.
    out = []
    cur = []                           # the subset being built
    def go(i):
        if i == len(nums):
            out.append(cur[:])         # COPY — cur keeps mutating
            return
        go(i + 1)                      # choice 1: exclude nums[i]
        cur.append(nums[i])            # choice 2: include nums[i]
        go(i + 1)
        cur.pop()                      # undo before returning (backtrack)
    go(0)
    return out

# power_set([1, 2]) -> [[], [1], [2], [1, 2]]  (mask order 00,01,10,11)

sections.title: Pattern: Prefix XOR + Binary Trie (Maximum XOR Subarray)
sections.content:
**Recognize it when**: the problem says "maximum XOR" over pairs or subarrays. The sheet question is *Maximum XOR Subarray*; the identical trie also solves *Maximum XOR of Two Numbers* and *Maximum XOR Queries* in the Tries topic — one structure, three problems.

**Step 1 — prefix XOR turns ranges into pairs.** Define P[i] = nums[0] ^ ... ^ nums[i], with P[-1] = 0. Because XOR is its own inverse (a ^ a = 0), xor(l..r) = P[r] ^ P[l-1]: the shared prefix cancels. So "best subarray XOR" becomes "best XOR between two prefix values" — the same shape of reduction that prefix sums perform for *Largest Subarray with 0 Sum* and *Count Subarrays with Given XOR* in Arrays.

**Step 2 — the trie answers 'best partner' greedily.** Store every prefix as a 32-level root-to-leaf bit path, most significant bit first. To find the stored value that XORs best with x, walk from the root and at each level try the child holding the OPPOSITE of x's bit: opposite bits XOR to 1, and a 1 at bit i outweighs 1s at ALL lower bits combined (2^i > 2^(i-1) + ... + 1) — that inequality is why the greedy high-to-low choice is safe and why the walk must start at the TOP bit.

**The invariant of the scan**: before processing index r, the trie holds exactly P[-1..r-1]; query with P[r] to find its best left boundary, then insert P[r]. One insert and one query per element: O(N * 32) total, O(N * 32) trie nodes. The brute force checks all O(N^2) subarrays — mention that gap when you present the design.

sections.title: Pitfalls & Common Mistakes
sections.content:
**LFU traps.** Forgetting `min_freq = 1` when a new key is inserted — eviction later drains an empty bucket and crashes. Forgetting the tie-break: eviction inside the min-frequency bucket must remove the LEAST RECENT key, so buckets must preserve recency order. On put of an existing key, the frequency must bump AND the value must overwrite — doing one without the other passes half the tests. Capacity 0 must make put a no-op. And after moving a key out of bucket f, only raise min_freq when f was the floor AND its bucket emptied.

**Stock span traps.** Using `<` instead of `<=` when popping — equal prices count toward the span, so days equal to today must be absorbed. Storing bare prices without spans forces a rescan and quietly reverts the solution to O(N^2). Claiming next() is O(1) flat is wrong; the correct claim is amortized O(1), worst single call O(N).

**Power set traps.** Appending `cur` instead of `cur[:]` in backtracking — every stored subset aliases the same list and finishes empty. Writing `range(2 ** n)` is fine but `range(1 << n) - 1` style off-by-ones are not: the mask range is 0 to 2^n - 1 inclusive, which `range(1 << n)` already gives. Attempting n = 40: 2^40 subsets can never be enumerated — switch techniques instead.

**XOR trie traps.** Iterating bits low-to-high breaks the greedy proof — the walk must go high-to-low. Forgetting to insert P[-1] = 0 makes every subarray that starts at index 0 invisible. Hard-coding 32 bits fails when values exceed 2^32 — size with `max(nums).bit_length()` when unsure. Querying before the first insert would walk a childless root; the insert-0-first ordering removes that case.

sections.title: Interview Recognition Checklist
sections.content:
**Cues that map a problem to this tab's patterns**: the phrase "design ... in O(1)" with a capacity and an eviction rule means a composed hash-map + linked-list structure (LRU if recency, LFU if frequency, with a recency tie-break). "Span", "streak", "consecutive previous elements smaller/greater", or any per-element look-back in a stream means a monotonic stack holding (value, span) pairs. "All subsets/combinations" with n <= 20 means bitmask enumeration or backtracking. "Maximum XOR" means a bit trie, and "subarray XOR" adds the prefix-XOR reduction in front of it.

**30-second pre-coding checklist**:

```
1. What is the per-operation budget?  O(1)?  amortized O(1)?  O(bits)?
2. Which invariant makes that budget possible?  Say it in one sentence:
     LFU  -> "min_freq names a non-empty bucket; buckets keep recency"
     span -> "stack prices strictly decrease; spans partition history"
     mask -> "subset <-> integer bijection, 2^n total"
     trie -> "opposite bit first, high bit to low bit"
3. What breaks ties / edge cases?
     capacity 0, equal prices, empty subset, prefix P[-1] = 0
4. What is the memory cost?  O(capacity) / O(N) stack / O(2^n) output
     / O(N * bits) trie nodes.
5. Can I trace 4-5 operations on paper before coding?  Do it.
```

If an interviewer extends the problem — "make LFU thread-safe", "make the span window bounded", "count subsets with a given XOR instead of the max" — the invariant you stated in step 2 is what you adapt; the structures rarely change. That is the meta-lesson of the whole tab: invariant first, structure second, code last.

implementations.title: LFU Cache from Scratch (hand-rolled doubly linked lists + frequency buckets)
implementations.code:
class Node:
    """Doubly linked list node: key/value plus its current frequency."""
    __slots__ = ("key", "val", "freq", "prev", "next")

    def __init__(self, key=0, val=0):
        self.key = key
        self.val = val
        self.freq = 1                  # every new key starts at frequency 1
        self.prev = None
        self.next = None


class DList:
    """Doubly linked list with sentinels: O(1) splice at either end."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.head = Node()             # sentinel: holds no real data
        self.tail = Node()             # sentinel
        self.head.next = self.tail     # empty list: head <-> tail
        self.tail.prev = self.head
        self.size = 0

    def push_front(self, node):
        # Splice node right after head (the most-recently-used end).
        node.next = self.head.next
        node.prev = self.head
        self.head.next.prev = node     # old front now points back at node
        self.head.next = node
        self.size += 1

    def unlink(self, node):
        # Remove node wherever it sits: neighbors bypass it. O(1).
        node.prev.next = node.next
        node.next.prev = node.prev
        self.size -= 1

    def pop_back(self):
        # The least-recently-used real node sits just before tail.
        node = self.tail.prev
        self.unlink(node)
        return node


class LFUCache:
    """O(1) get/put. Evicts least-frequent key; ties -> least recent.

    nodes : key -> Node                 (reach any key in O(1))
    lists : freq -> DList at that freq  (recency order inside each)
    minf  : lowest frequency present    (the eviction bucket)
    """

    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.cap = capacity
        self.nodes = {}
        self.lists = {}
        self.minf = 0

    def _bump(self, node):
        # Move node from frequency f to f+1, keeping every invariant.
        f = node.freq
        self.lists[f].unlink(node)
        if self.lists[f].size == 0:
            del self.lists[f]          # drop the now-empty bucket
            if self.minf == f:
                self.minf = f + 1      # floor rises: node moved up
        node.freq = f + 1
        if node.freq not in self.lists:
            self.lists[node.freq] = DList()
        self.lists[node.freq].push_front(node)     # newest at freq f+1

    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.nodes:
            return -1
        node = self.nodes[key]
        self._bump(node)               # a read counts as a use
        return node.val

    def put(self, key, value):
        if self.cap <= 0:
            return                     # capacity 0: store nothing
        if key in self.nodes:
            node = self.nodes[key]
            node.val = value           # overwrite, then count the use
            self._bump(node)
            return
        if len(self.nodes) >= self.cap:
            # Evict: minf bucket, least-recent (back) end of its list.
            victim = self.lists[self.minf].pop_back()
            del self.nodes[victim.key]
            if self.lists[self.minf].size == 0:
                del self.lists[self.minf]      # keep buckets tidy
        node = Node(key, value)        # fresh node arrives at freq 1
        self.nodes[key] = node
        if 1 not in self.lists:
            self.lists[1] = DList()
        self.lists[1].push_front(node)
        self.minf = 1                  # a freq-1 key certainly exists now


if __name__ == "__main__":
    c = LFUCache(2)
    c.put(1, 1)
    c.put(2, 2)
    print(c.get(1))                    # 1   (key 1's freq becomes 2)
    c.put(3, 3)                        # evicts key 2 (lowest freq)
    print(c.get(2))                    # -1  (gone)
    print(c.get(3))                    # 3
    c.put(4, 4)                        # 3 and 1 tie on freq 2 -> evict 1?
    print(c.get(1), c.get(3), c.get(4))    # 1 was less recent: -1 3 4

implementations.title: Bitwise Trie: Max XOR Pair and Max XOR Subarray
Monotonic Stack Toolkit: StockSpanner + Next Greater Element
implementations.code:
class StockSpanner:
    """Streaming stock span with a monotonic stack of (price, span).

    Invariant: prices on the stack strictly decrease bottom -> top,
    and the spans on the stack partition every day seen so far.
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.stack = []                # [(price, span), ...]

    def next(self, price):
        span = 1                       # today counts itself
        while self.stack and self.stack[-1][0] <= price:
            _, s = self.stack.pop()    # a day <= today can never be a
            span += s                  #   future answer: absorb its span
        self.stack.append((price, span))
        return span                    # amortized O(1) per call


def next_greater_elements(nums):
    # Offline cousin: for each i, the first value to the RIGHT that is
    # strictly greater (-1 if none). Same monotonic-stack accounting.
    n = len(nums)
    ans = [-1] * n
    stack = []                         # indices with unresolved answers
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        while stack and nums[stack[-1]] < x:
            ans[stack.pop()] = x       # x is their next greater element
        stack.append(i)                # wait for something bigger
    return ans                         # leftovers keep -1: nothing bigger


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sp = StockSpanner()
    for p in [100, 80, 60, 70, 60, 75, 85]:
        print(sp.next(p), end=" ")     # 1 1 1 2 1 4 6
    print()
    print(next_greater_elements([2, 1, 2, 4, 3]))  # [4, 2, 4, -1, -1]

implementations.title: Power Set Three Ways (bitmask, backtracking, iterative doubling)
implementations.code:
def power_set_bitmask(nums):
    # Subset <-> n-bit integer bijection. O(n * 2^n), output-bound.
    n = len(nums)
    out = []
    for mask in range(1 << n):         # masks 0 .. 2^n - 1
        subset = [nums[i] for i in range(n) if mask >> i & 1]
        out.append(subset)             # bit i set -> nums[i] included
    return out


def power_set_backtrack(nums):
    # Include/exclude decision tree; 2^n leaves = 2^n subsets.
    out = []
    cur = []                           # the subset under construction
    def go(i):
        if i == len(nums):
            out.append(cur[:])         # COPY: cur keeps mutating
            return
        go(i + 1)                      # branch 1: exclude nums[i]
        cur.append(nums[i])            # branch 2: include nums[i]
        go(i + 1)
        cur.pop()                      # backtrack: undo the include
    go(0)
    return out


def power_set_doubling(nums):
    # Iterative doubling: each new element forks every existing subset.
    out = [[]]                         # start with the empty subset
    for x in nums:
        out += [s + [x] for s in out]  # copy-with-x of everything so far
    return out                         # sizes: 1 -> 2 -> 4 -> ... -> 2^n


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(power_set_bitmask([1, 2]))       # [[], [1], [2], [1, 2]]
    print(power_set_backtrack([1, 2]))     # [[], [2], [1], [1, 2]]
    print(power_set_doubling([1, 2]))      # [[], [1], [2], [1, 2]]
    # All three emit the same 2^n subsets, in different orders.

Greedy.summary:
A greedy algorithm builds a solution one step at a time and, at every step, takes the choice that looks best right now — then never goes back to change it. That is the entire technique. There is no recursion tree, no memo table, no backtracking. The catch is that "looks best right now" must be defined by exactly the right rule, because a greedy with the wrong rule produces confident, fast, wrong answers. Compare it with dynamic programming: DP tries many futures and keeps the best; greedy commits immediately and trusts a proof that commitment can never hurt. When that proof exists, greedy beats DP by a mile — usually O(N log N) time and O(1) extra space instead of a table.

Interviews love greedy because the code is tiny — typically one sort plus one linear pass — so the whole interview becomes a test of judgment: WHICH key do you sort by, and can you defend it? "N Meetings in One Room" looks like it wants sorting by start time or by duration; both are wrong, and only sort-by-end-time is provably optimal. "Greedy Coin Change" works for Indian or US denominations but silently fails on coins {1, 3, 4} for amount 6 — knowing when greedy breaks is worth as much as knowing when it works. The standard defense is the exchange argument: assume some optimal answer disagrees with your greedy at the first step, swap in the greedy choice, and show the answer got no worse.

The working mental model for this whole topic is: sort by the right key, then sweep.

```
intervals sorted by END:   |--A--|  |-B-|   |---C---|
sweep left to right:       take A -> B starts after A ends? yes -> take B ...
```
Every sheet problem in this topic is that picture with a different key: end time (meetings), event time (platforms), profit (job sequencing), value density (fractional knapsack), denomination size (coin change).
preRequisites: Python sorting idioms: arr.sort(key=lambda x: x[1]), sorted(..., reverse=True), and the fact that Python's Timsort is stable (equal keys keep their original order).
How tuples compare in Python — (2, 5) < (2, 7) < (3, 0) element by element — because greedy state is usually a list of tuples.
Big-O of sorting: O(N log N) comparisons; almost every greedy's total cost is the sort plus an O(N) scan.
Unpacking pairs in loops: for start, end in intervals — you will write this constantly.
heapq basics (heappush/heappop are O(log N)) — a few greedy problems need a running 'best available' set mid-scan.
The difference between a locally decidable choice (greedy) and a choice whose quality depends on how subproblems resolve (dynamic programming).
What an exchange argument is: swap an optimal solution's first differing choice for the greedy one and show the result is no worse.
cheatSheet: Interval scheduling (max non-overlapping): sort by END time; take interval if start >= last_end. O(N log N).
Min platforms / meeting rooms = MAX OVERLAP: sort arrivals and departures separately, sweep with a counter, track the peak.
Job sequencing: sort by profit DESC; place each job in the LATEST free slot <= deadline. O(N*D) naive, O(N log N) with DSU.
Fractional knapsack: sort by value/weight DESC; take whole items until one doesn't fit, then take the fitting fraction. O(N log N).
Greedy coin change: largest denomination first via divmod — correct ONLY for canonical systems (1,2,5,10,...); {1,3,4} amount 6 breaks it -> DP.
Greedy correctness = greedy-choice property + exchange argument; one counterexample kills the greedy — then reach for DP.
Sorting by the WRONG key is the classic trap: meetings by start time or duration both fail; end time wins.
Typical complexity signature: O(N log N) time (the sort dominates), O(1)-O(N) extra space.
When each step needs 'best among currently available': sort one dimension, push candidates into a heap for the other.

sections.title: What & Why
sections.content:
A greedy algorithm makes a sequence of choices, and each choice is the best-looking one at that moment, judged by a single fixed rule. Once made, a choice is never revisited. Think of a cashier giving change: to hand you 87 rupees they grab the biggest note that fits (50), then the next biggest (20), then 10, 5, 2 — largest first, no second-guessing. Or think of you planning your day from a list of meetings: if you always accept the meeting that ends earliest, you leave yourself the most free time for whatever comes next, and you provably attend the maximum number of meetings.

Real systems run on greedy decisions because they are fast and need no lookahead: Huffman coding (used inside ZIP, JPEG, MP3) greedily merges the two rarest symbols; Dijkstra's shortest path greedily settles the closest unvisited node; OS schedulers like Shortest-Job-First greedily pick the quickest task; Kruskal's minimum spanning tree greedily adds the cheapest safe edge. Interviewers use greedy problems to test judgment rather than memorization: the code is five lines, so the entire signal is whether you can (a) find the one sorting key that makes the local choice safe, and (b) argue why it is safe — or spot the counterexample proving it is not.

sections.title: Memory Model & Representation
sections.content:
Greedy is a technique, not a data structure, so its memory footprint is refreshingly small: the input reorganized (usually sorted) plus a handful of scalars that summarize everything decided so far. For "N Meetings in One Room" the entire algorithm state is one sorted list of (start, end) tuples, an integer count, and last_end — the finish time of the last accepted meeting. That single number compresses the whole past: nothing about earlier choices matters except when the room frees up.

```
sorted by end:  [(1,2), (3,4), (0,6), (5,7), (8,9)]
                    ^taken  ^taken  ^skip   ^taken ^taken
state:          count=4          last_end=9
```
For sweep problems like "Minimum Number of Platforms" the memory picture is a timeline of events. Sort arrivals and departures into two arrays and walk them with two pointers; the only live state is a counter of trains currently in the station and the peak that counter ever reached:

```
time  -> 900   940   950  1100  1130  1500
event -> arr   arr   arr   dep   arr   dep
count ->  1     2     3     2     3     2      peak = 3 platforms
```
This is why greedy answers are usually O(1) or O(N) extra space: the algorithm deliberately forgets everything a few scalars can summarize. If you find yourself wanting a 2-D table of intermediate answers, you have drifted into dynamic programming territory.

sections.title: Core Operations & Complexity
sections.content:
Greedy solutions are assembled from a tiny toolbox. Know the cost of each piece and you can price any greedy algorithm in seconds — the sort almost always dominates.

```
Operation                     Time         Why
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
sort by chosen key            O(N log N)   comparison sort lower bound
single sweep / scan           O(N)         each element examined once
two-pointer merge of events   O(N + M)     each pointer only moves forward
heap push / pop mid-scan      O(log N)     sift through tree height
slot search (job seq, naive)  O(D) each    walk back day by day to a free slot
DSU find with compression     ~O(1) amort  paths flatten after first walk
divmod per denomination       O(1)         integer division hardware op
```
Combine them: meetings = sort + sweep = O(N log N) time, O(N) for the tuple list (O(1) extra beyond it). Platforms = two sorts + two-pointer merge = O(N log N). Job sequencing = sort + N slot searches = O(N log N + N*D) naive, improved to O(N log N) when a Disjoint Set Union hands you the latest free slot in near-constant time. Fractional knapsack = sort by density + one pass = O(N log N). Coin change with a fixed denomination table is O(C) for C coin types — effectively constant. The WHY column matters in interviews: saying 'the sort dominates, the sweep is linear' is exactly the complexity discussion the interviewer wants.

sections.title: How Python Does It
