sections.content: Python gives you everything greedy needs in three tools: list.sort / sorted with a key function, tuple comparison, and heapq for the occasional 'best available right now' set. Details that matter: sort is Timsort — O(N log N) worst case, stable, and in fact O(N) on already-sorted data. list.sort() mutates in place and returns None (a classic bug: writing arr = arr.sort() leaves arr as None); sorted() returns a new list and accepts any iterable. The key= function is called once per element, so key=lambda j: -j[2] is cheap; for descending order prefer reverse=True over negating, since negation breaks on non-numeric keys. Stability is genuinely useful: sorting jobs by profit descending keeps equal-profit jobs in input order, which makes results deterministic and tie-breaking explicit. heapq implements a min-heap on a plain list — push a tuple (key, payload) and the smallest key surfaces first; for a max-heap push the negated key. There is no built-in sorted-set; when an interviewer's C++ solution uses std::multiset, your Python answer is usually heapq plus, if needed, lazy deletion.
sections.code:
import heapq

# --- Sorting with a key: the heart of most greedy solutions ---------------
meetings = [(1, 2), (0, 6), (3, 4), (5, 7)]
meetings.sort(key=lambda p: p[1])          # in-place, stable, by END time
# meetings is now [(1, 2), (3, 4), (0, 6), (5, 7)]

jobs = [('a', 2, 100), ('b', 1, 19), ('c', 2, 27)]   # (id, deadline, profit)
by_profit = sorted(jobs, key=lambda j: j[2], reverse=True)   # new list, DESC

# --- Tuple comparison: sort by profit DESC, then deadline ASC -------------
tie_broken = sorted(jobs, key=lambda j: (-j[2], j[1]))   # negate only numbers

# --- heapq: a 'best available' set that changes mid-scan ------------------
available = []                       # min-heap of (end_time, meeting_id)
heapq.heappush(available, (4, 'm2')) # O(log N) insert
heapq.heappush(available, (2, 'm1'))
soonest = heapq.heappop(available)   # (2, 'm1') — smallest key wins

# --- divmod: the whole engine of canonical coin change --------------------
count, remainder = divmod(87, 50)    # 1 note of 50, 37 left over

# --- Gotcha: sort() returns None ------------------------------------------
arr = [3, 1, 2]
result = arr.sort()                  # result is None! arr itself was sorted

sections.title: Pattern: Interval Scheduling — Sort by End Time
sections.content:
Recognize it: you must pick the MAXIMUM NUMBER of non-overlapping intervals (meetings, activities, jobs on one machine). On this sheet it is exactly "N Meetings in One Room".

The rule: sort by END time and accept every interval that starts after the last accepted one ends. The invariant after each step: among all ways to schedule the intervals processed so far, the greedy schedule has the maximum count, and among schedules with that count it has the EARLIEST last-end-time — meaning no other schedule leaves more room for the future. That second half is the exchange argument in disguise: if an optimal schedule takes some interval X where greedy took G, then G ends no later than X (greedy picked the earliest finisher), so replacing X with G keeps the schedule valid and the count equal.

Why the tempting alternatives fail: sort by START time and one marathon meeting (0, 100) blocks everything; sort by DURATION and a short meeting straddling two others, like (4,6) against (1,5) and (5,9), picks 1 when 2 was possible. Interviewers will probe exactly this — have the counterexamples ready. Watch the boundary rule: this sheet's version says a meeting may start only strictly after the previous ends (s > last_end); LeetCode-style variants often allow touching intervals (s >= last_end). Ask which one is intended before coding.
sections.code:
def max_meetings(start, end):
    # Pair and sort by END time — the earliest finisher first,
    # because finishing early leaves maximum room for future meetings.
    meetings = sorted(zip(start, end), key=lambda p: p[1])

    count = 0
    last_end = float('-inf')       # finish time of the last accepted meeting
    for s, e in meetings:
        if s > last_end:           # room is free strictly after last_end
            count += 1             # commit greedily — never reconsidered
            last_end = e           # room now busy until e
        # else: skip — it overlaps the meeting we already committed to
    return count                   # O(N log N) time, O(N) for the pairs

sections.title: Pattern: Event Sweep — Maximum Overlap
sections.content:
Recognize it: you must find how many intervals overlap AT THE SAME MOMENT — minimum platforms, meeting rooms, maximum concurrent users. On this sheet it is "Minimum Number of Platforms". The key insight is a reframe: the minimum number of platforms is exactly the maximum number of trains simultaneously in the station. You are not scheduling anything; you are measuring peak load.

The technique: break every interval into two events — arrival (+1) and departure (-1) — sort each event stream, and sweep time forward with two pointers, maintaining a live counter. The invariant: after processing all events up to time t, the counter equals the number of trains present at t, and best holds the peak so far. Since both pointers only move forward, the sweep is O(N) after the O(N log N) sorts.

The classic edge case: a train arrives at the exact minute another departs. If the platform can NOT be reused instantly (the usual convention), process the arrival first — the tie-break arrivals[i] <= departures[j] increments before it decrements, correctly counting both trains at that instant. Flip the <= to < only if the problem states instant reuse is allowed. This same sweep answers "Merge Overlapping Intervals"-style peak questions and appears in load-balancer capacity planning; the alternative implementation pushes departure times into a min-heap (pop while the earliest departure <= new arrival), which generalizes to allocating WHICH room each meeting gets.
sections.code:
def min_platforms(arrivals, departures):
    # Sort both event streams — we replay the day in time order.
    arrivals.sort()
    departures.sort()

    i = j = 0                      # i -> next arrival, j -> next departure
    in_station = best = 0          # live train count and its peak
    n = len(arrivals)
    while i < n:                   # every arrival must be processed
        if arrivals[i] <= departures[j]:
            in_station += 1        # train pulls in before earliest one leaves
            best = max(best, in_station)   # record the peak overlap
            i += 1
        else:
            in_station -= 1        # earliest departure frees a platform
            j += 1
    return best                    # peak simultaneous trains = platforms

sections.title: Pattern: Deadline Scheduling by Profit
sections.content:
Recognize it: unit-time jobs, each with a deadline and a profit; maximize total profit. On this sheet this is the "Job Sequencing Problem". Two greedy decisions stack here, and both need defending.

Decision 1 — order: sort jobs by profit DESCENDING and commit to rich jobs first. Exchange argument: if an optimal schedule omits a high-profit job that greedy fit, swapping it in for whatever occupies its slot cannot lower the total, because greedy processes profits in decreasing order.

Decision 2 — placement: put each job in the LATEST free slot at or before its deadline, not the earliest. Why: a job with deadline 5 placed on day 5 leaves days 1-4 open for jobs with tighter deadlines; placed on day 1 it might evict a deadline-1 job entirely. The invariant: after processing each job, the set of filled slots is one that some optimal schedule also fills.

Complexity: sorting is O(N log N); the naive latest-slot search walks back day by day, O(D) per job for maximum deadline D, so O(N*D) total — fine for interviews, and say so. The elegant upgrade replaces the walk with a Disjoint Set Union where find(t) returns the latest free day <= t and placing a job unions it to t-1; total drops to effectively O(N log N). Mentioning the DSU version unprompted is a strong senior signal, and the full code is in the implementations below.
sections.code:
def job_sequencing(jobs):
    # jobs: list of (job_id, deadline, profit); one unit of time each.
    # Greedy decision 1: richest jobs first.
    jobs = sorted(jobs, key=lambda j: j[2], reverse=True)

    max_deadline = max(j[1] for j in jobs)
    slot = [None] * (max_deadline + 1)   # slot[t] = job scheduled on day t (1-based)

    count = total = 0
    for job_id, deadline, profit in jobs:
        # Greedy decision 2: latest free day <= deadline,
        # leaving earlier days open for tighter-deadline jobs.
        t = deadline
        while t >= 1 and slot[t] is not None:
            t -= 1                       # that day is taken; try one earlier
        if t >= 1:                       # found a free day in time
            slot[t] = job_id             # commit — never moved again
            count += 1
            total += profit
        # else: job is dropped — every day up to its deadline is full
    return count, total                  # O(N log N + N*D) with this slot walk

sections.title: Pattern: Ratio Sort — Fractional Choices
sections.content:
Recognize it: maximize value under a capacity, and you may take FRACTIONS of items. On this sheet it is "Fractional Knapsack". The divisibility is what unlocks greedy: sort items by value density (value/weight) descending, take whole items while they fit, and when one no longer fits, take exactly the fraction that fills the bag. Done — no table, no recursion.

The exchange argument is at its cleanest here: suppose an optimal answer carries a kilogram of a cheaper-density item while some higher-density item is not fully taken. Swap that kilogram for a kilogram of the denser item: weight unchanged, value strictly up — contradiction, so the optimal answer is density-ordered, which is exactly what greedy produces. The invariant during the scan: the bag always holds the maximum possible value for the weight used so far.

Now the trap the interviewer is fishing for: the moment fractions are forbidden — 0/1 knapsack — this greedy collapses. Capacity 10 with items (value 60, weight 10) and two items (40, 5) each: density greedy grabs the 60/10 item for value 60, but taking the two 40/5 items yields 80. Indivisibility means a locally dense choice can block a better combination, so "0/1 Knapsack" on the Dynamic Programming sheet needs a DP table. Saying exactly this — fractional is greedy, 0/1 is DP, and why — is the expected talking point. Cost: O(N log N) for the sort, O(1) extra space.
sections.code:
def fractional_knapsack(items, capacity):
    # items: list of (value, weight); fractions of an item are allowed.
    # Sort by value density value/weight, best bang-per-kg first.
    items = sorted(items, key=lambda it: it[0] / it[1], reverse=True)

    total = 0.0
    for value, weight in items:
        if capacity == 0:                  # bag is exactly full — stop early
            break
        take = min(weight, capacity)       # whole item if it fits, else the rest
        total += value * (take / weight)   # proportional value for a partial take
        capacity -= take                   # shrink what remains of the bag
    return total                           # O(N log N) time, O(1) extra space

sections.title: Pattern: Canonical Coin Change
sections.content:
Recognize it: make an amount with the FEWEST coins/notes from standard denominations. On this sheet it is "Greedy Coin Change". The rule is the cashier's instinct: repeatedly take the largest denomination that still fits, which in code is one divmod per denomination walking from largest to smallest — O(C) for C coin types, with no loop over the amount at all.

The crucial theory: this is only correct for CANONICAL coin systems — systems (like Indian 1/2/5/10/20/50/100... or US 1/5/10/25) deliberately designed so that every larger coin 'dominates' combinations of smaller ones. The exchange argument holds there: any optimal solution can be rewritten, coin by coin, into the greedy one without increasing the count.

For arbitrary coin sets it FAILS, and you must produce the counterexample on demand: coins {1, 3, 4}, amount 6. Greedy takes 4, then 1, then 1 — three coins; optimal is 3 + 3 — two coins. Greedy overcommits to the 4 and nothing later can repair it. The moment denominations are arbitrary input, the problem is "Coin Change" on the Dynamic Programming sheet: dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - c]) over coins c, O(amount * C). Interviewers frequently ask the greedy version first and then remove the canonical assumption to watch whether you notice the ground shifting. Notice it out loud.
sections.code:
def greedy_coin_change(coins, amount):
    # CORRECT only for canonical systems (1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, ...).
    # Counterexample for arbitrary sets: coins {1,3,4}, amount 6 ->
    # greedy 4+1+1 (3 coins) vs optimal 3+3 (2 coins). Then use DP.
    used = []
    for c in sorted(coins, reverse=True):   # largest denomination first
        k, amount = divmod(amount, c)       # how many of coin c fit
        used.extend([c] * k)                # record k coins of value c
    if amount != 0:                         # smallest coin isn't 1 and change
        return None                         # cannot be completed exactly
    return used                             # O(C log C) sort + O(C) loop

sections.title: Proving a Greedy Correct: The Exchange Argument
sections.content:
An interviewer who accepts your greedy will often follow with "why is that optimal?" — and hand-waving here undoes a perfect solution. The standard tool is the exchange argument, and it always has the same three-move shape. Move 1: suppose some optimal solution OPT disagrees with your greedy solution G, and look at the FIRST place they differ. Move 2: show you can swap OPT's choice at that point for G's choice and OPT stays valid and gets no worse — this is where your sorting key earns its keep (the earliest-ending meeting ends no later than whatever OPT chose, so the swap cannot create an overlap; a denser knapsack kilogram is worth no less, so the swap cannot lose value). Move 3: repeat — after finitely many swaps OPT has been transformed into G without ever getting worse, so G is optimal.

Two companion ideas complete the toolkit. The greedy-choice property says some optimal solution contains the greedy's first choice — exactly what moves 1-2 establish. Optimal substructure says that after committing the choice, what remains is a smaller instance of the same problem. And the fastest practical test is the hunt for a counterexample: before trusting any greedy, spend sixty seconds trying to break it on a 3-element input, the way {1,3,4}/6 breaks coin change and duration-sort breaks meetings. If you cannot break it AND an exchange sketch goes through, code it; if you break it, pivot to DP and say why.

sections.title: Pitfalls & Common Mistakes
sections.content:
1) Sorting by the wrong key. Meetings sorted by start time or by duration both fail (marathon-meeting and straddling-meeting counterexamples). Fix: for max-count interval problems, end time is the provably safe key — and keep the counterexamples ready to justify it.

2) Assuming greedy applies because it feels natural. 0/1 knapsack by density and arbitrary-coin change by largest-first are the two famous frauds. Fix: hunt for a small counterexample first; if choices are indivisible or denominations arbitrary, default to DP.

3) Boundary bugs at equal timestamps. Meetings: s > last_end vs s >= last_end changes answers; platforms: arrival tied with departure must count both trains unless instant reuse is stated. Fix: ask, then encode the convention in the comparison operator deliberately.

4) arr = arr.sort() — sort() mutates and returns None, so arr becomes None. Fix: arr.sort() alone, or arr = sorted(arr) when you need a copy.

5) Filling the EARLIEST slot in job sequencing. It can evict tight-deadline jobs; latest-free-slot is the correct placement. Fix: walk back from the deadline (or use DSU).

6) Integer division in density sorts. In Python 2 habits, value//weight truncates; in Python 3 use / for the ratio, or avoid float error entirely by comparing cross-products (v1*w2 > v2*w1).

7) Claiming O(N) out loud while sorting inside. The sort is O(N log N) and dominates. Fix: state 'sort dominates, sweep is linear' every time.

sections.title: Interview Recognition Checklist
sections.content:
Cues that a problem is greedy: the ask is a single optimal NUMBER (max count, min platforms, max profit) rather than an enumeration of ways; items are independent with no chained consequences; choices are divisible (fractions allowed) or intervals/deadlines are involved; N is large (10^5+) so exponential search is out and a sort feels affordable; the phrase 'maximum non-overlapping', 'minimum resources at once', or 'deadline' appears. Counter-cues pushing toward DP instead: 'count the number of ways', indivisible items with a capacity (0/1 knapsack), arbitrary denominations, or any hint that a local choice changes the value of future choices.

30-second pre-code checklist: (1) What single key am I sorting by, and can I say in one sentence why that key is safe? (2) Did I spend a minute trying a 3-element counterexample — and does an exchange-argument sketch survive it? (3) What exactly is my loop state (last_end, counter, remaining capacity) — the fewer scalars the better? (4) Ties and boundaries: > or >=, arrival-equals-departure, zero capacity, empty input? (5) Complexity ready to state: O(N log N) sort + O(N) sweep, O(1) or O(N) space? If any answer is shaky — especially (2) — say the counterexample out loud and pivot to DP with confidence; recognizing greedy's limits scores as high as using it.

implementations.title: N Meetings in One Room — complete greedy with proof in comments
implementations.code:
# Interval scheduling: choose the maximum number of meetings one room
# can host, where a meeting may start only strictly after the previous ends.
#
# WHY sort by end time (exchange argument, in short):
#   Let G be greedy's first pick (earliest finisher) and X the first pick of
#   any optimal schedule OPT. Since G ends no later than X, replacing X by G
#   keeps OPT valid and the same size. Repeat -> OPT morphs into greedy's
#   schedule without losing meetings, so greedy is optimal.

def n_meetings(start, end):
    # Bundle (start, end, original 1-based index) so we can report WHICH
    # meetings were chosen, not just how many.
    meetings = sorted(
        ((s, e, i + 1) for i, (s, e) in enumerate(zip(start, end))),
        key=lambda m: m[1],          # earliest END time first
    )

    chosen = []                      # indices of accepted meetings, in order
    last_end = float('-inf')         # when the room frees up

    for s, e, idx in meetings:
        if s > last_end:             # strictly after: room must be empty
            chosen.append(idx)       # commit to this meeting forever
            last_end = e             # room busy until e
        # overlapping meetings are skipped and never reconsidered

    return chosen                    # len(chosen) = max number of meetings


if __name__ == '__main__':
    start = [1, 3, 0, 5, 8, 5]
    end = [2, 4, 6, 7, 9, 9]
    picked = n_meetings(start, end)
    # Expected: 4 meetings, e.g. order 1, 2, 4, 5 (1-based indices)
    print(len(picked), picked)

implementations.title: Minimum Platforms — two-pointer sweep AND heap variant
implementations.code:
import heapq

# Reframe: min platforms = MAX number of trains in the station at once.
# Variant A sorts the two event streams and sweeps; Variant B keeps a
# min-heap of departure times (generalizes to 'which room does each
# meeting get'). Both are O(N log N) time.

def min_platforms_sweep(arrivals, departures):
    arr = sorted(arrivals)           # replay arrivals in time order
    dep = sorted(departures)         # replay departures in time order

    i = j = 0                        # i -> next arrival, j -> next departure
    live = best = 0                  # trains currently in station; the peak
    while i < len(arr):
        # Tie (arrival == departure): count the arriving train too, because
        # a platform cannot be vacated and reused in the same instant.
        if arr[i] <= dep[j]:
            live += 1                # one more train inside
            best = max(best, live)   # remember the peak load
            i += 1
        else:
            live -= 1                # earliest train has left
            j += 1
    return best


def min_platforms_heap(arrivals, departures):
    # Process trains sorted by arrival; the heap holds departure times of
    # trains currently occupying platforms (root = first platform to free).
    trains = sorted(zip(arrivals, departures))
    occupied = []                    # min-heap of departure times
    best = 0
    for arr_t, dep_t in trains:
        # Free every platform whose train departed strictly before arrival.
        while occupied and occupied[0] < arr_t:
            heapq.heappop(occupied)  # that platform is available again
        heapq.heappush(occupied, dep_t)      # this train takes a platform
        best = max(best, len(occupied))      # heap size = platforms in use
    return best


if __name__ == '__main__':
    arrivals = [900, 940, 950, 1100, 1500, 1800]
    departures = [910, 1200, 1120, 1130, 1900, 2000]
    print(min_platforms_sweep(arrivals, departures))   # expected 3
    print(min_platforms_heap(arrivals, departures))    # expected 3

implementations.title: Job Sequencing — slot array and the DSU-optimized version
implementations.code:
# Unit-time jobs (id, deadline, profit): maximize profit, one job per day.
# Greedy: richest first; place each in the LATEST free day <= its deadline.
# Version A walks days backwards: O(N log N + N*D).
# Version B replaces the walk with a Disjoint Set Union where find(t)
# returns the latest free day <= t in near-constant amortized time.

def job_sequencing_slots(jobs):
    jobs = sorted(jobs, key=lambda j: j[2], reverse=True)   # profit DESC
    max_d = max(j[1] for j in jobs)
    slot = [None] * (max_d + 1)      # slot[t]: job scheduled on day t (1-based)

    count = total = 0
    for job_id, deadline, profit in jobs:
        t = deadline                 # try the latest legal day first
        while t >= 1 and slot[t] is not None:
            t -= 1                   # taken — step one day earlier
        if t >= 1:                   # found a free day before the deadline
            slot[t] = job_id
            count += 1
            total += profit
    return count, total


def job_sequencing_dsu(jobs):
    jobs = sorted(jobs, key=lambda j: j[2], reverse=True)   # profit DESC
    max_d = max(j[1] for j in jobs)

    # parent[t] = latest free day <= t. Initially every day is free, so
    # parent[t] = t. Day 0 acts as the 'no slot available' sentinel.
    parent = list(range(max_d + 1))

    def find(t):
        # Path compression: hop to the representative and flatten the path,
        # so repeated queries on full days become O(1) amortized.
        root = t
        while parent[root] != root:
            root = parent[root]      # climb to the latest free day
        while parent[t] != root:
            parent[t], t = root, parent[t]   # flatten for next time
        return root

    count = total = 0
    for job_id, deadline, profit in jobs:
        day = find(deadline)         # latest free day <= deadline
        if day >= 1:                 # 0 means everything up to deadline is full
            parent[day] = day - 1    # occupy it: next query slides earlier
            count += 1
            total += profit
    return count, total


if __name__ == '__main__':
    jobs = [('a', 2, 100), ('b', 1, 19), ('c', 2, 27), ('d', 1, 25), ('e', 3, 15)]
    print(job_sequencing_slots(jobs))   # expected (3, 142): jobs c, a, e
    print(job_sequencing_dsu(jobs))     # expected (3, 142) — same answer

implementations.title: Fractional Knapsack and Canonical Coin Change
implementations.code:
# Two ratio/denomination greedies side by side, with the exact boundary
# where each stops being valid noted in comments.

def fractional_knapsack(items, capacity):
    # items: (value, weight). Fractions ALLOWED — that's what makes greedy
    # optimal; forbid fractions (0/1 knapsack) and this breaks, e.g.
    # capacity 10, items (60,10),(40,5),(40,5): greedy 60 < optimal 80.
    items = sorted(items, key=lambda it: it[0] / it[1], reverse=True)

    total = 0.0
    for value, weight in items:
        if capacity == 0:                 # bag exactly full — done early
            break
        take = min(weight, capacity)      # whole item, or whatever still fits
        total += value * (take / weight)  # value scales with fraction taken
        capacity -= take                  # remaining room shrinks
    return total                          # max achievable value


def coin_change_greedy(coins, amount):
    # Valid ONLY for canonical systems like (1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100).
    # Arbitrary sets break it: coins (1, 3, 4), amount 6 ->
    # greedy [4, 1, 1] but optimal [3, 3]. That version needs DP.
    used = []
    for c in sorted(coins, reverse=True):   # biggest denomination first
        k, amount = divmod(amount, c)       # k coins of value c fit
        used.extend([c] * k)                # record them
    if amount != 0:                         # can't finish without a 1-coin
        return None
    return used


if __name__ == '__main__':
    items = [(60, 10), (100, 20), (120, 30)]
    print(fractional_knapsack(items, 50))   # expected 240.0
    inr = [1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 2000]
    print(coin_change_greedy(inr, 87))      # expected [50, 20, 10, 5, 2]

Heap.summary:
A heap is a complete binary tree with one rule: every parent is no larger than its children (min-heap) or no smaller (max-heap). That single rule buys you three things: the minimum (or maximum) is always at the root, readable in O(1); inserting keeps order in O(log N); and removing the root also costs O(log N). Nothing else is sorted — siblings can be in any order — and that deliberate looseness is exactly why a heap is cheaper to maintain than a fully sorted structure. The magic implementation detail: because the tree is complete (every level full except possibly the last, filled left to right), it needs no pointers at all. It lives in a flat array where the node at index i has children at 2i+1 and 2i+2 and its parent at (i-1)//2.

```
        1            index:  0  1  2  3  4  5  6
      /   \           value: [1, 3, 2, 8, 5, 4, 7]
     3     2          parent(i) = (i-1)//2
    / \   / \         children(i) = 2i+1, 2i+2
   8   5 4   7
```

Interviews lean on heaps whenever the phrase 'K' or 'stream' appears: Kth largest, top-K frequent, merge K sorted things, running median. The shared insight is that you rarely need everything sorted — you need fast access to the current best while data keeps arriving, and a heap maintains exactly that and nothing more. In Python the tool is the heapq module: min-heap only, operating on a plain list, with the max-heap trick of pushing negated keys. Master three patterns — a size-K heap for top-K, a K-front heap for K-way merge, and two opposing heaps for streaming median — and all five sheet questions fall out of them.
preRequisites: Python lists and index arithmetic — the whole heap is arr[0..n-1] with children at 2i+1 and 2i+2, so off-by-one comfort is essential.
Logarithms as tree height: a complete binary tree with N nodes has height floor(log2 N), which is where every O(log N) comes from.
The difference between a heap and a BST: a BST orders left < node < right for searching; a heap only orders parent vs child for fast min/max — you cannot binary-search a heap.
heapq module basics: heappush, heappop, heapify all operate on a plain Python list and implement a MIN-heap only.
Tuple comparison — (3, 'a') < (5, 'a') element by element — because heap entries are usually (priority, tiebreak, payload) tuples.
collections.Counter for frequency tables — Top K Frequent Elements is Counter + heap glued together.
Why list.pop(0) is O(N) (everything shifts) — motivation for why a heap, not a sorted list, backs a priority queue.
cheatSheet: Min-heap invariant: a[i] <= a[2i+1] and a[i] <= a[2i+2] for all valid i; the root a[0] is the global minimum.
Index math (0-based): parent(i) = (i-1)//2, left(i) = 2i+1, right(i) = 2i+2; last internal node = n//2 - 1.
push = append + sift-up: O(log N). pop = swap root with last, shrink, sift-down: O(log N). peek = a[0]: O(1).
Build a heap from N items with heapify in O(N) (sum of subtree heights), NOT by N pushes (O(N log N)).
Kth largest: min-heap capped at size K; anything beating the root replaces it; final root = answer. O(N log K), space O(K).
Max-heap in Python: push -x, negate again on pop; or negate the key field of a tuple.
K-way merge: heap holds one (value, src, pos) per list front; pop the min, push its successor. O(T log K) for T total items.
Streaming median: max-heap 'lo' (lower half) + min-heap 'hi' (upper half); keep len(lo) - len(hi) in {0, 1}; median = -lo[0] or the average of both roots.
heapq.nlargest(k, it, key=...) / nsmallest: one-shot top-K in O(N log K) without hand-rolling the loop.
heapreplace(h, x) = pop-then-push in one O(log N) sift; heappushpop(h, x) = push-then-pop (returns x itself if x <= root).

sections.title: What & Why
sections.content:
A heap is the data structure behind a priority queue: a bag of items where you can always grab the most urgent one instantly, and adding or removing items stays cheap no matter how large the bag grows. The real-world analogy is a hospital emergency room. Patients do not form a first-come-first-served line; a triage nurse ensures the most critical patient is seen next. Nobody keeps the whole waiting room sorted — that would be wasted effort, since only the front matters — and that is precisely a heap's philosophy: maintain just enough order to know the best element, and no more.

Heaps run everywhere in real systems: operating system schedulers pick the highest-priority task; Dijkstra's algorithm and A* pathfinding pop the closest frontier node; timer wheels and event loops (including parts of Python's asyncio) pop the soonest deadline; external merge sort — how databases sort files larger than RAM — is one giant K-way heap merge; Huffman coding repeatedly merges the two rarest symbols via a heap.

Interviewers reach for heaps because they cleanly separate the students who memorized 'sort it' from those who see that sorting all N items to answer a question about K of them is waste. Every sheet question here — Kth Largest Element, Top K Frequent Elements, Merge K Sorted Arrays, Merge K Sorted Linked Lists, Find Median from Data Stream — is a variation on 'keep only the order you actually need'.

sections.title: Memory Model & Representation
sections.content:
A heap is conceptually a tree but physically a flat array — no node objects, no pointers. This works because the tree is COMPLETE: every level is full except possibly the last, which fills left to right with no gaps. Completeness means the nodes, read level by level, map onto array slots 0, 1, 2, ... with pure index arithmetic:

```
         tree                       array

          1                idx:   0  1  2  3  4  5  6
        /   \              val: [ 1, 3, 2, 8, 5, 4, 7 ]
       3     2
      / \   / \            parent(i) = (i - 1) // 2
     8   5 4   7           left(i)  = 2*i + 1
                           right(i) = 2*i + 2
```
Check it: node 3 sits at index 1; its children 8 and 5 sit at 2*1+1 = 3 and 2*1+2 = 4. The min-heap property is visible in the array as a[i] <= a[2i+1] and a[i] <= a[2i+2] wherever those indices exist — note the array is NOT sorted (3 appears before 2), and does not need to be.

This layout is why heaps are fast in practice, not just in theory: one contiguous block of memory, cache-friendly sequential-ish access, zero pointer chasing, zero per-node allocation. It is also why heapq can operate directly on a plain Python list. The cost of completeness: you can only cheaply add or remove at specific places (append a leaf at the end, remove the root by swapping in the last leaf) — which is exactly how push and pop are implemented.

sections.title: Core Operations & Complexity
sections.content:
Every heap operation is built from two primitives. Sift-up: a node smaller than its parent swaps upward until order is restored — used after inserting at the end. Sift-down: a node larger than a child swaps with its SMALLER child, falling until order is restored — used after replacing the root. Both touch at most one node per level, so both are O(height) = O(log N).

```
Operation           Time        Why
---------------------------------------------------------------------
peek min            O(1)        the root always sits at index 0
push x              O(log N)    append as last leaf, sift it up
pop min             O(log N)    move last leaf to root, sift down
replace root        O(log N)    one sift-down (cheaper than pop+push)
build from N items  O(N)        sift-down all internal nodes bottom-up
delete arbitrary    O(log N)*   *needs a position map to find it first
search / contains   O(N)        siblings unordered — no way to prune
heapsort            O(N log N)  N pops of O(log N) each
```
Two rows deserve emphasis. Build being O(N) — not O(N log N) — surprises people; the reason is that most nodes sit near the bottom with tiny sift-down distances (fully explained in the heapify section). And search being O(N) is the price of a heap's laziness: nothing relates left subtrees to right subtrees, so 'is 42 in the heap?' must scan. If you need fast membership or arbitrary deletion, pair the heap with a dict (position map or lazy deletion), a trick worth naming in interviews.

sections.title: How Python Does It
sections.content:
Python's heap lives in the stdlib heapq module, and its design is unusual: there is no Heap class. Every function operates on a plain Python list that you own, and the list IS the heap as long as you only mutate it through heapq functions. heapify(lst) rearranges in place in O(N); heappush and heappop are O(log N); lst[0] peeks the min in O(1). Two fused operations save a sift each: heapreplace(h, x) pops the root then pushes x (always removes the old root), while heappushpop(h, x) pushes then pops (returns x itself when x is smaller than the root). For one-shot top-K there are heapq.nlargest(k, iterable, key=...) and nsmallest — O(N log K), and they accept a key function, which plain heap entries do not.

The gotchas every interview touches: (1) heapq is MIN-heap only — simulate a max-heap by pushing -x, or negating the priority field of a tuple. (2) Entries compare as whole tuples: (priority, payload) breaks with a TypeError the moment two priorities tie and Python tries to compare payloads that lack __lt__ (linked-list nodes!). Insert a unique counter as tiebreak: (priority, counter, payload). (3) There is no decrease-key like textbook Dijkstra wants; the Pythonic substitute is lazy deletion — push the updated entry and discard stale ones as they surface. (4) sorted() then indexing is O(N log N); if you only need K of them, the heap wins.
sections.code:
import heapq
import itertools

nums = [5, 1, 8, 3, 2]
heapq.heapify(nums)                  # O(N), IN PLACE: nums is now a valid heap
heapq.heappush(nums, 0)              # O(log N) insert
smallest = heapq.heappop(nums)       # O(log N) — returns 0, the minimum
peek = nums[0]                       # O(1) — read the root without removing

# --- Max-heap: negate on the way in, negate on the way out ----------------
mx = []
for x in [5, 1, 8]:
    heapq.heappush(mx, -x)           # store negatives
largest = -heapq.heappop(mx)         # 8 — biggest original value

# --- Tuples + counter tiebreak (payloads may not define __lt__) -----------
counter = itertools.count()          # unique, always-increasing tiebreak
tasks = []
heapq.heappush(tasks, (2, next(counter), 'write tests'))
heapq.heappush(tasks, (2, next(counter), 'review PR'))   # tie is safe now
priority, _, task = heapq.heappop(tasks)   # FIFO among equal priorities

# --- Fused ops: one sift instead of two -----------------------------------
h = [3, 7, 9]
old_root = heapq.heapreplace(h, 5)   # pop 3, push 5 — root always removed
maybe_x = heapq.heappushpop(h, 1)    # 1 <= root so 1 comes straight back

# --- One-shot top-K with a key function -----------------------------------
words = {'apple': 5, 'pear': 9, 'plum': 2}
top2 = heapq.nlargest(2, words, key=words.get)   # ['pear', 'apple']

sections.title: Pattern: Top-K with a Size-K Heap
sections.content:
Recognize it: 'Kth largest', 'K closest', 'K best' — you need K winners out of N items and K is much smaller than N. On this sheet: "Kth Largest Element" directly, and "Top K Frequent Elements" after a counting step (next section).

The counter-intuitive core: to track the K LARGEST items, use a MIN-heap. Keep the heap capped at size K; its root is then the weakest of your current top K — the bouncer at the door. Each new element faces one question: do you beat the weakest member? If not (x <= root), discard it in O(1). If yes, heapreplace evicts the root and admits x in O(log K). The invariant after every element: the heap holds exactly the K largest seen so far, with the Kth largest at the root — so when the scan ends, the root IS the answer.

Complexity: O(N log K) time, O(K) space — versus O(N log N) for full sorting. For N = 10^6 and K = 10 that is the difference between ~20 million and ~3 million comparisons, and the heap version works on a STREAM: it never needs all N in memory, which is the standard follow-up ('what if the numbers arrive from a network feed?'). Alternatives worth naming: sorting (simpler, O(N log N)), and Quickselect (O(N) average, O(N^2) worst, in-memory only). Mirror rule for K smallest: use a max-heap (negate values). The streaming class version is in the implementations below.
sections.code:
import heapq

def kth_largest(nums, k):
    # Min-heap of the K largest seen so far. Root = current Kth largest,
    # i.e. the WEAKEST member of the club — the one challengers must beat.
    heap = nums[:k]
    heapq.heapify(heap)              # O(K) build from the first K items

    for x in nums[k:]:               # each remaining element challenges
        if x > heap[0]:              # beats the weakest of the top K?
            heapq.heapreplace(heap, x)   # evict root + admit x: one O(log K)
        # else: x can't be in the top K — dropped in O(1)

    return heap[0]                   # root = Kth largest overall
    # O(N log K) time, O(K) space — and stream-friendly.

sections.title: Pattern: Counting + Heap
sections.content:
Recognize it: the ranking key is not the element itself but a DERIVED statistic — usually frequency. On this sheet it is "Top K Frequent Elements": first build a frequency table, then run top-K on the (element, count) pairs. Two stdlib pieces snap together: collections.Counter builds the table in O(N), and either heapq.nlargest(k, freq.keys(), key=freq.get) or a hand-rolled size-K min-heap of (count, element) tuples extracts the winners in O(U log K), where U is the number of DISTINCT elements. Total: O(N + U log K) time, O(U) space — and since U <= N, that beats sorting the table at O(U log U) whenever K is small.

Two details interviewers poke at. First, when you push tuples the count must come FIRST — (count, element) — because tuples compare element by element and you rank by count; flip the order and you rank alphabetically. If elements can tie on count and are not comparable, insert a counter tiebreak. Second, know the O(N) alternative for the follow-up: bucket sort by frequency. A frequency can be at most N, so make buckets[f] = list of elements appearing f times and read buckets from N down to 1 collecting K elements — O(N) time flat, no heap at all. Mentioning the bucket upgrade unprompted, after shipping the clean heap version, is exactly the progression the question is designed to reward.
sections.code:
import heapq
from collections import Counter

def top_k_frequent(nums, k):
    freq = Counter(nums)             # O(N): element -> how many times it appears
    # nlargest runs a size-k min-heap over U distinct items: O(U log k).
    return heapq.nlargest(k, freq.keys(), key=freq.get)


def top_k_frequent_manual(nums, k):
    # Same idea without the convenience wrapper — the loop you may be
    # asked to write out by hand.
    freq = Counter(nums)
    heap = []                        # min-heap of (count, element), size <= k
    for element, count in freq.items():
        if len(heap) < k:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (count, element))   # room left — admit
        elif count > heap[0][0]:     # beats the least-frequent member?
            heapq.heapreplace(heap, (count, element))  # evict + admit
    return [element for _, element in heap]   # any order; sort if required

sections.title: Pattern: K-Way Merge
sections.content:
Recognize it: K sources, each ALREADY sorted, and you need one combined sorted output. On this sheet: "Merge K Sorted Arrays" and "Merge K Sorted Linked Lists". The naive approaches both waste the given order — concatenate-and-sort costs O(T log T) for T total elements, and merging lists one into another costs O(K*T). The heap approach costs O(T log K): since each source is sorted, the next output element must be one of the K front elements, so keep a heap of just those K candidates.

The loop: seed the heap with each source's first element as (value, source_index, position). Pop the minimum — that is the next output — then push the popped source's NEXT element, keeping at most one candidate per source. The invariant: the heap always contains the current front of every non-exhausted source, so the popped minimum is the global minimum of everything unmerged. Every element enters and leaves the heap exactly once: T operations on a K-sized heap = O(T log K), with O(K) working space.

For linked lists the entry is (node.val, tiebreak, node) — and the tiebreak counter is NOT optional: when two node values tie, Python compares the next tuple field, and ListNode objects without __lt__ raise TypeError. This pattern is external merge sort's core (databases merging sorted runs from disk) and also powers heapq.merge in the stdlib, which returns a lazy iterator over exactly this loop.
sections.code:
import heapq

def merge_k_sorted_arrays(arrays):
    # Heap holds ONE candidate per array: its current front element.
    heap = []
    for src, arr in enumerate(arrays):
        if arr:                              # skip empty sources entirely
            heap.append((arr[0], src, 0))    # (value, which array, index)
    heapq.heapify(heap)                      # O(K) initial build

    out = []
    while heap:
        val, src, pos = heapq.heappop(heap)  # global min of all fronts
        out.append(val)                      # emit it to the merged output
        nxt = pos + 1
        if nxt < len(arrays[src]):           # that source has more elements
            heapq.heappush(heap, (arrays[src][nxt], src, nxt))
    return out                               # O(T log K) time, O(K) extra

sections.title: Pattern: Two Heaps — Streaming Median
sections.content:
Recognize it: numbers arrive one at a time and you must answer an ORDER-STATISTIC query (median, percentile) at any moment. On this sheet it is "Find Median from Data Stream". Re-sorting per query costs O(N log N) each time; a single heap cannot help because the median is the middle, not an extreme. The trick is to make the median an extreme: split the numbers into halves and point two heaps at each other. lo is a MAX-heap holding the smaller half (its root = largest of the small numbers); hi is a MIN-heap holding the larger half (its root = smallest of the large numbers). The median lives at the roots.

Two invariants, restored after every insertion: (1) ordering — every element of lo <= every element of hi; (2) balance — len(lo) - len(hi) is 0 or 1. The bulletproof insertion does three fixed steps: push the new number into lo; move lo's root into hi (this guarantees ordering, because whatever crosses over is lo's maximum); if hi has grown larger than lo, move hi's root back. Both invariants now hold with no case analysis on the incoming value. Median query: odd total count -> lo's root; even -> average of the two roots.

Costs: O(log N) per insertion, O(1) per median query, O(N) space. In Python lo stores NEGATED values (heapq is min-only), so lo's true maximum is -lo[0] — the single most common sign bug in this problem. The standard follow-up is a sliding-window median, which adds lazy deletion of expired elements to the same skeleton.
sections.code:
import heapq

class MedianFinder:
    def __init__(self):
        self.lo = []   # MAX-heap via negation: the smaller half of the data
        self.hi = []   # min-heap: the larger half
        # Invariants: max(lo) <= min(hi), and len(lo) - len(hi) in {0, 1}.

    def add_num(self, num):
        heapq.heappush(self.lo, -num)        # 1) everything enters lo first
        moved = -heapq.heappop(self.lo)      # 2) lo's max crosses to hi —
        heapq.heappush(self.hi, moved)       #    this enforces max(lo) <= min(hi)
        if len(self.hi) > len(self.lo):      # 3) rebalance: lo may equal or
            back = heapq.heappop(self.hi)    #    exceed hi by exactly one
            heapq.heappush(self.lo, -back)

    def find_median(self):
        if len(self.lo) > len(self.hi):      # odd count: lo holds the middle
            return float(-self.lo[0])        # un-negate the stored max
        # even count: average of the two inner roots
        return (-self.lo[0] + self.hi[0]) / 2.0

sections.title: Heapify in O(N) and Heapsort
sections.content:
Building a heap by pushing N items one by one costs O(N log N). heapify does it in O(N), and interviewers love asking why. The method: leaves (indices n//2 .. n-1, half the nodes) are already valid one-element heaps, so start at the LAST INTERNAL node, index n//2 - 1, and sift each node DOWN, walking backward to the root. When you reach any node, both its subtrees are already heaps, so one sift-down fixes its whole subtree.

The accounting: a sift-down costs the node's HEIGHT (distance to the leaves), not log N. About n/2 nodes have height 0 (cost 0), n/4 have height 1, n/8 have height 2...

```
total = n/4*1 + n/8*2 + n/16*3 + ...  =  n * SUM(h / 2^(h+1))  <  n * 1
```
The series converges to a constant, so building is O(N). Intuition: almost all nodes sit near the bottom where sifting is nearly free; only one node (the root) can pay the full log N. Contrast with N pushes, where each sift-UP cost is the node's DEPTH — and almost all nodes are DEEP, so that sum genuinely is Theta(N log N).

Heapsort falls out immediately: build a max-heap in O(N), then repeatedly swap the root (current maximum) with the last element, shrink the heap boundary by one, and sift the new root down — sorting in place in O(N log N) worst case with O(1) extra memory. It is not stable, and Python's Timsort usually beats it in practice, but 'sorts in place with guaranteed O(N log N) and no extra memory' is the exam answer for why heapsort matters. Full code in the implementations below.

sections.title: Pitfalls & Common Mistakes
sections.content:
1) TypeError on tuple ties. Pushing (priority, node) works until two priorities tie and Python compares nodes lacking __lt__ — a crash that appears only on tie-heavy input, classically in Merge K Sorted Linked Lists. Fix: (priority, unique_counter, node) with itertools.count().

2) Max-heap sign slips. Push -x then forget to negate on pop, or negate the payload instead of the priority. Fix: negate at exactly two boundaries — push and pop — and nowhere else; in two-heap problems write -self.lo[0] with the sign in one place.

3) Mutating the list around heapq. sort(), remove(), insert(), or arr[i] = x on a heapified list silently breaks the invariant; later pops return non-minimums with no error. Fix: after any raw mutation, heapify again — or never mutate raw.

4) Building with N pushes when heapify exists: O(N log N) versus O(N), and interviewers notice. Fix: heapq.heapify(lst) on the initial data.

5) Using a size-N heap where size-K suffices: pushing all N then popping K is O(N log N); the capped heap is O(N log K). Fix: cap at K with heapreplace.

6) Wrong heap polarity for top-K: K LARGEST needs a MIN-heap (root = eviction candidate), not a max-heap. Fix: 'keep the K best, root = worst of the best'.

7) Believing the heap array is sorted, or that heap[1] is the second-smallest — it can be the largest of the top three levels' children. Only heap[0] is guaranteed. Fix: pop repeatedly (or nsmallest) for ordered output.

8) Treating decrease-key as available. heapq has none. Fix: lazy deletion — push updated entries, skip stale ones when popped (check against a 'current value' dict).

sections.title: Interview Recognition Checklist
sections.content:
Cues that scream heap: the letter K in the ask ('Kth largest', 'top K', 'K closest', 'merge K') — a heap capped at K almost always beats sorting; the word 'stream' or 'online' — data arrives incrementally and sorting is off the table, as in Find Median from Data Stream; 'median/percentile so far' — two heaps; several ALREADY-SORTED inputs to combine — K-way merge, as in Merge K Sorted Arrays and Merge K Sorted Linked Lists; scheduling by priority/earliest-deadline; repeatedly needing the current min or max while items keep being added — the defining priority-queue workload.

30-second pre-code checklist: (1) Min-heap or max-heap? K-largest -> min-heap of size K; K-smallest -> max-heap; write the polarity down before coding. (2) What tuple am I pushing, is the sort key its FIRST field, and can ties reach a payload without __lt__? If yes, add a counter tiebreak now. (3) Heap size: K or N? That decides O(N log K) vs O(N log N) — say the difference out loud. (4) Am I building from existing data? heapify is O(N); N pushes are not. (5) Do I need heapreplace/heappushpop to fuse a pop+push? (6) Negation audit for max-heaps: minus sign on push, minus sign on pop, nowhere else. (7) Could sorting actually be simpler and fast enough? For one-shot small inputs, sorted(...)[k-1] is honest — mention the heap upgrade and let the interviewer choose the constraint.

implementations.title: Binary Min-Heap from scratch (push, pop, heapify, heapsort)
MedianFinder — two heaps for a running median
implementations.code:
import heapq

# Find Median from Data Stream. Split numbers into halves:
#   lo = MAX-heap (negated values) holding the SMALLER half
#   hi = min-heap holding the LARGER half
# Invariants: max(lo) <= min(hi) and len(lo) - len(hi) in {0, 1}.
# The median is then read off the roots in O(1).

class MedianFinder:
    def __init__(self):
        self.lo = []                 # negated values: -lo[0] is lo's true max
        self.hi = []                 # plain values: hi[0] is hi's min

    def add_num(self, num):
        # Three fixed steps restore BOTH invariants with no case analysis:
        heapq.heappush(self.lo, -num)          # 1) enter the lower half
        crossing = -heapq.heappop(self.lo)     # 2) lo's max crosses over,
        heapq.heappush(self.hi, crossing)      #    guaranteeing lo <= hi
        if len(self.hi) > len(self.lo):        # 3) hi grew too big —
            back = heapq.heappop(self.hi)      #    send its min back so lo
            heapq.heappush(self.lo, -back)     #    stays equal or +1 ahead

    def find_median(self):
        if len(self.lo) > len(self.hi):
            return float(-self.lo[0])          # odd count: lo holds the middle
        # even count: the two inner elements are the roots — average them
        return (-self.lo[0] + self.hi[0]) / 2.0


if __name__ == '__main__':
    mf = MedianFinder()
    for x, expected in [(5, 5.0), (15, 10.0), (1, 5.0), (3, 4.0)]:
        mf.add_num(x)                # stream arrives one number at a time
        assert mf.find_median() == expected   # O(1) median query each step
    print('running medians OK')

implementations.title: K-way merge — K sorted arrays and K sorted linked lists
implementations.code:
import heapq
import itertools

# One pattern, two inputs. Heap holds ONE candidate per source (its current
# front), so popping always yields the global minimum of all unmerged data.
# T total elements across K sources -> O(T log K) time, O(K) heap space.

def merge_k_arrays(arrays):
    heap = [(arr[0], src, 0) for src, arr in enumerate(arrays) if arr]
    heapq.heapify(heap)              # O(K) seed: each source's front element
    out = []
    while heap:
        val, src, pos = heapq.heappop(heap)   # smallest of the K fronts
        out.append(val)
        if pos + 1 < len(arrays[src]):        # advance within that source
            heapq.heappush(heap, (arrays[src][pos + 1], src, pos + 1))
    return out


class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, nxt=None):
        self.val = val               # node payload
        self.next = nxt              # pointer to the next node (or None)


def merge_k_lists(lists):
    # CRUCIAL: ListNode has no __lt__, so on tied vals Python would try to
    # compare nodes and raise TypeError. A unique counter breaks ties first.
    tiebreak = itertools.count()
    heap = [(node.val, next(tiebreak), node) for node in lists if node]
    heapq.heapify(heap)              # one entry per non-empty list

    dummy = ListNode()               # dummy head avoids empty-result edge cases
    tail = dummy
    while heap:
        val, _, node = heapq.heappop(heap)    # global minimum node
        tail.next = node             # splice it onto the merged list
        tail = node
        if node.next:                # its source list continues —
            heapq.heappush(heap, (node.next.val, next(tiebreak), node.next))
    return dummy.next                # first real merged node


if __name__ == '__main__':
    print(merge_k_arrays([[1, 4, 7], [2, 5], [3, 6, 8, 9]]))
    # Build 1->4->5, 1->3->4 as linked lists and merge them:
    a = ListNode(1, ListNode(4, ListNode(5)))
    b = ListNode(1, ListNode(3, ListNode(4)))
    node, vals = merge_k_lists([a, b]), []
    while node:                      # walk the merged list to verify
        vals.append(node.val)
        node = node.next
    print(vals)                      # [1, 1, 3, 4, 4, 5]

implementations.title: KthLargest — streaming top-K class with a capped min-heap
implementations.code:
import heapq

# Streaming version of Kth Largest Element: numbers keep arriving and each
# add() must report the CURRENT Kth largest. A min-heap capped at size K
# holds the K largest so far; its root is the Kth largest — the 'weakest
# member of the club' that newcomers must beat.

class KthLargest:
    def __init__(self, k, nums):
        self.k = k
        self.heap = list(nums)
        heapq.heapify(self.heap)     # O(N) build from the initial batch
        while len(self.heap) > k:    # trim down to the K largest:
            heapq.heappop(self.heap) # popping removes the SMALLEST each time

    def add(self, val):
        # O(log K) per arriving number, O(K) memory total — stream-safe.
        if len(self.heap) < self.k:
            heapq.heappush(self.heap, val)    # club not full yet — admit
        elif val > self.heap[0]:              # beats the weakest member?
            heapq.heapreplace(self.heap, val) # evict root + admit, one sift
        # else: val is too small to matter — O(1) rejection
        return self.heap[0]          # root = current Kth largest


if __name__ == '__main__':
    kl = KthLargest(3, [4, 5, 8, 2])          # 3rd largest of {4,5,8,2} is 4
    print([kl.add(x) for x in [3, 5, 10, 9, 4]])   # [4, 5, 5, 8, 8]

Linked List.summary:
A linked list stores a sequence one node at a time. A node is a tiny object with two fields: `val` (the data it carries) and `next` (a reference to the following node, or None at the end). The whole list is nothing more than a reference to the first node, called the head; every other node is reachable only by following `next` arrows one hop at a time. Think of a scavenger hunt: each clue holds a prize and the address of the next clue. You cannot jump straight to clue 7 — you must walk the chain. An array, by contrast, is a numbered row of lockers where locker 7 is one address computation away. That single difference — pointers instead of positions — creates the entire topic.

Interviews love linked lists because the questions are cheap to state and merciless about precision. They test whether you understand aliasing (two variables naming the same object), whether you can rewire structure without losing half the list, and whether you handle the silent edge cases — empty list, single node, head being replaced — without being reminded. They also force O(1)-space thinking: most sheet problems forbid copying values into a Python list and demand in-place pointer surgery instead.

The mental model that carries you through all 13 sheet questions: you only ever hold two or three "fingers" (references such as prev, curr, nxt) on the chain, and each loop iteration re-points one arrow while the fingers slide forward under an invariant you can state out loud. Before coding, draw boxes and arrows for a 3-node list and simulate your loop twice on paper. Nearly every question here is a combination of five or six reusable finger patterns — reversal, fast/slow, dummy-plus-merge, fixed-gap, pointer switching — and this tab teaches each one with its invariant and template.
preRequisites: Python references: a variable holds a reference to an object, so `a = b` makes two names for ONE node — it never copies the node.
Class basics: define `class ListNode: def __init__(self, val): self.val = val; self.next = None` and read/write attributes with dot syntax.
Tuple assignment evaluates the whole right side first: `curr.next, prev, curr = prev, curr, curr.next` is safe, but the same three statements in the wrong order destroy the list.
`is` vs `==`: cycle and intersection questions compare node IDENTITY with `is`; `==` on values gives wrong answers when values repeat.
Loop invariants: be able to finish the sentence 'at the top of every iteration it is true that ...' for any while loop you write.
Big-O basics: following k pointers costs O(k); arrays get O(1) indexing from address arithmetic, linked lists never do.
None-safety: `fast.next.next` crashes if `fast.next` is None — guard with `while fast and fast.next` in that exact order.
cheatSheet: Reverse in place: prev, curr = None, head; each step: nxt = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev, curr = curr, nxt — O(N) time / O(1) space.
Middle: slow moves 1, fast moves 2 with `while fast and fast.next`; slow stops on the middle (the SECOND middle when length is even).
Cycle (Floyd): if fast is slow ever holds, there is a cycle; then reset one pointer to head, move both by 1 — they meet at the cycle's first node (a = c).
N-th from end: from a dummy, advance lead n+1 steps, then move lead and trail together; trail stops on the PREDECESSOR of the target.
Dummy node: `dummy = ListNode(0); dummy.next = head` removes every 'head might change' special case; return dummy.next.
Merge two sorted lists: tail.next = smaller head, advance that list, advance tail — O(N+M) time / O(1) space, no new nodes.
Intersection: when a pointer hits None it jumps to the OTHER list's head; both travel lenA+lenB steps, so they meet at the joint node or at None.
Rotate right by k: close the list into a ring, walk n - (k % n) - 1 steps from head to the new tail, cut the ring — O(N) / O(1).
Palindrome: find middle, reverse the second half, compare halves, optionally re-reverse to restore — O(N) time / O(1) space.
Delete a node without head access: node.val = node.next.val; node.next = node.next.next — O(1), impossible for the tail node.

sections.title: What & Why
sections.content:
A linked list is a sequence built from independent node objects, each carrying a value and a reference to its successor. Nothing about a node says where it sits in the sequence; order exists ONLY in the arrows. That makes the structure cheap to re-arrange (re-point an arrow) and expensive to index (walk the arrows).

Real-world analogy: a scavenger hunt. Each clue contains a prize and the location of the next clue. Adding a stop in the middle of the hunt means editing one clue — nobody else moves. Finding the 7th clue, though, means visiting the first six.

Where it appears in real systems: an LRU cache is a hash map pointing into a doubly linked list so both lookup and recency-reordering are O(1) (the sheet's LRU Cache question in Stack & Queue is exactly this); hash tables resolve collisions by chaining nodes; memory allocators keep free blocks on free lists; text editors, undo stacks and music players model previous/next; OS schedulers keep run queues linked so a task can be unlinked in O(1) no matter where it sits.

Why interviewers reach for it: the problems need almost no setup, yet they expose exactly the skills production code needs — reasoning about aliasing, mutating shared structure safely, and covering edge cases (empty list, one node, operation lands on the head) without prompting. Every question in this tab is solved by a small set of reusable pointer patterns, so the topic rewards understanding over memorization.

sections.title: Memory Model & Representation
sections.content:
An array is one contiguous block of memory, so the k-th slot lives at address base + k × slot_size — a single multiplication gives O(1) indexing. A linked list abandons contiguity: each node is allocated wherever the heap has room, and the only thing tying the sequence together is the `next` reference stored inside each node.

```
Python list (array of pointers):      Singly linked list:
index:    0     1     2               head
        +-----+-----+-----+            |
        | p0  | p1  | p2  |            v
        +-----+-----+-----+     addr 0x51C0      addr 0x9A40      addr 0x2F80
        contiguous slots        +-----+------+   +-----+------+   +-----+------+
        address math ->         |  7  |  *---|-->|  3  |  *---|-->|  9  | None |
        O(1) indexing           +-----+------+   +-----+------+   +-----+------+
                                nodes scattered anywhere on the heap
```

Three consequences follow. (1) No random access: reaching position k costs k hops, O(k), because there is no arithmetic that predicts where node k lives. (2) O(1) local surgery: holding a reference to a node lets you insert or delete just after it by rewriting one or two arrows — nothing shifts, which is the whole selling point over arrays. (3) Weak cache locality: hopping between scattered addresses defeats the CPU cache that makes array scans fast, so linked lists often lose in wall-clock time even when Big-O ties. Memory cost matters too: in CPython a node is a full object (roughly 56 bytes even with __slots__) while a list slot is one 8-byte pointer, so the chain can cost several times the array. When a node becomes unreachable (no references left), Python's garbage collector reclaims it — deletion is just unlinking.

sections.title: Core Operations & Complexity
sections.content:
Every complexity below follows from one fact: you can only touch what you hold a reference to, and each hop follows one arrow.

```
Operation                     Time     Space   Why
push_front                    O(1)     O(1)    new node points at old head; head re-points
push_back (no tail pointer)   O(N)     O(1)    must walk to the last node first
push_back (with tail pointer) O(1)     O(1)    tail reference skips the walk
pop_front                     O(1)     O(1)    head = head.next
get k-th / index              O(k)     O(1)    no address arithmetic — k hops
search by value               O(N)     O(1)    scan node by node
insert AFTER a held node      O(1)     O(1)    rewrite two arrows, nothing shifts
delete AFTER a held node      O(1)     O(1)    bypass one node with one arrow write
delete by value               O(N)     O(1)    must find the PREDECESSOR first
reverse in place              O(N)     O(1)    flip each of N arrows exactly once
```

Two rows deserve emphasis. First, `insert after a held node` being O(1) is why linked lists exist: an array pays O(N) to shift elements for the same edit. Second, `delete by value` is O(N) even though the unlink itself is O(1), because a singly linked node cannot see its predecessor — you must arrive there by scanning from the head. Doubly linked lists fix exactly this (each node also stores `prev`), buying O(1) deletion of a HELD node at the price of one extra pointer per node — the trade LRU Cache makes.

sections.title: How Python Does It
sections.content:
Python ships no singly linked list — in every interview you define a two-field `ListNode` class yourself, and that is expected. What the stdlib does give you: `collections.deque`, implemented as a doubly linked list of fixed-size blocks. It offers O(1) `append`, `appendleft`, `pop` and `popleft`, which is why deque (not list) is the right queue; but indexing `dq[k]` walks blocks in O(k), so deque is not an array substitute.

Know the costs of faking a linked list with a plain `list`: `lst.pop(0)` and `lst.insert(0, x)` shift every element and cost O(N) — a classic hidden-quadratic bug in loops. Also remember CPython's default recursion limit (about 1000 frames): a recursive reversal of a 100 000-node list crashes with RecursionError, so the iterative versions in this tab are not a style choice, they are a correctness requirement. `sys.setrecursionlimit` exists but merely trades the exception for a possible interpreter crash — say that in the interview and write the loop.

Two more Python facts the patterns rely on. Node objects compare by identity by default, so `a is b` (and even `a == b` on bare nodes) asks "same object?" — use `is` deliberately when hunting cycles or intersections. And Python's garbage collector frees any node you unlink, so 'deleting' is nothing more than removing the last reference to it.
sections.code:
from collections import deque

# Python has NO built-in singly linked list. In interviews you define the node:
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, nxt=None):
        self.val = val          # payload stored in this node
        self.next = nxt         # reference to the next node, or None at the tail

# collections.deque is the closest stdlib relative: a doubly linked list of
# fixed-size blocks. Both ENDS are O(1); the middle is not.
dq = deque([1, 2, 3])
dq.appendleft(0)    # O(1)  -- a plain list pays O(N) for insert(0, x)
dq.popleft()        # O(1)  -- list.pop(0) shifts every element: O(N)
dq.append(4)        # O(1)  -- same as list.append (amortized)

# Gotcha: dq[k] costs O(k) from the nearer end, NOT O(1) like a list.
# Gotcha: list.insert(0, x) and list.pop(0) are O(N) — never call them in loops.
# Gotcha: default recursion limit is ~1000; a 10^5-node list will blow the
#         stack in recursive solutions — prefer iterative loops.

def build(values):
    # Build a linked list from a Python list (handy for testing solutions).
    dummy = ListNode()          # dummy head: no special case for the first node
    tail = dummy                # tail always references the last node built
    for v in values:
        tail.next = ListNode(v) # append a fresh node after the current tail
        tail = tail.next        # advance the tail onto it
    return dummy.next           # the real head sits right after the dummy

sections.title: Pattern: In-Place Reversal
sections.content:
Recognize it: the problem says "reverse", "reorder", or "in groups", or it demands O(1) extra space for something you could do trivially by copying values out to a Python list. Copying values is the rookie answer; the interviewer wants arrows re-pointed in place.

The invariant that makes the loop safe: prev is the head of the already-reversed prefix, curr is the head of the untouched suffix, and the single dangerous moment is overwriting curr.next — so you save it into nxt FIRST, every iteration, no exceptions. Each iteration flips exactly one arrow and moves both fingers forward, so the loop terminates after N flips with prev as the new head.

Sheet questions using it: Reverse Linked List is the pure template above. Reverse Nodes in K Group runs the same flip exactly k times per block, then splices the block back between its neighbours (the block's old first node becomes its tail — full solution in the implementations below). Check if Linked List is Palindrome reverses only the SECOND half (found via the fast/slow pattern), compares the two halves front-to-front, and ideally re-reverses to restore the input — mention the restore step out loud; it signals care.

A trap worth naming: after any partial reversal the original sub-head still points into the old order, so the caller must re-wire it. Draw the 5-node, k=2 case once and the re-linking writes itself.
sections.code:
def reverse_list(head):
    # INVARIANT: prev heads the fully-reversed prefix; curr heads the untouched
    # suffix; every arrow to the left of curr already points backwards.
    prev = None                 # reversed prefix starts empty
    curr = head
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next         # 1) save the suffix BEFORE breaking the arrow
        curr.next = prev        # 2) flip this node's arrow to point backwards
        prev = curr             # 3) reversed prefix grows by this node
        curr = nxt              # 4) step into the saved suffix
    return prev                 # when curr is None, prev is the new head


def reverse_first_k(head, k):
    # Same engine, but stop after exactly k flips.
    # Returns (new_head_of_block, head_of_the_rest).
    # This is the inner subroutine of Reverse Nodes in K Group.
    prev, curr = None, head
    for _ in range(k):          # exactly k arrows get flipped
        nxt = curr.next         # save suffix
        curr.next = prev        # flip
        prev = curr             # advance prev
        curr = nxt              # advance curr
    # NOTE: the original head is now the TAIL of the reversed block;
    # the caller must re-link head.next = <whatever follows>.
    return prev, curr

sections.title: Pattern: Fast & Slow Pointers (Floyd)
sections.content:
Recognize it: "find the middle", "is there a cycle", "where does the loop start", or any question where you need a structural position (half-way point, cycle entry) without knowing the length in advance. Two pointers at different speeds convert those positions into meeting events.

Why the meeting is guaranteed: once both pointers are inside a cycle, the gap between them shrinks by exactly 1 each step (relative speed 2 − 1 = 1), so the fast pointer cannot jump over the slow one — the gap hits 0 in at most cycle-length steps. If there is no cycle, fast reaches None in N/2 steps and you are done.

Why phase 2 finds the entry: let a = distance head→entry, b = entry→meeting point, c = rest of the cycle (so cycle length L = b + c). At the meeting, slow has walked a + b and fast exactly twice that: 2(a + b) = a + b + kL for some laps k ≥ 1. Rearranging gives a = (k − 1)L + c, meaning: walking a steps from the head lands on the entry, and walking a steps from the meeting point ALSO lands on the entry (c steps plus whole laps). So two speed-1 pointers, one from head, one from the meeting point, collide precisely at the entry. Say this derivation in the interview — it is the difference between knowing Floyd and reciting it.

Sheet questions using it: Find Middle of Linked List (template above; note the even-length convention — slow stops on the SECOND middle), Detect Cycle in Linked List (phase 1 alone), Find Starting Point of Loop (both phases), and Check if Linked List is Palindrome uses `middle` as step one before reversing the second half.
sections.code:
def middle(head):
    # Hare moves 2, tortoise moves 1 -> tortoise covers exactly half.
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:   # this exact order: fast may be None already
        slow = slow.next        # 1 step
        fast = fast.next.next   # 2 steps
    return slow                 # even length: this is the SECOND middle


def cycle_start(head):
    # Phase 1: detect a meeting inside the cycle (or fall off the end).
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:        # identity check: same NODE, not equal value
            # Phase 2: distance head->entry equals meeting->entry (a == c),
            # so two speed-1 pointers from head and meeting collide at entry.
            slow = head
            while slow is not fast:
                slow = slow.next
                fast = fast.next
            return slow         # first node of the cycle
    return None                 # fast reached the end -> acyclic

sections.title: Pattern: Dummy Node & Merge Building
sections.content:
Recognize it: you are BUILDING an output list node by node — merging sorted lists, summing digit lists, flattening structures. Two tools define the pattern. The dummy node kills the "is this the first node?" branch: you never know the result's head up front, so you hang everything off a throwaway node and return dummy.next. The tail pointer carries the invariant: everything from dummy.next through tail is finished and correct; each iteration appends exactly one node and advances tail.

Sheet questions using it: Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists is the canonical form — note it re-links EXISTING nodes (O(1) extra space) rather than allocating copies. Add Two Numbers as Linked Lists is the same builder with a carry: the loop condition `while l1 or l2 or carry` is the whole difficulty, because forgetting `or carry` drops the final digit of 5 + 5 = 10. Flatten a Linked List (each node has `next` across and `bottom`/`child` down, every vertical chain sorted) is merge applied repeatedly: treat each vertical chain as one sorted list and fold them — merging right-to-left keeps the code clean because each step merges the current chain with the already-flattened result to its right.

Complexity: merge is O(N + M) time, O(1) extra space. Flatten by left-to-right folding is O(total · lists) in the worst case; folding pairwise (like merge sort's ladder, used in Merge K Sorted Linked Lists from the Heap tab) improves it — worth mentioning unprompted.
sections.code:
def merge_two(l1, l2):
    dummy = ListNode(0)         # result head unknown until first comparison
    tail = dummy                # INVARIANT: chain up to tail is final and sorted
    while l1 and l2:
        if l1.val <= l2.val:    # <= keeps the merge stable (ties keep order)
            tail.next = l1      # link the smaller NODE itself — zero allocation
            l1 = l1.next        # consume from that list
        else:
            tail.next = l2
            l2 = l2.next
        tail = tail.next        # built chain grew by exactly one node
    tail.next = l1 or l2        # one side is empty; append the leftovers whole
    return dummy.next           # real head sits after the dummy


def add_two_numbers(l1, l2):
    # Digits stored least-significant first, e.g. 342 is 2 -> 4 -> 3.
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    tail, carry = dummy, 0
    while l1 or l2 or carry:    # run while ANY source of digits remains
        s = (l1.val if l1 else 0) + (l2.val if l2 else 0) + carry
        carry, digit = divmod(s, 10)   # carry = s // 10, digit = s % 10
        tail.next = ListNode(digit)    # emit one result digit
        tail = tail.next
        l1 = l1.next if l1 else None   # advance only non-exhausted lists
        l2 = l2.next if l2 else None
    return dummy.next

sections.title: Pattern: Fixed-Gap Two Pointers & Ring-and-Cut
sections.content:
Recognize it: the problem measures position FROM THE END ("n-th from the end", "rotate right by k") but the list only walks forward. The trick: convert the from-the-end distance into a fixed gap between two forward-moving pointers, so one pass suffices.

The invariant for Remove Nth Node From End: after the setup loop, lead is exactly n + 1 nodes ahead of trail; that gap never changes while both slide; therefore when lead steps off the end (None), trail stands on the PREDECESSOR of the n-th-from-end node — precisely where you must stand to bypass it. Why n + 1 and not n: to delete a node you need its predecessor, and starting both pointers from a dummy (not head) makes "delete the head itself" (n equals the length) fall out of the same code path with zero special cases.

Rotate a Linked List is the same idea executed through a ring: walking to the old tail gives you the length n for free; joining tail to head makes rotation a pure re-labeling problem — choose where the list now BEGINS. The new tail sits n − (k mod n) − 1 hops from the old head; cut after it. Two habits graders look for: reduce k with `k %= n` first (k can be 2·10^9 while n is 5), and sever the ring with `new_tail.next = None` — omitting that line turns your answer into an infinite loop for whoever traverses it.

Both are O(N) time, O(1) space, single structural pass.
sections.code:
def remove_nth_from_end(head, n):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)   # target might be the head -> dummy saves us
    lead = trail = dummy
    for _ in range(n + 1):      # gap of n+1 parks trail on the PREDECESSOR
        lead = lead.next
    while lead:                 # slide the fixed gap until lead falls off
        lead = lead.next
        trail = trail.next
    trail.next = trail.next.next    # bypass the n-th node from the end
    return dummy.next


def rotate_right(head, k):
    if not head or not head.next:
        return head             # 0 or 1 node: rotation is a no-op
    n, tail = 1, head           # 1) measure length, find the old tail
    while tail.next:
        tail = tail.next
        n += 1
    k %= n                      # rotating by n is identity; k may be huge
    if k == 0:
        return head             # nothing to do — avoid pointless surgery
    tail.next = head            # 2) close the list into a ring
    new_tail = head             # 3) new tail sits n-k-1 hops from old head
    for _ in range(n - k - 1):
        new_tail = new_tail.next
    new_head = new_tail.next    # 4) head follows the new tail
    new_tail.next = None        # 5) cut the ring — forgetting this leaves a cycle
    return new_head

sections.title: Pattern: Pointer Switching for Alignment
sections.content:
Recognize it: two lists that share a suffix ("Y shape"), and you must return the first shared NODE — same object in memory, not merely equal value. Intersection of Two Linked Lists is this tab's instance.

The elegant solution is pointer switching. Let a = the part of list A before the junction, b = the same for list B, and c = the shared suffix. Pointer pa walks a + c and then restarts on B; pointer pb walks b + c and restarts on A. By the time either can reach the junction on its second list, both have travelled exactly a + b + c steps — so they arrive together, and the loop's `pa is not pb` test catches it. If the lists never intersect, both pointers hit None on the same step (each has travelled a + c + b + c'… more precisely lenA + lenB), None is None, and the loop exits returning None — the no-intersection case needs zero extra code, which is why this version beats the alternatives in an interview.
