The plainer alternative — compute both lengths, advance the longer list's pointer by the difference, then walk in lockstep until the nodes match — is equally O(N + M) time and O(1) space and completely acceptable; know both, offer either. The hash-set version (store every node of A in a set, walk B until a node is already present) costs O(N) extra space and is the fallback if pointer reasoning deserts you mid-interview. Never compare by `.val`: distinct nodes may carry equal values, and the whole question is about identity.
sections.code:
def get_intersection(a, b):
    # Each pointer walks its own list, then SWITCHES to the other list's head.
    # Pointer A travels lenA + lenB steps; pointer B travels lenB + lenA.
    # Equal totals -> from the switch onward they are step-synchronized and
    # reach the first shared node at the same instant.
    pa, pb = a, b
    while pa is not pb:              # identity comparison, never value
        pa = pa.next if pa else b    # fell off the end -> restart on OTHER list
        pb = pb.next if pb else a
    # Exit: pa is pb — either the intersection node, or None when both
    # pointers fell off together (the lists never meet).
    return pa

sections.title: Pattern: Value Overwrite Deletion
sections.content:
Recognize it: Delete a Given Node hands you a pointer to the node that must disappear — and nothing else. No head, no predecessor. Every deletion you have written so far worked by making the predecessor skip over the victim, and here the predecessor is unreachable, so the standard move is impossible by construction. That impossibility IS the question.

The trick reframes the goal: the list must merely LOOK as if the node were deleted. So you overwrite the given node's value with its successor's value, then bypass the successor. To any traversal from the head, the sequence of values is exactly what deletion would have produced. Both steps are O(1), no traversal at all.

An interviewer will probe the seams, so raise them first: it cannot work on the tail node (no successor exists to copy — and the problem statement guarantees the node is not the tail for exactly this reason); if outside code holds a reference to the successor node, that reference now points at a node that has been spliced out; and if the values were huge objects, the 'copy' is just a reference assignment in Python, so cost stays O(1). This pattern also generalizes: the same impersonation idea shows up when deleting from a singly linked structure given only local access, and understanding WHY it is a workaround (not a real deletion) is what the question actually measures.
sections.code:
def delete_given_node(node):
    # You are handed ONLY this node — the head (and thus the predecessor)
    # is unreachable, so a normal bypass is impossible.
    # Solution: IMPERSONATE the successor, then remove the successor.
    node.val = node.next.val        # 1) copy the next node's value into here
    node.next = node.next.next      # 2) unlink the next node instead
    # Limits worth stating out loud in the interview:
    #  - undefined for the TAIL node: there is no successor to impersonate
    #    (the classic problem guarantees the node is not the tail)
    #  - any external reference held to the bypassed successor is now stale
    #  - node identity changes meaning: the "deleted" object still exists

sections.title: Pitfalls & Common Mistakes
sections.content:
Each mistake below has sunk real interviews; each fix is one habit.

1) Losing the suffix: writing `curr.next = prev` before saving `curr.next`. Everything after curr becomes unreachable. Fix: `nxt = curr.next` is ALWAYS the first line of the loop body (or use one tuple assignment, whose right side is evaluated before any write).

2) No dummy when the head can change: deleting/merging with branchy special cases for the first node breeds bugs. Fix: any operation that might replace the head starts with `dummy = ListNode(0, head)` and returns `dummy.next`.

3) Wrong guard order: `while fast.next and fast` raises AttributeError when fast is None. Fix: `while fast and fast.next` — `and` short-circuits left to right.

4) Value comparison where identity is meant: using `==`/`.val` in cycle or intersection checks breaks on duplicate values. Fix: compare nodes with `is`.

5) Off-by-one in the gap: advancing lead n instead of n+1 from the dummy leaves trail ON the target instead of before it. Fix: state where trail must STOP (the predecessor), then count the gap; dry-run on a 2-node list.

6) A branch that advances nothing: in merge-style loops, an `elif` chain where some branch forgets to move a pointer loops forever. Fix: check every branch advances at least one finger.

7) Leaving an accidental cycle: rotate/reorder solutions that join the list into a ring and forget `new_tail.next = None`. Fix: every "close the ring" line gets a paired "cut the ring" line before returning.

8) Recursion on long inputs: an elegant recursive reversal dies at ~1000 depth; sheet inputs reach 10^5 nodes. Fix: iterate; keep recursion for trees, where depth is log-ish.

9) Forgetting `k %= n`: Rotate with k = 2·10^9 walks the ring for minutes. Fix: reduce k modulo length immediately after measuring the list.

10) Even-length middle drift: `while fast and fast.next` stops slow on the SECOND middle; palindrome and split logic must match that convention. Fix: pick the convention once, test with 2-node and 4-node lists before submitting.

sections.title: Interview Recognition Checklist
sections.content:
Cues that a problem is a linked-list pointer problem: the input is given as a head node (not an array); the statement says "in place", "O(1) extra space", or "without modifying values"; positions are measured from the end; the words cycle, loop, intersection, middle, or "in groups of k" appear; or you are handed a node WITHOUT the head. Map the cue to the pattern: reverse/groups → in-place reversal; middle/cycle/loop-start → fast & slow; build-a-result (merge, digit sum, flatten) → dummy + tail; from-the-end positions or rotation → fixed gap / ring-and-cut; shared suffix → pointer switching; no-head deletion → value overwrite.

The 30-second pre-code checklist:
- Empty list and single-node list: does my loop even start? What do I return?
- Can the HEAD change? If yes, dummy node now, return dummy.next.
- Do I need the PREDECESSOR of the node I operate on? Park a pointer one step early.
- Which finger can be None mid-loop? Write the guard in short-circuit order.
- Does every branch of the loop advance a pointer? (termination)
- Am I comparing nodes by identity (`is`) or accidentally by value?
- Did I sever any ring I created, and restore anything I reversed (palindrome)?
- State the invariant in one sentence; if I cannot, I am not ready to type.

Finally, narrate the plan on a 3-node drawing before coding — interviewers score the drawing and the invariant sentence as highly as the code itself.

implementations.title: SinglyLinkedList — full class from scratch
implementations.code:
class Node:
    # One cell of the chain: a value plus a reference to the next cell.
    __slots__ = ("val", "next")         # no per-instance __dict__ -> smaller nodes

    def __init__(self, val, nxt=None):
        self.val = val                  # payload
        self.next = nxt                 # successor node or None


class SinglyLinkedList:
    # Maintains BOTH head and tail pointers so push_back is O(1),
    # plus a size counter so len() is O(1) instead of an O(N) walk.
    def __init__(self):
        self.head = None                # first node or None when empty
        self.tail = None                # last node or None when empty
        self._size = 0                  # number of nodes, kept in sync

    def __len__(self):
        return self._size               # O(1): updated by every insert/delete

    def __iter__(self):
        # Generator walk: enables `for v in lst` and list(lst).
        curr = self.head
        while curr:
            yield curr.val              # hand out the value, keep the node private
            curr = curr.next            # follow the arrow

    def push_front(self, val):
        # O(1): new node adopts the old head as its successor.
        self.head = Node(val, self.head)
        if self.tail is None:           # list was empty -> node is also the tail
            self.tail = self.head
        self._size += 1

    def push_back(self, val):
        # O(1) thanks to the tail pointer (would be O(N) without it).
        node = Node(val)
        if self.tail:
            self.tail.next = node       # old tail links forward to the new node
        else:
            self.head = node            # empty list: new node is head too
        self.tail = node                # either way it is the new tail
        self._size += 1

    def insert_at(self, idx, val):
        # O(idx): walk to the predecessor, then rewrite two arrows.
        if idx <= 0:                    # clamp: treat as push_front
            self.push_front(val)
            return
        if idx >= self._size:           # clamp: treat as push_back
            self.push_back(val)
            return
        prev = self.head
        for _ in range(idx - 1):        # stop ON the predecessor of slot idx
            prev = prev.next
        prev.next = Node(val, prev.next)    # new node adopts prev's old successor
        self._size += 1

    def delete_value(self, val):
        # O(N): unlink the FIRST node holding val; True if found.
        dummy = Node(None, self.head)   # dummy -> deleting the head is not special
        prev = dummy
        while prev.next and prev.next.val != val:
            prev = prev.next            # walk until prev precedes the victim
        if prev.next is None:
            return False                # value absent — nothing changed
        if prev.next is self.tail:      # removing the last node moves the tail
            self.tail = prev if prev is not dummy else None
        prev.next = prev.next.next      # bypass the victim (GC reclaims it)
        self.head = dummy.next          # head may have changed via the dummy
        self._size -= 1
        return True

    def get(self, idx):
        # O(idx): no address arithmetic exists — must hop idx times.
        if not 0 <= idx < self._size:
            raise IndexError("linked list index out of range")
        curr = self.head
        for _ in range(idx):
            curr = curr.next            # one hop per index step
        return curr.val

    def reverse(self):
        # O(N) time / O(1) space: the classic three-finger flip, in place.
        prev, curr = None, self.head
        self.tail = self.head           # old head will end up as the tail
        while curr:
            nxt = curr.next             # save the suffix BEFORE overwriting
            curr.next = prev            # flip this arrow backwards
            prev, curr = curr, nxt      # slide both fingers forward
        self.head = prev                # last flipped node is the new head

    def to_list(self):
        # Snapshot as a Python list — convenient for tests and printing.
        return list(self)               # uses __iter__ above


if __name__ == "__main__":
    lst = SinglyLinkedList()
    for x in (1, 2, 3):
        lst.push_back(x)                # 1 -> 2 -> 3
    lst.push_front(0)                   # 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3
    lst.insert_at(2, 9)                 # 0 -> 1 -> 9 -> 2 -> 3
    assert lst.to_list() == [0, 1, 9, 2, 3]
    assert lst.delete_value(9)          # back to 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3
    lst.reverse()                       # 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> 0
    assert lst.to_list() == [3, 2, 1, 0]
    assert len(lst) == 4 and lst.get(0) == 3
    assert lst.tail.val == 0            # tail tracked through the reversal
    print("SinglyLinkedList OK")

implementations.title: DoublyLinkedList with sentinels (LRU skeleton)
implementations.code:
class DNode:
    # Doubly linked node: arrows in BOTH directions.
    __slots__ = ("val", "prev", "next")

    def __init__(self, val=None):
        self.val = val                  # payload (None for sentinels)
        self.prev = None                # predecessor
        self.next = None                # successor


class DoublyLinkedList:
    # Two permanent SENTINEL nodes (head/tail) that never hold data.
    # Every real node therefore always has a live prev AND next, so
    # insert/remove need ZERO None-checks. This exact skeleton powers
    # the LRU Cache question: dict for lookup + this list for recency.
    def __init__(self):
        self.head = DNode()             # sentinel before the first real node
        self.tail = DNode()             # sentinel after the last real node
        self.head.next = self.tail      # empty list: sentinels hold hands
        self.tail.prev = self.head
        self._size = 0

    def __len__(self):
        return self._size               # O(1)

    def _insert_between(self, node, left, right):
        # Wire node between two EXISTING neighbours: 4 writes, O(1).
        node.prev = left
        node.next = right
        left.next = node                # left now points forward to node
        right.prev = node               # right now points back to node
        self._size += 1

    def push_front(self, val):
        node = DNode(val)
        # insert right after the head sentinel
        self._insert_between(node, self.head, self.head.next)
        return node                     # caller keeps this for O(1) removal later

    def push_back(self, val):
        node = DNode(val)
        # insert right before the tail sentinel
        self._insert_between(node, self.tail.prev, self.tail)
        return node

    def remove(self, node):
        # O(1) removal GIVEN the node — the whole reason LRU uses a DLL.
        node.prev.next = node.next      # left neighbour skips over node
        node.next.prev = node.prev      # right neighbour skips back over node
        node.prev = node.next = None    # fully detach (prevents stale-pointer bugs)
        self._size -= 1
        return node.val

    def move_to_front(self, node):
        # The LRU "touch": unlink + relink at the front, O(1).
        node.prev.next = node.next      # unlink from current position
        node.next.prev = node.prev
        self._size -= 1                 # _insert_between will add it back
        self._insert_between(node, self.head, self.head.next)

    def pop_back(self):
        # Evict the least-recently-used node in LRU terms.
        if self._size == 0:
            raise IndexError("pop from empty list")
        return self.remove(self.tail.prev)  # last REAL node sits before sentinel

    def to_list(self):
        out, curr = [], self.head.next
        while curr is not self.tail:    # walk sentinel to sentinel
            out.append(curr.val)
            curr = curr.next
        return out


if __name__ == "__main__":
    dll = DoublyLinkedList()
    a = dll.push_back(1)                # keep the node handle for O(1) ops
    dll.push_back(2)
    dll.push_front(0)                   # 0 <-> 1 <-> 2
    dll.move_to_front(a)                # 1 <-> 0 <-> 2
    assert dll.to_list() == [1, 0, 2]
    assert dll.pop_back() == 2          # evict from the back
    assert dll.to_list() == [1, 0] and len(dll) == 2
    print("DoublyLinkedList OK")

implementations.title: Floyd cycle toolkit: detect, entry, length
implementations.code:
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, nxt=None):
        self.val = val                  # payload
        self.next = nxt                 # successor or None


def has_cycle(head):
    # Floyd phase 1 only: does a cycle exist?
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:           # fast is the only pointer that can fall off
        slow = slow.next                # tortoise: 1 step
        fast = fast.next.next           # hare: 2 steps
        if slow is fast:                # met INSIDE the cycle (identity, not value)
            return True
    return False                        # reached None -> the list terminates


def cycle_entry(head):
    # Full Floyd: return the node where the cycle begins, else None.
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:
            break                       # meeting point found inside the cycle
    else:
        return None                     # while-else: no break happened -> acyclic
    # MATH: a = head->entry, b = entry->meeting, L = cycle length (b + c).
    # slow walked a+b; fast walked 2(a+b) = a+b+kL  =>  a = (k-1)L + c.
    # Hence a steps from head == c steps (plus laps) from the meeting point:
    # two speed-1 pointers collide exactly at the entry.
    slow = head
    while slow is not fast:
        slow = slow.next                # both at speed 1 now
        fast = fast.next
    return slow


def cycle_length(head):
    # Detect, then lap the cycle once, counting steps.
    meet = None
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:
            meet = slow                 # remember any node inside the cycle
            break
    if meet is None:
        return 0                        # acyclic list has cycle length 0
    steps, curr = 1, meet.next
    while curr is not meet:             # walk one full lap back to the start node
        curr = curr.next
        steps += 1
    return steps


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Build 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5, then loop 5 back to node 3.
    nodes = [ListNode(i) for i in range(1, 6)]
    for i in range(4):
        nodes[i].next = nodes[i + 1]    # straight chain first
    nodes[4].next = nodes[2]            # create the loop at value 3
    assert has_cycle(nodes[0]) is True
    assert cycle_entry(nodes[0]) is nodes[2]    # entry is the node valued 3
    assert cycle_length(nodes[0]) == 3          # 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> back
    nodes[4].next = None                # break the loop
    assert has_cycle(nodes[0]) is False
    assert cycle_entry(nodes[0]) is None
    print("Floyd toolkit OK")

implementations.title: Reverse Nodes in K Group — complete solution
implementations.code:
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, nxt=None):
        self.val = val                  # payload
        self.next = nxt                 # successor or None


def reverse_k_group(head, k):
    # Reverse every consecutive block of k nodes, in place, O(1) extra space.
    # A final block shorter than k stays in original order (LeetCode 25 rules).
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)           # head will change -> dummy owns the answer
    block_prev = dummy                  # node JUST BEFORE the current block
    while True:
        # 1) Probe: is there a full block of k nodes left? kth = block's last node.
        kth = block_prev
        for _ in range(k):
            kth = kth.next
            if kth is None:
                return dummy.next       # fewer than k remain -> leave them, done
        block_next = kth.next           # first node AFTER this block
        # 2) Reverse exactly the k nodes of the block (standard 3-finger flip).
        #    Seeding prev with block_next pre-links the block's future tail.
        prev, curr = block_next, block_prev.next
        while curr is not block_next:   # stop when the block is consumed
            nxt = curr.next             # save suffix
            curr.next = prev            # flip arrow
            prev = curr                 # advance prev
            curr = nxt                  # advance curr
        # 3) Reconnect: the block's old first node is now its LAST node.
        old_first = block_prev.next
        block_prev.next = kth           # kth leads the reversed block
        block_prev = old_first          # next block hangs after the old first


def build(vals):
    # Helper: python list -> linked list (dummy + tail builder pattern).
    dummy = ListNode()
    t = dummy
    for v in vals:
        t.next = ListNode(v)            # append fresh node
        t = t.next                      # advance tail
    return dummy.next


def to_list(head):
    out = []                            # collect values front to back
    while head:
        out.append(head.val)
        head = head.next                # follow the chain
    return out


if __name__ == "__main__":
    assert to_list(reverse_k_group(build([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]), 2)) == [2, 1, 4, 3, 5]
    assert to_list(reverse_k_group(build([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]), 3)) == [3, 2, 1, 6, 5, 4]
    assert to_list(reverse_k_group(build([1, 2]), 3)) == [1, 2]  # short block untouched
    assert to_list(reverse_k_group(build([]), 2)) == []          # empty list safe
    print("reverse_k_group OK")

Linked List & Arrays.summary:
Quick recap of the two parent tabs: arrays give O(1) indexed access into one contiguous block, and in-place edits mean overwriting slots; linked lists give O(1) local rewiring of scattered nodes that are reachable only through pointers, and in-place edits mean re-aiming arrows. This tab is the sheet's hybrid set — five problems chosen because one discipline solves them all: several cooperating pointers, each with a job description and a movement rule that provably never skips an answer. The layout (index or node) changes the syntax; the reasoning is identical.

Interviewers adore this cluster. 3 Sum and Trapping Rain Water are among the most-asked questions at MAANG because they separate candidates who can PROVE a pointer may move from those who pattern-match and pray. Clone Linked List with Random Pointer is the cleanest identity-vs-value test in the catalogue: it cannot be solved by copying values, only by reasoning about which object is which. Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array and Max Consecutive Ones look easy, and that is the trap — they are graded on whether your invariant is airtight, not on whether the output happens to be right.

The mental model for the whole tab: before moving any pointer, finish this sentence — "moving this pointer cannot skip a valid answer because …". For 3 Sum the reason comes from sortedness; for Trapping Rain Water it comes from knowing which wall is the binding constraint; for the compaction problems it comes from the write index never overtaking the read index; for the clone it comes from a bijection between original and copied nodes. If you can finish the sentence, the code is ten lines. If you cannot, no amount of typing will save the solution.
preRequisites: The Linked List tab: traversal, dummy nodes, and in-place rewiring — Clone with Random Pointer builds directly on them.
Array two-pointer basics from the Arrays tab (Two Sum, Sort Colors) — this tab generalizes them to converging pointers with proofs.
list.sort() is in-place Timsort at O(N log N) and returns None; sorted() returns a new list — 3 Sum starts by sorting.
dict operations are O(1) on average, and node OBJECTS are valid dict keys (hashed by identity) — the clone's hash-map solution depends on this.
Slicing copies: a[1:] builds a new O(k) list, so in-place O(1)-space solutions must index, never slice.
enumerate and range(len(a)) idioms for walking an array with an index you also write through.
min/max running bookkeeping: maintaining a best-so-far in one variable instead of recomputing with max(list) each step.
cheatSheet: 3 Sum: sort; fix anchor i; converge l,r on the suffix; sum<target → l+=1, sum>target → r-=1; skip duplicates at i, l, r — O(N^2) time / O(1) extra.
Trapping water at i: min(max_left[i], max_right[i]) − h[i]; two-pointer version keeps left_max/right_max and always processes the SMALLER side — O(N)/O(1).
Remove duplicates (sorted): write index w=1; if nums[r] != nums[w-1]: nums[w]=nums[r]; w+=1; answer is nums[:w] — O(N)/O(1).
Max consecutive ones: streak = streak+1 if x==1 else 0; best = max(best, streak) — O(N)/O(1), the zero-budget sliding window.
Random-pointer clone (hash): pass 1 builds {old: new} for every node; pass 2 wires new.next = map[old.next], new.random = map[old.random] — O(N)/O(N).
Random-pointer clone (O(1) space): splice A→A'→B→B'; set copy.random = orig.random.next; unzip and RESTORE the original — three passes.
Two-pointer legality: a pointer may only move in a direction that provably cannot skip a valid answer — say the proof before moving it.
Sort first when answers are VALUE combinations (3 Sum); never sort when the answer needs original INDICES (Two Sum).
Compaction safety: the write pointer never passes the read pointer (w ≤ r), so overwriting forward can never destroy unread input.

sections.title: What & Why
sections.content:
Recap in one breath: the Linked List tab taught O(1) pointer surgery on scattered nodes, and the Arrays tab taught O(1) indexing into contiguous slots. This tab exists because the interviewer's favourite skill — several cooperating pointers moving under a provable rule — is layout-independent, and these five questions are its cleanest exam across both layouts.

What the five questions each certify: 3 Sum certifies that you can turn sortedness into a licence for pointer movement (and dedupe without a set). Trapping Rain Water certifies that you can carry just enough state (two running maxima) to replace whole precomputed arrays. Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array certifies the read/write compaction contract that every in-place array rewrite uses. Max Consecutive Ones certifies streak bookkeeping — the embryo of every sliding window. Clone Linked List with Random Pointer certifies that you understand object identity: two nodes with equal values are still different nodes, and a correct clone is a bijection, not a value copy.

Where this shows up in real systems: compaction is how databases vacuum dead rows and how garbage collectors defragment heaps; running-maxima scans power skyline and water-fill computations in graphics; deep-copying object graphs with arbitrary cross-references (the random pointer, generalized) is exactly what serializers and `copy.deepcopy` do with a memo dictionary. These are not puzzle tricks; they are production idioms shrunk to interview size.

sections.title: Memory Model: Arrays vs Linked Lists Side by Side
sections.content:
The two layouts store the same sequence in opposite ways, and every pattern in this tab exploits one layout's superpower.

```
Array (contiguous block)              Linked list (scattered nodes)
+-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+      head -> [3|*] -> [1|*] -> [4|*] -> [1|/]
|  3  |  1  |  4  |  1  |  5  |      each node anywhere on the heap;
+-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+      a "position" is a node REFERENCE,
   ^l                    ^r          not a number; only next-hops exist
 two indices l, r: O(1) jumps,
 O(1) reads/writes at any slot
```

Why compaction (Remove Duplicates) is an array-only trick: it OVERWRITES slot w while reading slot r, which needs O(1) writes by position — a linked list would instead unlink duplicate nodes, a different operation with the same spirit. Why converging pointers (3 Sum, Trapping Rain Water) are array-first: `r -= 1` moves BACKWARD in O(1), which a singly linked list cannot do at all. Why Clone with Random Pointer is a list-only problem: the structure being copied IS the pointer graph; an array's structure is implicit in positions, so there is nothing interesting to clone. Cache locality seals the practical gap: an array scan streams sequential addresses the prefetcher loves, while a list walk chases pointers across the heap — at equal Big-O the array is often several times faster in wall-clock terms. Choose the layout whose O(1) superpower (indexed overwrite vs local rewire) your algorithm actually needs.

sections.title: Core Operations & Complexity — the Comparison Table
sections.content:
One table to internalize — the same logical operation, priced under each layout, with the reason in one clause.

```
Operation                      Array (list)       Linked list      Why they differ
read k-th element              O(1)               O(k)             address math vs k hops
overwrite k-th element         O(1)               O(k)             same
append at end                  O(1) amortized     O(1) w/ tail     over-allocation vs tail ref
insert/delete at FRONT         O(N)               O(1)             every slot shifts vs re-point head
insert AFTER a held position   O(N)               O(1)             shifting vs 2 arrow writes
delete AFTER a held position   O(N)               O(1)             shifting vs 1 arrow write
move a pointer BACKWARD        O(1)  (i -= 1)     impossible*      indices are numbers; next is one-way
search by value (unsorted)     O(N)               O(N)             both must scan
binary search (sorted)         O(log N)           useless          needs O(1) random access
memory per element             1 pointer slot     whole node       object header + next per node
```

(*) backward motion needs a doubly linked list, which pays an extra pointer per node. Read the table as a decision procedure: converging two-pointer algorithms (3 Sum, Trapping Rain Water) need `r -= 1`, so they live on arrays; O(1) splicing (Clone's interleave trick) needs insert-after-a-node, so it lives on lists; compaction (Remove Duplicates) needs overwrite-by-index, arrays again. When an interviewer swaps the container mid-question ("now the input is a list, not an array"), this table tells you instantly which parts of your algorithm survive and which must be redesigned.

sections.title: How Python Does It
sections.content:
Four Python facts carry this whole tab. First, `list.sort()` is Timsort: O(N log N) worst case, in place, returns None (assigning `a = a.sort()` silently gives you None — a classic bug). 3 Sum's entire strategy is buying sortedness up front. Second, `dict` gives O(1) average lookup, and — crucially for the clone problem — plain objects are hashable BY IDENTITY, so a dictionary keyed by node objects distinguishes two nodes with equal values. Keying by `node.val` instead is the classic wrong clone.

Third, slices copy. `nums[1:]` allocates a new list in O(k) time and space, so writing 'in-place' solutions with slices quietly violates the O(1)-space contract; index with `nums[r]` and overwrite with `nums[w] = ...` instead. Similarly `del nums[i]` and `nums.remove(x)` shift every later element (O(N) each) — calling them in a loop is the hidden O(N²) that compaction exists to avoid.

Fourth, appends are amortized O(1) because CPython over-allocates capacity geometrically, which is why building a result list with `res.append(...)` is fine, while inserting at the front is O(N) per call. For the linked-list half of this tab, everything from the Linked List tab applies unchanged: define your own Node class, prefer iteration to recursion, and compare nodes with `is`.
sections.code:
# A Python list is an array of POINTERS in one contiguous block.
a = []
# Amortized O(1) append: CPython over-allocates capacity in growth spurts,
# so most appends never move memory (~1.125x growth factor).
for x in (3, 1, 4, 1, 5):
    a.append(x)

a.sort()                     # Timsort: O(N log N) worst, O(N) on nearly-sorted runs
b = sorted(a, reverse=True)  # sorted() COPIES; .sort() is in place and returns None

# dict lookups/inserts are O(1) average — and node OBJECTS are hashable
# by identity, so {old_node: new_node} works with no id() calls.
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val):
        self.val = val
        self.next = None
        self.random = None       # the pointer that makes cloning interesting

n1, n2 = Node(1), Node(1)        # equal values, DIFFERENT identities
clone_of = {n1: Node(1), n2: Node(1)}    # keys are the node objects themselves
assert clone_of[n1] is not clone_of[n2]  # value-keyed maps would collide here

# Slicing copies: a[1:] allocates a NEW list — O(k) time AND space.
# In-place O(1)-space solutions must therefore index, never slice.
tail_copy = a[1:]            # fine in tests; a space-limit violation in solutions

# Deleting from the middle of a list shifts every later element: O(N).
# That is why Remove Duplicates overwrites forward instead of calling del.

sections.title: Pattern: Sort + Converging Two Pointers
sections.content:
Recognize it: "find all triples/pairs whose values satisfy an equation", answers are VALUE combinations (not indices), duplicates in the output are forbidden. Values-not-indices is the green light to sort; sorting is what turns pointer movement from a guess into a proof.

The structure: fix an anchor nums[i], then find all pairs in the sorted suffix summing to −nums[i] with two converging pointers. The invariant: every valid pair for this anchor lies within the current window [l, r]. The movement proof — the sentence you must be able to say: if nums[l] + nums[r] < target, then nums[l] paired with ANY r' ≤ r is also < target (the array is sorted, so nums[r'] ≤ nums[r]); l can appear in no remaining answer, so discarding l is safe. Symmetrically, an overshoot discards r. Each step discards one index forever, so the pair phase is O(N) per anchor and the whole algorithm is O(N²) — beating the O(N³) brute force and avoiding the hashing-and-dedupe swamp of set-based solutions.

Deduplication has exactly three rules: skip a repeated anchor BEFORE using it (`i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i-1]`), and after recording a hit, advance l past equal values and r past equal values. Nothing else is needed — no result set, no sorting of triples. Sheet connections: this generalizes the Arrays tab's Two Sum (which forbids sorting because it wants indices) and is the inner engine of Four Sum (one more anchor loop around the same core). The `nums[i] > 0` early break is a free optimization worth saying aloud.

sections.title: Pattern: Two Ends with Running Maxima
sections.content:
Recognize it: bars/heights, and the answer at each position depends on the best value on BOTH sides of it (here: the tallest wall left and right). The physics first: water settles at min(tallest_left, tallest_right), so the water above bar i is min(maxL[i], maxR[i]) − height[i], never negative because each maximum includes bar i itself.

Three solutions, in the order you should present them. Brute force: for each bar scan both directions for the maxima — O(N²), name it and move on. Prefix/suffix arrays: precompute maxL (left-to-right) and maxR (right-to-left), then one summing pass — O(N) time but O(N) space, and completely fine as a first correct answer. The two-pointer refinement removes the arrays with one observation: you never need BOTH maxima at a position, only the smaller one — and when height[l] < height[r], the right side is guaranteed to hold a wall at least height[l] tall, so the left maximum alone is the binding constraint at l. Process that side, advance, repeat. The invariant: every position outside [l, r] has already had its water counted exactly once, using a bound that was provably tight.

That "the smaller side is fully decidable" argument is the entire interview. It is the same converging-pointer geometry as 3 Sum, but the state carried is two running maxima instead of a sum — seeing that connection is what this tab is for. Sheet question: Trapping Rain Water. Related shape: the classic Container With Most Water uses the same movement rule with a different objective.
sections.code:
def trap(height):
    # Water above bar i = min(tallest-to-left, tallest-to-right) - height[i].
    # Two pointers maintain those maxima WITHOUT prefix/suffix arrays.
    l, r = 0, len(height) - 1
    left_max = right_max = 0        # tallest bar seen so far from each side
    water = 0
    while l < r:
        if height[l] < height[r]:
            # Some bar >= height[l] exists on the right (height[r] itself),
            # so min(left_wall, right_wall) at position l is decided by the
            # LEFT side alone — right_max cannot be the binding constraint.
            left_max = max(left_max, height[l])
            water += left_max - height[l]   # 0 when height[l] sets a new max
            l += 1                  # position l is fully settled — move on
        else:
            # Mirror image: the left wall is at least height[r], so the
            # right maximum decides the level at position r.
            right_max = max(right_max, height[r])
            water += right_max - height[r]
            r -= 1
    return water                    # O(N) time, O(1) space, single pass

sections.title: Pattern: Read/Write Pointer Compaction
sections.content:
Recognize it: "remove/keep elements IN PLACE, O(1) extra space, return the new length". The contract is subtle and worth restating to the interviewer: you do not shrink the list; you pack the survivors into the front and return their count, and everything past index w−1 is unspecified garbage the judge never reads.

Two pointers with different jobs: r (read) visits every element exactly once; w (write) marks the boundary of the finished output. The invariant: nums[:w] is exactly the deduplicated version of nums[:r] seen so far, in order, final. The safety argument that makes overwriting legal: w ≤ r at all times — w starts equal to r's start and advances at most once per r step — so `nums[w] = nums[r]` can only overwrite a slot that has already been read. That one inequality is the whole correctness proof; say it.

Compare against nums[w−1] (the last kept value), which reads naturally as "is this a new value?" — on a sorted array comparing with nums[r−1] happens to work too, but the w−1 form is the one that survives variations. And the variations are the point: keep-at-most-two-duplicates changes the test to `nums[r] != nums[w-2]`; Move Zeroes and Remove Element are the same skeleton with a different keep-predicate. Why not `del` or `remove` in a loop? Each call shifts the tail — O(N) per deletion, O(N²) total, plus the classic skip-an-element bug when deleting while iterating. Sheet question: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array — O(N) time, O(1) space, one pass.
sections.code:
def remove_duplicates(nums):
    # INVARIANT: nums[:w] is the deduped prefix — strictly increasing,
    # final, and never touched again. r scans every element once.
    if not nums:
        return 0
    w = 1                           # nums[0] is always kept
    for r in range(1, len(nums)):
        if nums[r] != nums[w - 1]:  # compare against the last KEPT value
            nums[w] = nums[r]       # overwrite forward; r >= w always,
            w += 1                  # so no unread element is ever destroyed
    return w                        # caller reads nums[:w]; the tail is garbage

sections.title: Pattern: Streak Counting (Degenerate Sliding Window)
sections.content:
Recognize it: "longest run of X", "maximum streak", any question about consecutive elements satisfying a predicate. The state is one integer — the length of the run ENDING at the current element — and the update is binary: extend on success, reset to zero on failure. Recording the best immediately inside the extend branch (rather than after the loop) means an array that ends mid-streak needs no postscript, a small habit that prevents a real off-by-one family.

Why this is worth a section for a one-liner problem: it is the degenerate sliding window. A window is a pair of pointers [left, right] where right extends and left retreats just enough to restore validity; here "validity" is "contains no zeros", so any zero snaps left all the way past it — collapsing the window to nothing, which is exactly `streak = 0`. See it that way once and the generalization is mechanical: allow at most k zeros inside the window and you get the standard budgeted window (`while zeros > k: shrink from the left`) of Max Consecutive Ones III; track last-seen positions instead and you get Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters from the Arrays tab. Interviewers deliberately open with the streak version and then add the budget — answer the easy form in a way that sets up the follow-up.

The reset is also the reason this is O(N) and not O(N²): the naive "for each index, count forward" rescans runs repeatedly; the streak counter never re-reads an element. Sheet question: Max Consecutive Ones.

sections.title: Pattern: Cloning by Bijection (Hash Map & Interleaving)
sections.content:
Recognize it: deep-copy a structure whose pointers can aim ANYWHERE — Clone Linked List with Random Pointer gives every node a `next` and a `random` that may point forward, backward, at itself, or be None. A single forward pass cannot work naively: when you meet a node whose random aims three nodes AHEAD, the target's copy does not exist yet. Every correct solution is a way of establishing a bijection old→new before wiring.

Solution 1 — hash map, O(N) space: pass 1 creates a copy of every node and records the pairing in a dict keyed by the ORIGINAL NODE OBJECTS (identity, not value — two nodes may share a value). Pass 2 wires `copy.next = map[orig.next]` and `copy.random = map[orig.random]`; seeding the map with {None: None} erases all the None branches. This is precisely how `copy.deepcopy` uses its memo dict — say that and you sound like an engineer, not a puzzle-solver.

Solution 2 — interleaving, O(1) extra space: encode the bijection in the list itself.

```
Original:  A ──▶ B ──▶ C
Step 1:    A ─▶ A' ─▶ B ─▶ B' ─▶ C ─▶ C'     (each copy spliced after its original)
Step 2:    A'.random = A.random.next           (a copy always sits right after its original)
Step 3:    unzip copies out; RESTORE A ─▶ B ─▶ C  (graders check the restore)
```

The splice makes "find the copy of X" a one-hop operation (X.next), replacing the dict. Three passes, O(N) time, O(1) extra space beyond the output. The linked-list skills doing the work here — splicing after a held node, careful unzip without losing a chain — are exactly the Linked List tab's surgery, which is why this question lives in the hybrid tab. Full interleave code with a verifier is in the implementations below.
sections.code:
def clone_random_hash(head):
    # Pass 1: bare-copy every node; remember the pairing old -> new.
    clone_of = {None: None}         # None maps to None -> no branches in pass 2
    curr = head
    while curr:
        clone_of[curr] = Node(curr.val)     # keys are node IDENTITIES
        curr = curr.next
    # Pass 2: wire next and random THROUGH the map. Any forward reference
    # already has a copy waiting — that is why two passes are needed.
    curr = head
    while curr:
        clone_of[curr].next = clone_of[curr.next]       # mirror the next arrow
        clone_of[curr].random = clone_of[curr.random]   # mirror the random arrow
        curr = curr.next
    return clone_of[head]           # O(N) time, O(N) extra space

sections.title: Pitfalls & Common Mistakes
sections.content:
1) 3 Sum duplicate output: forgetting the anchor skip (`i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i-1]`) or the pointer skips after a hit yields repeated triples. Fix: dedupe in exactly three places, and skip BEFORE using an anchor, not after — skipping after can jump over a legitimately different anchor.

2) Sorting away the answer: sorting is legal only when the output is value-based. Two Sum wants ORIGINAL indices — sort and you return positions in the wrong coordinate system. Fix: ask "values or indices?" before the first line.

3) Trapping Rain Water, moving the wrong side: advancing the taller side breaks the "smaller side is decidable" proof and undercounts. Fix: process and advance the side with the SMALLER current bar; on ties either side is fine — pick one branch shape and keep it.

4) Compaction that isn't: building `res = []` and appending survivors is correct output but violates the O(1)-space contract; `del nums[i]` inside a loop is O(N²) and skips elements. Fix: read/write pointers, overwrite forward, return w.

5) `l <= r` in converging loops: letting the pointers meet reuses one element twice (3 Sum) or double-counts a bar (Trapping). Fix: `while l < r` unless the problem explicitly needs l == r.

6) Clone keyed by value: `{node.val: copy}` collides when values repeat, silently cross-wiring randoms. Fix: key by the node object itself. Related: forgetting that random can be None (seed the map with {None: None}) and, in the interleave version, returning without UNZIPPING — the original list must come back intact, and graders check.

7) Streak best updated too late: computing best only when a zero arrives misses an array that ends on its longest run. Fix: update best at the moment the streak grows (or once more after the loop — pick one and be consistent).

8) `a = a.sort()`: sort() returns None; the array is now gone. Fix: call `a.sort()` as a statement, or use `sorted(a)` when you need a copy.

sections.title: Interview Recognition Checklist
sections.content:
Cues that a problem belongs to this hybrid family: "all pairs/triples with a value property" on an array → sort + converging pointers; "answer at each index depends on the best to its left AND right" → running maxima from both ends; "in place, O(1) extra space, return the new length" → read/write compaction; "longest run/streak" → extend-or-reset counter; "deep copy a structure with arbitrary cross-pointers" → bijection first (hash map), then the O(1) interleave upgrade.

The 30-second pre-code checklist:
- Does the answer need VALUES or INDICES? (decides whether sorting is legal)
- For every pointer I plan: what is its job, and can I finish the sentence "moving it cannot skip an answer because…"?
- Converging pointers: is the loop `l < r` or `l <= r`, and can they use the same element twice?
- Any write to the array: is w ≤ r guaranteed so I never clobber unread input?
- Duplicates: where exactly do I skip them (anchor, left, right), and is it before or after use?
- Linked structure: am I keying maps by node identity, and does None have a mapping?
- Am I obliged to restore the input (interleaved clone, reversed halves)?
- Complexity sanity: sort O(N log N) + pointers O(N) or O(N²) — does that meet the stated bound?

If the problem resists all five patterns, re-read it: interviewers routinely disguise one of these (Container With Most Water is Trapping's movement rule; Four Sum is 3 Sum plus a loop; Move Zeroes is compaction with a different predicate).

implementations.title: Clone Linked List with Random Pointer — both solutions + verifier
implementations.code:
class Node:
    # Node with the extra "random" pointer that makes cloning non-trivial.
    def __init__(self, val):
        self.val = val
        self.next = None
        self.random = None              # may aim anywhere in the list, or None


def clone_random_hash(head):
    # O(N) time, O(N) space: two passes over the list with an identity map.
    clone_of = {None: None}             # None -> None kills all branches below
    curr = head
    while curr:                         # PASS 1: create every copy, unwired
        clone_of[curr] = Node(curr.val)
        curr = curr.next
    curr = head
    while curr:                         # PASS 2: wire both arrows via the map
        clone_of[curr].next = clone_of[curr.next]
        clone_of[curr].random = clone_of[curr.random]
        curr = curr.next
    return clone_of[head]


def clone_random_interleave(head):
    # O(N) time, O(1) EXTRA space: encode the old->new pairing in the list.
    if not head:
        return None
    curr = head
    while curr:                         # STEP 1: splice copies -> A,A',B,B',...
        copy = Node(curr.val)
        copy.next = curr.next           # copy adopts the original's successor
        curr.next = copy                # original now points at its copy
        curr = copy.next                # hop over the copy to the next original
    curr = head
    while curr:                         # STEP 2: randoms via adjacency
        if curr.random:                 # copy of X sits at X.next by design
            curr.next.random = curr.random.next
        curr = curr.next.next           # original -> original hop
    curr = head
    clone_head = head.next              # first copy leads the cloned list
    while curr:                         # STEP 3: unzip AND restore the original
        copy = curr.next
        curr.next = copy.next           # original chain restored one link
        if copy.next:                   # a following original exists
            copy.next = copy.next.next  # so its copy follows it in clone chain
        curr = curr.next                # advance along restored originals
    return clone_head


def _check(orig_head, clone_head):
    # Verifier: same values, same random STRUCTURE, zero shared nodes.
    idx_o, idx_c = {}, {}
    o, i = orig_head, 0
    while o:                            # index the original nodes 0,1,2,...
        idx_o[id(o)] = i
        o, i = o.next, i + 1
    c, i = clone_head, 0
    while c:                            # index the clone nodes the same way
        idx_c[id(c)] = i
        c, i = c.next, i + 1
    o, c = orig_head, clone_head
    while o and c:
        assert o.val == c.val           # values mirror
        assert id(c) not in idx_o       # deep copy: no node is shared
        ro = None if o.random is None else idx_o[id(o.random)]
        rc = None if c.random is None else idx_c[id(c.random)]
        assert ro == rc                 # random aims at the SAME position
        o, c = o.next, c.next
    assert o is None and c is None      # equal lengths


def _build(vals, randoms):
    # Build a list where randoms[i] is the index node i's random points to.
    nodes = [Node(v) for v in vals]
    for i in range(len(nodes) - 1):
        nodes[i].next = nodes[i + 1]    # straight next-chain
    for i, ri in enumerate(randoms):
        nodes[i].random = None if ri is None else nodes[ri]
    return nodes[0] if nodes else None


if __name__ == "__main__":
    vals, rnds = [7, 13, 11, 10, 1], [None, 0, 4, 2, 0]   # LeetCode 138 example
    for cloner in (clone_random_hash, clone_random_interleave):
        orig = _build(vals, rnds)
        _check(orig, cloner(orig))      # clone is a faithful deep copy
        # after interleave-clone the ORIGINAL must be restored intact:
        o, expect = orig, iter(vals)
        while o:
            assert o.val == next(expect)
            o = o.next
    print("clone_random OK")

implementations.title: Trapping Rain Water — brute, prefix arrays, two pointers
implementations.code:
def trap_brute(height):
    # O(N^2) reference version: rescan both sides for every bar.
    n = len(height)
    total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        left = max(height[:i + 1])      # tallest bar at-or-left of i (includes i)
        right = max(height[i:])         # tallest bar at-or-right of i
        total += min(left, right) - height[i]   # never negative: both maxima >= h[i]
    return total


def trap_prefix(height):
    # O(N) time, O(N) space: precompute both running maxima, then one sum pass.
    n = len(height)
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    left = [0] * n                      # left[i] = max(height[0..i])
    right = [0] * n                     # right[i] = max(height[i..n-1])
    left[0] = height[0]
    for i in range(1, n):
        left[i] = max(left[i - 1], height[i])       # extend prefix maximum
    right[n - 1] = height[n - 1]
    for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):
        right[i] = max(right[i + 1], height[i])     # extend suffix maximum
    # water at i = binding wall minus floor height
    return sum(min(left[i], right[i]) - height[i] for i in range(n))


def trap_two_pointer(height):
    # O(N) time, O(1) space: keep only the two maxima that matter.
    l, r = 0, len(height) - 1
    left_max = right_max = 0            # tallest seen so far from each end
    water = 0
    while l < r:
        if height[l] < height[r]:
            # right side guarantees a wall >= height[l], so the LEFT max
            # is the binding constraint at position l — settle l now.
            left_max = max(left_max, height[l])
            water += left_max - height[l]
            l += 1
        else:
            right_max = max(right_max, height[r])   # mirror case
            water += right_max - height[r]
            r -= 1
    return water


if __name__ == "__main__":
    cases = [
        ([0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1, 3, 2, 1, 2, 1], 6),  # classic LeetCode 42
        ([4, 2, 0, 3, 2, 5], 9),
        ([3, 3, 3], 0),                              # flat: no water
        ([5], 0),                                    # single bar: no walls pair
        ([], 0),                                     # empty input
    ]
    for arr, want in cases:
        # all three implementations must agree with the expected answer
        assert trap_brute(list(arr)) == want if arr else True
        assert trap_prefix(list(arr)) == want
        assert trap_two_pointer(list(arr)) == want
    print("trapping rain water OK")

implementations.title: Array two-pointer toolkit: 3 Sum, compaction, streaks
implementations.code:
def three_sum(nums):
    # All unique triples summing to 0. O(N^2) time, O(1) extra space.
    nums.sort()                         # licence for pointer movement + dedupe
    res = []
    n = len(nums)
    for i in range(n - 2):              # anchor of the triple
        if nums[i] > 0:
            break                       # sorted: everything ahead is positive too
        if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]:
            continue                    # duplicate anchor -> duplicate triples
        l, r = i + 1, n - 1
        target = -nums[i]
        while l < r:
            s = nums[l] + nums[r]
            if s < target:
                l += 1                  # raise the sum (proof: sorted order)
            elif s > target:
                r -= 1                  # lower the sum
            else:
                res.append([nums[i], nums[l], nums[r]])
                l += 1
                r -= 1
                while l < r and nums[l] == nums[l - 1]:
                    l += 1              # skip equal left values
                while l < r and nums[r] == nums[r + 1]:
                    r -= 1              # skip equal right values
    return res


def remove_duplicates(nums):
    # In-place dedupe of a SORTED array; returns count of unique elements.
    if not nums:
        return 0
    w = 1                               # nums[:w] = finished unique prefix
    for r in range(1, len(nums)):
        if nums[r] != nums[w - 1]:      # new value vs last KEPT value
            nums[w] = nums[r]           # safe: w <= r always holds
            w += 1
    return w


def max_consecutive_ones(nums):
    # Longest run of 1s. O(N) time, O(1) space.
    best = streak = 0
    for x in nums:
        if x == 1:
            streak += 1                 # extend the run
            if streak > best:
                best = streak           # record immediately (end-of-array safe)
        else:
            streak = 0                  # zero kills the run
    return best


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # three_sum: canonical example, plus all-zero dedupe stress
    assert three_sum([-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4]) == [[-1, -1, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]
    assert three_sum([0, 0, 0, 0]) == [[0, 0, 0]]   # one triple, not four
    assert three_sum([1, 2, 3]) == []               # early break path
    # remove_duplicates: verify BOTH the count and the packed prefix
    a = [0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4]
    k = remove_duplicates(a)
    assert k == 5 and a[:k] == [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
    assert remove_duplicates([]) == 0               # empty input safe
    # max_consecutive_ones: run at the END must be counted
    assert max_consecutive_ones([1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1]) == 3
    assert max_consecutive_ones([0, 0]) == 0
    print("two-pointer toolkit OK")

Recursion.summary:
Recursion is the technique of solving a problem by having a function call itself on a smaller version of the same problem, until the input becomes so small that the answer is immediate. That immediate-answer case is the base case; the self-call on a smaller input is the recursive case. The magic is trust: you write the function assuming the recursive call already works for smaller inputs, and you only wire up (a) when to stop and (b) how to combine the smaller answer into the bigger one. Interviewers love recursion because it exposes whether you can decompose a problem — and because a whole family of classic questions (subsets, combinations, partitions, permutations) can ONLY be solved by systematically exploring choices, which recursion expresses in five lines.

The mental model for this sheet's questions is the recursion tree of choices. At every index of the input you make a decision — pick this element or don't, cut the string here or don't — and each decision spawns a child call. The leaves of that tree are the complete answers. For n elements the pick/not-pick tree has 2^n leaves, which is exactly why there are 2^n subsets:

```
                 solve(0, [])
              pick 1 /      \ skip 1
        solve(1,[1])          solve(1,[])
        pick 2 /  \ skip      pick 2 /  \ skip
   [1,2]        [1]        [2]         []      <- 2^2 = 4 leaves
```

Under the hood, every call pushes a stack frame holding its local variables; frames pop in reverse order when calls return. Depth equals one frame per undecided index, so space is O(n) for the stack even though the tree has exponentially many nodes — the tree is explored one root-to-leaf path at a time, never stored whole. Master the handful of templates in this tab (pick/not-pick, for-loop recursion with duplicate skipping, target-sum recursion with reuse, string partitioning, and counting with factorials instead of enumerating) and all six sheet problems here become variations on code you already know.
preRequisites: Python functions and scoping: each call gets its OWN local variables; an inner function can read (and mutate) lists from the enclosing scope without `nonlocal`.
List mechanics: `path.append(x)` and `path.pop()` are O(1) at the end; `path[:]` or `list(path)` makes an O(n) snapshot copy — you must copy before saving an answer.
Big-O for exponential families: n items have 2^n subsets and n! orderings; printing each answer of length n multiplies the bound by n.
The call stack as a LIFO structure: the most recent call must finish before its caller resumes — this is why 'undo after the call' restores state correctly.
`list.sort()` and why sorting groups equal values next to each other (the precondition for every duplicate-skipping trick).
Integer tools: `divmod(a, b)` returns `(a // b, a % b)` in one step, and `math.factorial(n)` — both power the K-th Permutation Sequence pattern.
cheatSheet: Every recursion = base case + strictly smaller subproblem + combine step; missing any one of the three gives a wrong answer or RecursionError.
Pick/not-pick: solve(i+1, path + [a[i]]) and solve(i+1, path) — binary tree, 2^n leaves, depth n, stack space O(n).
Enumerating all subsets costs O(2^n * n) time (copying each answer) and O(2^n * n) output space — the copy, not the recursion, dominates.
Duplicate skip (sorted input, for-loop recursion): `if j > start and a[j] == a[j-1]: continue` — skip repeats at the SAME tree level, never down a path.
Combination Sum reuse rule: recurse with the SAME index i when an element may be reused; with i+1 when each element is used at most once.
Prune target-sum branches with `remain < 0` (unsorted) or `break` when `a[j] > remain` (sorted) — pruning changes nothing about correctness, only speed.
Palindrome Partitioning: try every prefix cut, recurse on the suffix only if the prefix is a palindrome — O(n * 2^n) worst case (all-equal string).
K-th permutation: first digit index = (k-1) // (n-1)!, then recurse with rank (k-1) % (n-1)! — O(n^2) total, no enumeration of n! options.
Python's default recursion limit is ~1000 frames and there is NO tail-call optimization; raise it with sys.setrecursionlimit only when depth is provably bounded.

sections.title: What & Why
sections.content:
Recursion is delegation to a smaller copy of yourself. Think of Russian nesting dolls: to count the dolls, open one and ask "how many dolls are inside you?" — the inner doll asks the same of its inner doll, until the smallest doll answers "just me" (the base case), and the counts add up on the way back out. Formally, a recursive function does three things: (1) detects an input small enough to answer directly, (2) calls itself on a strictly smaller input, and (3) combines the returned sub-answer into its own answer.

Recursion is everywhere in real systems because so much data is self-similar: a filesystem directory contains files and more directories; a JSON object contains values that are themselves JSON; a compiler's expression contains sub-expressions. Merge sort, quicksort, tree traversals, and the entire divide-and-conquer family are recursion in production clothing.

For this sheet, recursion's killer application is exhaustive enumeration of choices. Questions like Subset Sums, Subsets II, Combination Sum, Combination Sum II and Palindrome Partitioning all say, in disguise, "generate every valid selection". A loop cannot express 'for every subset' directly — but recursion can, because each call handles one decision and delegates the remaining decisions. Interviewers use these problems to check three skills at once: can you find the decision structure, can you translate it into a clean template, and can you state the exponential complexity honestly.

sections.title: Memory Model: The Call Stack
sections.content:
Every function call pushes a stack frame: a block of memory holding the call's parameters, local variables, and where to resume in the caller. Frames pop in reverse (LIFO) order. For factorial(4), four frames stack up before any multiplication happens, then results flow back down as frames pop:

```
CALL PHASE (stack grows down)        RETURN PHASE (stack unwinds)
+----------------+
| factorial(4)   | waits for f(3)     f(1) returns 1
|  +-------------+                    f(2) returns 2*1 = 2
|  | factorial(3)| waits for f(2)     f(3) returns 3*2 = 6
|  |  +----------+                    f(4) returns 4*6 = 24
|  |  | f(2)     | waits for f(1)
|  |  |  +-------+
|  |  |  | f(1)  | base case -> 1
+--+--+--+-------+
```

Two consequences matter for enumeration problems. First, space: the stack only ever holds ONE root-to-leaf path of the recursion tree, so depth (not tree size) determines stack memory — O(n) frames for subsets of n items, even though the tree has 2^n leaves. Second, state restoration: when you mutate a shared list (`path.append`) before a call, the frame that did the append is still alive underneath, so executing `path.pop()` right after the call returns restores the exact state — this append/recurse/pop rhythm is the backbone of every template in this tab. A Python frame costs a few hundred bytes, and CPython refuses to grow the stack past `sys.getrecursionlimit()` (default ~1000) to protect the underlying C stack — deep-but-bounded recursions need that limit raised.

sections.title: Core Operations & Complexity: Costing a Recursion
sections.content:
The universal formula: total time = (number of nodes in the recursion tree) x (work done per node, excluding the recursive calls). Space = (maximum depth) x (frame size) + (size of stored answers). To use the formula you identify the branching factor (children per node) and the depth, then multiply per-node work. The table below covers every shape this topic's questions use:

```
Shape of recursion            | Tree size / leaves      | Total time
------------------------------+-------------------------+---------------------
Chain: T(n)=T(n-1)+O(1)       | n nodes, 1 leaf         | O(n)      (factorial)
Pick/not-pick over n indices  | 2^(n+1)-1 nodes, 2^n lv | O(2^n * n) with copies
For-loop recursion (subsets)  | one node PER subset     | O(2^n * n)
Permutation building          | ~ e * n! nodes          | O(n! * n)
Palindrome partition, len n   | up to 2^(n-1) cut sets  | O(2^n * n)
Naive fib: T(n)=T(n-1)+T(n-2) | ~ phi^n nodes           | O(1.618^n)
K-th permutation (counting)   | n calls (a chain!)      | O(n^2) via list.pop
```

Two refinements. (1) The "* n" factors come from copying an answer of length up to n into the result list — the recursion bookkeeping itself is O(1) per node, so on enumeration problems the OUTPUT dominates and no algorithm can beat it. (2) Pruning (e.g. abandoning a branch whose running sum already exceeds the target in Combination Sum) shrinks the tree that is actually visited, often massively, but the worst-case bound stays exponential — say both facts in an interview. Stack space is O(depth): O(n) for every problem in this tab.

sections.title: How Python Does It
sections.content:
Python recursion has four platform facts you must know cold. (1) Depth limit: CPython caps the interpreter stack at `sys.getrecursionlimit()` frames, default around 1000, and raises RecursionError beyond it. Enumeration recursions here have depth <= n, so they are safe, but linked-list or deep-tree recursions of 10^5 nodes are not — raise the limit only when depth is provably bounded. (2) No tail-call optimization: even a perfectly tail-recursive function grows one frame per call; Python will never turn your recursion into a loop for you. (3) Frames are heap-allocated objects and function calls carry real overhead, so an iterative rewrite is constant-factor faster — but interviewers care about the O-class and the clarity, and recursion usually wins on clarity. (4) Closures: an inner `def solve(...)` can read and mutate `res` and `path` from the enclosing function without passing them around — the standard structure for every template in this tab.

The single most important idiom is the shared-path pattern in the snippet: one `path` list lives across the whole exploration, `append` marks a choice, `pop` erases it, and `path[:]` snapshots an answer. The two classic traps: appending `path` itself (aliasing — every saved answer later mutates into the same final value) and mutable default arguments (`def f(path=[])` creates ONE list at definition time, silently shared by all calls).
sections.code:
import sys

# --- Fact 1: the recursion depth limit ------------------------------
print(sys.getrecursionlimit())      # typically 1000
# Raise it ONLY when depth is provably bounded (each frame ~ hundreds of bytes):
sys.setrecursionlimit(10_000)

# --- The shared-path idiom every template in this tab uses ----------
def subsets(nums):
    res = []                        # collected answers
    path = []                       # the CURRENT root-to-leaf branch, shared by all frames
    def solve(i):
        if i == len(nums):          # base case: every index decided
            res.append(path[:])     # path[:] COPIES; res.append(path) would alias!
            return
        path.append(nums[i])        # choice A: pick nums[i]
        solve(i + 1)                # explore with it included
        path.pop()                  # undo -> path is bit-for-bit as before append
        solve(i + 1)                # choice B: skip nums[i]
    solve(0)
    return res

print(subsets([1, 2]))              # [[1, 2], [1], [2], []]

# --- Trap: mutable default argument (created ONCE, shared forever) --
def bad(path=[]):                   # DON'T: second call sees the first call's data
    path.append(1)
    return path
def good(path=None):                # DO: make a fresh list inside the call
    if path is None:                # None is the safe immutable sentinel
        path = []
    path.append(1)
    return path

# --- Fact 2: no tail-call optimization ------------------------------
def countdown(n):                   # still consumes n stack frames,
    if n == 0:                      # even though the recursive call is
        return                      # the very last thing the function does
    countdown(n - 1)

sections.title: Pattern: Pick / Not-Pick (Subset Enumeration)
sections.content:
Recognize it when the problem says "all subsets", "all subsequences", or "every possible sum of a subset" — anything where each element is independently in or out. The invariant: when `solve(i, state)` runs, indices 0..i-1 have each been irrevocably decided (picked or skipped) along this branch, and `state` reflects exactly those decisions. Each call makes the two possible decisions for index i and delegates indices i+1..n-1. The tree is binary with depth n, so there are exactly 2^n leaves — one per subset — which both proves correctness (every subset appears exactly once) and gives the complexity O(2^n) leaves.

On this sheet, Subset Sums is the purest instance: carry a running sum instead of a list, and record the sum at each leaf — 2^n numbers out. Subsets II starts from the same idea but the input contains duplicates, which breaks pick/not-pick (picking the first 2 and skipping the second produces the same subset as the reverse), so it upgrades to the for-loop form in the next pattern. The pick/not-pick shape is also the seed of 0/1 Knapsack and every subset-DP you will meet later: DP is this exact tree with repeated states cached. If the interviewer asks for subsets themselves rather than sums, swap the integer accumulator for the append/recurse/pop idiom.
sections.code:
def subset_sums(a):
    # Returns the sums of all 2^n subsets, in pick-first order.
    out = []                           # one entry per leaf of the binary tree
    def solve(i, running):             # INVARIANT: a[0..i-1] decided; running = sum of picks
        if i == len(a):                # all n decisions made -> this is one subset
            out.append(running)        # record the leaf
            return
        solve(i + 1, running + a[i])   # decision 1: PICK a[i]
        solve(i + 1, running)          # decision 2: NOT-PICK a[i]
    solve(0, 0)                        # start: nothing decided, sum 0
    return out

# Example: [3, 1] -> [4, 3, 1, 0]
#          pick both, pick 3 only, pick 1 only, pick none
print(subset_sums([3, 1]))

sections.title: Pattern: For-Loop Recursion + Duplicate Skipping
sections.content:
Recognize it when answers are collected at every node (not just leaves) or when the input has duplicates that must not produce duplicate answers — Subsets II is the canonical sheet question, and the same skip rule reappears in Combination Sum II. Structure: instead of a binary pick/skip split, each call runs `for j in range(start, n)` and tries every element that could occupy the NEXT position; recursing with `j + 1` guarantees elements are taken in left-to-right index order, so each subset is generated exactly once and no permutation duplicates arise. The invariant: `path` holds a valid answer built from indices < start, and every extension uses indices >= start.

Duplicate handling requires two steps that only work together. First sort, so equal values are adjacent. Then, inside the loop: `if j > start and a[j] == a[j-1]: continue`. Read it precisely — it skips a value that equals its left neighbor only when that neighbor was ALREADY tried at this same tree level (`j > start`). Choosing two equal values in sequence down a path (j == start after recursing) remains allowed, which is why [1, 2, 2] still appears in the output for input [1, 2, 2]. Getting this level-vs-path distinction wrong is the classic bug: skipping whenever `a[j] == a[j-1]` regardless of `j > start` wrongly deletes answers that legitimately use the duplicate twice. Complexity is O(2^n * n) worst case — sorting adds only O(n log n).
sections.code:
def subsets_with_dup(nums):
    # All unique subsets of a multiset (Subsets II).
    nums.sort()                        # step 1: group equal values together
    res, path = [], []
    def solve(start):
        res.append(path[:])            # EVERY node is a complete subset -> record now
        for j in range(start, len(nums)):
            # step 2: at this LEVEL, a value equal to its left neighbor
            # has already produced this exact branch -> skip the repeat.
            if j > start and nums[j] == nums[j - 1]:
                continue
            path.append(nums[j])       # choose nums[j] as the next member
            solve(j + 1)               # j+1: later members come from the right only
            path.pop()                 # un-choose before trying the next j
    solve(0)
    return res

# [1,2,2] -> [], [1], [1,2], [1,2,2], [2], [2,2]   (no duplicates)
print(subsets_with_dup([2, 1, 2]))

sections.title: Pattern: Target-Sum Recursion (Reuse vs No-Reuse)
sections.content:
Recognize it when the problem asks for all combinations reaching a target sum — Combination Sum and Combination Sum II on this sheet. The entire pattern hinges on one index decision that students routinely mix up. If an element may be REUSED unlimited times (Combination Sum), then after picking `cands[i]` you recurse with the SAME index i — the element remains available. If each element may be used AT MOST ONCE (Combination Sum II), you recurse with `i + 1` (or `j + 1` in the for-loop form). One character in the code, completely different search space.

The invariant: `path` sums to `target - remain`, and only candidates at index >= i (pick/not-pick form) or >= start (for-loop form) may still be chosen — this ordering discipline is what prevents [2,3] and [3,2] from both appearing. Combination Sum II additionally has duplicate values in the input, so it combines this pattern with the previous one: sort first, then apply the `j > start and cands[j] == cands[j-1]` skip. Sorting buys a second prize: once `cands[j] > remain`, every later candidate also overshoots, so `break` prunes the whole rest of the level. Complexity: O(2^n) branches in the worst case with up to O(n) copying per stored answer — pruning helps enormously in practice but does not change the worst case, and you should volunteer that distinction in an interview.
sections.code:
def combination_sum(cands, target):
    # Each candidate may be reused any number of times.
    res, path = [], []
    def solve(i, remain):              # remain = target minus sum(path)
        if remain == 0:                # exact hit -> record a full combination
            res.append(path[:])
            return
        if i == len(cands) or remain < 0:
            return                     # dead end: candidates exhausted or overshot
        path.append(cands[i])          # PICK cands[i] ...
        solve(i, remain - cands[i])    # ... and STAY at i  -> reuse allowed
        path.pop()                     # undo the pick
        solve(i + 1, remain)           # NOT-PICK: abandon i for good
    solve(0, target)
    return res


def combination_sum2(cands, target):
    # Each candidate used at most once; input may contain duplicates.
    cands.sort()                       # enables both the skip rule and the break prune
    res, path = [], []
    def solve(start, remain):
        if remain == 0:
            res.append(path[:])
            return
        for j in range(start, len(cands)):
            if j > start and cands[j] == cands[j - 1]:
                continue               # duplicate value at the same level -> already tried
            if cands[j] > remain:
                break                  # sorted: everyone to the right overshoots too
            path.append(cands[j])      # choose
            solve(j + 1, remain - cands[j])   # j+1 -> NO reuse (the one-char difference)
            path.pop()                 # un-choose
    solve(0, target)
    return res

print(combination_sum([2, 3, 5], 8))       # [[2,2,2,2],[2,3,3],[3,5]]
print(combination_sum2([1, 1, 2, 5], 8))   # [[1,2,5],[1,1,...]] style, no duplicates

sections.title: Pattern: Partitioning a String
sections.content:
Recognize it when the problem asks to split a sequence into consecutive pieces where every piece satisfies a predicate — Palindrome Partitioning on this sheet (every piece must be a palindrome), and the identical skeleton solves Word Break in the Recursion & Backtracking tab (every piece must be a dictionary word). The reframe that unlocks it: a partition is a set of CUT POSITIONS. Between every pair of adjacent characters you either cut or don't — n-1 binary decisions, hence up to 2^(n-1) partitions, hence the exponential worst case (string "aaaa" really does have 8 all-palindrome partitions).

The template: `solve(start)` means "the prefix s[0..start-1] is already cut into valid pieces sitting in `path`". Try every `end` from `start` to n-1; if s[start..end] satisfies the predicate, append that piece, recurse on `solve(end + 1)`, then pop. The predicate check IS the pruning: an invalid prefix kills the entire subtree under it before any work happens, which is why real inputs run far faster than the 2^n bound. Two implementation notes that earn interview points: check palindromes with two pointers over indices instead of `s[l:r+1] == s[l:r+1][::-1]` to avoid building throwaway strings, and for repeated queries precompute a pal[l][r] table in O(n^2) so each check is O(1) (shown in the implementations below). Complexity: O(2^n * n) time worst case, O(n) recursion depth.
sections.code:
def partition(s):
    # All ways to split s so that every piece is a palindrome.
    res, path = [], []
    def is_pal(l, r):                  # test s[l..r] in place, no slicing copies
        while l < r:
            if s[l] != s[r]:
                return False           # mismatch -> not a palindrome
            l += 1
            r -= 1
        return True
    def solve(start):                  # INVARIANT: s[0..start-1] already cut into path
        if start == len(s):            # whole string consumed -> complete partition
            res.append(path[:])
            return
        for end in range(start, len(s)):
            if is_pal(start, end):     # PRUNE: only cut after a palindromic prefix
                path.append(s[start:end + 1])   # take s[start..end] as one piece
                solve(end + 1)         # recurse on the untouched suffix
                path.pop()             # undo the cut, try a longer piece
    solve(0)
    return res

# "aab" -> [["a","a","b"], ["aa","b"]]
print(partition("aab"))

sections.title: Pattern: Counting Instead of Enumerating (Factorial Number System)
sections.content:
Recognize it when the problem asks for the K-th item of an exponentially large ordered family — K-th Permutation Sequence on this sheet asks for the k-th permutation of 1..n in sorted order, where n can be 9 (362,880 permutations). Enumerating all permutations and indexing is O(n! * n) and is exactly what the interviewer hopes you will NOT do. The insight: sorted permutations come in blocks. All permutations starting with the smallest digit come first — and there are (n-1)! of them — then the block starting with the second digit, and so on. So the leading digit is simply block number (k-1) // (n-1)! in the sorted list of remaining digits, and the problem recurses on the remaining digits with the remaining rank (k-1) % (n-1)!.

This is the factorial number system: writing k-1 in mixed radix where position weights are (n-1)!, (n-2)!, ..., 1!, 0!. The invariant: before each step, `digits` holds the unused digits in sorted order and `k` is the 0-indexed rank among permutations of exactly those digits. Each step does one divmod and one `list.pop(idx)` (O(n) because elements shift), giving O(n^2) total — for n = 9 that is ~81 operations versus ~3.3 million for enumeration. The same block-counting idea answers the reverse question (given a permutation, what is its rank?) and 'k-th subset/combination in order' variants — recognize the family, not just this one problem.
sections.code:
import math

def kth_permutation(n, k):
    # k is 1-indexed among the n! sorted permutations of 1..n.
    digits = list(range(1, n + 1))     # unused digits, kept in sorted order
    def solve(k):                      # k: 0-indexed rank among perms of `digits`
