        if not digits:                 # no digits left -> empty suffix
            return ''
        block = math.factorial(len(digits) - 1)   # perms per leading-digit block
        idx, rest = divmod(k, block)   # which block -> leading digit; offset inside it
        lead = digits.pop(idx)         # claim that digit (O(n) shift, fine)
        # remaining digits are still sorted, so the same logic recurses cleanly
        return str(lead) + solve(rest)
    return solve(k - 1)                # convert to 0-indexed once, up front

# n=4: the 24 perms in order; the 9th is "2314"
print(kth_permutation(4, 9))           # -> 2314

sections.title: Pitfalls & Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Saving a reference instead of a copy: `res.append(path)` stores the live list; after the recursion finishes every "answer" has mutated into the same empty list. Fix: `res.append(path[:])` at the moment of recording.
- Forgetting the undo: `path.append(x)` before a call with no `path.pop()` after it poisons every sibling branch. Fix: append and pop must be visually paired lines around the recursive call — write them together, then fill in the call.
- Wrong duplicate skip: skipping whenever `a[j] == a[j-1]` (without `j > start`) deletes legitimate answers that use a duplicated value twice, e.g. [2,2] vanishes from Subsets II. Fix: the skip fires only at the same tree LEVEL — `if j > start and a[j] == a[j-1]`.
- Reuse index off by one: in Combination Sum, recursing with `i + 1` after a pick forbids reuse and silently loses answers like [2,2,2,2]; in Combination Sum II, recursing with `j` allows illegal reuse. Fix: same index = reuse allowed, next index = single use; say the rule out loud before coding.
- Slicing instead of indexing: passing `s[1:]` or `a[i:]` to the recursive call copies O(n) per frame, degrading O(2^n) to O(2^n * n) extra and wrecking linear recursions to O(n^2). Fix: pass an index, keep one shared sequence.
- Missing or unreachable base case: `solve(i)` that never tests `i == len(a)` recurses past the array and dies with IndexError or RecursionError. Fix: write the base case FIRST, then the choices.
- Mutable default argument: `def solve(path=[])` shares one list across all top-level calls of the function. Fix: default to None and create the list inside.
- Assuming Python optimizes tail calls: it never does; a 10^6-deep 'tail' recursion still crashes. Fix: bounded depth or convert to a loop.

sections.title: Interview Recognition Checklist
sections.content:
Cues that a problem belongs to this topic: the statement says "all possible" / "generate every" / "print all" subsets, combinations, partitions or ways; n is small (<= 20 for subsets, <= 10-12 for permutations) — small n is the interviewer whispering "exponential is intended"; the answer is a list of lists rather than a single number; or the problem asks for the k-th member of an ordered exponential family (that one wants counting, not enumeration).

The 30-second pre-coding checklist: (1) What is one DECISION? (include element i? where to cut next?) — this fixes the recursion signature. (2) Leaf answers or node answers? Pick/not-pick records at leaves; for-loop recursion records at every node. (3) Reuse allowed? Same index on pick if yes, i+1 if no. (4) Duplicates in input? Sort + same-level skip. (5) What prunes? remain < 0, sorted break, predicate check before recursing. (6) State the complexity before coding: 2^n or n! leaves, times O(n) copying, O(n) stack depth. (7) Confirm the three code habits: base case first, append/pop paired, `path[:]` when recording. If the interviewer bumps n to 10^5, recursion-as-enumeration is dead — the follow-up is asking for DP or a closed form, and noticing that pivot quickly is worth more than the code itself.

implementations.title: Recursion Tracer: Watch the Call Stack Live
Subset & Combination Toolkit From Scratch
implementations.code:
# Every enumeration template from this tab, runnable end to end:
# pick/not-pick subsets, subset sums, Subsets II (duplicate skipping),
# Combination Sum (reuse) and Combination Sum II (no reuse + duplicates).

def subsets(nums):
    # Pick / not-pick: binary tree, 2^n leaves, one subset per leaf.
    res, path = [], []
    def solve(i):
        if i == len(nums):            # every index decided
            res.append(path[:])       # snapshot -- never append the live list
            return
        path.append(nums[i])          # PICK nums[i]
        solve(i + 1)                  # explore with it in
        path.pop()                    # undo -> state restored for the sibling
        solve(i + 1)                  # NOT-PICK nums[i]
    solve(0)
    return res

def subset_sums(a):
    # Same tree as subsets(), but carry a running sum instead of a list.
    out = []
    def solve(i, running):
        if i == len(a):               # leaf -> one complete subset's sum
            out.append(running)
            return
        solve(i + 1, running + a[i])  # pick: add a[i] to the sum
        solve(i + 1, running)         # skip: sum unchanged
    solve(0, 0)
    return out

def subsets_with_dup(nums):
    # Subsets II: for-loop recursion, answers at every NODE, sorted + skip.
    nums.sort()                       # duplicates must be adjacent for the skip
    res, path = [], []
    def solve(start):
        res.append(path[:])           # every node is a valid unique subset
        for j in range(start, len(nums)):
            if j > start and nums[j] == nums[j - 1]:
                continue              # equal value already tried AT THIS LEVEL
            path.append(nums[j])      # choose
            solve(j + 1)              # future picks come strictly from the right
            path.pop()                # un-choose
    solve(0)
    return res

def combination_sum(cands, target):
    # Unlimited reuse: after a pick, recurse with the SAME index.
    res, path = [], []
    def solve(i, remain):
        if remain == 0:               # exact target -> record
            res.append(path[:])
            return
        if i == len(cands) or remain < 0:
            return                    # exhausted or overshot -> dead branch
        path.append(cands[i])         # pick cands[i]
        solve(i, remain - cands[i])   # SAME i -> may pick it again
        path.pop()                    # undo
        solve(i + 1, remain)          # skip i permanently
    solve(0, target)
    return res

def combination_sum2(cands, target):
    # Single use + duplicate inputs: sort, level-skip, and break-prune.
    cands.sort()
    res, path = [], []
    def solve(start, remain):
        if remain == 0:
            res.append(path[:])
            return
        for j in range(start, len(cands)):
            if j > start and cands[j] == cands[j - 1]:
                continue              # duplicate branch at this level
            if cands[j] > remain:
                break                 # sorted -> all later values overshoot too
            path.append(cands[j])     # choose
            solve(j + 1, remain - cands[j])   # j+1 -> each element used once
            path.pop()                # un-choose
    solve(0, target)
    return res

if __name__ == '__main__':
    print(subsets([1, 2, 3]))               # 8 subsets
    print(sorted(subset_sums([5, 2, 1])))   # 8 sums: 0,1,2,3,5,6,7,8
    print(subsets_with_dup([1, 2, 2]))      # 6 unique subsets
    print(combination_sum([2, 3, 6, 7], 7)) # [[2,2,3],[7]]
    print(combination_sum2([10,1,2,7,6,1,5], 8))  # 4 unique combinations

implementations.title: Palindrome Partitioning, Two Ways (On-the-fly vs Precomputed Table)
implementations.code:
# Version A checks palindromes with two pointers at query time.
# Version B precomputes pal[l][r] for ALL substrings in O(n^2) first,
# making every in-recursion check O(1) -- the classic interview upgrade.

def partition_simple(s):
    res, path = [], []
    def is_pal(l, r):
        # walk the two ends toward the middle; indices only, no slices
        while l < r:
            if s[l] != s[r]:
                return False          # one mismatch settles it
            l += 1
            r -= 1
        return True
    def solve(start):
        if start == len(s):           # every character placed in some piece
            res.append(path[:])       # record a complete partition
            return
        for end in range(start, len(s)):
            if is_pal(start, end):    # prune: never cut after a non-palindrome
                path.append(s[start:end + 1])  # this slice IS the answer piece
                solve(end + 1)        # partition the remaining suffix
                path.pop()            # undo, then try a longer first piece
    solve(0)
    return res


def partition_fast(s):
    n = len(s)
    # pal[l][r] == True  iff  s[l..r] reads the same both ways.
    pal = [[False] * n for _ in range(n)]
    for r in range(n):                # grow the right end
        for l in range(r + 1):        # every left end up to r
            # ends match AND the inside is a palindrome (or too short to matter)
            if s[l] == s[r] and (r - l < 2 or pal[l + 1][r - 1]):
                pal[l][r] = True
    res, path = [], []
    def solve(start):
        if start == n:                # suffix empty -> partition complete
            res.append(path[:])
            return
        for end in range(start, n):
            if pal[start][end]:       # O(1) lookup instead of an O(n) scan
                path.append(s[start:end + 1])
                solve(end + 1)        # recurse past this piece
                path.pop()            # backtrack the cut
    solve(0)
    return res

if __name__ == '__main__':
    print(partition_simple("aab"))    # [['a','a','b'], ['aa','b']]
    print(partition_fast("aab"))      # identical output, faster checks
    # sanity: both agree on a stress string
    assert partition_simple("abba") == partition_fast("abba")

implementations.title: K-th Permutation: Brute Enumeration vs Factorial Counting, Cross-Checked
implementations.code:
# Two solvers for K-th Permutation Sequence.
#   kth_brute  : recursively ENUMERATES permutations in sorted order -- O(n! * n).
#   kth_fast   : COUNTS with the factorial number system            -- O(n^2).
# The __main__ block cross-checks them on every k for n = 4.

import math

def kth_brute(n, k):
    # Generate permutations in lexicographic order until the k-th appears.
    digits = list(range(1, n + 1))    # sorted -> generation order is sorted
    answers = []                      # filled permutation strings, in order
    path = []
    used = [False] * n
    def solve():
        if len(answers) >= k:         # early exit: the k-th is already found
            return
        if len(path) == n:            # a full permutation is assembled
            answers.append(''.join(map(str, path)))
            return
        for i in range(n):            # smallest available digit first
            if used[i]:
                continue              # digit already placed on this path
            used[i] = True            # choose digit i
            path.append(digits[i])
            solve()                   # fill the remaining slots
            path.pop()                # un-choose
            used[i] = False
    solve()
    return answers[k - 1]             # k is 1-indexed

def kth_fast(n, k):
    # Factorial number system: peel off one leading digit per step.
    digits = list(range(1, n + 1))    # unused digits, always sorted
    def solve(rank):                  # rank: 0-indexed among perms of `digits`
        if not digits:
            return ''                 # nothing left to place
        block = math.factorial(len(digits) - 1)   # size of each leading block
        idx, rest = divmod(rank, block)  # block index + rank inside that block
        lead = digits.pop(idx)        # the (idx+1)-th smallest unused digit leads
        return str(lead) + solve(rest)   # recurse with the leftover rank
    return solve(k - 1)               # switch to 0-indexed exactly once

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # exhaustive agreement check for n = 4 (24 permutations)
    for k in range(1, math.factorial(4) + 1):
        assert kth_brute(4, k) == kth_fast(4, k), k
    print('all 24 ranks agree for n=4')
    print(kth_fast(4, 9))             # -> 2314, the classic example
    print(kth_fast(9, 362880))        # last permutation of 1..9: 987654321

Recursion & Backtracking.summary:
Quick recap: the Recursion tab built the machinery — base case plus smaller subproblem, the call stack, the recursion tree of choices, and the append/recurse/pop rhythm for enumerating subsets, combinations and partitions. This tab is the advanced continuation: backtracking, which is recursion pointed at problems with CONSTRAINTS, where most branches of the choice tree are illegal and the whole game is detecting that early and undoing cleanly.

Backtracking is depth-first search through a state space with three verbs at every node: CHOOSE (make a tentative move and mutate shared state), EXPLORE (recurse), UN-CHOOSE (undo the mutation so the state is bit-for-bit identical for the next option). Think of walking a hedge maze with chalk: mark the corridor you enter, and if it dead-ends, walk back and erase the mark so it does not lie to you later. The un-choose step is what separates backtracking from plain recursion — state persists across calls, so every mutation must be reversed on the way out. The second pillar is pruning: check constraints BEFORE recursing, not at the leaves. Naive 4-queens tries 256 complete placements; pruned backtracking visits a few dozen nodes, and the gap widens astronomically with n.

```
        place queen in row 0
       /        |         \
   col 0      col 1      col 2 ...
     |          |           x  <- attacked: subtree PRUNED, never built
   row 1 ...  row 1 ...
```

This is the engine inside SAT solvers, regex engines, Prolog, and constraint schedulers. The sheet questions here are the canon: Print All Permutations (undo-by-swapping), N Queens and Sudoku Solver (constraint satisfaction on boards), M Coloring Problem (labels on a graph), Rat in a Maze (path search with visited marking), and Word Break (where memoization collapses exponential backtracking to polynomial — your bridge into DP).
preRequisites: The Recursion tab in full: pick/not-pick, for-loop recursion, the append/recurse/pop idiom, and why enumeration costs are output-bound.
Python sets: `x in s`, `s.add(x)`, `s.discard(x)` are O(1) average — the tool that turns O(n) board scans into O(1) constraint checks.
Building 2D grids correctly: `[[0] * m for _ in range(n)]`; the `[[0] * m] * n` form aliases one row n times and corrupts backtracking state.
Tuple swap `a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]` — the O(1) in-place exchange behind swap-based permutations.
Dictionaries / functools.lru_cache for memoization, and why cache keys must be immutable (use indices, not list slices).
Reading problems as graphs: board cells or vertices are nodes, legal moves are edges — backtracking is DFS over that implicit graph.
cheatSheet: Backtracking = CHOOSE -> EXPLORE -> UN-CHOOSE; shared state must be identical before and after every iteration of the choice loop.
Prune BEFORE recursing: validity checks at the choice point, not at the leaves — correctness identical, tree exponentially smaller.
N-Queens O(1) safety: column set + (row+col) set for one diagonal family + (row-col) set for the other; place/remove updates all three.
Swap permutations: fix slot i by swapping each j in [i, n) into it, recurse on i+1, swap back — O(n * n!) total, O(1) extra state.
One solution vs all: return True upward to freeze the first solution (Sudoku, M-Coloring); collect-and-continue for all (N-Queens list, maze paths).
Rat in a Maze: mark the cell BEFORE recursing, unmark AFTER — no visited mark means cycles and infinite recursion.
M-Coloring: for each vertex try colors 1..m, reject a color any neighbor wears — O(m^V) worst case, tiny in practice with pruning.
Sudoku bound: O(9^m) for m empty cells; box index = 3*(r//3) + c//3 maps any cell to its 3x3 box.
Word Break: pure backtracking O(2^n); memoize failure by start index -> O(n^2) checks with a word set — memoized backtracking IS top-down DP.

sections.title: From Recursion to Backtracking: What Actually Changes
sections.content:
Plain recursive enumeration (the previous tab) walks a choice tree where every leaf is an answer. Backtracking handles the harder case: most of the tree is ILLEGAL, and answers may be rare or unique. Three things change. First, shared mutable state: instead of passing fresh values down, you mutate one board / one path / a few sets, because copying a 9x9 Sudoku grid at every node would swamp the search itself. Second, the un-choose obligation: since state is shared, every mutation made before a recursive call must be exactly reversed after it returns — the caller's world must be restored whether the branch succeeded or failed. Third, pruning: a constraint check runs at the moment of choosing, so an illegal partial state kills its entire subtree unexplored.

The analogy: solving a paper Sudoku with pencil and eraser. You pencil in a digit that fits so far (choose), keep solving (explore), and when a contradiction appears you erase back to the last guess and try the next digit (un-choose). Nobody restarts the whole puzzle from scratch after each contradiction — that is the difference between backtracking and brute-force generation. In real systems this exact loop runs inside SAT/SMT solvers, Prolog's resolution engine, regex backtracking engines, package-dependency resolvers, and timetabling software. On this sheet, Print All Permutations, N Queens, Sudoku Solver, M Coloring Problem, Rat in a Maze and Word Break are all this one loop wearing six costumes.

sections.title: The State-Space Tree & Pruning Arithmetic
sections.content:
Model the search as a tree: each node is a partial state (queens in the first r rows; a partly filled board; a prefix of a path), each edge is one legal-looking choice, and each leaf is either a full solution or a dead end. Backtracking is depth-first traversal of this tree where pruning deletes subtrees before they are ever constructed.

```
                      ( no queens )                 4-queens
          c0        c1         c2        c3         <- row 0: 4 branches
           |          |          |          |
        row 1      row 1      row 1      row 1
        c0 x       c0 x       c0 x       c0 x       x = attacked -> subtree
        c1 x       c1 x       c1 x       c1 ok      never generated
        c2 ok      c2 x       c3 x       ...
        ...
```

The arithmetic that justifies the pattern: naive generation of 4-queens placements tries 4^4 = 256 complete boards (or C(16,4) = 1820 if any 4 cells allowed); pruned backtracking touches roughly 60 nodes, most shallow. For 8-queens: 8^8 is ~16.7 million naive, while backtracking finds all 92 solutions visiting on the order of two thousand nodes. Pruning power compounds with depth, because a rejection at depth d kills b^(n-d) descendants at once. Two rules follow. Check EVERY constraint you can as early as you can — a cheap check high in the tree beats a perfect check at the leaves. And keep checks O(1) where possible (sets, boolean arrays) so the per-node cost does not eat the savings: this is exactly why N Queens uses three hash sets instead of rescanning the board, and why Sudoku Solver checks one row, column and box rather than validating the whole grid per placement.

sections.title: Cost Model: Branching, Depth, Undo, and What to Quote
sections.content:
Time = nodes actually visited x per-node work; the worst case assumes no pruning helps, so quote it as branching^depth (or the count of complete candidates) times per-node cost. Space = recursion depth + the shared state, since backtracking stores ONE path at a time, never the whole tree. The table gives the bounds interviewers expect for this tab's questions:

```
Problem                  | Worst-case time        | Depth / extra space
-------------------------+------------------------+---------------------------
Print All Permutations   | O(n * n!)              | O(n) frames, O(1) extra
N Queens (all solutions) | O(n!) placements       | O(n) + three sets
Sudoku Solver            | O(9^m), m empty cells  | O(m) frames, board in place
M Coloring Problem       | O(m^V) label vectors   | O(V) + color array
Rat in a Maze            | O(4^(n^2)) crude bound | O(n^2) path + visited marks
Word Break (naive)       | O(2^n) cut patterns    | O(n) frames
Word Break (memoized)    | O(n^2) with a word set | O(n) memo + O(n) frames
```

Three speaking points. (1) These are ceilings, not predictions: pruning makes typical runs orders of magnitude smaller, but you cannot promise better in O-notation — say "worst case X, pruning makes it feasible in practice". (2) The undo step must be O(1)-ish: swapping back, popping, set.discard — if undo means recopying a structure, the state design is wrong. (3) Memoized Word Break shows the escape hatch: when subproblems repeat and are identified by a small key (a start index), caching collapses exponential search into polynomial DP; N Queens has no such small key (the whole column/diagonal state matters), which is why it stays exponential. Knowing WHICH problems admit memoization is the real lesson of the table.

sections.title: How Python Does It: Mutable State & O(1) Constraint Checks
sections.content: Backtracking performance in Python lives or dies on four mechanics. (1) Sets for constraints: `in`, `add`, `discard` are O(1) average, so occupied columns and both diagonal families in N Queens become three set lookups instead of an O(n) board scan. Encode each diagonal by its invariant — cells on one anti-diagonal share row+col, cells on one main diagonal share row-col. (2) In-place grid mutation: pass the same list-of-lists everywhere and write/erase cells; never copy the board per call. The construction trap: `[[0]*m]*n` repeats ONE row object n times, so 'erasing' a cell erases it in every row and the backtrack silently corrupts — always build with a comprehension. (3) Closure state beats parameter threading: define the recursive worker inside the solver so `board`, `res`, and the sets are shared lexically; you only need `nonlocal` to REBIND (e.g. a solution counter), not to mutate. (4) Memo keys must be immutable and small: memoize Word Break on the integer start index, never on a list slice (unhashable) or the suffix string (O(n) to hash each time). `functools.lru_cache` does this bookkeeping for you when arguments are already hashable. Bonus habit: append single characters to a list and `''.join` once at the end — repeated string concatenation in a deep recursion costs O(n^2).
sections.code:
# --- O(1) constraint bookkeeping: the N-Queens set trio -------------
cols  = set()      # columns already holding a queen
diag1 = set()      # anti-diagonals: row + col is constant along each
diag2 = set()      # main diagonals: row - col is constant along each

def safe(r, c):
    # one O(1) expression replaces scanning the whole board
    return c not in cols and (r + c) not in diag1 and (r - c) not in diag2

def place(r, c):
    cols.add(c); diag1.add(r + c); diag2.add(r - c)      # CHOOSE is O(1)

def unplace(r, c):
    cols.discard(c); diag1.discard(r + c); diag2.discard(r - c)  # UNDO is O(1)

# --- The 2D-grid aliasing trap --------------------------------------
bad = [[0] * 3] * 2            # ONE row object, referenced twice
bad[0][0] = 9                  # "both" rows change -- they are the same list
good = [[0] * 3 for _ in range(2)]   # fresh row per iteration
good[0][0] = 9                 # only row 0 changes, as intended
print(bad, good)               # [[9,0,0],[9,0,0]]  vs  [[9,0,0],[0,0,0]]

# --- Memo keys: hash an index, not a slice --------------------------
from functools import lru_cache

def word_break(s, words):
    word_set = set(words)      # O(1) membership per lookup
    @lru_cache(maxsize=None)   # cache keyed on the int argument
    def solve(start):          # "can s[start:] be segmented?"
        if start == len(s):    # empty suffix segments trivially
            return True
        # try every prefix cut; recurse only on real dictionary words
        return any(s[start:end] in word_set and solve(end)
                   for end in range(start + 1, len(s) + 1))
    return solve(0)

print(word_break("leetcode", ["leet", "code"]))   # True

sections.title: Pattern: Permutations by In-Place Swapping
sections.content:
Recognize it when the problem asks for all orderings of a collection — Print All Permutations on this sheet. The elegant trick: build each permutation inside the input array itself. `solve(i)` means positions 0..i-1 are finalized; the loop gives every element in positions i..n-1 a turn at slot i by swapping it in, recursing, and swapping back. The invariant is exact restoration: after `solve(i)`'s loop iteration for j finishes, the array is identical to before that iteration, so iteration j+1 starts from a clean state. The undo here is a second swap rather than a pop — same choose/explore/un-choose skeleton, different mutation.

Why prefer this over the visited-array approach (keep a `used[]` boolean array, append unused elements)? Swap-based runs in O(1) extra space beyond recursion and showcases the undo discipline interviewers probe; the visited-array version produces permutations in lexicographic order (when input is sorted) and adapts more cleanly to duplicate handling — mention both and let the interviewer pick. Complexity: the recursion tree has n!/(n-i)! nodes at depth i, ~e*n! nodes total; each leaf copies an n-element answer, so O(n * n!) time, O(n) stack. Caution: with duplicate values, plain swapping emits duplicate permutations; deduplicate with a per-level `seen` set of values tried at slot i. This pattern also back-fills the previous tab: K-th Permutation Sequence is exactly this tree with counting substituted for traversal.
sections.code:
def permutations(nums):
    # All orderings, built by swapping in place (Print All Permutations).
    res = []
    n = len(nums)
    def solve(i):                     # slots 0..i-1 are already FIXED
        if i == n:                    # every slot fixed -> one permutation done
            res.append(nums[:])       # snapshot: nums keeps mutating afterwards
            return
        for j in range(i, n):         # each remaining element tries slot i
            nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]   # CHOOSE: bring nums[j] to slot i
            solve(i + 1)              # EXPLORE: fix the remaining slots
            nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]   # UN-CHOOSE: exact swap-back
    solve(0)
    return res

def permutations_unique(nums):
    # Duplicate-safe variant: at each slot, never try the same VALUE twice.
    res = []
    n = len(nums)
    def solve(i):
        if i == n:
            res.append(nums[:])
            return
        seen = set()                  # values already placed at slot i (this level)
        for j in range(i, n):
            if nums[j] in seen:
                continue              # same value at same slot -> duplicate output
            seen.add(nums[j])         # remember the value, not the index
            nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]
            solve(i + 1)
            nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]
    solve(0)
    return res

print(permutations([1, 2, 3]))        # 6 orderings
print(permutations_unique([1, 1, 2])) # 3 orderings, no repeats

sections.title: Pattern: Row-by-Row Placement (N Queens)
sections.content:
Recognize it when items must be placed on a board so that no two conflict, and there is exactly one item per row/group — N Queens is the archetype. The structural insight that shrinks the search: since queens attack along rows, each row holds exactly one queen, so a solution is just a choice of one column per row — search row by row, and the state is `queens[r] = column`. That reframing alone cuts the space from C(n^2, n) cell subsets to n^n column vectors before any pruning.

The invariant: entering `solve(r)`, rows 0..r-1 hold mutually non-attacking queens, and three sets describe everything the next choice needs — occupied columns, occupied anti-diagonals (keyed by r+c, constant along each anti-diagonal), occupied main diagonals (keyed by r-c). A candidate column is safe iff it misses all three sets: an O(1) check replacing an O(n) rescan of earlier rows. Choose = record the column and add three set entries; un-choose = pop and discard three entries — perfect symmetry, and any asymmetry is a bug that corrupts sibling branches. Collect a snapshot at r == n for all solutions, or return True upward if only one is needed. Complexity: O(n!)-ish worst case (each row has at most n - r safe columns), O(n) depth. This exact "one per row + O(1) conflict sets" shape transfers to exam scheduling, register allocation, and any assignment problem with pairwise conflicts.
sections.code:
def solve_n_queens(n):
    # All solutions; each is a list where entry r = queen's column in row r.
    res = []
    queens = []                        # queens[r] = chosen column for row r
    cols, d1, d2 = set(), set(), set() # columns, anti-diagonals(r+c), main diagonals(r-c)
    def solve(r):                      # INVARIANT: rows 0..r-1 placed, conflict-free
        if r == n:                     # queen in every row -> full solution
            res.append(queens[:])      # snapshot the column list
            return
        for c in range(n):             # try every column for this row
            if c in cols or (r + c) in d1 or (r - c) in d2:
                continue               # attacked -> prune the whole subtree NOW
            queens.append(c)           # CHOOSE: three set adds + one append
            cols.add(c); d1.add(r + c); d2.add(r - c)
            solve(r + 1)               # EXPLORE the next row
            queens.pop()               # UN-CHOOSE: mirror every mutation exactly
            cols.discard(c); d1.discard(r + c); d2.discard(r - c)
    solve(0)
    return res

# n=4 has exactly 2 solutions: [1,3,0,2] and [2,0,3,1]
print(solve_n_queens(4))

sections.title: Pattern: Fill the First Empty Cell (Sudoku)
sections.content:
Recognize it when a partially filled structure must be completed under local consistency rules — Sudoku Solver here, and the same skeleton completes Latin squares, KenKen, and crossword fills. The loop: scan for the first undecided cell; try each candidate value that passes the constraint check (row, column, and 3x3 box — with the box's top-left corner at (3*(r//3), 3*(c//3))); write the value, recurse, and erase on failure. When the scan finds no empty cell, the board is complete — return True and let every caller return True without erasing, which freezes the solved board in place. That propagating-True idiom is the standard "stop at first solution" mechanism, and it contrasts with N Queens above, where all solutions are collected and the search always continues.

The invariant: the board is consistent (no rule violated) at every moment the function runs; writes happen only after a successful check, and every failed subtree erases its write on the way out. Two upgrades worth mentioning aloud: keep 27 sets (9 rows, 9 columns, 9 boxes) to turn the O(27) validity scan into three O(1) lookups, and pick the empty cell with FEWEST candidates first (minimum-remaining-values heuristic) instead of the first one — the same pruning logic, aimed better, often collapsing hard puzzles by orders of magnitude. Complexity: O(9^m) worst case for m empty cells, O(m) recursion depth, O(1) extra space since the board itself is the state.
sections.code:
def solve_sudoku(board):
    # board: 9x9 list of lists of str, '.' marks an empty cell. Solved in place.
    def valid(r, c, ch):
        br, bc = 3 * (r // 3), 3 * (c // 3)   # top-left corner of the 3x3 box
        for k in range(9):                    # one pass checks all three units
            if board[r][k] == ch:             # row clash
                return False
            if board[k][c] == ch:             # column clash
                return False
            if board[br + k // 3][bc + k % 3] == ch:
                return False                  # box clash
        return True
    def fill():
        for r in range(9):
            for c in range(9):
                if board[r][c] != '.':
                    continue                  # already decided -> keep scanning
                for ch in '123456789':        # try each digit in the empty cell
                    if valid(r, c, ch):
                        board[r][c] = ch      # CHOOSE: pencil the digit in
                        if fill():            # EXPLORE: solvable downstream?
                            return True       # yes -> freeze; no erasing on the way up
                        board[r][c] = '.'     # UN-CHOOSE: erase, try next digit
                return False                  # 1-9 all fail -> backtrack to caller
        return True                           # no empty cell -> board is complete
    fill()
    return board

sections.title: Pattern: Try Every Label per Vertex (M Coloring)
sections.content:
Recognize it when each of V items must receive one of m labels and certain PAIRS of items may not share a label — the M Coloring Problem asks exactly this on a graph: color vertices with at most m colors so no edge joins two same-colored vertices. This is the cleanest template of the whole tab: process vertices in a fixed order; at vertex v, try each color 1..m, rejecting any color already worn by a neighbor of v; assign, recurse to v+1, and reset to 0 on failure. Reaching v == V means every vertex is consistently colored — return True upward (the usual first-solution freeze).

The invariant: entering `solve(v)`, vertices 0..v-1 form a valid partial coloring, and `color[u] == 0` for all u >= v. The neighbor check only needs to look at ALREADY-colored neighbors, which the invariant guarantees are exactly those with nonzero color. Complexity: O(m^V) label vectors worst case with O(V + E) state — but graph coloring is NP-complete, so no polynomial algorithm is expected, and saying so is a credibility point. Practical accelerations to mention: order vertices by decreasing degree (most-constrained first), and skip symmetric color renamings by allowing vertex v to use at most (highest color used so far + 1). The pattern generalizes to register allocation (variables = vertices, interference = edges), exam timetabling (courses sharing students), and frequency assignment — recognizing "conflict pairs + limited labels = coloring" is the transferable skill.
sections.code:
def graph_coloring(adj, m):
    # adj: adjacency list (list of neighbor lists); colors are 1..m; 0 = none.
    n = len(adj)
    color = [0] * n                    # color[v] == 0 means v is uncolored
    def solve(v):                      # INVARIANT: vertices 0..v-1 validly colored
        if v == n:                     # every vertex colored consistently
            return True
        for c in range(1, m + 1):      # try each of the m labels at v
            if any(color[u] == c for u in adj[v]):
                continue               # a neighbor already wears c -> illegal here
            color[v] = c               # CHOOSE the color
            if solve(v + 1):           # EXPLORE the rest of the graph
                return True            # a full coloring exists -> freeze choices
            color[v] = 0               # UN-CHOOSE: erase before the next label
        return False                   # no label fits -> force an earlier change
    return color if solve(0) else None

# Triangle needs 3 colors: fails with m=2, succeeds with m=3.
triangle = [[1, 2], [0, 2], [0, 1]]
print(graph_coloring(triangle, 2))     # None
print(graph_coloring(triangle, 3))     # e.g. [1, 2, 3]

sections.title: Pattern: Grid Walk with Visited Marking (Rat in a Maze)
sections.content:
Recognize it when the problem asks for paths through a grid or graph where revisiting a cell is forbidden — Rat in a Maze: find every path from (0,0) to (n-1,n-1) through open cells (1s), moving up/down/left/right. The new hazard versus board-placement problems: the grid has CYCLES. Without a visited mark, the search walks right then left forever and recurses to death. So the pattern's signature move is temporal: mark the current cell visited BEFORE trying neighbors, and unmark it AFTER all four directions are exhausted — the unmark is essential because a cell blocked for the current path must remain available to a different path that reaches it another way. Marking by writing 0 into the grid itself (and restoring 1) saves a separate visited matrix; use an explicit visited set when the grid must not be mutated.

The invariant: cells on the current path (inclusive of the current cell) are marked; all other cells show their true open/blocked value; `path` spells the moves taken so far. The classic asks for paths in lexicographic order of the move letters, which falls out for free by iterating directions in D, L, R, U order — a detail interviewers use to check whether you control iteration order deliberately. Complexity: O(4^(n^2)) crude worst case (each cell branches at most 4 ways, path length at most n^2 due to visited marking), O(n^2) depth. Edge cases to state before coding: a blocked start or destination cell means zero paths, and a 1x1 open grid's answer is the empty path. This is DFS on an implicit graph — the direct ancestor of Number of Islands and Flood Fill in the Graphs topic.
sections.code:
def rat_paths(grid):
    # All paths (0,0) -> (n-1,n-1) through 1-cells, as move strings (Rat in a Maze).
    n = len(grid)
    res, path = [], []
    # D,L,R,U order -> results come out already lexicographically sorted
    moves = [('D', 1, 0), ('L', 0, -1), ('R', 0, 1), ('U', -1, 0)]
    def walk(r, c):
        if r == n - 1 and c == n - 1:  # reached the exit cell
            res.append(''.join(path))  # record the move string
            return
        grid[r][c] = 0                 # CHOOSE/mark: close the cell to this path
        for name, dr, dc in moves:
            nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc    # neighbor coordinates
            # inside the grid AND open AND (by the mark) not on the current path
            if 0 <= nr < n and 0 <= nc < n and grid[nr][nc] == 1:
                path.append(name)      # take the step
                walk(nr, nc)           # explore from the neighbor
                path.pop()             # undo the step letter
        grid[r][c] = 1                 # UN-CHOOSE/unmark: other paths may pass here
    if grid and grid[0][0] == 1 and grid[n - 1][n - 1] == 1:
        walk(0, 0)                     # blocked start or end -> no paths at all
    return res

maze = [[1, 0, 0, 0],
        [1, 1, 0, 1],
        [1, 1, 0, 0],
        [0, 1, 1, 1]]
print(rat_paths(maze))                 # ['DDRDRR', 'DRDDRR']

sections.title: Pattern: Prefix Cut + Memoization (Word Break) — the Bridge to DP
sections.content:
Recognize it when a string must be segmented into pieces from a dictionary and the answer is yes/no or a count — Word Break here. Structurally it is Palindrome Partitioning from the Recursion tab with the predicate swapped: cut a prefix, recurse on the suffix, but only when the prefix is a dictionary word. Run that naively and worst-case time is O(2^n) — for s = "aaaa...b" with words {"a","aa","aaa"}, the search re-proves that the same doomed suffix fails, once for every way of cutting the prefix before it.

The fix is the most important idea this tab teaches: the subproblem is fully identified by ONE integer — the start index of the suffix — so there are only n+1 distinct subproblems. Cache each suffix's verdict the first time; every later arrival at the same index is an O(1) lookup. Failure caching does the heavy lifting (successes short-circuit anyway). Time collapses to O(n^2) cut attempts (times O(n) slicing/hashing if you count it: O(n^3) pedantically; bound piece length by the longest dictionary word to tighten it), with O(n) memo space. Memoized backtracking IS top-down dynamic programming — same recursion, plus a dictionary — and this problem is the cleanest place to say that sentence to an interviewer. The contrast to internalize: Word Break memoizes because its state compresses to an index; N Queens cannot, because its state is the whole set of used columns and diagonals. Checking "does my state compress to a small key?" is how you decide, in 10 seconds, whether a backtracking problem hides a polynomial DP.

sections.title: Pitfalls & Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Asymmetric undo: choosing mutates three structures but un-choosing restores two (say, popping `queens` but forgetting `d2.discard`), silently poisoning sibling branches with phantom constraints. Fix: write choose and un-choose as adjacent mirror-image blocks before writing the recursive call between them.
- Aliased grid rows: building the board or visited matrix as `[[0]*m]*n` makes every row the same object, so one cell's undo 'undoes' a full column of state. Fix: `[[0]*m for _ in range(n)]`, always.
- No visited mark on cyclic structures: Rat in a Maze without marking recurses right-left-right forever until RecursionError. Fix: mark before the neighbor loop, unmark after it — and know WHY the unmark exists (the cell must reopen for other paths).
- Early return when all solutions are wanted: `if solve(...): return True` inside N Queens truncates the answer list to one solution. Fix: decide first-solution vs all-solutions BEFORE coding; propagate True for the first, collect-and-continue for all.
- Checking constraints at the leaves: generating complete boards and validating at depth n runs the full b^n tree. Fix: validate at the choice point — same answers, exponentially fewer nodes.
- Snapshotting mutable answers lazily: `res.append(nums)` in swap-permutations stores n! references to one array that ends up back in input order. Fix: `res.append(nums[:])` at the leaf.
- Memoizing on the wrong key: caching Word Break on the suffix STRING hashes O(n) characters per lookup, and caching on a list crashes (unhashable). Fix: key on the integer start index.
- Wrong duplicate-permutation dedup: sorting + adjacent skip (the Subsets II rule) does not transplant to swap-permutations, because swapping unsorts the tail. Fix: a per-level `seen` set of VALUES tried at the current slot.

sections.title: Interview Recognition Checklist
sections.content:
Cues that a problem is backtracking: the statement asks to place / arrange / color / fill / route under a "no two conflict" or "each piece must be valid" rule; it asks for ALL solutions or whether ANY solution exists (not the optimal one — optimal usually signals DP or greedy); the input is tiny (n <= 9-ish boards, V <= 20 vertices, strings <= 20 for pure search) — exponential is the intended shape; or the phrase "return to the previous state and try another option" is paraphrased anywhere in the prompt.

The 30-second pre-coding checklist: (1) Name the DECISION at each level (which column in this row? which digit in this cell? which color for this vertex? which direction from this cell? where does the next word end?). (2) Name the STATE and its constraint structures — and make each check O(1) if a set or boolean array can do it. (3) Write choose and un-choose as mirror lines; confirm every mutation has its inverse. (4) Where does pruning fire? It must be before the recursive call. (5) One solution or all? — pick the propagate-True or collect-and-continue skeleton accordingly. (6) Cycles possible? Then a visited mark with a matching unmark. (7) Does the state compress to a small key (an index, a bitmask)? If yes, memoize — you may have found the hidden DP, as in Word Break. (8) Quote the worst case honestly (n!, 9^m, m^V, 2^n) and add that pruning makes it run in practice. If you cannot name the un-choose step for your design, the design is not ready — fix that before typing.

implementations.title: N-Queens: All Solutions, Rendered Boards, and a Fast Counter
implementations.code:
# Full N-Queens toolkit:
#   solve_n_queens(n) -> every solution as a rendered board (list of strings)
#   count_n_queens(n) -> just the number of solutions (no board building)
# Both use the three-set O(1) safety check: columns, r+c diagonals, r-c diagonals.

def solve_n_queens(n):
    res = []
    queens = []                        # queens[r] = column of the queen in row r
    cols, d1, d2 = set(), set(), set() # occupied columns / anti-diags / main diags
    def place(r):
        if r == n:                     # all rows filled -> render and store
            board = []
            for c in queens:           # one row string per queen
                board.append('.' * c + 'Q' + '.' * (n - c - 1))
            res.append(board)          # board is fresh each time -> no aliasing
            return
        for c in range(n):
            # O(1) safety: not same column, not same anti-diag, not same main diag
            if c in cols or (r + c) in d1 or (r - c) in d2:
                continue               # attacked -> prune this branch
            queens.append(c)           # CHOOSE (4 mutations...)
            cols.add(c); d1.add(r + c); d2.add(r - c)
            place(r + 1)               # EXPLORE next row
            queens.pop()               # UN-CHOOSE (...and their 4 exact inverses)
            cols.discard(c); d1.discard(r + c); d2.discard(r - c)
    place(0)
    return res

def count_n_queens(n):
    # Counting-only variant: no boards, no lists -- just an integer.
    cols, d1, d2 = set(), set(), set()
    def place(r):
        if r == n:
            return 1                   # one complete placement found
        total = 0
        for c in range(n):
            if c in cols or (r + c) in d1 or (r - c) in d2:
                continue               # pruned
            cols.add(c); d1.add(r + c); d2.add(r - c)   # choose
            total += place(r + 1)      # count all completions below
            cols.discard(c); d1.discard(r + c); d2.discard(r - c)  # undo
        return total
    return place(0)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    for board in solve_n_queens(4):    # n=4 has exactly 2 solutions
        print('\n'.join(board))
        print()
    # known sequence: 1, 0, 0, 2, 10, 4, 40, 92 for n = 1..8
    print([count_n_queens(n) for n in range(1, 9)])

implementations.title: Sudoku Solver From Scratch (with 27-Set Speedup)
Rat in a Maze + M-Coloring: Two Classic Searchers
implementations.code:
# Two compact backtrackers demonstrating the two undo styles:
#   rat_paths      -> mark/unmark a GRID cell around the neighbor loop
#   graph_coloring -> assign/reset a LABEL around the recursive call

def rat_paths(grid):
    # All (0,0) -> (n-1,n-1) paths through 1-cells, lexicographic order.
    n = len(grid)
    res, path = [], []
    # trying D, L, R, U in this order yields sorted move strings for free
    moves = [('D', 1, 0), ('L', 0, -1), ('R', 0, 1), ('U', -1, 0)]
    def walk(r, c):
        if r == n - 1 and c == n - 1:  # standing on the exit
            res.append(''.join(path))  # one complete path recorded
            return
        grid[r][c] = 0                 # mark: cell closed to this path
        for name, dr, dc in moves:
            nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
            # in bounds, open, and not on the current path (mark guarantees it)
            if 0 <= nr < n and 0 <= nc < n and grid[nr][nc] == 1:
                path.append(name)      # choose the move letter
                walk(nr, nc)           # explore onward
                path.pop()             # undo the letter
        grid[r][c] = 1                 # unmark: reopen for OTHER paths
    if grid and grid[0][0] == 1 and grid[n - 1][n - 1] == 1:
        walk(0, 0)                     # blocked endpoints -> zero paths
    return res

def graph_coloring(adj, m):
    # Color vertices 0..n-1 with labels 1..m; adjacent vertices must differ.
    n = len(adj)
    color = [0] * n                    # 0 means "not yet colored"
    def solve(v):
        if v == n:                     # every vertex colored -> success
            return True
        for c in range(1, m + 1):
            # reject c if any already-colored neighbor wears it
            if any(color[u] == c for u in adj[v]):
                continue
            color[v] = c               # choose the label
            if solve(v + 1):           # explore the remaining vertices
                return True            # full coloring found -> freeze
            color[v] = 0               # reset before trying the next label
        return False                   # no label works -> backtrack
    return color if solve(0) else None

if __name__ == '__main__':
    maze = [[1, 0, 0, 0],
            [1, 1, 0, 1],
            [1, 1, 0, 0],
            [0, 1, 1, 1]]
    print(rat_paths(maze))             # ['DDRDRR', 'DRDDRR']
    square_plus_diag = [[1, 2, 3], [0, 2], [0, 1, 3], [0, 2]]
    print(graph_coloring(square_plus_diag, 3))   # a valid 3-coloring
    print(graph_coloring([[1, 2], [0, 2], [0, 1]], 2))  # triangle, m=2 -> None

implementations.title: Word Break: Exponential vs Memoized, With Call Counters
implementations.code:
# The same recursion twice -- once naive, once memoized -- with a counter
# proving the collapse from exponential to quadratic on an adversarial input.

def word_break_naive(s, words):
    word_set = set(words)              # O(1) membership
    calls = [0]                        # mutable counter shared with the closure
    def solve(start):
        calls[0] += 1                  # count every invocation
        if start == len(s):
            return True                # whole string segmented
        for end in range(start + 1, len(s) + 1):
            # recurse on the suffix only when the prefix is a real word
            if s[start:end] in word_set and solve(end):
                return True
        return False                   # failure result is thrown away -> re-derived
    ok = solve(0)
    return ok, calls[0]

def word_break_memo(s, words):
    word_set = set(words)
    memo = {}                          # start index -> cached verdict
    calls = [0]
    def solve(start):
        calls[0] += 1
        if start == len(s):
            return True
        if start in memo:              # this suffix was already settled
            return memo[start]
        for end in range(start + 1, len(s) + 1):
            if s[start:end] in word_set and solve(end):
                memo[start] = True     # cache success
                return True
        memo[start] = False            # cache FAILURE -- the crucial line:
        return False                   # each index is fully searched only once
    ok = solve(0)
    return ok, calls[0]

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Adversarial input: many ways to cut prefixes, and the answer is False,
    # so the naive version re-proves the same failing suffixes over and over.
    s = 'a' * 20 + 'b'
    words = ['a', 'aa', 'aaa']
    print(word_break_naive(s, words))  # (False, huge call count)
    print(word_break_memo(s, words))   # (False, tiny call count)
    # Sanity checks on satisfiable inputs
    print(word_break_memo('applepenapple', ['apple', 'pen']))   # (True, small)

Stack & Queue.summary:
A stack and a queue are the two simplest "ordered access" containers in computer science, and almost every harder structure or algorithm secretly uses one of them. A stack is Last-In-First-Out (LIFO): you may only add and remove at one end, called the top, like a pile of plates — the plate you put down last is the first one you pick up. A queue is First-In-First-Out (FIFO): elements enter at one end (the tail/rear) and leave from the other (the head/front), like a line at a ticket counter — whoever arrived first is served first. Neither structure lets you touch the middle; that restriction is the point, because it makes every allowed operation O(1) and makes the order of events predictable.

Interviews love this topic for two reasons. First, "implement X using Y" questions (stack with an array, queue with two stacks, and so on) test whether you understand the machinery instead of just calling a library. Second, and more importantly, a family of genuinely hard-looking problems — Next Greater Element, Largest Rectangle in Histogram, Maximum of Minimum for Every Window Size — all collapse to one idea called the monotonic stack, where the stack holds only elements still "waiting for their answer" and every element is pushed and popped exactly once, giving O(N) totals. If you can spot "each element needs its nearest larger/smaller neighbour," you can solve a whole tier of MAANG questions on sight.

```
Stack (LIFO)                 Queue (FIFO)
push/pop here                out <- [a][b][c][d] <- in
      |                          head        tail
      v
   | 30 | <- top
   | 20 |
   | 10 | <- bottom
```

The mental model to carry: a stack remembers "what is still open / most recent" (function calls, unmatched brackets, bars that have not met a shorter bar yet), while a queue remembers "who has waited longest" (task scheduling, breadth-first search frontiers). When a problem talks about undoing, nesting, or the nearest element in one direction, think stack; when it talks about fairness, levels, or shortest number of steps, think queue.
preRequisites: Python list basics: append(x) and pop() work at the END of the list and are amortized O(1); indexing my_list[-1] reads the last element without removing it.
collections.deque: a double-ended queue where append, appendleft, pop, and popleft are all O(1) — the correct tool for queues in Python.
Big-O and the idea of AMORTIZED cost: a loop containing an inner while can still be O(N) total if every element enters and leaves a structure at most once.
Dictionaries: dict get/set/delete are average O(1) — needed for the LRU Cache design question.
How references work in Python: a 'node' object holding pointers to other nodes is just an object whose attributes refer to other objects (needed for the linked-list-backed LRU Cache).
Recursion and the call stack: each active call keeps its local variables in a frame; Python's default recursion limit is about 1000 frames (sys.setrecursionlimit can raise it).
Guarded while loops: 'while stack and condition(stack[-1])' — the 'stack and' part prevents peeking into an empty list.
cheatSheet: Stack ops push/pop/peek/is_empty are all O(1); in Python use one list and touch ONLY its end: append / pop / [-1].
Queue ops enqueue/dequeue/front are all O(1) with collections.deque (append + popleft); list.pop(0) is O(N) because it shifts everything.
Monotonic stack template: for each i, `while stack and cmp(a[stack[-1]], a[i]): resolve(stack.pop())` then push i — O(N) total because each index is pushed once and popped once.
Next Greater Element: pop while top's value < current; each popped index's answer is the current value; whatever survives has answer -1.
Largest Rectangle: when bar i closes a taller bar h = heights[stack.pop()], width = i - stack[-1] - 1 (or i if stack empty); append a 0 sentinel to flush.
Balanced Parentheses: push openers; on a closer, the top MUST be the matching opener; string balanced iff stack empty at the end.
Queue using two stacks: push into `inbox`; pop from `outbox`; refill outbox from inbox ONLY when outbox is empty — amortized O(1) per operation.
Stack using one queue: after enqueueing x, rotate len(q)-1 elements from front to back so x sits at the front — push O(N), pop/top O(1).
LRU Cache = dict + doubly linked list: dict finds the node in O(1), the DLL reorders/evicts in O(1); or use OrderedDict.move_to_end + popitem(last=False).

Max of min per window size: element a[i] is the minimum of every window of length up to L = nextSmaller[i] - prevSmaller[i] - 1; record a[i] at length L, then sweep lengths from N down to 1 taking suffix maxima.

sections.title: What & Why
sections.content:
A stack is a container with one rule: all insertions (push) and removals (pop) happen at the same end, the top. Because only the top is reachable, the element you get back is always the most recently added one that has not been removed yet — Last-In-First-Out. A queue has the mirror rule: insertions (enqueue) happen at the tail, removals (dequeue) happen at the head, so the element you get back is always the oldest one — First-In-First-Out.

Real-world analogies map exactly. A stack is a stack of cafeteria plates, the Undo history in an editor, or the browser Back button: you always return to the most recent state first. A queue is any waiting line: a printer's job queue, a ride line at a theme park, customer-support tickets served in arrival order.

Real systems are full of both. Every running program uses a call stack: calling a function pushes a frame with its local variables, returning pops it — which is why infinite recursion produces a "stack overflow". Compilers use stacks to match brackets and evaluate expressions. Operating systems and web servers use queues to schedule tasks fairly; message brokers like Kafka and RabbitMQ are industrial-strength queues; breadth-first search — the basis of shortest-path-in-unweighted-graphs — is nothing but a queue of "nodes to visit next". Caches (the LRU Cache sheet question) combine a queue-like recency order with O(1) lookup.

Why interviewers care: the operations are trivial, so the questions test whether you can (a) build the structures from raw parts (arrays, linked nodes, or each other) and (b) recognize the non-obvious problems — nearest-greater/smaller, histogram areas, window minimums — where a stack with a maintained ordering invariant turns an O(N^2) brute force into O(N).

sections.title: Memory Model & Representation
sections.content:
Both structures need a place to keep elements and O(1) access to the "active" end(s). There are two standard physical layouts.

1) Array-backed. A stack is a dynamic array plus one integer `top` (index of the last used slot). Push writes at `top+1` and increments; pop reads at `top` and decrements. Nothing ever shifts, which is why both are O(1).

```
capacity = 8, top = 2
index:   0    1    2    3    4    5    6    7
       [ 10 ][ 20 ][ 30 ][ -- ][ -- ][ -- ][ -- ][ -- ]
                     ^ top (push writes at index 3 next)
```

An array-backed queue is trickier: if you dequeue by removing index 0, every remaining element must shift left — O(N). The fix is a circular buffer: keep `head` (index of the front) and `count`, and compute the tail slot as `(head + count) % capacity`, so indices wrap around the end of the array and no element ever moves.

```
capacity = 6, head = 4, count = 3   (logical order: C, D, E)
index:   0    1    2    3    4    5
       [ E  ][ -- ][ -- ][ -- ][ C  ][ D  ]
         ^ tail wrapped around      ^ head
enqueue writes at (4 + 3) % 6 = index 1
```

2) Linked. A stack is a singly linked list where push/pop happen at the list head. A queue is a singly linked list with pointers to BOTH head (for dequeue) and tail (for enqueue). Linked versions never resize but pay memory per node (pointer overhead) and lose CPU-cache friendliness because nodes are scattered across the heap.

Python's `collections.deque` is a hybrid: a doubly linked list of fixed-size blocks (64 pointers per block). Both ends are O(1) like a linked list, but elements sit in contiguous chunks, so it is cache-friendlier than one-node-per-element designs. Indexing the middle of a deque is O(N), though — it must walk the blocks.

sections.title: Core Operations & Complexity
sections.content:
Every core operation on a correctly built stack or queue is O(1). The table below states each operation, its cost, and the one-line reason. N is the number of stored elements.

```
Structure | Operation      | Time      | Why
----------+----------------+-----------+-------------------------------------------
Stack     | push(x)        | O(1)*     | write at index top+1, bump top
Stack     | pop()          | O(1)      | read index top, drop top by 1
Stack     | peek()/top()   | O(1)      | read index top, change nothing
Stack     | is_empty()     | O(1)      | check top == -1 (or len == 0)
Queue     | enqueue(x)     | O(1)*     | write at (head+count) % cap, bump count
Queue     | dequeue()      | O(1)      | read index head, head=(head+1)%cap
Queue     | front()        | O(1)      | read index head, change nothing
Queue     | is_empty()     | O(1)      | check count == 0
Either    | search/access  | O(N)      | NOT supported by the interface; you would
          | middle element |           | have to pop/dequeue your way to it
```

The `*` marks amortized cost for dynamic arrays: when the underlying array is full, a push triggers one O(N) grow-and-copy, but doubling capacity means a copy happens so rarely that the average cost per push stays O(1). (Aggregate argument: to reach N elements you copy at most 1+2+4+...+N/2 < N items total.)

Space is O(N) for the elements themselves, plus O(1) bookkeeping (a few integers) for array versions or O(N) extra pointers for linked versions.

Two interface details interviewers probe: (1) what pop/dequeue on an EMPTY structure should do — raise an error, return a sentinel like None, or be guarded by the caller; state your choice out loud. (2) whether peek mutates — it must not. Underflow (popping empty) and overflow (pushing into a full fixed-capacity array) are the standard edge cases for Implement Stack Using Array and Implement Queue Using Array.

sections.title: How Python Does It
sections.content:
Python has no built-in named "stack" or "queue"; you assemble them from three tools.

`list` as a stack: `append` and `pop` operate on the end. Both are amortized O(1) — CPython over-allocates capacity and grows it geometrically, so the occasional realloc-and-copy averages out. `stack[-1]` peeks. This is the idiomatic Python stack; use it in every interview.

`list` as a queue: do not. `list.pop(0)` and `list.insert(0, x)` shift all N elements — each O(N). A loop that dequeues N items this way is O(N^2) and is one of the most common hidden performance bugs in interview code.

`collections.deque`: the real queue. `append`/`popleft` give FIFO; `appendleft`/`pop` also work, so it doubles as a stack or a double-ended structure. All four end operations are O(1) worst case (block-linked-list layout), but `dq[i]` for a middle index is O(N). `deque(maxlen=k)` auto-evicts the far end on overflow — useful for sliding windows, surprising if unintended.

`queue.Queue`, `queue.LifoQueue`: thread-safe channels for producer/consumer threading code. They acquire locks on every call and `get()` BLOCKS forever on an empty queue instead of raising. Never use them for algorithms.

`collections.OrderedDict`: a dict that also maintains a doubly linked list of keys in insertion order, exposing `move_to_end(key)` and `popitem(last=False)` in O(1) — which is exactly the machinery LRU Cache needs (see that pattern below). Since Python 3.7 plain dicts remember insertion order too, but they cannot move a key or pop from the front efficiently, so OrderedDict still earns its keep here.
sections.code:
# --- Stack: a plain Python list, touching ONLY the end ---------------
stack = []                       # empty stack
stack.append(10)                 # push 10          -> [10]
stack.append(20)                 # push 20          -> [10, 20]
top = stack[-1]                  # peek -> 20 (nothing removed)
x = stack.pop()                  # pop  -> 20, stack is now [10]
empty = not stack                # truthiness test: [] is falsy

# --- Queue: collections.deque, NEVER list.pop(0) ---------------------
from collections import deque
q = deque()                      # empty queue
q.append('a')                    # enqueue at the tail
q.append('b')                    # tail is now 'b'
front = q[0]                     # peek at the head -> 'a'
y = q.popleft()                  # dequeue -> 'a', true O(1)

# WHY a list is a bad queue: list.pop(0) shifts every remaining
# element one slot left, so each dequeue costs O(N) -> O(N^2) loops.

# queue.Queue and queue.LifoQueue are for THREAD communication:
# they take locks and BLOCK when empty instead of raising -> never
# use them in algorithm code; they are slower and hide bugs.

# deque(maxlen=k) silently DROPS the opposite end when full --
# handy for "keep last k items", dangerous if you did not expect it.

sections.title: Pattern: Balanced Symbol Matching
sections.content:
Recognize it: the input is a sequence with nested opening/closing structure — brackets, HTML tags, function calls — and you must decide validity or find the deepest/longest well-formed part. Sheet question: Balanced Parentheses.

Why a stack is forced on you: nesting means the LAST thing opened must be the FIRST thing closed. "Most recent unfinished thing" is literally the definition of a stack top. Trying to solve bracket matching with counters alone fails the moment there is more than one bracket type: "([)]" has matching counts but is invalid because the types interleave wrongly.

The invariant to state in the interview: at any point while scanning left to right, the stack contains exactly the openers that have not yet been closed, in the order they were opened (deepest at the bottom, most recent on top). Three ways to fail: (1) a closer arrives and the stack is empty — nothing to close; (2) a closer arrives and the top is the wrong type — crossed nesting; (3) the scan ends with a non-empty stack — something was never closed. If none of these fire, the string is balanced.

Complexity: one pass, each character pushed/popped at most once — O(N) time, O(N) worst-case space (all openers, e.g. "((((").

Variations that reuse the same skeleton: minimum insertions/removals to balance (count the failures instead of returning False), longest valid parentheses substring (push INDICES and measure gaps), and expression evaluation (two stacks: values and operators). If you can write the template below from memory, all of these become edits, not new problems.

sections.title: Pattern: Monotonic Stack (Nearest Greater / Smaller)
sections.content:
This is the single most valuable pattern in the topic. Recognize it: every element needs its NEAREST greater/smaller element to the left or right — sometimes stated directly (Next Greater Element), sometimes hidden inside a geometry or window question (Largest Rectangle in Histogram, Maximum of Minimum for Every Window Size). Brute force compares every pair: O(N^2). The monotonic stack does it in O(N).

The invariant: the stack holds indices of elements that are still WAITING for their answer, and their values are kept sorted from bottom to top (decreasing for next-greater problems, increasing for next-smaller problems). When a new element x arrives, every stacked element that x "beats" gets its answer NOW (it is x, and x is the nearest such element because anything between them was already popped). Then x itself starts waiting. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the whole scan is O(N) amortized even though one step may pop many items.

How the three sheet questions use it:
- Next Greater Element: the template verbatim — pop while top's value < current; each popped index's next greater is the current value; survivors get -1.
- Largest Rectangle in Histogram: for each bar, the widest rectangle with that bar's height spans from just after its previous SMALLER bar to just before its next SMALLER bar. A single left-to-right pass with an increasing stack discovers both boundaries the moment a bar is popped: the popper is the right boundary, the new stack top is the left boundary. A 0-height sentinel appended at the end flushes every remaining bar.
- Maximum of Minimum for Every Window Size: compute, for each element, its previous-smaller and next-smaller indices (two monotonic passes, or one pass recording both on pop). Element a[i] is then the minimum of SOME window of length L = nextSmaller[i] - prevSmaller[i] - 1, and of no longer window. Write a[i] into ans[L] with max; finally sweep L from N-1 down to 1 doing ans[L] = max(ans[L], ans[L+1]), because a value that is the min of a long window is also achievable as a min of every shorter length. Total O(N).

Choosing the comparison is the classic trap: strict (<) versus non-strict (<=) decides which side "owns" ties. For counting/area problems you must make one side strict and the other non-strict so equal elements are not double-counted or lost; for Largest Rectangle, popping on strictly-greater works because the LAST bar of an equal run computes the full combined width.
sections.code:
def next_greater(nums):
    # ans[i] = first value to the RIGHT of i that is bigger; -1 if none.
    n = len(nums)
    ans = [-1] * n
    stack = []                            # indices still waiting; their values
                                          # DECREASE from bottom to top
    for i in range(n):
        # nums[i] answers every waiting index with a smaller value.
        while stack and nums[stack[-1]] < nums[i]:
            ans[stack.pop()] = nums[i]    # nums[i] is its nearest greater
        stack.append(i)                   # now i waits for ITS next greater
    return ans                            # O(N): each index pushed & popped once


def largest_rectangle(heights):
    # Largest axis-aligned rectangle under a histogram, O(N).
    ext = list(heights) + [0]             # 0-height sentinel flushes the stack
    stack = []                            # indices; their heights INCREASE upward
    best = 0
    for i, h in enumerate(ext):
        # A bar shorter than the top CLOSES the top bar's rectangle:
        # the closed bar cannot stretch past index i.
        while stack and ext[stack[-1]] > h:
            height = ext[stack.pop()]     # the bar being closed
            left = stack[-1] if stack else -1   # nearest smaller on the left
            best = max(best, height * (i - left - 1))  # width is the open gap
        stack.append(i)                   # current bar now waits to be closed
    return best

sections.title: Pattern: Implement One Structure With Another
sections.content:
Four sheet questions live here: Implement Stack Using Array, Implement Queue Using Array, Implement Stack Using Queue, and Implement Queue Using Stack. They test whether you understand the CONTRACT (LIFO vs FIFO) separately from the STORAGE, and whether you can pay a cost on one operation to keep another O(1).

Stack using array: keep a `top` index into a fixed array; push increments, pop decrements; raise or signal on overflow (top == capacity-1) and underflow (top == -1). Nothing subtle — the interviewer is checking edge-case discipline. (Full class in Implementations.)

Queue using array: the naive version dequeues by shifting — O(N). The expected answer is the circular buffer: `head` marks the front, `count` the size, and the tail slot is computed as `(head + count) % capacity`, so both operations are O(1) and slots are reused forever. (Full class in Implementations.)

Queue using (two) stacks: two stacks, `inbox` and `outbox`. Enqueue pushes onto inbox. Dequeue pops from outbox; if outbox is empty, first pour ALL of inbox into it — the double reversal (into inbox, then into outbox) restores arrival order. The key sentence for the interview: each element is moved at most once from inbox to outbox, so over any sequence of M operations the total work is O(M) — amortized O(1) per operation, even though a single dequeue can cost O(N). Never refill while outbox still has elements, or you interleave old and new items out of order.

Stack using (one) queue: after enqueueing the new element x, rotate the queue len(q)-1 times (popleft then append), which walks the older elements behind x. Now the queue's FRONT is always the NEWEST element, so pop and top are plain popleft and peek. Push is O(N), everything else O(1). The two-queue variant moves elements between queues instead; know that it exists, but the one-queue rotation is shorter and the one interviewers prefer.

sections.title: Pattern: Recursion as a Hidden Second Stack (Sort a Stack)
sections.content:
Recognize it: you must transform a stack (sort it, reverse it) but you are only allowed stack operations — push, pop, peek, is_empty — no arrays, no walking the middle. Sheet question: Sort a Stack.

The trick is that RECURSION gives you a second stack for free: the call stack. Each recursive call pops one element and holds it in its local frame; when the recursion bottoms out the stack is empty, and as the calls unwind, each held element is inserted back into its correct place.

Two mutually recursive routines do the job. `sort_stack`: if the stack is non-empty, pop the top into a local variable, recursively sort the rest, then call `insert_sorted` to weave the held value back in. `insert_sorted(stack, x)`: if the stack is empty or the top is <= x, just push x (it belongs on top); otherwise pop the bigger top, recurse to place x deeper, then push the bigger element back. The invariant that makes it correct: whenever `insert_sorted` runs, the stack below is already sorted with the largest element on top, so x only needs to sink past elements bigger than itself.

Complexity: `insert_sorted` can touch O(N) elements, and it runs once per element — O(N^2) time, O(N) call-stack space. That is expected and accepted; the question is about the technique, not speed. The same held-in-frames idea reverses a stack (insert each held element at the BOTTOM instead of in sorted position).

Practical caution: Python's recursion limit (~1000) means this is a teaching pattern, not a production sort. If an interviewer allows an extra explicit stack, you can do it iteratively: pop from the source, and while the auxiliary stack's top is bigger than the popped value, move elements back to the source, then push — an insertion sort across two stacks, same O(N^2), no recursion.

sections.title: Pattern: O(1) Design with Hash Map + Doubly Linked List (LRU)
sections.content:
Recognize it: a DESIGN question demanding several operations, each O(1), over a bounded collection with an eviction rule. Sheet question: LRU Cache — `get(key)` and `put(key, value)` in O(1), evicting the Least Recently Used entry when capacity is exceeded.

Reason out the data structures from the requirements. O(1) lookup by key forces a hash map. Eviction needs "the entry unused for the longest time" — a recency ORDER, oldest at one end, newest at the other: queue-like. But a plain queue fails, because a `get` on a middle entry must move that entry to the newest end, and queues cannot remove from the middle. A doubly linked list can: given a direct pointer to a node, unlinking it is O(1) (rewire node.prev.next and node.next.prev). So the design is: a hash map from key to DLL node, plus a DLL ordered by recency. `get`: find the node via the map, unlink it, re-insert at the most-recent end, return its value. `put`: if the key exists, update and refresh like a get; if new, insert at the most-recent end, and if over capacity, remove the node at the least-recent end AND delete its key from the map — which is why each node must store its key, not just its value.

Implementation details that separate a pass from a fail: use two sentinel nodes (dummy head and tail) so insert/unlink never special-case an empty or one-element list; refresh recency on BOTH get and put-of-existing-key; never forget the map deletion on evict.

In Python, `collections.OrderedDict` packages this exact machinery — `move_to_end(key)` refreshes recency and `popitem(last=False)` evicts the oldest, both O(1) — so the short version below is genuinely O(1) per operation. Interviewers usually accept it but often then ask for the raw version, so the from-scratch dict+DLL implementation is given in full under Implementations.

sections.title: Pitfalls & Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Using `list.pop(0)` as dequeue. It shifts all remaining elements: O(N) per call, O(N^2) loops. Fix: `collections.deque` with `popleft`.
- Peeking or popping an empty structure. `stack[-1]` on `[]` raises IndexError. Fix: guard every access — `while stack and ...`, `if not stack: ...` — and decide up front whether empty-pop raises or returns a sentinel.
- Wrong strictness in monotonic-stack comparisons. `<` vs `<=` decides who owns ties; with duplicates one choice double-counts areas or gives the wrong nearest index. Fix: pick one side strict and the other non-strict, and dry-run on an input with equal values like [2, 2].
- Forgetting to flush the monotonic stack. Elements still stacked after the scan never got processed. Fix: append a sentinel (0 height for Largest Rectangle in Histogram) or run a drain loop after the pass.
- Storing values instead of indices on the stack. Values cannot give you widths or positions when you need them (histogram width, window length). Fix: push indices; look values up via the array.
- Refilling `outbox` while it is non-empty in the two-stack queue. Interleaves old and new elements, breaking FIFO. Fix: pour inbox into outbox ONLY when outbox is empty.
- Off-by-one in the circular queue. Writing the tail at `(head + count - 1) % cap` or forgetting `% cap` corrupts the buffer. Fix: tail slot = `(head + count) % capacity`; test enqueue/dequeue across the wrap boundary.
- LRU Cache: not refreshing recency on `get`, or on `put` of an existing key, or forgetting to delete the evicted key from the dict (map grows forever, stale node returned later). Fix: every touch moves the node to the most-recent end; evict = unlink node AND `del map[node.key]`.
- Recursion-based Sort a Stack on large inputs hits Python's ~1000-frame recursion limit with RecursionError. Fix: mention `sys.setrecursionlimit` or present the iterative two-stack insertion sort.
- Using `queue.Queue` in algorithm code. `get()` on an empty queue BLOCKS the program forever instead of raising. Fix: `collections.deque`.

sections.title: Interview Recognition Checklist
sections.content:
Cues that scream STACK: "valid/balanced" over nested symbols; "next/previous greater/smaller element"; "nearest ... to the left/right"; histograms, spans, or areas under bars; "undo", "most recent", "backtrack one step"; matching or cancelling adjacent pairs; evaluating or parsing expressions.

Cues that scream QUEUE: "first come first served"; "process in arrival order"; "level by level"; "minimum number of steps/minutes" on a grid or graph (BFS); "sliding window" combined with both-ends removal (deque); producer/consumer buffering.

Cues that scream DESIGN COMBO: "implement X with O(1) get and put" plus an eviction rule — hash map + doubly linked list (LRU Cache).

30-second pre-coding checklist:
- Which end is which? Say out loud where push/pop or enqueue/dequeue happen, and what `[-1]` / `[0]` mean in your code.
- Empty-case contract: what do pop/peek/dequeue do when the structure is empty — raise, return None, or guaranteed-never-called?
- If monotonic: increasing or decreasing? Strict or non-strict comparison? Indices or values on the stack? What flushes leftovers at the end?
- Complexity claim ready: "each element is pushed once and popped at most once, so the loop is O(N) amortized" — rehearse saying it.
- Python tools chosen: list for stack, deque for queue, OrderedDict (or dict+DLL) for LRU — and NOT list.pop(0), NOT queue.Queue.
- One tiny dry run picked: include duplicates for monotonic problems, include a wrap-around for circular queues, include an update-existing-key for LRU.

implementations.title: Array-Backed Stack (fixed capacity, from scratch)
Circular Array Queue (from scratch)
implementations.code:
class CircularArrayQueue:
