    # Fixed-capacity FIFO queue on one array, O(1) enqueue AND dequeue.
    # 'head' = index of the front element; 'count' = how many stored.
    # The tail slot is COMPUTED: (head + count) % capacity -- indices
    # wrap around the array end, so nothing ever shifts.

    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.capacity = capacity          # fixed number of slots
        self.data = [None] * capacity     # pre-allocated storage
        self.head = 0                     # where the next dequeue reads
        self.count = 0                    # current number of elements

    def is_empty(self):
        return self.count == 0            # nothing stored

    def is_full(self):
        return self.count == self.capacity    # every slot in use

    def size(self):
        return self.count

    def enqueue(self, x):
        if self.is_full():
            raise OverflowError("enqueue into full queue")  # overflow guard
        tail = (self.head + self.count) % self.capacity     # wrap-around slot
        self.data[tail] = x               # write at the logical tail
        self.count += 1                   # one more element stored

    def dequeue(self):
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("dequeue from empty queue")    # underflow guard
        x = self.data[self.head]          # front element leaves first (FIFO)
        self.data[self.head] = None       # drop the reference
        self.head = (self.head + 1) % self.capacity   # advance front, wrapping
        self.count -= 1                   # one fewer element stored
        return x

    def front(self):
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("front of empty queue")        # underflow guard
        return self.data[self.head]       # peek WITHOUT removing


# self-test exercising the wrap-around boundary
q = CircularArrayQueue(3)
q.enqueue('a'); q.enqueue('b'); q.enqueue('c')   # full: [a, b, c]
assert q.dequeue() == 'a'                 # head advances to index 1
q.enqueue('d')                            # 'd' wraps into index 0
assert [q.dequeue() for _ in range(3)] == ['b', 'c', 'd']   # FIFO preserved

implementations.title: Queue Using Two Stacks (amortized O(1))
implementations.code:
class QueueUsingTwoStacks:
    # FIFO queue built from two LIFO stacks (plain Python lists).
    # inbox  : where new arrivals are pushed        (newest on top)
    # outbox : reversed arrivals, ready to pop      (oldest on top)
    # Each element moves inbox -> outbox AT MOST ONCE, so any M
    # operations cost O(M) total: amortized O(1) each.

    def __init__(self):
        self.inbox = []                   # enqueue side
        self.outbox = []                  # dequeue side

    def enqueue(self, x):
        self.inbox.append(x)              # O(1): just push

    def _refill(self):
        # Pour inbox into outbox ONLY when outbox is empty.
        # The double reversal (into inbox, then into outbox)
        # restores original arrival order on top of outbox.
        if not self.outbox:
            while self.inbox:
                self.outbox.append(self.inbox.pop())   # reverse transfer

    def dequeue(self):
        self._refill()                    # make sure oldest is on outbox top
        if not self.outbox:
            raise IndexError("dequeue from empty queue")   # underflow guard
        return self.outbox.pop()          # oldest element leaves first

    def front(self):
        self._refill()                    # same preparation as dequeue
        if not self.outbox:
            raise IndexError("front of empty queue")
        return self.outbox[-1]            # peek at the oldest element

    def is_empty(self):
        return not self.inbox and not self.outbox   # both stacks empty


# self-test: interleave enqueues and dequeues to prove FIFO holds
q = QueueUsingTwoStacks()
q.enqueue(1); q.enqueue(2)
assert q.dequeue() == 1                   # oldest first
q.enqueue(3)                              # arrives while outbox non-empty
assert q.dequeue() == 2 and q.dequeue() == 3   # order still correct
assert q.is_empty()

implementations.title: LRU Cache (dict + doubly linked list, from scratch)
implementations.code:
class _Node:
    # One entry of the recency list. Stores the KEY too, because on
    # eviction we must delete that key from the hash map.
    __slots__ = ('key', 'val', 'prev', 'next')   # compact node objects

    def __init__(self, key, val):
        self.key = key                    # needed for map cleanup on evict
        self.val = val
        self.prev = None                  # neighbour toward LRU end
        self.next = None                  # neighbour toward MRU end


class LRUCache:
    # O(1) get/put: dict finds nodes, doubly linked list orders them
    # by recency.  head sentinel <-> LRU ... MRU <-> tail sentinel.
    # Sentinels mean insert/unlink NEVER special-case empty lists.

    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.cap = capacity
        self.map = {}                     # key -> _Node
        self.head = _Node(None, None)     # sentinel BEFORE the LRU end
        self.tail = _Node(None, None)     # sentinel AFTER the MRU end
        self.head.next = self.tail        # empty list: sentinels linked
        self.tail.prev = self.head

    def _unlink(self, node):
        # Remove node from the list in O(1) by rewiring neighbours.
        node.prev.next = node.next        # bypass forward
        node.next.prev = node.prev        # bypass backward

    def _push_mru(self, node):
        # Insert node just before the tail sentinel (most-recent end).
        node.prev = self.tail.prev        # old MRU becomes node's prev
        node.next = self.tail
        self.tail.prev.next = node        # old MRU points to node
        self.tail.prev = node             # tail sentinel points back

    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.map:
            return -1                     # cache miss
        node = self.map[key]
        self._unlink(node)                # remove from current position...
        self._push_mru(node)              # ...and refresh as most recent
        return node.val

    def put(self, key, value):
        if key in self.map:
            node = self.map[key]
            node.val = value              # overwrite the stored value
            self._unlink(node)            # updating counts as a use:
            self._push_mru(node)          # refresh recency too
            return
        if len(self.map) == self.cap:
            lru = self.head.next          # real node at the LRU end
            self._unlink(lru)             # drop it from the list...
            del self.map[lru.key]         # ...AND from the map (key stored!)
        node = _Node(key, value)          # brand-new entry
        self.map[key] = node
        self._push_mru(node)              # newest entry is most recent


# self-test reproducing the classic LeetCode trace
c = LRUCache(2)
c.put(1, 1); c.put(2, 2)
assert c.get(1) == 1                      # touches key 1 -> key 2 is now LRU
c.put(3, 3)                               # evicts key 2, NOT key 1
assert c.get(2) == -1 and c.get(1) == 1 and c.get(3) == 3

Stack & Queue Part-II.summary:
Part-I built the machinery: LIFO stacks, FIFO queues, circular buffers, the monotonic stack for nearest-greater/smaller questions, and O(1) design with a hash map plus a linked list. This tab assumes all of that and goes further. Part-II is about AUGMENTING the two structures so they answer richer questions in O(1), and about using a queue as an algorithmic engine rather than a container.

Four upgrades cover this tab's questions. (1) The monotonic DEQUE: Sliding Window Maximum needs the maximum of a window that loses elements on the left while gaining them on the right — a stack cannot evict from its far end, so the monotonic idea moves onto a double-ended queue whose front always holds the current maximum. (2) The augmented stack: Min Stack demands getMin() in O(1) at every moment, which works only if each stack level carries the minimum-so-far along with its value — the answer travels with the data. (3) The streaming monotonic stack: Stock Span Problem is Next Greater Element turned online — prices arrive one at a time, forever, so the stack compresses history into (price, span) runs and answers each day in amortized O(1). (4) Multi-source breadth-first search: Rotten Oranges uses a queue not to store data but to sweep a grid outward from MANY starting cells at once, one minute per BFS level, which is exactly why BFS — and never DFS — computes minimum time.

```
Monotonic deque for window max (k = 3), nums = [1, 3, -1, -3, 5]
window [3, -1, -3]   deque: [ 3 ][ -1 ][ -3 ]   front = 3 = max
5 arrives            pop -3, pop -1, pop 3  ->  [ 5 ]
```

The unifying theme: pay a small, disciplined cost on every insert (pop dominated elements, store an extra field, seed all sources) so that the expensive question — max, min, span, distance — becomes a free read. If Part-I taught you what stacks and queues are, Part-II teaches you what they can carry.
preRequisites: Part-I's monotonic stack pattern (Next Greater Element): the pop-while-dominated loop and why it is O(N) amortized — Part-II generalizes it twice.
collections.deque with all four end operations — append, appendleft, pop, popleft — each O(1); the monotonic deque needs both ends of the same structure.
Amortized analysis vocabulary: 'each element is inserted once and removed at most once, so M operations cost O(M) total' — you will say this for every pattern here.
Level-order traversal on trees: processing a queue one 'ring' at a time with a size snapshot (for level in ...: for _ in range(len(q))) — grid BFS is the same loop.
Grid mechanics in Python: a grid as list of lists, bounds checks 0 <= r < rows and 0 <= c < cols, and iterating 4 neighbours via (dr, dc) pairs.
Tuples as records: storing (value, extra) pairs on a stack and unpacking them — the augmented-stack questions live on this idiom.
cheatSheet: Sliding Window Maximum: keep a deque of INDICES with values decreasing front-to-back; pop back while nums[back] <= x, pop front while front <= i - k; answer = nums[front]; O(N) total.
Monotonic deque invariant: front-to-back values strictly decrease -> the front is always the max of the current window.
Min Stack (pair method): push (x, min(x, current_min)); getMin = stack[-1][1]; every operation O(1), space 2N.
Min Stack (O(1) extra space): if x < mn push encoded 2*x - mn and set mn = x; on popping an encoded value e < mn, restore mn = 2*mn - e.
Stock Span: span = 1 + spans of all previous days with price <= today; keep a stack of (price, span) with prices strictly decreasing; amortized O(1) per day.
Stock span identity: span[i] = i - (index of previous STRICTLY greater price); ties are absorbed, not blockers.
Rotten Oranges: multi-source BFS — enqueue ALL initially rotten cells at minute 0, expand level by level; answer = last minute reached; return -1 if any fresh orange survives.
BFS distance law: the first time BFS reaches a cell is via a shortest path (in edges/minutes) — guaranteed because the queue is processed in non-decreasing distance order.
Mark grid cells visited WHEN ENQUEUED, not when dequeued — otherwise the same cell enters the queue many times.
Amortized accounting: give each element 2 tokens (1 to enter, 1 to leave); any pop-many step is prepaid -> total O(N) for all monotonic structures.

sections.title: Recap & What Part-II Adds
sections.content:
Quick recap of Part-I: a stack gives O(1) access to the most recent element (LIFO), a queue to the oldest (FIFO); Python supplies them via list.append/pop and collections.deque; and the monotonic stack answers every "nearest greater/smaller" question in O(N) because each index is pushed once and popped at most once. If any of that feels shaky, reread Part-I first — every section below builds on it without re-explaining it.

Part-II adds four tools, each matched to one sheet question. First, the monotonic DEQUE (Sliding Window Maximum): the monotonic idea from Part-I, rebuilt on a double-ended queue so the structure can also expire elements that fall out of a sliding window on the left. Second, the AUGMENTED stack (Min Stack): store a second field on every level so an aggregate (the minimum) is readable in O(1) at any time — the general trick behind "design a structure with O(1) X". Third, the STREAMING monotonic stack (Stock Span Problem): the same pop-while-dominated loop, but online — input arrives one item per call with no end in sight, so the stack must compress everything it has absorbed into (value, count) runs. Fourth, the queue as a BFS ENGINE (Rotten Oranges): multi-source breadth-first search over a grid, where the queue's FIFO discipline is precisely what makes "minutes elapsed" equal "BFS level".

A fair question: why do these four live in a stack-and-queue chapter rather than under arrays or graphs? Because in each one the DATA STRUCTURE is the algorithm. Sliding Window Maximum without the deque is O(NK); Min Stack without augmentation needs an O(N) scan per getMin; Stock Span without the stack re-scans history every day; Rotten Oranges with a stack (DFS) computes wrong times entirely. The structure is not bookkeeping — it is the reason the complexity drops.

sections.title: Pattern: Monotonic Deque (Sliding Window Maximum)
sections.content:
Problem shape: a window of fixed size k slides over an array; report the maximum of each window. Brute force recomputes each window's max: O(N*k). Sheet question: Sliding Window Maximum. The target is O(N).

Why Part-I's stack is not enough: a monotonic stack only ever discards from its top. A sliding window loses its OLDEST element each step — that element could be the current maximum, and it must be removable from the other end. So the structure needs controlled removal at both ends: a deque.

The two invariants, which you should state before coding: (1) the deque holds INDICES from the current window only — the front is expired (popped left) the moment it slides out, i.e. when front <= i - k; (2) values are DECREASING from front to back, enforced by popping the back while its value is <= the incoming value. Together they force the front to be the window maximum: everything larger and older was never popped, everything smaller is behind it.

The reasoning that makes invariant (2) legal is the heart of the pattern: when x arrives and some element y sits in the deque with y <= x, then y is both OLDER than x and NOT LARGER than x. In any future window that still contains y, x is also present and at least as big — y can never again be the answer. Deleting y loses nothing. This "older and dominated means dead" argument is exactly the Next Greater Element pop condition wearing window clothes.

Why indices, not values: expiry (invariant 1) needs to know WHERE the front element lives; a raw value cannot tell you whether it has slid out of range. Storing indices costs nothing and answers both questions — position for expiry, nums[idx] for comparisons.

Complexity: each index is appended once, popped (from either end) at most once — O(N) total, O(k) space. Note the emission guard: output starts only once the first window is complete, at i >= k - 1. This structure also generalizes: Maximum of Minimum for Every Window Size (Part-I) fixes the element and varies the window; this pattern fixes the window and slides it — knowing both directions is a strong interview signal.

sections.title: Pattern: Augmented Stack (Min Stack)
sections.content:
Problem shape: a stack that additionally answers getMin() in O(1) at every moment, surviving arbitrary push/pop interleavings. Sheet question: Min Stack. The same recipe builds Max Stack, or a stack tracking any aggregate that is recomputable from "aggregate before this push" plus the new value.

Why the naive ideas fail. Keeping a single `current_min` variable breaks on pop: if you pop the minimum itself, the variable must roll back to the PREVIOUS minimum, which a lone variable has forgotten. Scanning the stack on each getMin is O(N). The fix is the augmentation principle: the answer to getMin must travel WITH the stack levels, so that popping automatically restores the older answer — no recomputation, no history replay.

Method 1 — pair per level. Each slot stores (value, minimum of everything at or below this level). Push computes min(x, current_min) in O(1) from the pair beneath; getMin reads stack[-1][1]; pop discards both fields together, which is what makes rollback automatic. Space: two numbers per element. This is the version to write first in an interview — it is five lines and impossible to get wrong under pressure.

Method 2 — O(1) extra space by encoding. Keep one number per level plus a single `mn` variable, and maintain this invariant: an entry stores its real value UNLESS it was pushed as a new minimum, in which case it stores the encoded value e = 2*x - old_mn and mn becomes x. The arithmetic that makes decoding safe: since x < old_mn, we get e = x + (x - old_mn) < x = mn, so encoded entries are recognizable — they are strictly below the current mn. On pop, if the stored entry e < mn, the true popped value is mn itself and the previous minimum is recovered as old_mn = 2*mn - e; otherwise the entry is a plain value. Top must apply the same test. Caveats worth saying aloud: 2*x can overflow fixed-width integers (a real concern in Java/C++; Python integers are arbitrary precision so it is safe here), and the trick stores numbers only — method 1 works for any orderable payload.

The interview meta-lesson: when a design question demands O(1) for an aggregate query, the aggregate must be maintained incrementally at write time, not computed at read time. Min Stack is the smallest possible example of that principle; LRU Cache (Part-I) is the same principle applied to recency.

sections.title: Pattern: Streaming Monotonic Stack (Stock Span)
sections.content:
Problem shape: prices arrive one per call, and each day you must report its span — the number of consecutive days ending today with price less than or equal to today's. Sheet question: Stock Span Problem. Equivalently: span[i] = i - (index of the previous STRICTLY greater price), the mirror image of Part-I's Next Greater Element, computed ONLINE.

Online changes the rules in two ways. First, there is no "right side" yet — only previous-greater questions make sense. Second, the input has no known end, so anything you store must stay bounded by useful content, not by the raw history. The monotonic stack handles both, with one twist: compression.

The twist: when today's price absorbs previous days (pops them), a plain index stack would suffice offline — span = i - stack[-1] after popping. Online, it is cleaner and more instructive to store (price, span) pairs: pop while the top's price is <= today's, adding each popped pair's span to today's running span. The popped days are consecutive by construction, and every day in their spans also had price <= the popped price <= today's price, so their entire runs fold into today's span. What remains on the stack is a strictly decreasing sequence of prices, each carrying the length of history it has swallowed — the stack is a lossless-for-this-question compression of the entire past.

Why the comparison must be <= (non-strict): equal prices do not break a span — a day with price equal to today's is absorbed, because the span counts days with price less than OR equal. Using < would wrongly stop the count at the first equal price. This is the strictness discipline from Part-I's monotonic section, applied to a definition you must read carefully.

Complexity: each day is pushed exactly once and popped at most once across the whole lifetime of the streamer, so M calls cost O(M) — amortized O(1) per call — with worst-case O(M) space (strictly decreasing prices never pop). A single call can pop many entries; that is fine and expected — say "amortized" before the interviewer asks. The same streaming-monotonic skeleton reappears in online next-greater feeds and in temperature-span variants; recognize it whenever a per-arrival answer depends on a suffix of history that dominance lets you delete.
sections.code:
class StockSpanner:
    # Online 'previous strictly greater' via a monotonic stack that
    # COMPRESSES absorbed history into (price, span) runs.

    def __init__(self):
        self.st = []                      # (price, span); prices strictly
                                          # DECREASE from bottom to top

    def next(self, price):
        span = 1                          # today always counts itself
        # Absorb every previous run whose price is <= today's.
        # Everything inside that run was <= its head price <= today,
        # so the WHOLE run joins today's span.
        while self.st and self.st[-1][0] <= price:
            span += self.st.pop()[1]      # merge the absorbed run's length
        self.st.append((price, span))     # today becomes a new compressed run
        return span                       # amortized O(1) per call


# self-test on the classic sequence
sp = StockSpanner()
answers = [sp.next(p) for p in (100, 80, 60, 70, 60, 75, 85)]
assert answers == [1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 4, 6]   # spans absorb equal/lower runs

sections.title: Pattern: Queue as BFS Engine (Rotten Oranges)
sections.content:
Problem shape: a grid where some cells are sources of a spreading process (rot, fire, infection), spread moves to 4-directionally adjacent cells once per time unit, and you must report the time until everything reachable is covered — or detect that some cell never is. Sheet question: Rotten Oranges.

Why a queue, and specifically why breadth-first search: BFS processes cells in non-decreasing distance order, because the queue is FIFO — every cell at distance t is dequeued before any cell at distance t+1. Therefore the first time BFS reaches a cell, it has found a shortest route there, and "minutes until this orange rots" equals its BFS level. A stack (DFS) explores one deep path first and reaches cells by arbitrary, usually non-shortest routes — its arrival times mean nothing for this problem. When a problem says "minimum number of steps/minutes" on an unweighted grid or graph, the queue is not a choice; it is the answer.

The multi-source twist: rot starts from EVERY initially rotten orange at once. Handle it by seeding the queue with ALL rotten cells before the loop, each at minute 0. Conceptually you are running BFS from an imaginary super-source connected to every rotten cell — which is why no per-source loop or distance merging is needed; one plain BFS computes, for every fresh orange, the distance to its NEAREST rotten source.

Two bookkeeping rules carry the correctness. (1) Mark a cell visited AT ENQUEUE TIME (here: overwrite grid value 1 -> 2 as you append it). Marking at dequeue time lets the same fresh cell be enqueued by several neighbours, inflating the queue and, in counting problems, corrupting the fresh counter. (2) Count fresh oranges up front and decrement as they rot; at the end, any remainder means some orange was unreachable (walled off by empty cells) — return -1. Also handle the degenerate case: zero fresh oranges from the start means the answer is 0, not -1, even with no rotten oranges at all.

Tracking time has two equivalent styles: store (row, col, minute) triples in the queue, or process level-by-level — snapshot len(queue), loop that many dequeues, then increment the minute counter once per ring. Both appear in the wild; the level-size loop is shown in Implementations, the triple style in the code here. Complexity: every cell enters the queue at most once and each is examined with 4 neighbours — O(rows*cols) time, O(rows*cols) queue space worst case.

sections.title: Amortized Analysis, Rigorously
sections.content:
Every structure in this tab makes the same suspicious move: a single operation may trigger a long inner loop (the deque popping many back elements, StockSpanner absorbing many runs), yet we claim O(1) "amortized" per operation. Interviewers at the bar this tab targets will ask you to justify that word, so here is the argument in a form you can deliver in 30 seconds.

Aggregate method: over the entire run, count insertions and removals separately. Each element is INSERTED into the structure exactly once. Each element can be REMOVED at most once — after removal it is gone and can never be removed again. So across N operations, the total work of all inner pop-loops combined is at most N removals plus N insertions: O(N) total, hence O(1) on average per operation. The inner while-loop's length is irrelevant; what matters is that its iterations consume elements that were paid for when inserted.

Token (accounting) version of the same proof, if you prefer a picture: hand every element 2 tokens at insertion — one pays for the insert itself, one is taped to the element to pay for its eventual removal. Any pop-heavy operation spends only tokens already taped to the popped elements, so no operation ever needs new money beyond its constant insertion cost. Total tokens issued = 2N, so total work <= 2N.

Two important boundaries of the claim. First, amortized O(1) is NOT worst-case O(1): a single sliding-window step or StockSpanner.next call can cost O(N) — if a problem demands hard per-operation latency bounds (real-time systems), say so and discuss alternatives. Second, the argument requires that removed elements never return; if your code can re-insert what it popped (a common bug when "restoring" elements inside the same pass), the accounting collapses and so does the complexity. This is the same argument that justified Part-I's Next Greater Element and the two-stack queue; Part-II simply reuses it on richer structures — one proof, four questions.

sections.title: Pitfalls & Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Sliding Window Maximum: storing VALUES in the deque instead of INDICES. Values cannot be tested for expiry, so the front lingers after leaving the window. Fix: store indices; expire while dq[0] <= i - k.
- Sliding Window Maximum: expiring with the wrong inequality (dq[0] < i - k keeps one stale element; forgetting the check entirely returns maxima from outside the window). Fix: the window at step i is [i-k+1, i]; anything <= i-k is out.
- Sliding Window Maximum: emitting an answer before the first window is complete. Fix: append to output only when i >= k - 1.
- Monotonic deque with duplicates: popping the back on `<` keeps equal values queued (harmless but larger), while `<=` evicts them (leaner). Either is CORRECT for max — but be consistent and be able to say why both work: an equal newer element is always at least as good.
- Min Stack: keeping one global min variable with no history. Popping the minimum leaves the variable stale — getMin then returns a value no longer in the stack. Fix: the pair-per-level method, or the 2*x - mn encoding with its decode-on-pop.
- Min Stack encoded variant: forgetting that top() must ALSO decode (an encoded entry is not the real value), or porting the trick to fixed-width integers where 2*x overflows. Fix: test top() right after pushing a new minimum; mention overflow when not in Python.
- Stock Span: using strict < when absorbing. Equal prices must be absorbed (span counts days with price <= today); < stops the span one run early. Fix: pop while stack top price <= today.
- Rotten Oranges: marking cells visited at DEQUEUE time. The same fresh cell gets enqueued by multiple neighbours — the fresh counter goes negative and the queue balloons. Fix: mark (grid 1 -> 2) at the moment you append.
- Rotten Oranges: returning `minutes` without checking the fresh counter (walled-off oranges make the true answer -1), or returning -1 when there were zero fresh oranges to begin with (the answer is 0). Fix: count fresh at the start; final answer = -1 if fresh else minutes.
- Rotten Oranges with the level-loop style: incrementing the minute counter even for the final empty expansion, overshooting by one. Fix: increment only when the next level is non-empty, or track time on the queue entries as (r, c, t).

sections.title: Interview Recognition Checklist
sections.content:
Cues that pick the Part-II tool:
- "Maximum/minimum of every window of size k" or any per-window aggregate with fixed k -> monotonic deque, O(N) (Sliding Window Maximum).
- "Design a stack that also returns min/max in O(1)" -> augmented stack: carry the aggregate on every level (Min Stack).
- "Values arrive one at a time / streaming / API with a next() method" plus "how many previous items until a bigger one" -> streaming monotonic stack with (value, span) compression (Stock Span Problem).
- "Minimum time/steps for something to spread" on a grid, "all sources spread at once", "level by level" -> multi-source BFS with a queue (Rotten Oranges).
- The word "amortized" anywhere, or an interviewer poking at your inner while-loop -> deliver the each-element-in-once-out-once argument.

30-second pre-coding checklist:
- Deque problems: indices or values? (Indices, almost always.) Which end expires, which end absorbs? Write both invariants as comments FIRST, then fill in the loop.
- Ties decided? For each comparison, choose < vs <= from the PROBLEM'S definition (span counts equals; window max tolerates either) and say the choice out loud.
- Augmented stack: does every field pop together with its value? Any operation reading a stale aggregate after a pop is the bug to check.
- BFS: are ALL sources seeded before the loop? Visited marked on enqueue? Time tracked per-entry or per-level — pick one and stick to it. What is returned when nothing needed spreading, and when something was unreachable?
- Complexity sentence rehearsed: "insert once, remove at most once, so O(N) total" — and know whether your bound is amortized or worst-case before claiming it.

implementations.title: Min Stack — Pair Method and O(1)-Extra-Space Encoding
MaxQueue + Sliding Window Maximum (monotonic deque)
implementations.code:
from collections import deque

class MaxQueue:
    # A FIFO queue that also answers max() in O(1) amortized.
    # Two structures: 'q' holds ALL elements (real queue), 'dq' is a
    # monotonic deque of CANDIDATES, values decreasing front->back.
    # Front of dq == max of q at all times.

    def __init__(self):
        self.q = deque()                  # actual queue contents
        self.dq = deque()                 # decreasing candidate values

    def enqueue(self, x):
        self.q.append(x)                  # normal FIFO insert
        # x kills every candidate <= x: they are older and not larger,
        # so they can never be the maximum while x is still queued.
        while self.dq and self.dq[-1] <= x:
            self.dq.pop()                 # dominated candidate leaves
        self.dq.append(x)                 # x is now a live candidate

    def dequeue(self):
        x = self.q.popleft()              # oldest element leaves (FIFO)
        if self.dq and self.dq[0] == x:   # was it also the current max?
            self.dq.popleft()             # retire its candidacy too
        return x

    def max(self):
        return self.dq[0]                 # front candidate == queue max


def sliding_window_max(nums, k):
    # Window max in O(N): the window IS a MaxQueue of size k.
    mq = MaxQueue()
    out = []
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        mq.enqueue(x)                     # window gains x on the right
        if i >= k:
            mq.dequeue()                  # window drops nums[i-k] on the left
        if i >= k - 1:
            out.append(mq.max())          # window complete: record its max
    return out


# self-test against a brute-force check
nums = [1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7]
expect = [max(nums[i:i + 3]) for i in range(len(nums) - 2)]   # O(N*k) oracle
assert sliding_window_max(nums, 3) == expect == [3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7]

implementations.title: Stock Span — Streaming Class and Offline Index Stack
implementations.code:
class StockSpanner:
    # Streaming stock span: amortized O(1) per next() call.
    # Stack holds (price, span) runs with strictly decreasing prices;
    # each run compresses a block of consecutive absorbed days.

    def __init__(self):
        self.st = []                      # (price, span) compressed history

    def next(self, price):
        span = 1                          # today counts itself
        while self.st and self.st[-1][0] <= price:
            span += self.st.pop()[1]      # absorb the whole dominated run
        self.st.append((price, span))     # today starts a new run
        return span


def stock_spans(prices):
    # Offline version: span[i] = i - index_of_previous_strictly_greater.
    # Classic index-based monotonic stack, one pass, O(N).
    n = len(prices)
    ans = [0] * n
    stack = []                            # indices; prices strictly decrease
    for i in range(n):
        # Equal or smaller previous prices are absorbed, so pop them.
        while stack and prices[stack[-1]] <= prices[i]:
            stack.pop()                   # not a blocker for the span
        # Survivor (if any) is the previous STRICTLY greater price.
        ans[i] = i + 1 if not stack else i - stack[-1]
        stack.append(i)                   # today may block future days
    return ans


# self-test: streaming and offline versions must agree
prices = [100, 80, 60, 70, 60, 75, 85]
sp = StockSpanner()
assert [sp.next(p) for p in prices] == stock_spans(prices) == [1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 4, 6]

implementations.title: Rotten Oranges — Multi-Source BFS (level-loop style)
implementations.code:
from collections import deque

def oranges_rotting(grid):
    # Multi-source BFS, LEVEL-LOOP style: one outer iteration == one
    # minute. Contrast with the (r, c, t) triple style -- same result.
    rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    q = deque()                           # frontier: rotted this minute
    fresh = 0                             # oranges still to be rotted
    for r in range(rows):
        for c in range(cols):
            if grid[r][c] == 2:
                q.append((r, c))          # every source starts at minute 0
            elif grid[r][c] == 1:
                fresh += 1                # count what must eventually rot

    minutes = 0
    # Expand ring by ring; stop early once nothing is left to rot.
    while q and fresh:
        minutes += 1                      # this pass rots one more ring
        for _ in range(len(q)):           # snapshot: process ONE level only
            r, c = q.popleft()
            for dr, dc in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)):
                nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc   # 4-directional neighbour
                if 0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols and grid[nr][nc] == 1:
                    grid[nr][nc] = 2      # mark visited ON ENQUEUE
                    fresh -= 1            # one fewer fresh orange
                    q.append((nr, nc))    # joins the NEXT minute's ring
    # 'while q and fresh' exits before an empty final ring, so
    # 'minutes' is never overcounted; leftovers mean unreachable cells.
    return -1 if fresh else minutes


# self-tests: classic cases including unreachable and no-fresh grids
assert oranges_rotting([[2, 1, 1], [1, 1, 0], [0, 1, 1]]) == 4    # full spread
assert oranges_rotting([[2, 1, 1], [0, 1, 1], [1, 0, 1]]) == -1   # walled off
assert oranges_rotting([[0, 2]]) == 0     # nothing fresh: 0 minutes, not -1

String.summary:
A string is a sequence of characters stored one after another, like beads on a thread: "hello" is the characters 'h', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o' at positions 0 through 4. In Python a string is IMMUTABLE — once created it can never change. Every operation that looks like a modification (concatenation, slicing, upper-casing) quietly builds a brand-new string and copies characters into it. That single fact drives almost every performance decision in this topic: you think in terms of index arithmetic over a read-only array, and when you must build output you collect pieces in a list and join once at the end.

Interviews love strings for two reasons. First, easy-sounding problems hide sharp edge cases: reversing words must handle repeated spaces, atoi must handle signs and overflow clamping, Roman numerals hide a subtraction rule. These test whether you can turn a fuzzy spec into a precise linear scan. Second, strings carry three of the most beautiful algorithms in the standard interview canon — Rabin-Karp's rolling hash, KMP's prefix function, and the Z-function — which all answer the same question, "where does pattern P occur inside text T?", in O(n + m) instead of the naive O(n * m). Understanding WHY they are linear (they never re-examine text characters) is the real lesson.

```
text:    a b a b c a b a b c a b c      pattern: a b c
naive:   restart the pattern after every mismatch  -> O(n*m)
KMP/Z:   remember what already matched, never move
         the text pointer backwards            -> O(n+m)
```
The mental model for the whole topic: a string is a frozen array of small integers (code points). Scanning patterns (two pointers, expand-around-center, state machines) handle the ad-hoc problems; precomputed helper arrays (hash prefixes, LPS, Z) handle the matching problems. Master both halves and every question in this sheet becomes a variation you have already seen.
preRequisites: Array indexing and slicing in Python: s[i] is O(1), s[i:j] COPIES j-i characters into a new string, s[::-1] builds a full reversed copy.
ord() and chr(): ord('a') == 97 converts a character to its integer code point and back — the basis of frequency arrays and hashes.
The two-pointer technique from Arrays: two indices moving toward each other (reversal) or in tandem (run detection).
Modular arithmetic: (a * b + c) % m, and Python's pow(base, exp, mod) — needed to keep Rabin-Karp hashes bounded.
The ''.join(parts) idiom and WHY repeated s += piece inside a loop is O(N^2) on immutable strings.
Core str methods and their returns: split(), strip(), find(), startswith(), lower() — each returns a NEW string or list, never mutates.
Big-O comparison of nested versus single scans: O(n*m) double loop versus O(n+m) one-pass with preprocessing.
cheatSheet: Python str is immutable: s += ch in a loop costs O(N^2); collect in a list and ''.join(parts) for O(N).
LPS / prefix-function: lps[i] = length of the longest PROPER prefix of s[:i+1] that is also its suffix (its 'border').
KMP search: text pointer never moves backwards; on mismatch jump the pattern with j = lps[j-1] -> O(n+m) total.
Z-function: z[i] = length of the longest common prefix of s and s[i:]; maintain window [l, r) for O(n).
Rabin-Karp roll: h_new = ((h_old - ord(out)*B^(m-1)) * B + ord(in)) mod M; always verify a hash hit by real comparison.
Longest palindromic substring: 2n-1 centers (n odd, n-1 even gaps), expand around each -> O(n^2) time, O(1) space.
Longest common prefix vertical scan: compare column by column, stop at first disagreement -> O(total characters).
atoi state order: skip spaces -> read at most ONE sign -> accumulate digits -> clamp into [-2^31, 2^31 - 1].
Roman to Integer: if value(cur) < value(next) subtract it, else add it (IV = -1 + 5 = 4).
Choosing a matcher: single pattern -> KMP or Z; want hashes reusable for many substring compares -> Rabin-Karp.

sections.title: What & Why
sections.content:
A string is text: a finite sequence of characters indexed from 0. Think of a printed word as a row of letter tiles glued to a board — you can READ any tile instantly, but you cannot swap tiles; to 'change' the word you print a whole new board. That is exactly Python's contract: reading s[i] is O(1), but every apparent modification allocates a new string.

Strings are everywhere in real systems, which is why interviewers treat them as a proxy for day-one job skills: web servers parse URLs and headers (linear scans and state machines, like String to Integer (atoi)); editors and grep search text for patterns (KMP, Rabin-Karp, Z Function); bioinformatics matches DNA fragments against genomes (rolling hashes over 4-letter alphabets); compilers tokenize source code (run detection and lookahead, like Roman to Integer); autocomplete ranks by shared prefixes (Longest Common Prefix). The sheet's eight questions split cleanly into two families. The parsing family — Reverse Words in a String, Roman to Integer, String to Integer (atoi), Longest Common Prefix — tests careful single-pass scanning with edge cases. The matching family — Rabin Karp, KMP Algorithm, Z Function, plus Longest Palindromic Substring — tests whether you know the classic preprocessing tricks that turn quadratic brute force into linear (or near-linear) algorithms. Both families reward the same habit: state your invariant before you write the loop.

sections.title: Memory Model & Representation
sections.content:
CPython stores a string as one contiguous block: a small header (type pointer, reference count, length, a cached hash) followed by the character buffer. Since PEP 393, the buffer width adapts to the WIDEST character present: pure ASCII/Latin-1 text uses 1 byte per character, most other text 2 bytes, and emoji or rare symbols force 4 bytes per character for the whole string.

```
s = "HELLO"          (CPython object, compact 1-byte form)
+--------------------------------------------------+
| refcount | type=str | length=5 | cached hash | .. |   header
+--------------------------------------------------+
| 'H' | 'E' | 'L' | 'L' | 'O' |                        buffer
+-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+
  [0]   [1]   [2]   [3]   [4]

t = s + "!"   ->   NEW 6-slot object is allocated and
                    all 5 old chars are COPIED; s unchanged
```
Three consequences matter for algorithms. (1) len(s) is O(1) — it is read from the header, not counted. (2) hash(s) is O(n) the first time, then cached — dict lookups on repeated string keys are cheap. (3) Immutability means every slice s[i:j] is a physical copy, so writing recursion as f(s[1:]) hides an O(n) copy per call and turns a linear algorithm quadratic; pass indices instead. Python also 'interns' some small strings (identifiers, single characters), meaning identical literals may share one object — which is why 'a' is 'a' can be True. Never rely on it: compare text with ==, always.

sections.title: Core Operations & Complexity
sections.content:
Every string algorithm is assembled from a small set of primitives. Know the cost of each and WHY, because the difference between an accepted and a TLE solution is usually one hidden copy inside a loop.

```
Operation             | Time         | Why (one clause)
----------------------+--------------+------------------------------------
s[i]                  | O(1)         | direct offset into the char buffer
len(s)                | O(1)         | stored in the object header
s[i:j]                | O(j-i)       | copies the slice into a new string
s + t                 | O(n+m)       | allocates new buffer, copies both
s == t                | O(min(n,m))  | char-by-char compare, early exit
p in s / s.find(p)    | O(n*m) worst | optimized two-way scan, ~O(n) typical
''.join(parts)        | O(total)     | one allocation, one copy pass
s.split() / strip()   | O(n)         | single left-to-right scan
s.lower(), s.upper()  | O(n)         | builds a transformed copy
hash(s)               | O(n) once    | cached in the header afterwards
```
Two traps hide in this table. First, s + t is fine ONCE, but summing N pieces by repeated + performs 1 + 2 + ... + N copies = O(N^2); join fixes it. Second, 'p in s' looks O(1) because it is one operator, but it is a full substring search — calling it inside a loop over all positions silently builds an O(n^2 * m) brute force. The matching patterns below (Rabin-Karp, KMP, Z) exist precisely to beat that.

sections.title: How Python Does It
sections.content: Python has no separate 'char' type — s[0] is a length-1 string — and no mutable string type at all. The standard toolkit: str methods for scanning and splitting, a LIST OF CHARACTERS when you genuinely need in-place mutation (list(s), mutate, ''.join back), ord()/chr() for code-point math, and collections.Counter for frequency tables. str.find(sub) returns -1 when absent while str.index(sub) raises ValueError — prefer find in interview code. split() with NO argument collapses any run of whitespace and drops leading/trailing blanks, while split(' ') keeps empty pieces between consecutive spaces; this exact difference decides whether Reverse Words in a String works on '  hello   world  '. Under the hood 'sub in s' uses a variant of the Crochemore-Perrin 'two-way' algorithm, so in practice Python's built-in search is close to linear — interviewers still expect you to write KMP or Rabin-Karp yourself to prove you know why. The snippet shows the idioms that appear in nearly every string solution.
sections.code:
# --- Idioms every string solution leans on -------------------------

# 1) Build big strings with a list buffer + ONE join (O(total)).
def build_report(rows):
    parts = []                       # list append is amortized O(1)
    for r in rows:
        parts.append(",".join(r))    # join = single pass over pieces
    return "\n".join(parts)          # one final allocation, not N

# 2) Mutate via a char list — strings themselves cannot change.
def censor(s, bad_positions):
    chars = list(s)                  # O(n) copy into a MUTABLE list
    for i in bad_positions:
        chars[i] = "*"               # O(1) in-place writes
    return "".join(chars)            # freeze back into a string

# 3) Frequency table with ord() math (lowercase a-z assumed).
def letter_freq(s):
    freq = [0] * 26                  # one slot per letter
    for ch in s:
        freq[ord(ch) - ord("a")] += 1   # 'c' -> slot 2
    return freq

# 4) split() vs split(' ') — the whitespace trap.
#    "  a  b ".split()    -> ['a', 'b']        (runs collapsed)
#    "  a  b ".split(" ") -> ['', '', 'a', '', 'b', '']  (kept!)

sections.title: Pattern: Two Pointers, Reversal & Vertical Scanning
sections.content:
Recognize it: the problem asks you to rearrange, reverse, or compare strings without any searching — Reverse Words in a String and Longest Common Prefix are the sheet's examples. The invariant of a two-pointer reversal is: 'everything outside [lo, hi] is already in final position; each step fixes two more characters'. The invariant of a vertical scan is: 'all strings agree on every column before column i'.

For Reverse Words in a String, Python gives a one-liner via split/join, but interviewers often push for the O(1)-extra-space version used in C: reverse the WHOLE character buffer (word order becomes correct, letters inside each word become backwards), then reverse each word individually to repair it. Practice both — the follow-up is guaranteed. For Longest Common Prefix, compare column by column across all words: the moment any word disagrees (or ends), the answer is everything before that column. Total cost O(sum of lengths) worst case, and it usually exits far earlier. A useful bound to state out loud: the answer can never be longer than the shortest string, so iterate over that one.

sections.title: Pattern: Linear Parsing & State Machines
sections.content:
Recognize it: the input is a string encoding a VALUE (a number, a numeral, a token stream) and you must decode it while tolerating messy edges. String to Integer (atoi) and Roman to Integer are the sheet's examples. The winning mental model is a tiny state machine: list the states on paper first, then write one loop where each state consumes characters and hands off to the next. For atoi the states are exactly: (1) skip leading spaces, (2) consume at most ONE sign, (3) accumulate digits with num = num*10 + digit, (4) stop at the first non-digit, then clamp into the 32-bit range [-2^31, 2^31 - 1]. The invariant: after processing i characters, num holds the correctly parsed value of the digits seen so far.

Roman to Integer needs one insight instead of a state machine: reading left to right, a symbol SMALLER than its right neighbor is subtractive (the I in IV contributes -1), otherwise additive. One comparison per character replaces hardcoding all six subtractive pairs. State machines feel like overkill until you meet the edge cases: '+-12' (second sign ends parsing), '   42abc' (stop at 'a'), '' (empty input), clamping AFTER applying the sign. Walking your machine through those examples before coding is the difference between one submission and five.

sections.title: Pattern: Expand Around Center
sections.content:
Recognize it: the problem asks for the longest palindromic SUBSTRING (contiguous!) — the sheet's Longest Palindromic Substring. Brute force checks all O(n^2) substrings at O(n) each: O(n^3). The key observation: every palindrome has a center. There are exactly 2n - 1 possible centers — the n characters (odd-length palindromes like 'aba') and the n - 1 gaps between characters (even-length palindromes like 'abba'). Fix a center, then expand outward while the two ends match. Invariant during expansion: s[lo..hi] is a palindrome at the top of every loop iteration.

```
s = f o r g e e k s
center at gap between e,e:   g [e e] k     expand: 'ee'
                           [g e e k]?      g != k -> stop
```
Each of the 2n - 1 centers expands at most O(n), giving O(n^2) time and O(1) extra space — the expected interview answer. Mention (do not code) that Manacher's algorithm achieves O(n), and that the DP-table formulation (dp[i][j] = s[i] == s[j] and dp[i+1][j-1]) also works but costs O(n^2) space for no speed gain here. Classic bug: handling only odd centers, which silently fails on 'abba' — always run both expand(c, c) and expand(c, c + 1). Note the contrast with Part-II's Longest Palindromic Prefix, where the palindrome is anchored to position 0 and a smarter O(n) border trick applies.

sections.title: Pattern: Rolling Hash (Rabin-Karp)
sections.content:
Recognize it: you need substring search where hashing helps — one pattern against a long text, MANY patterns at once, or you want O(1) equality checks between substrings. The sheet's Rabin Karp question is the pattern in pure form, and the same rolling hash powers plagiarism detectors and rsync's block matching. Idea: treat a window of m characters as an m-digit number in base B, reduced mod a large prime M. Sliding the window one step right is O(1) arithmetic: subtract the leaving character's contribution (ord(out) * B^(m-1)), multiply by B, add the entering character.

```
window "abc":  h = ((a*B + b)*B + c) mod M          (Horner)
slide to "bcd": h' = ((h - a*B^2) * B + d) mod M     O(1)!
```
Invariant: after each slide, th equals the hash of the current window text[i..i+m-1]. Equal hashes do NOT prove equal strings — different windows can collide — so verify each hash hit with a real O(m) comparison. With a large prime M (say 10^9 + 7) collisions are rare, making the expected time O(n + m) while staying always-correct; extra-paranoid solutions hash with two independent (B, M) pairs. Against an adversarial test-setter, randomize B. Compared with KMP, Rabin-Karp is easier to extend (multiple patterns via a hash set of pattern hashes, 2D grids) but is expected-time rather than worst-case linear.

sections.title: Pattern: Prefix Function (KMP)
sections.content:
Recognize it: worst-case-linear substring search, or ANY problem about prefixes that are also suffixes — the sheet's KMP Algorithm here, and Part-II's Minimum Characters Needed for Palindrome and Longest Palindromic Prefix reuse it directly. The heart is the LPS array (also called the prefix function): lps[i] = length of the longest PROPER prefix of pattern[:i+1] that is also its suffix. Such a prefix-suffix is called a BORDER.

```
pattern:  a b a b a c
lps:      0 0 1 2 3 0
e.g. "ababa" -> border "aba" (prefix AND suffix), so lps[4]=3
```
Why it makes search linear: while scanning the text, suppose j pattern characters are matched and the next text character mismatches. The naive algorithm would move the text pointer back and restart. KMP instead observes that the last j text characters equal pattern[:j], so the longest possible re-alignment is the border of pattern[:j] — jump j to lps[j-1] and retry, WITHOUT moving the text pointer. Invariant: at every step, pattern[:j] equals the text suffix ending at the current position. Each text character is read once, and j can only decrease as often as it increased, so the whole search is O(n + m). The same amortized argument makes building lps O(m). Learn to compute lps by hand on 'aabaaab' — interviewers love asking for the array before the code.

sections.title: Pattern: Z-Function
sections.content:
Recognize it: you want, for EVERY position i, how long s[i:] agrees with the start of s — the sheet's Z Function question, and the cleanest tool whenever a problem compares suffixes against the prefix (periodicity, borders, pattern search). Definition: z[i] = length of the longest common prefix of s and s[i:] (with z[0] = n by convention — state your convention out loud).

```
s = a a b x a a b
z = 7 1 0 0 3 1 0     z[4]=3 because s[4:7]="aab" = s[0:3]
```
The O(n) trick mirrors KMP's amortization. Maintain the rightmost known 'prefix window' [l, r): a segment with s[l:r] == s[0:r-l]. For a new i inside the window, position i behaves like its mirror i-l near the start, so initialize z[i] = min(r - i, z[i - l]) for free, then extend by honest comparisons; if the match pushes past r, the window moves right. Since r only ever moves forward, total comparison work is O(n). Invariant: [l, r) is always the rightmost window matching a prefix.

Pattern search with Z: build combined = pattern + '#' + text, where '#' appears in neither string; every position with z[i] == len(pattern) marks a full occurrence in text. KMP and Z are interchangeable for plain search — Z is often easier to reason about ('how much of the prefix starts here?'), while KMP's lps drives the border tricks in String Part-II. Know both; derive one from the other if you blank.

sections.title: Pitfalls & Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1) Quadratic building: result += piece inside a loop copies the whole accumulator every time — O(N^2). Fix: append to a list, ''.join once. 2) Hidden slice copies: recursing on s[1:] or comparing s[i:i+m] inside a hot loop adds an O(n) copy per step. Fix: pass indices (i, j) and compare characters. 3) split(' ') vs split(): with an explicit separator, '  a  b '.split(' ') yields empty strings for every doubled space; no-arg split() collapses them — Reverse Words in a String breaks with the wrong one. 4) LPS misdefinition: lps[i] must use a PROPER prefix; allowing the whole string gives lps[i] = i+1 and infinite fallback loops. Also the fallback is k = lps[k-1], never k -= 1. 5) Unverified Rabin-Karp: reporting on hash equality alone fails on collisions. Fix: confirm with a real comparison (Python's % already returns non-negative values, one worry fewer). 6) Only-odd centers in expand-around-center silently misses 'abba'; always run expand(c, c) and expand(c, c+1). 7) atoi edge cases: '+-12' must stop at the second sign; clamp AFTER applying the sign; skip only spaces, not all whitespace, if the spec says spaces. 8) Comparing with 'is': interning makes 'a' is 'a' True in tests and False in production — always ==. 9) Z-array conventions: some sources define z[0]=0, others n; pick one, say it, and make z_search consistent with it. 10) Assuming 'in' is O(1): 'p in s' is a full substring search — never call it inside a per-position loop.

sections.title: Interview Recognition Checklist
sections.content:
Cues that a problem is a string problem in disguise: the input is text; words like substring, prefix, suffix, palindrome, anagram, pattern, occurrence, rotate, parse appear; the constraint is |s| up to 1e5 or 1e6 (a quadratic scan of 1e6 is 1e12 steps — you need the linear machinery).

30-second pre-coding checklist: (1) Alphabet — lowercase only? digits? Unicode? It decides array-of-26 versus dict/Counter. (2) Case sensitivity and whitespace rules — ask, do not assume. (3) Empty string and length-1 inputs — trace your loop on them mentally. (4) Am I searching (pattern in text -> KMP / Rabin-Karp / Z), parsing (value from text -> state machine), or transforming (rearrange -> two pointers + char list)? (5) Contiguous substring or subsequence? Palindromic SUBSTRING means expand-around-center here; palindromic SUBSEQUENCE is dynamic programming, a different topic. (6) Output building — list + join, never += in a loop. (7) If they say 'O(1) extra space', think char-list reversal tricks; if they say 'stream/online', think rolling hash. Map to the sheet: search machinery -> Rabin Karp, KMP Algorithm, Z Function; parsing -> String to Integer (atoi), Roman to Integer; scanning/rearranging -> Reverse Words in a String, Longest Common Prefix; palindromes -> Longest Palindromic Substring.

implementations.title: KMP Matcher From Scratch (LPS + Search)
implementations.code:
# ==================================================================
# KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt) substring search, built from scratch.
# Core idea: precompute, for every prefix of the pattern, its longest
# "border" — a proper prefix that is also a suffix. On a mismatch we
# slide the pattern onto its border instead of restarting, so the
# text pointer NEVER moves backwards. Total time: O(n + m).
# ==================================================================

def build_lps(pattern):
    # lps[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[:i+1]
    #          that is also a suffix of it (its "border").
    # Example: pattern = a b a b a c
    #          lps     = 0 0 1 2 3 0
    m = len(pattern)
    lps = [0] * m                 # lps[0] = 0 by definition (proper!)
    k = 0                         # length of the border being extended
    for i in range(1, m):
        # If pattern[i] cannot extend the current border, fall back
        # to the next smaller border (lps[k-1]) and try again.
        while k > 0 and pattern[i] != pattern[k]:
            k = lps[k - 1]
        if pattern[i] == pattern[k]:
            k += 1                # border extended by one character
        lps[i] = k                # record border length at position i
    return lps


def kmp_search(text, pattern):
    # Return every start index where pattern occurs inside text.
    n, m = len(text), len(pattern)
    if m == 0:
        return list(range(n + 1))     # empty pattern matches anywhere
    lps = build_lps(pattern)
    matches = []
    j = 0                             # pattern chars matched so far
    for i in range(n):                # i only ever moves forward
        # mismatch: reuse work by jumping j across known borders
        while j > 0 and text[i] != pattern[j]:
            j = lps[j - 1]
        if text[i] == pattern[j]:
            j += 1                    # extended the match by one char
        if j == m:                    # matched the entire pattern
            matches.append(i - m + 1) # match started m-1 chars back
            j = lps[m - 1]            # keep scanning: overlaps allowed
    return matches


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # quick self-checks (run this file directly)
    assert kmp_search("ababcababcabc", "abc") == [2, 7, 10]
    assert kmp_search("aaaa", "aa") == [0, 1, 2]   # overlapping hits
    assert build_lps("ababac") == [0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 0]
    print("KMP OK")

implementations.title: Rabin-Karp Matcher From Scratch (Rolling Hash)
implementations.code:
# ==================================================================
# Rabin-Karp substring search with a rolling polynomial hash.
# A window of m chars is read as an m-digit base-B number mod M.
# Sliding the window is O(1) arithmetic, so hashing all windows is
# O(n) instead of O(n*m). Hash hits are VERIFIED by real comparison,
# so the algorithm is always correct — the hash only decides when a
# comparison is worth doing.
# ==================================================================

B = 256                # base: one "digit" per possible byte value
M = 1_000_000_007      # large prime modulus keeps collisions rare

def poly_hash(s):
    # Horner's rule: "abc" -> ((a*B + b)*B + c) mod M
    h = 0
    for ch in s:
        h = (h * B + ord(ch)) % M
    return h

def rabin_karp(text, pattern):
    n, m = len(text), len(pattern)
    if m == 0:
        return list(range(n + 1))     # empty pattern matches anywhere
    if m > n:
        return []                     # pattern cannot fit at all
    high = pow(B, m - 1, M)           # weight of the char LEAVING the window
    ph = poly_hash(pattern)           # fixed target hash
    th = poly_hash(text[:m])          # hash of the first window
    matches = []
    for i in range(n - m + 1):
        # equal hashes -> PROBABLE hit; confirm to rule out collision
        if th == ph and text[i:i + m] == pattern:
            matches.append(i)
        if i + m < n:
            # roll the window one step right:
            th = (th - ord(text[i]) * high) % M   # drop outgoing char
            th = (th * B + ord(text[i + m])) % M  # append incoming char
    return matches

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # quick self-checks (run this file directly)
    assert rabin_karp("hello world hello", "hello") == [0, 12]
    assert rabin_karp("aaaa", "aa") == [0, 1, 2]   # overlapping hits
    assert rabin_karp("abc", "abcd") == []         # pattern too long
    print("Rabin-Karp OK")

implementations.title: Z-Algorithm From Scratch (Z-array + Search)
implementations.code:
# ==================================================================
# Z-algorithm: z[i] = length of the longest substring starting at i
# that matches a PREFIX of s. Computed in O(n) by maintaining the
# rightmost interval [l, r) already known to equal a prefix of s.
# Search application: run z over pattern + sep + text; every value
# equal to len(pattern) marks one occurrence.
# ==================================================================

def z_function(s):
    n = len(s)
    z = [0] * n
    if n == 0:
        return z
    z[0] = n                       # the whole string matches itself
    l, r = 0, 0                    # rightmost prefix-match window [l, r)
    for i in range(1, n):
        if i < r:
            # i sits inside a known prefix copy: its mirror is i-l.
            # We may not claim anything beyond the window edge r.
            z[i] = min(r - i, z[i - l])
        # extend the match by direct comparison past what is known
        while i + z[i] < n and s[z[i]] == s[i + z[i]]:
            z[i] += 1
        if i + z[i] > r:
            l, r = i, i + z[i]     # window now reaches further right
    return z

def z_search(text, pattern):
    # All start indices of pattern inside text. O(n + m) total.
    if not pattern:
        return list(range(len(text) + 1))
    sep = "\x00"                   # a char occurring in neither string
    z = z_function(pattern + sep + text)
    m = len(pattern)
    hits = []
    for i in range(m + 1, len(z)):
        if z[i] >= m:              # full pattern-length prefix match
            hits.append(i - m - 1) # combined index -> text index
    return hits

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # quick self-checks (run this file directly)
    assert z_function("aabxaab") == [7, 1, 0, 0, 3, 1, 0]
    assert z_search("ababcababcabc", "abc") == [2, 7, 10]
    print("Z-algorithm OK")

implementations.title: StringBuilder & Fixed-Alphabet Counter

String Part-II.summary:
In String Part-I you built the machinery: two-pointer scans, parsing state machines, expand-around-center, and the three linear-time matchers — Rabin-Karp's rolling hash, KMP's prefix function (the LPS array of 'border' lengths), and the Z-function. Part-II is about DEPLOYING that machinery on problems that do not announce which tool they need. The star exhibit is the border trick: gluing a string to its own reverse, s + '#' + reverse(s), and reading one LPS value to learn the longest PALINDROMIC PREFIX in O(n) — which instantly solves both Minimum Characters Needed for Palindrome and Longest Palindromic Prefix.

The remaining questions each crown a distinct reusable pattern. Anagram Check is frequency canonicalization: two strings are anagrams exactly when their character-count vectors are equal, so you compare 26 numbers instead of n! orderings. Count and Say is controlled simulation: each term is the run-length encoding of the previous one, generated with a two-pointer run scanner and a list buffer. Compare Version Numbers is tokenize-normalize-compare: split on dots, convert chunks to integers (killing leading zeros), pad the shorter side with zeros, compare left to right. Implement strstr() closes the loop on Part-I: you write the library function itself, first naive, then KMP when the interviewer asks for worst-case O(n + m).

The meta-skill of Part-II is recognition speed. None of these problems is hard once named; all of them are slow if you rediscover the idea live. After this tab you should hear 'make it a palindrome by adding characters in front' and immediately think 'longest palindromic prefix -> border of s#rev(s) -> LPS', the way you hear 'sorted array, find x' and think binary search.
preRequisites: String Part-I's KMP section: what a border is and how build_lps computes lps[i] in O(m) — Part-II reuses it verbatim.
s[::-1] reverses a string in O(n) — it allocates a brand-new reversed copy, it does not mutate.
collections.Counter: one-pass frequency dict; two Counters compare equal exactly when every character count matches.
str.split('.') vs str.split(): an explicit separator keeps empty chunks ('1..2' -> ['1','','2']), no-arg split collapses whitespace runs.
int('007') == 7 — int() discards leading zeros, which is precisely the normalization version comparison needs.
Two-pointer run detection from Part-I: advance j while characters stay equal to isolate one maximal run [i, j).
cheatSheet: Border recap: a proper prefix that is also a suffix; lps[-1] of (s + '#' + s[::-1]) = length of the longest palindromic PREFIX of s.
Minimum characters to prepend for a palindrome = n - lps[-1] of s + '#' + rev(s); the answer string is rev(tail) + s.
Separator rule: '#' must be a character outside the alphabet, or borders leak across the join (s='aaa' gives border 5 > n without it).
Anagram: length gate first, then Counter(a) == Counter(b) -> O(n) time, O(alphabet) space; sorted(a) == sorted(b) is O(n log n).
Count and Say: term k+1 = run-length encoding of term k spoken aloud ('1211' -> one 1, one 2, two 1s -> '111221').
Compare versions: split('.') -> int() each chunk -> pad shorter with zeros -> first differing revision decides; never compare as raw strings.
strstr(): naive is O((n-m+1)*m) worst case; KMP is O(n+m); CPython's own str.find uses the two-way algorithm, also linear worst case.
Longest palindromic prefix via Part-I tools would be expand-around-center O(n^2); the border trick does it in O(n).

sections.title: What & Why: From Machinery to Applications
sections.content:
Part-I gave you the string toolbox: two-pointer scans, parsing state machines, expand-around-center, and the linear matchers (KMP's LPS array, the Z-function, Rabin-Karp's rolling hash). Part-II is the field test: six problems that never say 'use KMP' out loud, yet fall in one line once you name the right tool. This tab does not re-teach the machinery — it teaches the recognition step in between.

The six questions map onto five patterns. Minimum Characters Needed for Palindrome and Longest Palindromic Prefix are the same problem wearing two hats, both solved by the palindromic border trick (LPS over s + '#' + reverse(s)). Anagram Check is frequency canonicalization — reduce both strings to a canonical form (a count vector) and compare the forms. Count and Say is run-length simulation — generate each term from the previous with a run scanner. Compare Version Numbers is tokenize-normalize-compare — the pattern behind every 'compare two structured strings' problem (versions, IPs, dates). Implement strstr() asks you to BE the library author and write substring search yourself, naive first, KMP under pressure. Interviewers pick these because each has a tempting slow-or-buggy path (reverse-and-check for palindromes, string comparison for versions, += loops for count-and-say) and one crisp fast path; which path you take within the first two minutes tells them how much pattern vocabulary you actually own.

sections.title: The Border Concept: One Trick, Two Problems
sections.content:
Recall from Part-I: a BORDER of a string is a proper prefix that is also a suffix, and lps[i] (the KMP prefix function) stores the longest border length of s[:i+1]. Part-II's key construction converts a PALINDROME question into a BORDER question. Glue the string to its own reverse with a separator that occurs in neither: combined = s + '#' + reverse(s). A suffix of reverse(s) is a reversed prefix of s. So any border of combined is a prefix of s that equals one of its own prefixes read backwards — in other words, a prefix that is a palindrome. The LAST value of lps(combined) is therefore the length of the longest palindromic prefix of s, computed in O(n).

```
s        = a a c e c a a a            n = 8
rev(s)   = a a a c e c a a
combined = a a c e c a a a # a a a c e c a a

last lps value of combined = 7
  prefix of combined: a a c e c a a   (first 7 chars of s)
  suffix of combined: a a c e c a a   (last 7 of rev(s))
  -> "aacecaa" reads the same both ways: palindromic prefix
```
Why the separator is not optional: lps values can never exceed the position they describe, but WITHOUT '#' a border could straddle the glue point and count characters of s against other characters of s. Concretely, s = 'aaa' gives combined = 'aaaaaa' and a last lps of 5, which is longer than s itself — nonsense. With 'aaa#aaa' the border is correctly capped at 3. Any character guaranteed absent from the alphabet works ('#', '\x00'). This one diagram powers both Minimum Characters Needed for Palindrome and Longest Palindromic Prefix in the next section.

sections.title: Pattern: Palindromic Border Trick
sections.content:
Recognize it: the palindrome in the problem is ANCHORED to one end of the string. Longest Palindromic Prefix asks for it directly; Minimum Characters Needed for Palindrome asks how few characters, added IN FRONT, make all of s a palindrome. They are the same computation: the characters you may keep untouched are exactly the longest palindromic prefix, and every character after it must be mirrored in front, one prepended character each. So the answer to the minimum-characters question is n - len(longest palindromic prefix), and the constructed palindrome is reverse(tail) + s.

Invariant to state: k = lps[-1] of s + '#' + reverse(s) is the largest k such that s[:k] is a palindrome (proved in the previous section). Walk the example: s = 'aacecaaa' gives k = 7 ('aacecaa'), so 1 character must be prepended, producing 'a' + 'aacecaaa' = 'aaacecaaa'. For s = 'abcd', k = 1, so 3 characters: 'dcb' + 'abcd' = 'dcbabcd'. Contrast with Part-I's Longest Palindromic Substring: there the palindrome floats anywhere, and expand-around-center's O(n^2) is the standard answer; here the anchor to position 0 unlocks O(n). Using expand-around-center on these two questions works but is the slow path interviewers hope you avoid at |s| = 1e5+. A Z-function variant of the same trick exists (build rev(s) + '#' + s and read z-values), which makes a great follow-up answer.

sections.title: Pattern: Frequency Canonicalization (Anagrams)
sections.content:
Recognize it: the problem asks whether two strings contain the SAME characters with the SAME multiplicities, order ignored — Anagram Check is the pure form, and the identical canonicalization idea underlies 'group anagrams' and every sliding-window 'find permutations of p in s' variant. The invariant: a string's identity, order ignored, IS its frequency vector. Two strings are anagrams if and only if their frequency vectors are equal — one vector comparison replaces checking n! orderings.

Three canonical forms, in rising quality: (1) sorted(a) == sorted(b) — O(n log n), one line, fine as an opener. (2) Counter(a) == Counter(b) — O(n) time, O(k) space for k distinct characters, works for any alphabet including Unicode. (3) A fixed 26-slot list with +1 for one string and -1 for the other — O(n) time, O(1) space, all zeros at the end means anagram; this is the version to write when the input is guaranteed lowercase a-z, because it avoids hashing entirely. Always start with the length gate: different lengths can never be anagrams, and it exits in O(1). Ask the clarifying questions that change the answer: is the check case-sensitive ('Listen' vs 'silent')? Do spaces and punctuation count ('dormitory' vs 'dirty room')? Unicode input may also need normalization (NFC vs NFD encode the same visible character differently) — mentioning that is a senior-level flourish.

sections.title: Pattern: Run-Length Simulation (Count and Say)
sections.content:
Recognize it: the problem defines term k in terms of term k-1 and asks you to produce term n — Count and Say is generation by SIMULATION, not by formula. Each term is the previous term read aloud: '1211' is 'one 1, one 2, two 1s', so the next term is '111221'. Reading aloud is exactly run-length encoding: scan the string, isolate each maximal run of equal digits, and emit str(run_length) + digit.

```
term 1: 1
term 2: 11        (one 1)
term 3: 21        (two 1s)
term 4: 1211      (one 2, one 1)
term 5: 111221    (one 1, one 2, two 1s)
```
The run scanner is the two-pointer micro-pattern from Part-I: i marks the run start, j advances while term[j] == term[i], the run is [i, j), then i jumps to j. Invariant: at the top of the outer loop, everything before i has been encoded into the parts list. Two implementation rules keep it clean. First, build each new term in a list and join once — with terms growing roughly 30% per step, += concatenation inside the run loop goes quadratic on the later terms. Second, let the [i, j) structure handle the final run naturally — the classic bug in the 'compare each char with the next' formulation is forgetting to flush the last run after the loop ends. Complexity: term length grows by a factor of about 1.3 per step (Conway's constant), so total work is dominated by the last term's length; each term is produced in one linear pass over the previous.
sections.code:
def count_and_say(n):
    term = "1"                     # term 1 of the sequence
    for _ in range(n - 1):         # each pass builds the next term
        parts = []                 # list buffer -> join once (O(len))
        i = 0
        while i < len(term):
            j = i
            # advance j to the end of the current run of equal digits
            while j < len(term) and term[j] == term[i]:
                j += 1
            # say "<run length><digit>": e.g. run "111" -> "31"
            parts.append(str(j - i))
            parts.append(term[i])
            i = j                  # next run starts where this ended
        term = "".join(parts)      # freeze the next term
    return term

sections.title: Pattern: Tokenize, Normalize, Compare (Version Numbers)
sections.content:
Recognize it: two strings encode STRUCTURED values (versions, IPs, dates, dotted paths) and you must order them by meaning, not by spelling — Compare Version Numbers is the sheet's example. Raw string comparison is the trap: '1.10' < '1.9' lexicographically because '1' < '9' at the third character, yet version 1.10 is NEWER than 1.9. The cure is a three-step pipeline. TOKENIZE: split each version on '.' into revision chunks. NORMALIZE: convert every chunk with int(), which erases leading zeros ('001' -> 1 — exactly what version semantics demand), then pad the shorter list with zeros so '1.0' and '1.0.0' compare equal. COMPARE: walk both lists left to right; the first differing revision decides, and if none differs the versions are equal.

Invariant: after normalization, both lists have equal length and each position holds the true integer revision, so ordinary tuple comparison order is version order. Cost: O(n + m) time, O(n + m) space for the token lists. The same skeleton — parse into comparable normalized tuples, then compare componentwise — handles IP addresses (four octets), semantic versions with pre-release tags, and chapter numbering. In Python you can finish with a zip over the padded lists, and it is worth saying that real-world code uses exactly this idea via tuple comparison: (1, 10) > (1, 9) is True even though '1.10' < '1.9' as strings.
sections.code:
def compare_version(v1, v2):
    # TOKENIZE on '.', NORMALIZE each chunk with int() —
    # int() erases leading zeros: "001" -> 1.
    a = [int(x) for x in v1.split(".")]
    b = [int(x) for x in v2.split(".")]
    # pad the shorter list with zeros: "1.0" == "1.0.0"
    n = max(len(a), len(b))
    a += [0] * (n - len(a))
    b += [0] * (n - len(b))
    # COMPARE left to right; first difference decides
    for x, y in zip(a, b):
        if x != y:
            return -1 if x < y else 1
    return 0                       # every revision matched

sections.title: Pattern: Building strstr() Like a Library Author
sections.content:
Recognize it: Implement strstr() asks for the index of the FIRST occurrence of needle inside haystack, or -1 — you are writing the C library function (and Python's str.find) yourself. This is the reverse of Part-I's matcher sections: there you learned the algorithms, here you must choose one and defend the choice.

```
approach        | worst time    | space | when to write it
----------------+---------------+-------+---------------------------
naive scan      | O((n-m+1)*m)  | O(1)  | first version, short inputs
KMP (Part-I)    | O(n + m)      | O(m)  | asked for linear worst case
Rabin-Karp      | O(n+m) expect | O(1)  | many patterns / 2D variant
CPython find    | O(n + m)      | O(1)  | real life (two-way algo)
```
Interview strategy: write the naive double loop FIRST — correct, O(1) space, and honestly fine for small inputs — while narrating its worst case (haystack 'aaaa...a', needle 'aaab' re-scans m characters at every alignment). Then offer the KMP upgrade: identical loop shape, but a mismatch jumps the needle pointer via lps instead of restarting, and the function returns at the FIRST full match rather than collecting all of them. Key edge cases the grader checks: empty needle returns 0 by convention; needle longer than haystack returns -1; the naive loop's range must be n - m + 1 (the last viable start), not n. Worth one closing sentence in the interview: CPython's own str.find implements the Crochemore-Perrin two-way algorithm — linear worst case with O(1) extra space — which is why 'just use find' is fast in practice but never the point of the exercise.
sections.code:
def strstr_naive(haystack, needle):
    # try every alignment; leave an alignment at its first mismatch
    n, m = len(haystack), len(needle)
    if m == 0:
        return 0                   # convention: empty needle -> 0
    for i in range(n - m + 1):     # last viable start is n - m
        j = 0
        # march j while characters agree at this alignment
        while j < m and haystack[i + j] == needle[j]:
            j += 1
        if j == m:
            return i               # matched all m characters
    return -1                      # every alignment failed
# worst case O((n-m+1)*m); the KMP version (see implementations)
# reuses matched-prefix knowledge to guarantee O(n + m)

sections.title: Pitfalls & Common Mistakes
