sections.content: 1) Dropping the separator in the border trick: lps over s + reverse(s) WITHOUT '#' lets borders straddle the glue point — s = 'aaa' yields combined 'aaaaaa' with last lps 5, longer than s itself. Fix: always insert a character that appears in neither half. 2) Taking lps of s alone: the palindrome property comes from matching s against its reverse; lps(s)[-1] answers a different question (longest border of s). 3) Anagram traps: forgetting the O(1) length gate; ignoring case and spaces when the statement includes them; assuming a-z and indexing a 26-array with Unicode input (IndexError or wrong slot) — use Counter when the alphabet is open. 4) Comparing versions as strings: '1.10' < '1.9' lexicographically but 1.10 is the newer version; convert chunks with int() and pad with zeros — and remember int('') raises ValueError, so malformed inputs like '1.' need a guard if the spec allows them. 5) Count and Say: in the 'compare with next char' formulation, forgetting to flush the final run drops the last group; the [i, j) run-scanner shape avoids the bug entirely. Also += inside the run loop makes later terms quadratic — use a parts list. 6) strstr off-by-one: the alignment loop must run to n - m + 1; writing range(n) either crashes on an index or silently skips the last valid start. Also decide the empty-needle convention (return 0) BEFORE coding. 7) Rebuilding Part-I habits: solving Longest Palindromic Prefix with expand-around-center is O(n^2) — correct, but the border trick's O(n) is the expected answer at large constraints.

sections.title: Interview Recognition Checklist
sections.content:
Cues that map straight to a Part-II pattern: 'add characters at the front/back to make a palindrome' or 'longest palindrome starting at index 0' -> palindromic border trick (Minimum Characters Needed for Palindrome, Longest Palindromic Prefix). 'Same letters rearranged', 'permutation of', 'contains the same characters' -> frequency canonicalization (Anagram Check). 'Term n is derived from term n-1' with small n -> simulate with run-length grouping (Count and Say). 'Compare two dotted/structured strings by meaning' -> tokenize-normalize-compare (Compare Version Numbers). 'Find first occurrence / implement find()' -> strstr, naive then KMP (Implement strstr()).

30-second pre-coding checklist: (1) Is the palindrome anchored to an end (border trick, O(n)) or floating (expand-around-center, O(n^2))? (2) What is the alphabet — 26 lowercase letters permit a fixed array; anything open-ended means Counter. (3) Which separator character is guaranteed absent from the input? Say it before writing s + '#' + rev(s). (4) For comparisons: what normalization is needed (leading zeros, unequal lengths, case)? (5) For simulations: what is the growth rate of the generated string, and is my building idiom join-based? (6) State the naive complexity out loud FIRST, then name the upgrade — interviewers reward candidates who can rank their own options.

implementations.title: Minimum Characters for Palindrome (KMP Border Trick)
implementations.code:
# ==================================================================
# Minimum characters to ADD IN FRONT of s so it becomes a palindrome.
# Key fact: the characters we may keep untouched form the LONGEST
# PALINDROMIC PREFIX of s; every character after it must be mirrored
# in front. We find that prefix in O(n) via the KMP prefix function
# on the combined string  s + "#" + reverse(s).
# ==================================================================

def build_lps(p):
    # standard prefix function (full derivation in String Part-I)
    lps = [0] * len(p)
    k = 0                          # current border length
    for i in range(1, len(p)):
        while k > 0 and p[i] != p[k]:
            k = lps[k - 1]         # shrink to the next smaller border
        if p[i] == p[k]:
            k += 1                 # border extended by one character
        lps[i] = k
    return lps


def longest_palindromic_prefix(s):
    # A suffix of reverse(s) IS a reversed prefix of s, so a border
    # of s + '#' + reverse(s) is a prefix equal to its own reverse:
    # a palindromic prefix. '#' blocks matches across the boundary.
    if not s:
        return ""
    combined = s + "#" + s[::-1]
    k = build_lps(combined)[-1]    # last value = longest such border
    return s[:k]


def min_chars_for_palindrome(s):
    # each character after the palindromic prefix needs one mirror
    keep = len(longest_palindromic_prefix(s))
    return len(s) - keep


def shortest_palindrome(s):
    # construct the palindrome: mirror the tail in front of s
    keep = len(longest_palindromic_prefix(s))
    return s[keep:][::-1] + s      # reversed tail + original


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # quick self-checks (run this file directly)
    assert min_chars_for_palindrome("aacecaaa") == 1
    assert shortest_palindrome("aacecaaa") == "aaacecaaa"
    assert min_chars_for_palindrome("abcd") == 3       # -> "dcbabcd"
    assert longest_palindromic_prefix("ababa") == "ababa"
    print("Palindrome border OK")

implementations.title: strstr() From Scratch (Naive + KMP)
Anagram Checker Three Ways
implementations.code:
# ==================================================================
# Anagram Check: are a and b the same multiset of characters?
# Three canonical forms, from simplest to fastest:
#   1) sort both            O(n log n) time
#   2) Counter comparison   O(n) time, O(k) space, any alphabet
#   3) 26-slot +1/-1 array  O(n) time, O(1) space, lowercase a-z only
# ==================================================================

from collections import Counter


def is_anagram_sort(a, b):
    # canonical form = sorted character sequence
    return sorted(a) == sorted(b)


def is_anagram_counter(a, b):
    # canonical form = frequency map; works for Unicode too
    if len(a) != len(b):
        return False               # O(1) length gate first
    return Counter(a) == Counter(b)


def is_anagram_array(a, b):
    # fixed 26 slots; valid only when input is lowercase a-z
    if len(a) != len(b):
        return False
    freq = [0] * 26
    for x, y in zip(a, b):         # single pass over both strings
        freq[ord(x) - 97] += 1     # char of a adds one
        freq[ord(y) - 97] -= 1     # char of b removes one
    # anagram <=> all counts cancelled exactly to zero
    return all(v == 0 for v in freq)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # all three versions must agree
    cases = [("listen", "silent", True),
             ("rat", "car", False),
             ("aab", "abb", False),   # same letters, wrong counts
             ("", "", True)]
    for a, b, want in cases:
        assert is_anagram_sort(a, b) is want
        assert is_anagram_counter(a, b) is want
        assert is_anagram_array(a, b) is want
    print("Anagram OK")

implementations.title: Count-and-Say Generator (Run-Length Simulation)
implementations.code:
# ==================================================================
# Count and Say: term 1 is "1"; each later term reads the previous
# aloud. "1211" -> one 1, one 2, two 1s -> "111221".
# Reading aloud IS run-length encoding: isolate each maximal run of
# equal digits with two pointers and emit "<length><digit>".
# ==================================================================

def next_term(term):
    # one run-length-encoding pass over the current term
    parts = []                     # list buffer: join once at the end
    i = 0
    while i < len(term):
        j = i
        # advance j to the end of the current run of equal digits
        while j < len(term) and term[j] == term[i]:
            j += 1
        parts.append(str(j - i))   # how many ...
        parts.append(term[i])      # ... of which digit
        i = j                      # next run starts where this ended
    return "".join(parts)          # single O(length) join


def count_and_say(n):
    term = "1"                     # term 1 by definition
    for _ in range(n - 1):         # apply the encoder n-1 times
        term = next_term(term)
    return term


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # the first five terms, straight from the definition
    expect = ["1", "11", "21", "1211", "111221"]
    for i, want in enumerate(expect, start=1):
        assert count_and_say(i) == want
    # each term must round-trip from its predecessor
    assert next_term("111221") == "312211"
    print("Count and Say OK")
